title: Leviticus 1:1–17
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 1:1–17 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 1:1–17 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 1:1–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the book of Leviticus, Yahweh gives the people of Israel more of the rules, laws, and instructions for their nation. At the beginning of the book, Yahweh focuses on telling Moses how the people of Israel and Yahweh's priests should offer the offerings, gifts, and sacrifices of animals and grain to Yahweh.

Before Yahweh explains this, though, a few important things have already happened.

For more information about what important things have happened, stop and listen to the introduction to the book of Leviticus. Pause this audio here.

So the book of Leviticus begins with Yahweh telling Moses to tell the people of Israel the instructions for how to bring different kinds of offerings to Yahweh. And Yahweh talks to Moses from the Tent of Meeting because that was the place on earth where Yahweh had put Yahweh's presence.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Where do people in your culture go to communicate with gods, ancestors, or spirits? Is there a specific location, or can people communicate with gods anywhere? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh gives the instructions to Moses because Moses is Yahweh's prophet and so Moses is Yahweh's messenger. Part of Moses' job as Yahweh's prophet is to listen to Yahweh and then tell the people of Israel what Yahweh said. In the book of Leviticus, this means that it is Moses' responsibility to listen to Yahweh's instructions about how to worship Yahweh and then explain those instructions to the people of Israel so that everyone would know how to worship Yahweh in the correct way.

The beginning of Leviticus focuses on how to offer the burnt offerings. The word that Yahweh uses for burnt offerings in the original language means "go up." Yahweh probably calls this sacrifice the "go-up" offering because every part of the animal except the hide burns up on the bronze altar and becomes smoke that goes up to the sky. The hide of an animal is its outside skin.

Stop here and look at a picture of the bronze altar. Pause this audio here.

Burnt offerings were not a new kind of offering. If you remember the story of Noah, after Noah left the ark, Noah offered a burnt offering to Yahweh. Later, when the people of Israel went through the ritual to officially become Yahweh's people, and for Yahweh to be the people's only God, the people offered burnt offerings as part of that ritual. The people of Israel were not the only people who sacrificed this kind of offering. People in other countries offered burnt offerings to their gods and goddesses as a gift or as a way to ask for a favor.

However, after the people of Israel officially promised to be Yahweh's people and that Yahweh would be their only God, Yahweh no longer allowed the Israelites to offer burnt offerings or any other kind of sacrifice to anyone or anything except Yahweh. Because of that, Yahweh gave Moses instructions for how the people of Israel were supposed to offer burnt offerings to Yahweh. There are three main sets of instructions that are different depending on which kind of animal the person offering the sacrifice gives to Yahweh. The instructions start by focusing on how to offer the most expensive animals, and the instructions end with how to offer the least expensive animals.

So the instructions start with how to sacrifice an animal from the herd. "From the herd" means a large herd animal like a bull or ox, or another large animal people kept for milk or meat.

Stop here and look at a picture of a bull and an ox. Pause this audio here.

So, when a person chooses one of these large herd animals to offer to Yahweh, the person who offers the sacrifice is supposed to choose a male animal that is perfect. That means that the animal has no physical defects. The animal must not be blind or deformed or have any bruises or injuries. The animal must not have any kind of skin disease or be missing any body part. The animal has to be physically perfect.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, when people want to offer something to a god, ancestor, or spirit, what kinds of offerings are acceptable? What kinds of offerings are unacceptable? Pause this audio here.

Once the offeror has chosen a perfect animal, the offeror should bring the animal to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. Then the offeror should place their hand on the animal's head. The Bible does not explain exactly why the offeror had to put their hand on the animal's head. Some people think the purpose was a ritual way to say, "This animal is mine and not the priest's." This would be similar to how some people use a signature or stamp when they send a letter or a package to someone as a way to identify themself as the sender. Other people think the purpose was to say, "This animal is me, and I should be dying here." Still other people think the purpose was to transfer uncleanness or ritual dirtiness to the animal, which would then cleanse the offeror. People at this time used words like "clean" and "dirty" to talk about the world and people's actions. For example, doing something wrong would make someone unclean or ritually dirty. For the people of Israel, it was important for the Israelites to be "clean." This was because Yahweh had dedicated the Israelites to Yahweh and made the Israelites holy. Anything that was holy also had to be "clean." So, one possible reason the person offering the animal for the burnt offering put their hand on the animal's head was to move whatever ritual dirt was on that person onto the animal. When people killed and burned the animal on the altar, the person offering the animal would be "clean" again.

Next, Yahweh tells Moses one of the purposes of offering a burnt offering. That purpose is to "make atonement," or make amends, for the offeror. The word for this in this original language focuses on cleansing and making things right.

So, for the ancient Israelites, when someone wronged another person or wronged Yahweh, three things would happen. The first thing was that there would be a separation between the two people. When one person wronged a second person, that second person might feel upset or angry. That person might avoid or attack the first person.

The second thing that would happen was that the wrong thing would make the person who did the wrong thing ritually "dirty." However, it would not only affect the person who did the wrong thing. That dirt would also affect that person's family, community, and environment.

The third thing is that the spiritual dirt that came on a person marked that person for punishment or judgment that would happen sometime in the future. People from other nations who were not the people of Israel believed that one of the many gods and goddesses that those people believed in would punish the person who did wrong. However, the Bible teaches that Yahweh is the only God. That means that Yahweh is the One who would judge and punish the person who did wrong. Yahweh might use a human, disease, wild animal, or anything else to judge and punish the person, but the ultimate judge is always Yahweh.

"Making atonement," or making amends, would resolve these three problems. The act of atoning, or making amends, would do three things. First, it would restore the relationship between the person who did the wrong and the person whom the first person wronged. Second, it would cleanse the person who did the wrong, as well as their family and environment, from guilt and spiritual dirt. Third, because the person was now clean from the guilt of the wrong, that person did not have to worry about Yahweh judging and punishing that person. While there were other sacrifices that focused more specifically on atoning and making amends, one of the purposes of the burnt offering was to do this as well.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do people in your culture make amends when someone has wronged somebody else? Pause this audio here.

After the offeror puts their hand on the animal, the offeror is supposed to kill the animal in front of Yahweh. It is unclear exactly where the offeror is supposed to kill the animal, but it is probably somewhere in the courtyard area between the entrance of the Tent of Meeting and the bronze altar. It is possible that the offeror killed the animal right next to the bronze altar since people still considered the altar as part of the entrance, but no one knows for certain.

Stop here and look at a picture of the courtyard in the Tent of Meeting. Notice the possible locations for where the person should kill the animal. Pause this audio here.

After the offeror kills the animal, Aaron's descendants, who were the priests, are supposed to take the blood of the animal and splash it all around on the bronze altar. People thought blood contained the life of a person or animal, and so the people of Israel used the blood of animals to atone, or make amends, after the Israelites had wronged Yahweh or other people.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do people in your culture think about blood? How is that similar or different from how the people of Israel thought about blood? Pause this audio here.

After a person splashes the blood around the bronze altar, someone is supposed to skin the animal and cut the meat into pieces. It is unclear whether the person doing this is the priest, the offeror, or someone else. Next, the priest is supposed to light a fire on the altar and arrange wood on the fire. Then the priest is supposed to arrange the animal meat, head, and fat on top of the wood that is on the altar. After that, someone is supposed to wash the animal's legs and the inside organs with water. Again, it is unclear whether the person doing this is the priest, the offeror, or someone else. Finally, the priest is then supposed to burn the animal's innards and legs up on the altar as well.

The end result is that everything except for the hide is supposed to burn up on the altar. The smoke from the animal is like incense that would make a good smell to please and honor Yahweh. People in other cultures at this time thought that offering sacrifices to their gods and goddesses was a way to give the gods food. Other people thought that the gods and goddesses would eat the animals, grain, and wine that people sacrificed to gods. But Yahweh is different. Yahweh does not need to eat food or drink wine. The sacrifices and offerings that the people of Israel gave to Yahweh were a way to honor Yahweh, not a way to give Yahweh something to eat.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What are some other reasons that people might make an offering to a god, ancestor, or spirit? How is that similar or different to why the people of Israel are offering animals to Yahweh? Pause this audio here.

Part two focuses on what to do if the person offering the sacrifice sacrificed an animal from the flock. This refers to smaller animals like sheep or goats. Like with the bull or ox, the sheep or goat that the person sacrificed had to be a male that was physically perfect.

Stop here and look at a picture of sheep and goats. Pause this audio here.

A person is supposed to kill this animal on the north side of the bronze altar in front of Yahweh. After the person killed the animal, the priests were supposed to splash the blood around on the altar, and then someone was supposed to cut the animal into pieces. It is unclear whether the person doing this is the priest, the offeror, or someone else. Then the priest is supposed to arrange the pieces of meat along with the head and fat on the wood that is burning on the altar. Next, someone is supposed to wash the legs and innards with water. It is unclear whether the person doing this is the priest, the offeror, or someone else. Finally, the priest is supposed to burn the legs and innards on the altar as well. Once again, the smoke from the animal is like incense that would make a good smell to please and honor Yahweh.

Part three focuses on what to do if the person who sacrificed the animal sacrificed a bird. These specific birds are different kinds of pigeons and doves. These kinds of birds only eat plants and grains. Later, when Yahweh tells Moses what kinds of animals and birds are clean and which ones are not, Yahweh says these birds were "clean," which meant it is okay to eat and to sacrifice these birds to Yahweh.

Stop here and look at a picture of different kinds of pigeons and doves. Pause this audio here.

When someone sacrifices a bird as a burnt offering, the priest is supposed to bring the bird to the bronze altar. Then, the priest is supposed to wring off the bird's head and burn the head on the altar. After that, the priest is supposed to drain the blood on the side of the altar. Then, the priest is supposed to remove the digestive tract and feathers. The digestive tract refers to the part of the bird that digests food.

Stop here and look at a picture of a bird's digestive tract. Pause this audio here.

After the priest removes the digestive tract and feathers, the priest is supposed to throw both on the east side of the altar. This is the same place where the priest would put the ashes that were left behind after the fat from a sacrifice burned up. People called this place the place where the fat ashes went.

Stop here and look at a picture of the bronze altar. Note the east side where the fat ashes are. Pause this audio here.

After that, the priest is supposed to tear open the bird's wings without completely splitting the bird in half. Finally, the priest is supposed to burn the rest of the bird on the wood that is burning on the altar. Once again, the smoke from the bird would be like incense that would make a good smell to please and honor Yahweh.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 1:1–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

In the first scene: We hear an introduction to the passage and learn who is talking, to whom, where, and about what. Yahweh speaks to Moses in the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh tells Moses what the people of Israel need to do if they bring Yahweh an offering or a gift of animals to sacrifice as a burnt offering.

In the second scene: Yahweh tells Moses what to tell the people of Israel to do if someone sacrifices a bull, ox, or other large animal from the herd. These are animals that people used for milk and meat.

In the third scene: Yahweh tells Moses what to tell the people of Israel to do if someone sacrifices a sheep or goat from the flock.

In the fourth scene: Yahweh tells Moses what to tell the people of Israel to do if someone sacrifices a small bird like a pigeon or dove.

The characters in this passage include:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The sons, or people, of Israel
  • The person who offers an animal sacrifice
  • And Aaron and his sons, who are the priests

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In this scene, Yahweh talks about the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, the bronze altar, and the courtyard between the entrance and the bronze altar.

Stop here and look at a picture of the bronze altar. Pay special attention to the top and sides of the bronze altar. Also, pay special attention to the north side and the east side of the bronze altar. Pause the audio here.

In scene one, Yahweh speaks to Moses from the Tent of Meeting. This happens after the people of Israel made and set up the Tent of Meeting, the way Yahweh told Moses to do. In the previous book of Exodus, we hear that Yahweh told Moses how Yahweh wanted the people of Israel to make the Tent of Meeting and all of the parts, as well as how to set up the Tent of Meeting and where to put all of the parts. After the people of Israel set up everything in the middle of the Israelites' camp at Mount Sinai, Yahweh's presence and glory filled the Tent of Meeting.

Since Yahweh's presence was then living with the people of Israel, Yahweh began to give Moses further instructions about how the people of Israel needed to live. Yahweh begins by talking about what the people of Israel needed to do if a person wanted to bring Yahweh offerings, gifts, or sacrifices of animals.

Since Moses is acting as Yahweh's messenger, Yahweh tells Moses what to tell the people. Yahweh begins by focusing on what the people needed to do if they wanted to sacrifice an animal to Yahweh. Even though the storyteller does not use the word in the original language for a burnt offering, the entire passage focuses on that particular type of sacrifice.

Before going further, stop and describe a ritual ceremony that your community does. Pay attention to how the storyteller describes the process. What words does the storyteller use to explain who does what in what order? Pause this audio here.

Scene two begins the instructions about how to sacrifice an animal from the herd for a burnt offering. These kinds of animals include bulls, oxen, and other large animals that people kept for milk or meat.

Stop and discuss: What kinds of large herd animals do people in your culture keep for milk or meat? Would any of those animals be appropriate to sacrifice to a god, ancestor, or other spiritual being? Pause this audio here.

The instructions begin with what the person offering the sacrifice is supposed to do. The person should choose a male animal without any physical defect. Then the person should bring the animal to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. The person puts their hand on the head of the animal. Then the person kills the animal in front of Yahweh. This probably means in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting, somewhere between the entrance and the bronze altar.

When the Bible talks about killing the animal in front of Yahweh, it means that the person is killing the animal in Yahweh's presence. This does not mean that the person went into the tent itself to kill the animal in front of the ark of the covenant. Rather, it means that the person killed the animal in Yahweh's presence in the courtyard area. Make sure you find a way to translate this phrase that implies the person kills the animal in Yahweh's presence without implying that they went into the tent itself, but rather stayed in the courtyard.

The person offering the sacrifice is supposed to do these things so that Yahweh will accept the sacrifice as a way to atone, or make amends. Next, the priests take some of the blood from the animal and splash the blood around on the bronze altar.

Stop and do this activity: Grab some liquid, like water, and throw it onto a wall or similar structure. Discuss how you think the priests would have thrown the blood onto the sides of the altar, and try to do the same thing. Pause this audio here.

It is not clear who does the next step, but it is likely the offeror. The person should skin the animal and then cut the meat into pieces.

Then the priests should light the fire on the bronze altar and put wood on the fire. Next, the priests should arrange the meat, head, and fat on the wood on the bronze altar.

It is unclear who is doing the next step. It is likely that the offeror is the one doing it, but that is not certain. The step, however, is clear: wash the legs and inside organs with water. The inside organs were probably the animal's stomach and intestines.

Finally, a priest is supposed to burn everything on the altar.

Scene two ends by explaining that this burnt offering is a gift with fire to Yahweh, and it is like incense that is supposed to smell good and make Yahweh happy. Remember that the purpose of the offering is not to feed Yahweh. Instead, the purpose is to atone, or make amends, for the person who did something wrong and to honor Yahweh with the gift.

Scene three focuses on the instructions about how to sacrifice an animal from the flock as a burnt offering. This kind of animal includes smaller herd animals like sheep and goats.

Stop and discuss: What kinds of smaller herd animals do people in your culture keep? Would any of those animals be appropriate to sacrifice to a god, ancestor, or other spiritual being? Pause this audio here.

The instructions begin with what the person who offers the sacrifice is supposed to do. Again, the person must choose a male animal without any physical defect. The person should kill the animal on the north side of the altar in front of Yahweh.

Stop here and look at a picture of the bronze altar as a group. Note where the north side is. Find a way to explain where that is. Pause this audio here.

Remember, when a person kills an animal "in Yahweh's presence," this probably means that the person kills the animal in the courtyard.

The priests splash some of the animal's blood around on the bronze altar. It is not clear who does the next step, but it is likely the offeror. The step, however, is clear. Someone cuts the meat into pieces.

Next, a priest arranges the meat, head, and fat on the wood on the bronze altar. It is not clear who does the next step, but it may be the priests. The step, however, is clear. Someone washes the legs and the inside organs with water. Finally, a priest should burn everything on the altar.

Like with the previous scene, scene three ends by explaining that this burnt offering is a gift with fire to Yahweh. This offering is like incense that is supposed to smell good and make Yahweh happy. Remember that the purpose of the offering is not to feed Yahweh. Instead, the purpose is to atone for the person who did something wrong and to honor Yahweh with the gift.

Scene four focuses on the instructions about how to sacrifice a bird, such as a turtledove or young pigeon, as a burnt offering. These pigeons ate only plants.

Stop and discuss: What kinds of birds are nearby that only eat plants? Would people consider any of those animals appropriate to sacrifice to a god, ancestor, or other spiritual being? Pause this audio here.

The instructions begin with what the person offering the sacrifice is supposed to do. The person should bring the birds to the Tent of Meeting. Then the priest wrings the bird's neck and burns the head on the bronze altar. Next, the priest drains the blood on the side of the bronze altar. Then the priest must remove the digestive tract and feathers and put them on the east side of the bronze altar, where the fat ashes go. Then the priest should tear the wings, but not fully split the bird. Finally, the priest should burn everything on the wood on the bronze altar.

The east side is where the sun comes up in the morning. For the people of Israel, the east side of the altar is where the priests would put the ashes from the fat that would burn up on the altar. Although the priests and the people of Israel were allowed to eat some of the other animal sacrifices, no one was ever allowed to eat the fat. The fat always burned up on the altar, so it needed a place for the ashes to go.

Stop here and look at a picture of the bronze altar as a group. Note where the east side is. That is the place where the fat ashes went. Discuss a way to describe where the "east side" is. Pause this audio here.

Like with the previous two scenes, scene four ends by explaining that this burnt offering is a gift with fire to Yahweh. This offering is like incense that is supposed to smell good and make Yahweh happy. Remember that the purpose of the offering is not to feed Yahweh. Instead, the purpose is to atone for the person who did something wrong and to honor Yahweh with the gift.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 1:1–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The sons, or people, of Israel
  • The person who offers an animal sacrifice
  • And Aaron and his sons, who are the priests

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In scene one, Yahweh starts talking to Moses from the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh tells Moses, "Tell the people of Israel: 'If any of you want to bring an animal to Yahweh as a gift from either the herd or the flock, you should bring it near.'"

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I feel happy to hear what Yahweh has to say; or
  • I hope the Israelites listen and obey this time.
Continue the drama.

In scene two, Yahweh continues to tell Moses what to tell the people of Israel. Yahweh says, "If the burnt offering is an animal from the herd, it needs to be a male that is physically perfect. Then the offeror needs to bring the animal to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting so that Yahweh will accept the sacrifice. The offeror needs to lay their hand on the head of the animal so that Yahweh will accept it to make atonement and amends for that person."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person bringing the animal, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I feel sad that the animal has to die; or
  • I feel happy that Yahweh has made a way to restore our relationship.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh says, "Next, the offeror needs to kill the young bull in front of Yahweh. After that, Aaron's sons, who are the priests, will bring the blood and splash it around on the sides of the bronze altar. The altar is near the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. Then the offeror will skin the animal and cut the meat into pieces.

"After that, the priest will light the altar and put wood on the fire. Then the priest will arrange the pieces of meat along with the head and fat on the wood on the altar. Then, the offeror will wash the innards and legs with water. Finally, the priest will burn everything on top of the altar. This burnt offering is a gift with fire that will smell good to Yahweh and please Yahweh."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am happy that the offeror cares enough about our relationship to bring an animal; or
  • I am happy with the person offering the animal; or
  • I am glad this person wants to honor me.
Continue the drama.

In scene three, Yahweh continues to tell Moses what to tell the people of Israel. Yahweh says, "If the burnt offering is a sheep or goat from the flock, it needs to be a male that is physically perfect. The person who offers the animal will kill it on the north side of the altar in front of Yahweh. After that, Aaron's sons, who are the priests, will bring the blood and splash it around on the sides of the bronze altar. Then the offeror will cut the meat into pieces.

"After that, the priest will arrange the pieces of meat along with the head and fat on the wood on the altar. Then, someone will wash the innards and legs with water. Finally, the priest will burn everything on top of the altar. This burnt offering is a gift with fire that will smell good to Yahweh and please Yahweh."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am happy to help the offeror restore their relationship with Yahweh; or
  • My clothes have a lot of blood on them; or
  • I am glad to be able to honor Yahweh this way.
Continue the drama.

In scene four, Yahweh continues to tell Moses what to tell the people of Israel. Yahweh says, "If the burnt offering for Yahweh is a bird, it should be a turtledove or young pigeon. The priest will bring the bird to the altar. Then the priest will wring off the bird's head and burn the head on the altar. Next, the priest will drain the bird's blood on the side of the altar. After that, the priest will remove the digestive tract and the feathers and throw both on the east side of the altar, where the fat ashes are. Then, the priest will tear open the wings but not split the bird completely in half. Finally, the priest will burn the rest of the bird on the wood that is on the altar. This burnt offering is a gift with fire that will smell good to Yahweh and please Yahweh."

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 1:1–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

This passage begins with Yahweh talking to Moses. "Yahweh" was the personal name that the one true God told Moses at the beginning of the book of Exodus. When Yahweh told Moses to bring Yahweh's people out of slavery in Egypt, Moses asked Yahweh what name to tell the people of Israel so that the Israelites would know who sent Moses. So Yahweh told Moses that Yahweh's name was "Yahweh" and that is what Moses should tell the people. When the people of Israel heard this name for God, the name would remind the Israelites of the covenant and promise that Yahweh made with the Israelites' ancestors to take care of the Israelites.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for Yahweh. Look up Yahweh in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh talks with Moses at the Tent of Meeting, which in other places Moses calls the tabernacle. The Tent of Meeting referred to the tent and courtyard that Yahweh chose and set aside as Yahweh's personal space. The Tent of Meeting was sacred to Yahweh, and so everyone needed to treat it with extra respect and care. Only the priests and Moses were allowed to go into the tent itself.

Stop here and look at a picture of the Tent of Meeting as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the Tent of Meeting. Look up tabernacle in the Master Glossary for more information. Remember that although the Tent of Meeting and tabernacle are the same thing in Leviticus, Moses calls it the Tent of Meeting here. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells Moses what to tell the people of Israel. In the original language, the phrase literally means "Israel's sons," but it refers to everyone—both men and women—who were descended from a man named Israel and his 12 sons. Israel was Abraham's grandson, and his original name was Jacob. When Jacob first left his dad's home to travel to get married, Jacob made a promise to Yahweh that Yahweh would be Jacob's only God if Yahweh would keep Jacob safe until Jacob came back home to Jacob's dad. While Jacob was away, Jacob married two wives and two concubines and had twelve sons and one daughter. After being away from home for many years, Jacob and Jacob's family traveled back to Jacob's dad's home. On the way, Jacob wrestled with one of Yahweh's angels, and so Yahweh changed Jacob's name to "Israel." This new name meant "he wrestles with God." Not long after that, Jacob realized that Yahweh had kept Jacob safe throughout all of Jacob's travels, so Jacob told Jacob's family to get rid of all household idols in order to worship Yahweh only. The "people of Israel" referred to the descendants of Israel's 12 sons who got rid of their idols and whom their patriarch Israel commanded to worship only Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the people of Israel. Look up Israelites and Israel in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

In this chapter, Yahweh tells Moses to tell the people of Israel how to offer their offerings. Yahweh specifically talks about how to offer a burnt offering. The word in the original language literally means "go up." This is probably because people would burn the entire animal except the hide for a burnt offering. All of the meat and fat became smoke that would "go up" to the sky. There were many different reasons why someone might sacrifice a burnt offering. Sometimes it was to thank or honor Yahweh. Sometimes it was to restore their relationship with Yahweh and to cleanse themselves from the contamination of doing something wrong. Burnt offerings were also part of the daily morning and evening sacrifices that the people of Israel offered Yahweh to honor Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the general word for offering and for the burnt offering. Look up offering and burnt offering in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

In these instructions, Yahweh tells Moses what the person who brings the offering should do, as well as what the priests should do. The word "priest" referred to Moses's brother Aaron and Aaron's male descendants. The priests were responsible for offering the sacrifices. The priests were also the only ones who could go into Yahweh's tent itself, which was the most sacred area in the Tent of Meeting. And the priests were the only ones who could touch the most sacred things. It was dangerous for everyday people to be in the sacred space of Yahweh's courtyard and to be near Yahweh's most sacred things. If the everyday people touched the most sacred things or went into the tent itself, then the people could die. To protect the people, Yahweh gave the priests the responsibility to go into the tent itself, offer the sacrifices, perform the religious rituals, and make sure everyone did everything correctly. The priests also had the responsibility to teach the people of Israel how to love and honor Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the priests. Look up priest in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh gives Moses three different sets of instructions based on the type of animal that the people offered. Yahweh starts with instructions for the animals from the herd. These animals were large animals that the people of Israel kept for milk or meat. One specific type of herd animal in this chapter is a young bull.

Stop here and look at a picture of bulls again as a group, as needed. Pause this audio here.

The second set of instructions is for animals from the flock. Flock animals were smaller herd animals that the people of Israel kept for milk or meat. Two specific types of flock animals that we hear about in this chapter are goats and sheep.

Stop here and look at a picture of goats and sheep again as a group, as needed. Pause this audio here.

The third set of instructions is for birds. These were small birds that only ate plants. These birds did not hunt for meat or scavenge from dead animals. Yahweh talks about pigeons and turtledoves or doves.

Stop here and look at a picture of pigeons and turtledoves as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use for the herd, bull, flock, goat, sheep, pigeon, and turtledove. For more information, look at dove in the Master Glossary. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, use the same words that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

When Yahweh tells Moses what kinds of herd and flock animals to sacrifice, Yahweh says that the animals have to be physically perfect. The word here for "physically perfect" refers to something that is complete, whole, and without fault. For sacrifices, this meant that the animal could not have any physical defects or skin diseases. Some translations use the word "spotless" for this word. However, this word does not mean that the animal could not have different colors or spots of color. Instead, it meant that the animal could not be blind or lame. The animal could not have any injuries, deformities, bruises, or any kind of skin disease. What the animal looked like was not important. What was important was that the animal was physically perfect.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the physically perfect. Look up perfect in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, decide if it is appropriate to use the same word here. Use the same word throughout the book of Leviticus. Pause this audio here.

Once the person offering the animal brought the animal to the Tent of Meeting, that person would lay their hand on the head of the animal so that it would be accepted to make atonement for the person. This word focuses on cleansing and making things right.

In the ancient Israelite worldview, when someone wronged another person or wronged Yahweh, three things would happen. The first thing was that there would be a separation between the two people. When one person wronged a second person, that second person might feel upset or angry. That person might avoid or attack the first person.

The second thing was that the wrong thing would make the person who did the wrong thing ritually and spiritually "dirty." However, it would not only affect the person who did the wrong thing. That dirt would also affect that person's family, community, and environment.

The third thing is that because the person was ritually and spiritually dirty, that person would receive punishment or judgment sometime in the future. People from other nations who were not the people of Israel believed that one of the many gods and goddesses that those people believed in would punish the person who did wrong. However, the Bible teaches that Yahweh is the only God. That means that Yahweh is the One who would judge and punish the person who did wrong. Yahweh might use a human, disease, wild animal, or anything else to judge and punish the person, but the ultimate judge is always Yahweh.

"Making atonement," or making amends, would resolve these three problems. The act of atoning, or making amends, would do three things. First, it would restore the relationship between the person who did the wrong and the person whom the first person wronged. Second, it would cleanse the person who did the wrong, as well as their family and environment, from being guilty and ritually dirty. Third, because the person was now clean from the guilt of the wrong, that person did not have to worry about Yahweh judging and punishing that person.

Most of the time, people made atonement, or made amends, by offering a gift to apologize and then doing whatever the victim wanted as a way to make amends. In Leviticus, we hear that when people wronged Yahweh, those people offered Yahweh a gift of an animal sacrifice as a way to apologize and make amends.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for atonement. Look up atonement in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, decide if it is appropriate to use the same word here. Use the same word throughout the book of Leviticus. Pause this audio here.

The person would slaughter, or kill, the animal. Moses uses a special word for kill here to mean to cut through an animal, especially for a sacrifice.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for slaughtering an animal. Pause this audio here.

Then the priests would splash or throw some of the blood around on the sides of the bronze altar. Bronze was a metal that people made when they combined copper and tin. The altar was near the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. People considered the altar extra sacred, so only the priests were allowed to touch the altar. This altar was where people sacrificed all of the animals.

Stop here and look at a picture of the bronze altar as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the bronze altar. Look up bronze and altar in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will talk about the priest splashing or throwing the blood on the side of the altar. Pause this audio here.

For animals from the herd or from the flock, different things happened to different parts of the animal. The priest arranged the meat, fat, and head on the bronze altar and burned them up. But someone washed the legs and organs with water before the priest burned the pieces on the altar.

Stop here and look at a diagram of a cut-up animal as a group. Notice the different parts of the animal. Also, notice what the inside organs are. Decide how to translate these different parts of the animal. Use the same words throughout the book of Leviticus. Pause this audio here.

For birds, the priest wrung off the head and burned it on the bronze altar. Then the priest removed the digestive tract and feathers. The "digestive tract" probably refers to the part of the bird where the excrement is. Since that was dirty, the priest removed the whole digestive tract, along with the feathers. Then the priest would tear open the wings without splitting the bird completely in half, and then burn the bird on the altar.

Stop here and look at a diagram of a bird as a group. Notice where the digestive tract and feathers are. Decide how to refer to the different parts of the bird. Use the same words throughout the book of Leviticus. Pause this audio here.

The priest is supposed to throw the bird's digestive tract and feathers on the east side of the altar, where the fat ashes go. The east side is where the sun comes up in the morning. The east side of the altar was where the priests would put the ashes from the fat that burned up on the bronze altar.

Stop here and look at a picture of the bronze altar as a group. Note where the east side is, where the fat ashes went. Find a way to communicate about where the fat ashes went. Use that same word or phrase throughout the book of Leviticus. Pause this audio here.

Each section ends by noting that the burnt offering was one of the kinds of offerings that people called a gift with fire. This word in the original language likely referred to a gift of food that people gave to a god that would burn up on an altar. These sacrifices were not food for Yahweh, but instead a way to honor Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for a gift with fire. For more information on gift with fire, refer to fire offering in the Master Glossary. Be sure to choose a word or phrase that does not mean that Yahweh eats the sacrifices. Use the same word or phrase throughout the book of Leviticus. Pause this audio here.

This animal sacrifice would burn up as incense before Yahweh and be a sweet smell for Yahweh. Incense is a mixture of natural materials like spices and gums that smells good when people burn it. People would burn incense on an altar or in a censer as a way to worship a god or goddess. People at that time burnt incense as a way to honor and worship the gods, and so different communities in the Bible would worship their own gods and goddesses by burning incense. Burning incense smells good. People also thought of the smoke and smell of sacrifices as this same kind of good smell. In this chapter, Yahweh says the smoke and smell of the sacrifices are like incense. That means that the sacrifice was a way to honor and worship Yahweh, and that it would smell good to Yahweh, and that good smell would make Yahweh happy.

Stop here and discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use for incense and sweet smell. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, decide if it is appropriate to use the same words here. Use the same words or phrases throughout the book of Leviticus.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
