title: Leviticus 2:1–16
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 2:1–16 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 2:1–16 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 2:1–16 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

The second chapter on Leviticus focuses on offerings of grain and different kinds of bread and crackers. People often translate this kind of offering as the "grain offering." In the original language, people often used this word to talk about the kind of tribute someone might give to a king or ruler. People also used this word to talk about the kinds of gifts someone would give to someone else in order to ask for a favor. After Yahweh rescued the people of Israel out of slavery in Egypt, Yahweh used Moses to bring the Israelites to the Sinai Mountain. Then, Yahweh and the people of Israel made a covenant, or a binding agreement, with each other that the people of Israel would be special to Yahweh and that Yahweh would be the Israelites' only God. As part of that covenant, Yahweh became the king and ruler of the Israelite nation. This grain offering was one of the ways that the people of Israel could honor Yahweh as the Israelites' king and ruler, and ask Yahweh for favors.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What kind of gifts do people in your culture bring to honor or ask rulers, chiefs, and government officials for a favor? If Yahweh were in charge of your community, what kind of gifts would you bring to Yahweh? Pause this audio here.

This passage focuses on three different kinds of grain offerings that the people gave to Yahweh. The first kind of grain offering was an offering of uncooked flour. This particular kind of flour was probably semolina flour and was of very high quality. People often used this kind of flour to make meals for kings and other royals.

To prepare this offering, the person offering it would pour oil on the flour. People probably made this oil by pressing olives. After that, the person would put frankincense on top of the oil and flour. Frankincense was a kind of tree sap, or resin, that was both valuable and expensive. Frankincense smelled good when people burned it. People would have also added salt to the offering, but the storyteller does not mention that yet.

After the person prepared the offering, that person would bring the offering to the priests. The priests were Aaron's descendants. In order to bring the offering to the priest, the person presenting the offering probably carried it in a dish or some other sort of vessel. The person would bring this offering to the Tent of Meeting so that the priests could offer it on the bronze altar. This is the same altar that the priests offered the burnt offering and all of the other sacrifices and offerings on.

Once the priest received the offering, the priest would take a full handful of the fine flour and oil, as well as all of the frankincense, and then burn all of this on the altar as incense. The people called the part of the flour and oil that burned up "the memorial portion." Some people think that this portion was supposed to help the people of Israel remember the covenant between Yahweh and his people. Other people think it was supposed to call Yahweh's attention to the reason the person was offering the gift, whether that was to honor, thank, or ask Yahweh for a favor, or for another reason. This memorial portion was a gift with fire that would smell good to Yahweh.

After the memorial portion burned up along with all of the frankincense, the priests would keep the rest of the flour and oil. As Yahweh's close servants and representatives, the priests could share in the gifts that the people gave to King Yahweh. This was also a way for Yahweh to provide for the priests since Yahweh did not give the priests a portion of the promised land to farm. Instead, Yahweh was their portion, so Yahweh took care of the priests through the sacrifices and offerings of animals and grain that the people of Israel brought to Yahweh.

So the priests could eat everything left over after the memorial portion burned up on the bronze altar. However, because the grain offering was extra holy, Yahweh said that no one except the priests could eat that offering. We hear later that the priests needed to eat that offering in the holy place around the Tent of Meeting.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: When people in your culture give a food offering to a god, an ancestor, or a spirit, can anyone else eat that offering? If someone else may eat the food, why can that person eat that food? Pause this audio here.

People cooked the second kind of grain offering. There were three different ways to cook it, with instructions about each way. The first way was to cook the offering in an oven. There were two different kinds of ovens. People made both kinds of ovens from clay.

Stop here and look at a picture of both kinds of ovens as a group. Pause this audio here.

There were two kinds of bread that people made in these ovens. One bread was a ring shape. The other bread was a flat, round bread. People made both kinds of bread with the same high-quality flour that the storyteller mentioned earlier. People mixed olive oil with the flour to make the ring-shaped bread. People anointed or smeared the flat, round loaf with olive oil. It was important that people did not add any leavening or yeast to this bread when people cooked it. The two kinds of bread were high-quality, soft, flat bread.

Stop here and look at a picture of both kinds of bread as a group. Pause this audio here.

The second way was to cook the offering on a griddle. People probably made this griddle from iron or clay and made it so that the griddle was slightly curved in shape. People would put the griddle on the fire with the curved side facing up, and then put the dough on top of the curved side.

Stop here and look at a picture of this kind of griddle as a group. Pause this audio here.

Once again, people needed to make this offering with olive oil and the same high-quality flour. Like before, this offering could not have any leavening or yeast in it. This kind of dough made a hard and thin cracker that people needed to break into pieces and then pour oil on the pieces. This would make it easier for the priest to grab some of the cracker as a memorial portion.

The third way was to cook the offering in a pan. This type of pan was probably similar to a frying pan or bowl that might have had a lid with it.

Stop here and look at a picture of this kind of pan as a group. Pause this audio here.

Once again, people needed to make this offering with olive oil and the same high-quality flour. This kind of bread was softer and thicker.

Once someone made the cooked kind of grain offering in one of these three ways, that person would bring the bread or cracker to the priest at the Tent of Meeting. The priest would then approach the bronze altar and lift up a part of the offering as a memorial portion. Then the priest would burn that memorial portion on the bronze altar as a kind of incense to Yahweh. This memorial portion was a gift with fire that would smell good to Yahweh.

Like before, Yahweh gave the priests the rest of the offering to eat. Because this offering was very holy, the priests had to eat it in the holy space of the Tent of Meeting. It is possible that priests ate this meal in the holy space of the courtyard surrounding Yahweh's tent, just like trusted servants sharing a meal with their ruler and king, King Yahweh.

Before Yahweh gave instructions about the third kind of grain offering, Yahweh gave Moses general instructions and rules that applied to all three kinds of grain offerings.

The first rule was that people could not add yeast or honey to any of the grain offerings. The people of Israel often added leavening, or yeast, to other breads to make the bread fluffier. If someone added leaven and honey or sugar to dough, the leaven would eat the honey or the sugar, which would result in gas, which would cause the bread to rise.

However, when offering a gift of bread to Yahweh, the people of Israel were not allowed to use leavening, yeast, or honey. There are a few possible reasons for this rule. One possible reason is that the leavening process resulted in a kind of decay and death. Yahweh values life so much that Yahweh considered any death aside from the ritual animal sacrifices "unclean." If Yahweh called something "unclean," then that meant it was ritually dirty. Yahweh did not allow anything unclean in Yahweh's holy space. Grain offerings were unique because part of their purpose was to be a gift of tribute to honor Yahweh as king. Since death would contaminate Yahweh's space, a gift of tribute that had death as a part of its creation process would not be an appropriate gift to King Yahweh. Another possible reason was that people thought of leavening as alive, and the people could not burn anything that was alive on the altar.

A third possible reason is that the leavening process was chaotic in the way it "changed" the bread. Yahweh values order. When Yahweh created everything, Yahweh turned chaos into order, made everything stable, and assigned everything its roles and responsibilities. Since Yahweh values order, a gift of tribute that had a chaotic creation process would be an inappropriate gift to King Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Think about what you know about who Yahweh is and what Yahweh values. Why do you think that Yahweh did not allow people to add leavening, yeast, and honey to this kind of offering? Pause this audio here.

So leavening, yeast, and honey could not burn up on the altar as a gift with fire to Yahweh, but people could bring those foods to Yahweh as a separate gift. This separate gift would have been part of the gift of "firstfruits." People brought "firstfruits" at the beginning of the harvest season as a gift to thank Yahweh for providing a harvest. When people brought leavening, yeast, and honey, this provided more food for the priests without dishonoring Yahweh by burning up an offering of leavening, yeast, and honey on the altar.

The final rule the storyteller talks about in this section was that the person who presented the grain had to add salt to every offering of grain given to Yahweh as a gift or to honor Yahweh as king. This salt is the "salt of the covenant of your God." A covenant is a binding agreement or promise between two people or groups. In a covenant, these two people or groups promise to be loyal to each other. Yahweh and the people of Israel made a covenant, or a binding agreement, to be loyal to each other—Yahweh would take care of the people of Israel, and the people of Israel would rely on and worship Yahweh as their only God. Adding salt to this kind of offering was a way to remember that covenant and promise of loyalty.

For the people of Israel and the other people groups at this time, eating a meal together was a normal part of making a covenant with each other. Food with salt was a common part of this meal, and so sometimes people at this time talked about "eating salt" or "tasting salt" as a way to talk about the loyalty relationship that existed between the two people, or groups of people, who made a covenant with each other. For the people of Israel, to add salt to the grain offering would have been a constant reminder of the covenant and loyal relationship between the Israelites and Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: When people in your culture make covenants, binding agreements, or promises of loyalty to each other, what do people do to show that those people have promised to be loyal to each other? Pause this audio here.

After talking about the rules and guidelines that applied to all of the grain offerings, Yahweh gave Moses the instructions for the third kind of grain offering. This third kind is specifically a gift or tribute of "firstfruits." The gift of "firstfruits" means the gift that people gave to Yahweh at the beginning of the harvest to thank Yahweh for taking care of the people by providing the harvest. For the people of Israel, this gift was grain that someone roasted over the fire and then crushed or rubbed out through a sieve. The result was a kind of coarse, roasted grain that was a normal, everyday food for the people of Israel. When giving it as a gift of firstfruits, the people were supposed to put oil on the grain and then add frankincense on top.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do people in your culture give thanks for a good harvest? Who do people thank? Pause this audio here.

The person would bring the grain to the priests at the Tent of Meeting. The priest would then take a portion of the roasted grain and oil, as well as all of the frankincense that was resting on top of the mixture, and burn all of this on the altar as incense. The priests burned this portion on the altar as the memorial portion. It was a gift with fire for Yahweh.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 2:1–16 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh gives instructions about what to do if someone is offering a gift of uncooked grains.

In the second scene: Yahweh gives instructions about what to do if someone is offering a gift of cooked grains.

In the third scene: Yahweh gives rules for all kinds of grain offerings that the people gave to honor Yahweh as king or to give Yahweh a gift.

In the fourth scene: Yahweh gives instructions about what someone should do when they offer a gift of the firstfruits at the beginning of the harvest.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron's descendants, who are the priests
  • And the person who will one day bring an offering

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

A lot of this passage happens near or on the bronze altar. This bronze altar was in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting near the entrance of the tent. This was the altar where the priests burned all of the sacrifices.

Scene one focuses on how to offer Yahweh uncooked grain as a gift to honor Yahweh as king or ask Yahweh for a favor. Yahweh begins these instructions by stating that people have to use high-quality flour to make the grain offering.

Next, the person who offers the uncooked grain needs to pour olive oil on high-quality flour. Then, the person has to put frankincense on top of the oil and flour mixture. Finally, the person needs to bring the oil and flour mixture with the frankincense on top of it to the priests.

Then the priest needs to take a full handful of the oil and flour mixture, along with all of the frankincense, as a memorial portion. The priest needs to burn up this memorial portion on the bronze altar as incense and a gift with fire to smell good to Yahweh. The remainder of the flour and oil mixture that the priest did not burn became food for the priests, who were Aaron's descendants. This offering was very sacred.

Stop here and, as an activity, give instructions to someone about how to do a simple task that involves two people doing different things. How does the person who gives the instructions make it clear who does what? How does the person who gives the instructions make the order of instructions clear? Pause this audio here.

Scene two focuses on how people give Yahweh cooked grain as a gift to honor Yahweh as king or ask Yahweh for a favor. People made this grain into flour. There were three different ways to cook the flour.

The first way was to bake the offering in an oven. There were two kinds of bread that people baked in these ovens. One bread was a ring shape. The other bread was a flat, round bread. People needed to make both kinds of bread with the same high-quality flour as before. For the ring-shaped bread, the person needed to mix olive oil with the high-quality flour to make the bread. For the flat round bread, the person needed to anoint the bread. The word "anoint" could just mean that people smeared olive oil on top of the bread. However, Yahweh probably used this word to remind the people of Israel that people specially dedicated the grain offering to Yahweh. It was important that none of this bread had yeast or leaven in it.

The second way was to cook the offering on a griddle. Like before, people needed to make this offering with olive oil and the same high-quality flour. Like before, this offering could not have any leaven or yeast in it. In this way, the person would prepare the offering by first cooking the dough on a griddle. This made a hard, brittle cracker. Then, the person needed to break the cracker into pieces. Finally, the person needed to pour olive oil on top of the broken pieces.

The third way was to cook the offering in a pan. Once again, people needed to make this offering with olive oil and the same high-quality flour.

Once someone made the cooked kind of grain offering in one of these three ways, the person would bring the bread or cracker to the priest at the Tent of Meeting. After that, the priest first approached the bronze altar with the offering. Then, the priest would lift up part of the offering as a memorial portion. Finally, the priest would burn the memorial portion on the bronze altar as a kind of incense and gift with fire that would smell good to Yahweh.

Stop here and, as an activity, give instructions to someone about how to do a simple task that involves three different ways to do the same thing. How does the person who gives the instructions make it clear that there are three different ways to do the same thing? Pause this audio here.

The remainder of the flour and oil mixture that the priest did not burn became food for the priests, who were Aaron's descendants. This offering was very sacred, or very holy.

Scene three explains the general rules for all grain offerings that people gave to Yahweh to honor Yahweh as king or ask Yahweh for a favor. There are two main rules in this section. After Yahweh explains the first rule, Yahweh explains one situation that is a little different from the first rule. For the first rule, Yahweh says that people cannot ever include any kind of leaven, yeast, or any kind of honey with the grain offering. If the grain offering has leaven, yeast, or honey, people cannot burn it on the bronze altar as a kind of incense. The one situation that is a little different is at the beginning of the harvest. At that time, people could bring something with leaven, yeast, or honey as a gift to Yahweh at the beginning of the harvest. However, people could not burn it on the altar. This means that people would give the offering to the priests as Yahweh's representatives, but the priests would not burn any memorial portion on the bronze altar. For the second rule, Yahweh said that people always had to add salt to the grain offering. The salt represented the covenant and binding agreement between Yahweh and Yahweh's people. And this rule did not only apply to the grain offering. Every kind of offering that anyone gave to Yahweh had to include salt.

Stop here and, as an activity, give instructions to someone about how to do a simple task that has some important rules about how to do it. How does the person emphasize how important the rules are? Pause this audio here.

Scene four focuses on how to offer Yahweh a gift of the first produce from the harvest. People often translate this first produce as the "firstfruits" of the harvest. This kind of offering is one kind of grain offering that people only offered at specific times during the year.

Stop here and, as an activity, give instructions to someone about how to do a task differently from how people normally do it. For example, give instructions for how to cook a meal for a special holiday instead of how to cook a meal on normal days. How does the person who gives the instructions make sure the listener knows that this is a special task that only happens at certain times? Pause this audio here.

People made the gift of firstfruits that Yahweh talked about in this section from grain that people roasted over the fire and then crushed or rubbed out through a sieve. The person then needed to put oil on the grain and then add frankincense on top of the mixture.

After the person finished preparing the gift, the person would bring the gift to the priests at the Tent of Meeting. Next, the priest would do his part. First, the priest would take a portion of the roasted grain and oil, as well as all of the frankincense that was resting on top of the mixture, as a memorial portion. Then the priest would burn the memorial portion on the altar as incense and a gift with fire for Yahweh.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 2:1–16 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron's descendants, who are the priests
  • And the person who will one day bring an offering

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In scene one, Yahweh continues to tell Moses what to tell the people of Israel. This time, the focus is on uncooked grain. Yahweh says, "If someone wants to offer a gift to Yahweh or tribute to honor Yahweh as king, that person needs to make the gift with high-quality flour. The person will pour olive oil on the gift and then put frankincense on top. Then, that person will bring that gift to the priests. These priests are Aaron's descendants. The priest will take a full handful of the oil and flour mixture, along with all of the frankincense, and burn it all on the bronze altar as incense. This is a gift with fire that smells good to Yahweh."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who brings the offering, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I want to thank Yahweh for what Yahweh has done for me; or
  • I want to ask Yahweh for a favor; or
  • I hope Yahweh likes this gift; or
  • I am so glad Yahweh is our king.
Continue the drama.

Then Yahweh says, "The rest of the gift of grain belongs to Aaron's descendants, the priests, to eat. This leftover oil and flour mixture is very holy compared to the other gifts with fire that people give to Yahweh."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am happy that the person who offers the grain wants to honor Yahweh; or
  • I hope Yahweh gives the person what the person asks for; or
  • The bread and crackers look good to eat; or
  • I am glad Yahweh allows me and the other priests to enjoy this gift with Yahweh.
Continue the drama.

In scene two, Yahweh continues to tell Moses what to tell the people of Israel. This time, the focus is on cooked grain. Yahweh says, "If someone wants to offer a gift that the person baked in an oven, that person needs to make the bread with high-quality flour. This bread cannot have leaven or yeast. The person should mix the flour with olive oil. If the person bakes the dough as a flat round bread, the bread also cannot have leaven or yeast in it. The person should smear oil on this bread to dedicate it to Yahweh.

"And if someone wants to offer a gift that the person cooked on a griddle, the person needs to make the dough with high-quality flour. The person needs to mix the flour with olive oil. The dough must not have leaven or yeast in it. Once the person cooks the dough, that person needs to break the bread into pieces and pour oil on top of it. This is a gift to Yahweh or tribute to honor Yahweh as king.

"And if someone wants to offer a gift that the person cooked on a pan, the person needs to make the dough with high-quality flour and olive oil.

"Once that person has cooked the gift, that person will need to bring it to Yahweh at the Tent of Meeting and give it to the priest. Then, the priest will bring the gift to the bronze altar. The priest will lift up a portion of the grain offering as a memorial portion. Next, the priest will burn the memorial portion on the bronze altar as incense. This offering is a gift with fire that smells good to Yahweh."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am glad that my people want to honor me as their king; or
  • I am glad my people are coming to me to ask for help instead of going to other gods and goddesses.
Continue the drama.

Then Yahweh says, "The rest of the gift of bread or crackers belongs to Aaron's descendants to eat. This leftover portion of the bread or crackers is very holy compared to the other gifts with fire that people give to Yahweh."

In scene three, Yahweh continues to tell Moses what to tell the people of Israel. This time, the focus is on general rules for all kinds of grain offerings that people give to honor Yahweh as king or to give Yahweh a gift. Yahweh says, "There cannot be any leaven or yeast or honey in the grain offerings that people give to honor Yahweh as king or to give Yahweh a gift. You cannot burn anything that you made with leaven, yeast, or honey on the altar. Honey, yeast, and leaven cannot be in any of the gifts with fire that you burn to smell good to Yahweh.

"Now, the offerings that people give at the beginning of the harvest can have leaven or yeast or honey, and people can give these gifts to Yahweh. But people cannot burn these gifts on the altar to smell good to Yahweh.

"Also, every grain offering that you bring to Yahweh to honor Yahweh as king or give Yahweh as a gift has to have salt in the offering. This salt represents the covenant between your God, Yahweh, and his people, and so you cannot offer a gift of grain to honor Yahweh as king or to ask Yahweh for a favor without including that salt. In fact, all of your offerings and sacrifices need to have salt."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who brings the offering, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I want to be careful not to include leaven or yeast or honey when I bring Yahweh this gift; or
  • I am so glad Yahweh gave us specific instructions so that I know what to do; or
  • I am so glad Yahweh cares about our relationship enough to remember our covenant.
Continue the drama.

In scene four, Yahweh continues to tell Moses what to tell the people of Israel. This time, the focus is on the specific kind of grain offering called the "firstfruits." Yahweh says, "If you offer a grain offering as the first produce from the harvest to honor Yahweh as king or to give Yahweh a gift, you need to give heads of grain that you have roasted on the fire and then beaten or crushed to separate the kernels.

"Then you will put olive oil on it and set some frankincense on top. This is a gift of grain to honor Yahweh as king or to give Yahweh a gift. Then, the priest will burn a memorial portion of the grain and oil mixture on the altar, along with all of the frankincense. The priest will burn it as incense, a gift with fire to Yahweh."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am glad that my people want to honor me as their king; or
  • I am glad that my people are trusting me to give them a good harvest; or
  • This gift smells good. It reminds me of how special these people are to me.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 2:1–16 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this chapter, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about the grain offering. The word in the original language that people commonly translate as "grain offering" is actually a word that refers to gifts people gave to honor a king or to ask someone in a higher position for a favor. There were a few different reasons why someone might give Yahweh this kind of offering. Sometimes, a person might want to honor Yahweh as the king of their nation. Other times, a person might want to ask Yahweh for a favor or give Yahweh a gift to thank Yahweh for what Yahweh already did for that person. This kind of offering was also part of the daily morning and evening sacrifices that the people of Israel offered Yahweh to honor Yahweh. Use the same word for Yahweh that you used previously. For more information about Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the grain offering. Look up grain offering in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

In these instructions, Yahweh says that this gift must be of high-quality flour. This specific kind of flour was probably semolina flour. However, the important part is that the flour was high-quality. It was appropriate to use this flour to make food to serve a king at a royal feast.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the fine or high-quality flour. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The person offering the gift will pour oil on it. People made this particular kind of oil from pressed olives. If you do not have olive oil in your area, consider using a general term for oil or a different oil that people make from plants. If your language has more than one way to refer to oil, make sure to use the word that means oil from plants and not animals.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the oil. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Next, the person offering the gift needs to put frankincense on top. Frankincense is a kind of tree sap that has hardened into resin. Frankincense was valuable and expensive. People burned frankincense because it smelled good.

Stop here and look at a picture of frankincense as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the frankincense. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Then, the person will bring their gift of grain to the priests. These priests are Aaron's descendants. Use the same term as you did in the first chapter of Leviticus. Look up priest in the Master Glossary for more information.

The priest will take a full handful of the oil and flour mixture, along with all of the frankincense, and burn it all on the bronze altar as incense. Use the same term that you did in the first chapter of Leviticus to refer to burning things on the altar as incense. For more information about the bronze altar, refer to altar in the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for the bronze altar as you used in the previous passage.

People often translate the part of the grain offering that the priests burn on the altar as the memorial portion. In the original language, people connect this word to the idea of remembering. Some people think that the memorial portion was a physical way for people to remember the covenant between Yahweh and Yahweh's people. Other people think it was supposed to call Yahweh's attention to the reason the person was offering the gift, whether that was to honor, thank, or ask Yahweh for a favor, or for another reason.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the memorial portion. For more information, refer to "memorial portion" in the Master Glossary. If you have already translated this idea in another book of the Bible, use the same word or phrase that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

This is a gift with fire that smells good to Yahweh. Use the same phrase to describe a fire gift as you used in the first chapter. For more information on gift with fire, refer to fire offering in the Master Glossary.

The rest of the gift of grain will be for Aaron's descendants, the priests, to eat. This leftover oil and flour mixture is extra holy or more holy than the other gifts with fire that people gave to Yahweh. People often translate this phrase "extra sacred" as "most holy." The three sacrifices that Yahweh said were "most holy" were the sin or purification offering, the guilt offering, and the grain offering. If something or someone touches one of the "most holy" things, then that thing or person becomes holy and sacred themselves. However, if someone other than a priest touched something that was "most holy," that person would die. Yahweh only allowed the priests to touch what was "most holy."

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for most holy. Look up holy in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh then explains the instructions for what to do if someone wanted to offer a gift that the person had baked in an oven.

Stop here and look at a picture of the ovens as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the oven. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

People needed to make bread that those people baked in an oven as a grain offering with the same high-quality flour and olive oil as before. There were two different kinds of bread that people baked this way. One bread was a ring shape. The other bread was a flat, round bread. Both kinds of bread would have been soft and high-quality.

Stop here and look at a picture of both kinds of bread as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use for the ring-shaped bread and the flat, round bread. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, use the same words that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

When offering the flat round bread, the person needed to anoint the bread with olive oil to specially dedicate it to Yahweh. To anoint something means to put oil on something to choose that thing for a specific purpose. People often anointed something or someone to dedicate that thing or person to Yahweh. Here, "anoint" could just mean that someone smeared the olive oil on top of the bread. However, Yahweh probably also used the word "anoint" to remind the people of Israel that the grain offering specially belonged to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for anoint. Look up anoint in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

It was important that none of this bread had yeast or leaven in it. Yeast and leaven are two different ways to describe something that people add to dough to help the dough become fluffier after baking. When people mix yeast or leaven with a mixture of flour, water, and sugar, the yeast and leaven will eat the sugar. The leaven creates tiny pockets of air that become trapped in the dough. These pockets of air help the bread "rise" and become fluffier. Yahweh said that no one could burn anything on the altar that the person had made with yeast or leaven.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for yeast or leaven. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Now, if someone offered a gift that the person had cooked on a griddle, that person also needed to make the offering with high-quality flour and olive oil. This griddle was likely iron or clay and slightly curved in shape. People would put the griddle on the fire with the curved side facing up, and then put the dough on top of the curved side.

Stop here and look at a picture of a griddle as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the griddle. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, decide if it is appropriate to use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

This kind of offering also could not have leaven or yeast in it. After cooking the offering, the person offering the gift needed to break it into pieces and pour oil on top of it.

Now, if someone offered a gift that the person had cooked on a pan, that person needed to make the offering with high-quality flour and olive oil. This type of pan was probably similar to a frying pan or bowl that might have had a lid with it.

Stop here and look at a picture of a pan as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the pan. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, decide if it is appropriate to use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Once the person had baked the offering, the person needed to bring the offering to Yahweh at the Tent of Meeting and give the offering to the priest. Then, the priest brought the offering to the bronze altar. The priest lifted up a portion of the grain offering as a memorial portion and then burned the memorial portion on the bronze altar as incense. This offering was a fire offering, or a gift with fire that smelled good to Yahweh. Use the same phrases to describe burning something as incense, and something smelling good to Yahweh, as you used in the first chapter. Translate "fire offering" in the same way you did previously in this passage.

Yahweh gave the rest of the gift of bread or crackers to Aaron's descendants to eat. This leftover portion of the bread or crackers was extra sacred compared to the other gifts with fire that people gave to Yahweh.

Before Yahweh gave instructions about the third kind of grain offering, Yahweh gave Moses general instructions and rules that applied to all three kinds of grain offerings.

The first rule was that people could not make any of the grain offerings with leaven, yeast, or honey. Honey is a kind of natural sugar that small insects called bees make. Bees probably made this kind of honey from the blossoms of fruit trees.

Stop here and look at a picture of honey as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for honey. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Nothing that the priests burned on the altar could have yeast, leaven, or honey in it. Also, none of the gifts with fire that the priests burned as incense to Yahweh could have yeast, leaven, or honey in it. However, the offerings that people gave to Yahweh at the beginning of the harvest could have leaven, yeast, or honey. But people could not burn these gifts on the altar to smell good to Yahweh.

We do not know if the word that people typically translate here as "offerings that people give at the beginning of the harvest" refers to the "firstfruits" that Yahweh talks about later. This word could either refer to the first produce from the harvest or to food that people made from the first produce of the harvest. Discuss with your team whether you want to translate it the same or differently.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for "offerings that people give at the beginning of the harvest." For more information about firstfruits, refer to the Master Glossary. Pause this audio here.

The second rule was that people had to add salt to every grain offering that people gave to Yahweh. Salt is a kind of seasoning that people used to preserve food and help prevent the food from rotting. People also added salt to every offering and sacrifice of either grain or animals that people gave to Yahweh.

Stop here and look at a picture of salt as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for salt. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh calls this salt the "salt of the covenant of your God." A covenant is a binding agreement or promise between two people or groups. In a covenant, these two people or groups promise to be loyal to each other. These two promise to be at peace with each other and to help each other. If one person is in danger, the other person promises to help the other person.

Yahweh and the people of Israel made a covenant, or a binding agreement, to be loyal to each other, too. In this covenant, the people of Israel promised that Yahweh would be their only God. The people of Israel promised to only worship and serve Yahweh and to do whatever Yahweh said. Yahweh promised to protect and take care of the people of Israel. Yahweh promised that the Israelites would be special to Yahweh and that Yahweh would provide for and live with the Israelites.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for covenant. Look up covenant in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, decide if it is appropriate to use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

In the final section, Yahweh gives Moses instructions for a specific kind of grain offering, which is the "firstfruits." The word in the original language refers to the "first" "fruits" of anything. For example, in this culture, a woman's oldest son is the first fruit of the woman's womb. The first animal born to a mother animal is the first fruit of that animal's womb. The initial harvest of grain from a grain field was the first fruit from the land. The initial harvest of fruit was the first fruit of the vine or trees. All of these different kinds of "first" "fruits" are related in the original language. In this section, the specific kind of firstfruits that Yahweh is talking about is the initial harvest of grain, fruit, and other plant crops.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for firstfruits. Again, look up firstfruits in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, decide if it is appropriate to use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

If someone wanted to offer firstfruits to Yahweh as a grain offering to give Yahweh a gift or to honor Yahweh as king, that person needed to roast heads of grain over a fire and then beat or crush the roasted grain.

Stop here and look at a picture of roasted grain as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for roasted grain. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, decide if it is appropriate to use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Next, the person needed to put olive oil on top of the roasted grain and then set some frankincense on top of the mixture. This was a gift of grain to honor Yahweh as king or to give Yahweh a gift. Then, the priest would burn a memorial portion of the grain and oil mixture on the bronze altar, along with all of the frankincense, as incense, a fire offering, or gift with fire, to Yahweh.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 3:1–17
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 3:1–17 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 3:1–17 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 3:1–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Before this passage, Yahweh gave laws about how to offer burnt offerings and grain offerings. Now, Yahweh gives laws about how to offer a peace or fellowship offering. Later, Yahweh will explain that the people do not need to make these fellowship offerings at a specific time each day or when people sin. Instead, a fellowship offering was an offering that people offered to make their relationship with Yahweh stronger or better. People also offered a fellowship offering to have fellowship with Yahweh and with the people in their community.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you make your relationship with God or other people better? How do you talk about things that help relationships get better? Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Yahweh gives instructions about how to offer three different animals as fellowship offerings. The fellowship offering was a sacrifice where the priest only burned part of the animal on the altar. The person needed to kill the animal in a specific way, and then the priest would burn specific parts of the animal as a sacrifice to Yahweh. Yahweh also forbids the Israelites from eating fat or blood.

In the first section, Yahweh gives instructions for how to offer something from the herd as a fellowship offering. A herd was a group of cattle. A herd included male and female cows.

Stop here and look at a picture of a cow as a group. Pause this audio here.

Here, Yahweh says that the sacrifice could be one of the male or female cattle. Yahweh also says that the animal needs to be physically perfect. You will remember that a perfect animal had no physical defects. The animal must not be blind or deformed or have any bruises or injuries. This animal must not have any kind of skin disease or be missing any body part. The animal had to be physically perfect. The person who offers the sacrifice needs to bring the animal to Yahweh. You will remember that Yahweh told the Israelites that Yahweh's presence is at the Tent of Meeting, or the tabernacle. The person who is offering the sacrifice needs to put their hand on the head of the animal. Then the person needs to kill the animal in front of the Tent of Meeting. The person would kill the animal the same way a person kills a bull for the burnt offering in Leviticus 1. Then the priests need to throw the blood on the altar. The priests would not touch the altar, but just throw the blood onto the sides of the altar. Yahweh also calls the priests "Aaron's sons," because Yahweh told the Israelites that the priests would be the men who descended from Aaron. Then the priest needs to put specific parts of the animal on the altar. Yahweh says the priest needs to put those parts of the burnt offering on the altar. Every morning, the priests put a burnt offering on the altar, so the fellowship offering would go on top of it. On the altar, the priest should put the fat from around the internal organs, or the stomach and intestines; the kidneys and the fat that is around them; and the fatty part of the liver.

Stop here and look at pictures of a cow's kidney and liver as a group. Pause this audio here.

Also, stop here and discuss this question as a group: Talk about who deals with animals' organs in your culture. What do people do with the animals' organs? Pause this audio here.

Also, stop here and discuss this question as a group: What are the best parts of an animal to eat in your culture? Do people in your culture eat kidneys or liver? How does your culture divide the parts of the liver? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh tells Moses that the burned pieces of the animal will be a special gift that smells good to Yahweh and honors Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Discuss a time when you smelled something that made you happy. Why did that smell make you happy? Why do you think this smell made Yahweh happy? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh gives instructions for how to offer something from the flock as a fellowship offering. A flock was a group of sheep or goats that included male and female sheep or goats. Here, Yahweh says that the sacrifice could be a male or female. First, Yahweh gives the instructions for offering sheep.

Stop here and look at a picture of a sheep as a group. Pause this audio here.

You will notice that the laws for animals from the herd and the laws for animals from the flock are similar, but there are some small differences. Yahweh says that the sheep needs to be physically perfect. The person who offers the sacrifice needs to put their hand on the head of the sheep. Then the person needs to kill the sheep in front of the Tent of Meeting. The person would kill the sheep the same way a person kills a sheep for the burnt offering in Leviticus 1. Then Aaron's sons, the priests, need to put some of the blood on the altar the same way people do when the fellowship offering is a cow. Then the priest needs to put specific parts of the sheep on the altar. Yahweh says the priest needs to put the sheep on top of the burnt offering on the altar. When the fellowship offering is a sheep, the parts of the fellowship offering that go on the altar are slightly different. First, the sheep's tail goes on the altar. Yahweh says that the person needs to cut the tail off the sheep right where the tail touches the sheep's spine.

Stop here and look at a picture of a sheep's tail as a group. Pause this audio here.

The priests also need to burn all the fat around the sheep's stomach and intestines; the kidneys and the fat that is around them; and a specific lobe, or part, of the liver.

Stop here and look at pictures of a sheep's kidney and liver as a group. Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh tells Moses that the burned pieces of the sheep will be a special gift of food to Yahweh. Though people give this food to Yahweh, this is not food for Yahweh to eat. Yahweh does not say the parts of the bull that people burn as part of the fellowship offering will be food. But the bull is probably also the same kind of food offering for Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: Is there any way people in your culture give food to gods or spirits? How do people do this? Why do people give food to gods or spirits? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh tells Moses how to offer a goat, another animal from the herd, as a fellowship offering.

Stop here and look at a picture of a goat as a group. Pause this audio here.

You will notice that the rules for offering sheep and the laws for offering goats are similar. Yahweh says that the goat needs to be physically perfect. The person who offers the sacrifice needs to put their hand on the head of the sheep. Then the person needs to kill the goat in front of the Tent of Meeting. The person would kill this goat the same way a person kills a goat for the burnt offering in Leviticus 1. Then Aaron's sons, the priests, need to put some of the blood on the altar the same way the priests do when the fellowship offering is a cow. Then the priest needs to put specific parts of the animal on the altar. Yahweh says the priest needs to put the pieces on top of the burnt offering on the altar. When someone offers a goat as a fellowship offering, the parts that go on the altar are the same as when someone offers a cow as a fellowship offering. The priests need to burn all the fat around the stomach and intestines, the kidneys and the fat that is around them, and a specific lobe, or part, of the liver.

Stop here and look at pictures of a goat's kidney and liver as a group. Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh tells Moses that the burned pieces of the goat will be a special gift that smells good to Yahweh.

Finally, Yahweh tells Moses that all fat from animals belongs to Yahweh. Yahweh tells Moses a statute that the Israelites need to follow forever, no matter where the Israelites live. The law is that the Israelites cannot eat animal blood or fat. Yahweh does not allow the Israelites to eat the animal fat because the fat belongs to Yahweh. Yahweh does not explain why the Israelites must not eat blood here, but in Genesis, Yahweh explains that the blood of an animal is its life, and that is why the Israelites must not eat blood.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Are there any parts of an animal that no one in your culture may eat? Why must people not eat it? Why do you think that Yahweh does not allow the Israelites to eat blood or fat?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 3:1–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh gives specific instructions about how to offer cattle as a peace or fellowship offering.

In the second scene: Yahweh gives specific instructions about how to offer a sheep as a fellowship offering.

In the third scene: Yahweh gives specific instructions about how to offer a goat as a fellowship offering.

In the fourth scene: Yahweh tells Moses that Yahweh will never allow the Israelites to eat fat or blood.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • A person who offers a fellowship offering
  • The priests
  • And the Israelites

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In this passage, remember that Yahweh is still giving Moses instructions for how the Israelites are supposed to live now that the Israelites have a covenant with Yahweh. In the first part of the book of Leviticus, Yahweh gives Moses the laws the Israelites need to follow when someone offers a sacrifice to Yahweh. Remember, before this passage, Yahweh explained the laws for how to offer a burnt offering and a grain offering.

It was common in Moses' time that people who gave laws, such as kings and other leaders, would repeat a lot of information and instructions as the leader explained the ritual laws. This made these laws easier to remember and showed how the laws were important. Also, remember that the structure of these laws is, "If this is what you are doing, then this is how you need to do it." Yahweh expected people to make these offerings a lot, so you can also say, "When you do this, this is how you need to do it."

In the first scene, remember that when a person offers a bull or cow from the herd, there are several actions that the person needs to do. The animal needs to be "spotless," or physically perfect. The person needs to bring the animal to Yahweh. This means that the person needs to bring the animal to the front of the Tent of Meeting because God's presence is in the Tent of Meeting.

Stop here and look at a diagram of the layout of the tabernacle, or Tent of Meeting, again. Pause this audio here.

The person puts their hand on the animal's head, and then the person kills the animal. Then the priests take the blood and throw the blood on the sides of the altar. This is the same action that Yahweh described in earlier passages.

The person cuts the animal open and removes the fat around its stomach and intestines. The person also removes the kidneys and the fat around them, and removes a certain lobe, or part, of the liver. The priest burns all those pieces on the altar, and Yahweh enjoys the smell.

In the second and third scenes, Yahweh gives the laws for how to offer an animal from a flock as a fellowship offering. In the second scene, Yahweh specifically explains the laws for offering a sheep as a fellowship offering. These are the same laws for offering a cow as a fellowship offering, except that the person needs to cut off the tail of the sheep where it connects to the spine, and the priest burns that on the altar too.

Stop here and look at pictures of a sheep again as a group if needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and answer this question as a group: How will you explain the rules for sheep? Is there a way in your language to repeat information naturally? What is the best way to communicate these laws together? Pause this audio here.

Also, stop here and discuss this question as a group: When you repeat information in a story, do you ever repeat the same information slightly differently? Are there ever differences in the repeated information that do not mean there is new information? Why are there differences that do not mean there is new information? Why do you think there are differences here if they do not mean there is different information? Pause this audio here.

The sheep needs to be physically perfect. The person who is offering the sheep as a fellowship offering needs to be in front of the tabernacle, which is the Tent of Meeting. The person puts their hand on the sheep's head, and that person kills the sheep. Then the priests take the blood and throw the blood on the side of the altar. The person cuts the sheep open and removes the fat around its stomach and intestines. The person also removes the kidneys and the fat around the kidneys, and the person removes only the best part of the liver. The person also cuts off the tail at the point it connects to the spine. The priest burns all those pieces on the altar as a food offering to Yahweh.

In the third scene, Yahweh gives the laws for how to offer a goat as a fellowship offering.

Stop here and look at pictures of a goat again as a group, if needed. Pause this audio here.

These are the same laws for offering a cow as a fellowship offering. The goat needs to be physically perfect. The person who is offering the goat as a fellowship offering needs to be in front of the Tent of Meeting. The person puts their hand on the goat's head, and the person kills the goat. Then the priest takes the blood and throws the blood on the side of the altar. The person cuts the goat open and removes the fat around the stomach and intestines. The person also removes the kidneys and the fat around them, and removes only the best part of the liver. The priest burns all those pieces on the altar as a food offering to Yahweh, and Yahweh enjoys the smell.

In the fourth scene, Yahweh tells Moses that all fat belongs to Yahweh. Yahweh tells Moses that it will be a statute for the Israelites forever that the Israelites cannot eat fat or blood, no matter where the Israelites are. A statute is a rule that usually explains how to do something that involves the tabernacle or temple. A statute may also refer to a special requirement for living in a specific society.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 3:1–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • A person who offers a fellowship offering
  • The priests
  • And the Israelites

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh tells Moses the laws for how to offer different animals as a fellowship offering. Yahweh tells Moses that if someone offers an animal from the herd, it can be a bull or a cow, but the animal must be perfect. The person puts their hand on the animal's head, and then that person cuts the animal's throat with a knife to kill the animal. Then the priests throw some of the blood onto the sides of the altar. Then the person cuts the animal open and removes the fat around the internal organs, the kidneys and the fat around them, and the best part of the liver. The priest burns those parts on the altar, and Yahweh likes the smell.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who offers a fellowship offering, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so happy that Yahweh allows me to give Yahweh this offering. I really want to know Yahweh better; or
  • I really love Yahweh, and I am glad I got to show Yahweh appreciation with this cow; or
  • I think this cow was really expensive.
Continue the drama.

Then Yahweh tells Moses that if someone offers an animal from the flock, it can be a male or female, but it must be perfect. If someone offers a sheep, the person puts their hand on the sheep's head while that person is in front of the Tent of Meeting. Then the person cuts the sheep's throat with a knife to kill the sheep. Then the priests throw some of the blood onto the sides of the altar. Then the person cuts off the tail at the spine, cuts the sheep open, and removes the fat around the internal organs, the kidneys and the fat around them, and the best part of the liver. The priest burns those parts on the altar as a gift of food to Yahweh.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am happy with the person who made this offering; or
  • I really like the smell of this sheep; it makes me happy; or
  • It is good that this person wants to have a closer relationship with me and that the priest is helping that person do it.
Continue the drama.

Then Yahweh tells Moses that if someone offers a goat, the person puts their hand on the goat's head while the person is in front of the tabernacle. Then the person cuts the goat's throat with a knife to kill the goat. Then the priests throw some of the blood onto the side of the altar. Then the person cuts the sheep open and removes the fat around the internal organs, the kidneys and the fat around them, and the best part of the liver. The priest burns those parts on the altar as a gift of food to Yahweh, and Yahweh likes the smell.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am glad I get to help this person have a better relationship with Yahweh; or
  • All this blood from killing the animal is disgusting; or
  • I am very used to this because this is my job.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh tells Moses that all fat belongs to Yahweh. Yahweh also tells Moses that Yahweh will never allow the Israelites to eat blood or fat, no matter where the Israelites are.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 3:1–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Yahweh gives instructions for when a person offers a bull or a cow as a peace or fellowship offering. A fellowship offering is a sacrifice someone makes to have a better relationship, or "fellowship," with Yahweh and the person's community. A person makes a sacrifice when they give a gift to God. The person will eat part of the sacrifice with other people.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for sacrifice and peace or fellowship offering. Look up sacrifice and peace or fellowship offering in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, use the same words that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The animal must be perfect or spotless. The person takes the animal to Yahweh. Yahweh's presence is in the Tent of Meeting, so the person takes the animal to the front of the Tent of Meeting and puts their hand on the animal's head. Use the same words or phrases for perfect, Yahweh, and Tent of Meeting as you have used in previous passages. Look up perfect, Yahweh, and tabernacle in the Master Glossary for more information.

Then that person kills the animal. The priest will throw the blood onto the sides of the altar. Use the same words or phrases for throwing the blood on the sides of the altar as previously. Use the same words for altar and priest that you used in previous passages. For more information on altar and priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

Then the person will cut out certain parts of the animal's organs. The first is the fat on the internal organs, which may be the animal's stomach and intestines. Then the person removes the lobe of the liver. This is the best part of the animal's liver, and you may simply say "the best part of the liver" in your translation. These, along with the two kidneys, would be good portions of the animal. If you have already translated the book of Exodus, use the same words or phrases for kidneys and lobe of the liver as you used in Exodus 29:13. Use the same words or phrases for kidneys and lobe of the liver throughout the book of Leviticus.

This is a gift with fire that smells good to Yahweh. Use the same phrase to describe this fire offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on fire offering, refer to fire offering in the Master Glossary.

The smell will be a sweet smell or pleasing aroma to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for pleasing aroma as you used in previous passages.

There are also the rules for if someone wants to offer a sheep, and Yahweh also requires the priest to burn the sheep's tail. There are rules for if someone wants to offer a goat. Use the same words for sheep and goat that you have used in previous passages.

Then Yahweh tells Moses that all the fat is Yahweh's. That means that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to eat the fat in animals because the fat belongs to Yahweh. Yahweh also tells Moses this is a statute forever. No Israelite can eat fat or blood no matter where the Israelites are. A statute is a rule that focused specifically on the religious rules about how to celebrate festivals, perform religious rituals, and offer sacrifices of animals and grain. Yahweh also used this word to talk about the rules for what the priests needed to do.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for statute. Look up statute in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

This statute will last through all the generations of the Israelites.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for generations. Look up generations in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
