title: Leviticus 5:1–13
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 5:1–13 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 5:1–13 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 5:1–13 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous passage, Yahweh gave Moses laws for how people need to make a sin or purification offering. Yahweh now talks about the circumstances that require a purification offering. In this passage, Yahweh gives examples of circumstances in which someone becomes unclean or ritually dirty because that person has not done something that person needs to do. Therefore, that person needs to make a purification offering. Yahweh does not describe everything that makes a person ritually dirty.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Describe times when someone in your community has not done something they are supposed to do. How do other people feel about that person? What does that person need to do to make things right again? Pause this audio here.

The first example is when a leader or someone with authority commands people to talk about something that people saw or learned about. If a person does not talk about what that person saw or learned about, that person makes themselves guilty. Yahweh is probably talking about when the leaders in a community would ask for people to give the leaders information about a person who disobeyed a community law. People who do not give information to the leaders are guilty.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you investigate crimes in your community? What do you call the people who have information about crimes? What do you do if someone knows important information about a crime but will not share it? Pause this audio here.

The second example is when someone touches something that is unclean or ritually dirty. This makes that person become ritually dirty too and guilty. Unclean did not just mean physically dirty. Yahweh was talking about being ritually clean or dirty. Because Yahweh deserves a lot of respect as the creator of the universe and as the one who ruled over the Israelites, Yahweh used this system of clean and dirty to help the Israelites understand how to respect Yahweh. Yahweh did not want anything ritually dirty to touch anything holy, so Yahweh had various rules to keep literally dirty people, animals, and objects from touching holy objects or people. If a person touched a ritually dirty animal's dead body, that person became ritually dirty too. Ritually dirty animals were animals that Yahweh did not allow the Israelites to eat. Those animals also made the things the animals touched ritually dirty.

Stop and discuss this question as a group: What are your culture's rules about how to interact with the dead bodies of animals? What does someone who touches a dead animal have to do? Pause this audio here.

Stop and discuss this question as a group: Are there any animals that people in your culture must not eat? Why? What do you call animals that you must not eat? Pause this audio here.

When Yahweh talks about the ritually dirty animals, Yahweh talks about three different types of animals. Yahweh talks about animals that are livestock, which people also call domesticated animals. These were animals that people have tamed and used for food or work. Yahweh talks about wild animals, which people also call beasts. These were all the other animals that people have not tamed. Yahweh also talks about swarming creatures, or things that move on the earth. These were small creatures like rodents or insects. Yahweh talks about these categories of animals because these were the major categories of animals for the Israelites. When someone talked about wild animals and domesticated animals, that person was talking about all animals.

Stop and discuss this question as a group: How do people in your culture talk about different types of animals? How do people put different types of animals in groups that are similar? How do people in your culture talk about all the different kinds of animals at once? Pause this audio here.

Sometimes a person might accidentally touch the dead body of a ritually dirty animal, but does not realize that they have touched a ritually dirty animal. Then that person goes to the Tent of Meeting or participates in a religious ritual before that person has made themselves ritually clean again. That person is guilty. When that person realizes what they have done, that person must make a purification offering to Yahweh.

Another example is when someone touches another human's dirtiness. It does not matter that the person does not know that the other person is ritually dirty. That first person is now ritually dirty and guilty, too. A human's dirtiness is a way to refer to something that the human body produces, like excrement, blood, or semen, that makes people ritually dirty if those people touch it. It also refers to diseases, like specific types of rashes or skin diseases, that make a person ritually dirty. Yahweh will explain later what things specifically will make people ritually dirty if someone touches those things.

Stop and discuss this question as a group: How do people in your community treat things the human body produces? Do you treat different things, like spit or blood, differently? Talk about a time when someone could not be around other people because of something that person's body was producing. Pause this audio here.

A person who touches a human's dirtiness but does not make themselves ritually clean again is guilty for the same reason that a person who touches the dead body of a ritually dirty animal is guilty.

The fourth example is when a person swears an oath without thinking seriously about the oath. That person is also guilty. This is true whether the oath was good or bad. An oath was good if it was helpful and bad if it was harmful to someone. Yahweh cares a lot about making oaths, so if someone makes an oath, Yahweh's law says that person needs to do what that person said they would do. Yahweh cared because when a person swore an oath, that person said that their god would punish that person if the person did not do what that person said. Since Yahweh is the Israelite's God, Yahweh will punish that person if that person does not do what that person swore to do.

Stop and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time someone in your culture swore an oath or made a strong promise that that person would do something, and then that person did not do it. What happened to that person? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that if someone did any of the things Yahweh just talked about, then that person needs to confess that they are guilty. That person needs to bring a purification offering to Yahweh at the Tent of Meeting, and the priest will make atonement for the person's sin. This means that the priest will offer the animal as a purification offering, and then Yahweh will restore Yahweh's relationship with that person. Yahweh will forgive that person, and Yahweh will not punish the person for what that person did wrong.

The next section explains what someone needs to do for a purification offering if that person cannot afford a sheep. This rule is also for someone who cannot afford a goat. Yahweh is giving this rule because Yahweh wants to help the poor Israelites.

Stop and discuss this question as a group: How does your society help poor people, or people who need extra help, to worship your God or gods? How do poor people worship God in different ways than wealthy people do? Pause this audio here.

If someone cannot afford a sheep or a goat, that person needs to bring two doves or two pigeons. It is unclear what the difference is between a dove and a pigeon in this passage. People sacrificed these birds because these birds represented purity and innocence.

Stop here and look at a picture of doves and pigeons as a group. Pause this audio here.

The person offers one of the birds as a purification offering and one bird as a burnt offering. The person brings the birds to the priest, and the priest offers the first bird as a purification offering. The priest twists the bird's neck until the bird dies and pulls until the head starts to come off the body. The priest needs to make sure the head is still partially attached to the bird's dead body. As the blood pours out of where the bird's neck has ripped open, the priest needs to take some of the blood and sprinkle the blood onto the side of the altar. The priest will drain the rest of the blood from the bird at the base of the altar of burnt offering.

Stop here and look at a picture of the altar of burnt offering as a group. Pause this audio here.

Then the priest offers the second bird as a burnt offering by following the laws Yahweh explained earlier in Leviticus. Yahweh explains that this is how the priest will make atonement for the person's sin, and Yahweh will forgive the person.

Yahweh continues to help poor people by explaining what someone can do if someone cannot afford two doves or two pigeons for a purification offering. Yahweh says that the person needs to bring one-tenth of an ephah of good-quality flour to offer as a purification offering. An ephah was probably a large basket that people used to carry and measure flour. One tenth of an ephah was about 2.25 liters. In weight, it was about 1 to 2 kilograms. People crush the grain as small as they can to make good-quality flour.

Stop here and look at a picture of good-quality flour as a group. Pause this audio here.

The person must not add any oil or frankincense of any kind to the flour because this is a purification offering.

Stop here and look at a picture of oil and of frankincense as a group. Pause this audio here.

The person takes the flour to the priest, and the priest takes a handful of the flour and puts it on the altar to burn. This is a memorial portion. You will remember that some people think a memorial portion helps the Israelites remember Yahweh's covenant, or perhaps call Yahweh's attention to the reason the person was offering the flour. Yahweh explains that the flour will go with the other offerings that are already in the fire. This process will be how the priest will make atonement for the person's sin, and Yahweh will forgive the person. The person who brought the flour will give the rest of the flour to the priest, as a person does for a grain offering.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 5:1–13 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains what sort of sins require someone to offer a sin or purification offering.

In the second scene: Yahweh explains how to offer two doves or two pigeons as a purification offering if someone cannot afford to offer a sheep.

In the third scene: Yahweh explains how to offer flour for a purification offering if someone cannot afford to offer doves or pigeons.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The leaders who tell people to testify if people have seen something bad happen
  • The person who offers a purification offering because they have accidentally sinned
  • And a priest

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the passage, remember that Yahweh is still giving Moses these laws from the Tent of Meeting. These laws are about how and when the Israelites are supposed to bring offerings. Remember that in the previous passage, Yahweh gave Moses laws for what different types of people must do for purification offerings. In this passage, Yahweh is giving Moses examples of what types of sins require a purification offering, and what people can bring if people cannot afford to bring the certain animals. Also, remember that in this passage, Yahweh says, "If someone does this thing, another thing will happen." In each of these examples, Yahweh is talking about when someone does something that makes that person guilty or ritually dirty. Yahweh is talking about events that have not actually happened yet.

In the first scene, Yahweh describes things a person could do that would make that person guilty or ritually dirty. The first is if someone does not tell leaders what that person knows about a crime when the leaders ask about it. The second is if someone touches the dead body of an unclean animal, but that person does not realize it and does not make themselves clean. The third is if someone touches some human dirtiness that makes the person unclean, but that person does not realize it and does not make themselves clean. The fourth is if someone makes an oath to do something without thinking about the oath seriously.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: Talk about a list of potential actions someone might do, such as ways a person could get across a river or ways a person could start a story. Listen for words that you use to show these are all examples and potential things someone could do. Pause this audio here.

When someone realizes that they are guilty, that person needs to bring a purification offering to the priest and confess what that person has done. The purification offering needs to be a sheep or a goat. The priest will make atonement for the person with the offering, which will make the ritually dirty person clean again, so Yahweh will not punish that person. Here, Yahweh does not say Yahweh will forgive the person. That does not mean that Yahweh will not forgive the person. Yahweh probably does not say Yahweh will forgive the person because Yahweh already said he would forgive the person in the last passage, when Yahweh explained how to offer a purification offering.

In the second scene, Yahweh explains how to offer two doves or pigeons as a purification offering if the person cannot afford a sheep. Yahweh means a sheep or a goat here. Yahweh is giving another way for people who cannot afford a sheep or a goat for a purification offering.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: How do you give different options for ways people can do a certain task? As an activity, give someone multiple options, such as different ways they could get to a certain location or different ways to clean a house. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh explains that one dove or pigeon will be a purification offering, and one dove or pigeon will be for a burnt offering. Yahweh gives the details for how to offer a bird as a sin offering. First, the priest twists the bird's head partly off and sprinkles some of the blood onto the side of the altar. That means that the priest makes sure a few drops of blood drip from the priest's hand onto the side of the altar without touching the altar. Then the priest drains the rest of the blood at the bottom of the altar. Yahweh says again that this is a purification offering. Yahweh says that because the purification offering is the only offering in which the priests will pour the blood onto the base of the altar.

Stop here and, as a group, act out how the priest will sprinkle or throw some of the bird's blood on the side of the altar. Then act out how the priest will drain the rest of the bird's blood onto the base of the altar. How will you describe this in your translation? Remember how you have described these actions in previous passages. Pause this audio here.

Then the priest offers the second bird as a burnt offering. This entire process is how the priest makes atonement for the person, and Yahweh will forgive that person.

In the third scene, Yahweh explains how to use one tenth of an ephah of well-milled flour as a purification offering if a person cannot afford two doves or two pigeons. Yahweh explains how the flour cannot have any oil or frankincense in it. The priest burns a handful of the flour on the altar to show that the person remembers Yahweh and Yahweh's laws. The priest will put this flour on top of the other fire offerings, or the animal offerings, that are already on the altar. This process is how the priest makes atonement for the person, and Yahweh will forgive that person. Then the person who brings the flour is supposed to give the rest of the flour to the priest.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 5:1–13 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The leaders who tell people to testify if people have seen something bad happen
  • The person who offers a purification offering because they have accidentally sinned
  • And a priest

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

You may choose to have the characters act out each possible situation as Yahweh gives these instructions through Moses.

Yahweh tells Moses to say to the Israelites: "If you are a witness to a crime but you do not tell your leaders when your leaders ask you to say what you know, then you are guilty."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the leaders, "What are you thinking or feeling?" The person might answer things like:

  • I really want to know who committed this crime; or
  • I hope people tell us about what happened; or
  • No one told us about what happened, and now I am sad and frustrated.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh says, "If you touch the dead body of any kind of unclean animal, even if you do not realize it, then you are guilty. If you touch something that humans make that is unclean, even if you do not realize it, then you are guilty. If you make an oath to do something without thinking seriously about it, you are guilty. When you realize you are guilty, you need to take a sheep or a goat to the priest to make a purification offering."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who is bringing a purification offering, "What are you thinking or feeling?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so embarrassed that I forgot one of these things! or
  • I feel guilty because I did something wrong; or
  • I do not understand why I have to make a sacrifice since this was just an accident.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh then tells Moses to say to the Israelites, "If you cannot afford to use a sheep for the purification offering, then you need to take two doves or two pigeons to the priest. One of the birds will be a purification offering, and one will be a burnt offering. The priest will twist the bird's head until it comes mostly off the body but is still a little attached. Then the priest will get a little of the bird's blood on the priest's hand and sprinkle the blood onto the side of the altar. The priest will make sure the rest of the blood falls onto the ground at the base of the altar. The priest will use the second bird as a burnt offering, and the priest needs to follow the rules Yahweh said earlier about how to offer a dove or pigeon as a burnt offering. When the priest sacrifices the birds, the priest will make atonement for the person, which makes the person ritually clean from the thing that person did wrong so that Yahweh will not punish that person."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you thinking or feeling?" The person might answer things like:

  • I forgive this person because this person did what I asked the Israelites to do; or
  • I love this person so much. I am glad I gave people a way to restore their relationship with me, even though this person can not afford a sheep.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh then tells Moses to say to the Israelites: "If you cannot afford two doves or two pigeons, then you need to bring one tenth of an ephah of flour. The flour needs to be very small pieces of grain, and it cannot have any oil or frankincense in it. The priest will take a small amount of the flour and put it on the altar with the other food sacrifices. This shows that the person who brings the flour remembers Yahweh and the laws Yahweh told the Israelites to follow. When this happens, the priest makes atonement for the person. Yahweh will forgive the person and restore Yahweh's relationship with that person so that Yahweh does not punish that person. Then the person who brought the flour gives the rest of the flour to the priest, just like people give the flour from the grain offering to the priest."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who is bringing the purification offering, "What are you thinking or feeling?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so glad that I can restore my relationship with God, even though I do not have a lot of money; or
  • I hope Yahweh forgives me, even though this sacrifice is not as valuable as sheep.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 5:1–13 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this section of Leviticus, Yahweh gives Moses more laws for the Israelites about how to make offerings to Yahweh. The laws in this passage are about when and how to offer a sin or purification offering. Use the same word or phrase for purification offering that you used in the previous passage. Purification offering is in the Master Glossary.

The first example is when a leader commands people to testify, or talk about something people saw or learned about. If someone does not talk about that thing, that person is guilty. Use the same word or phrase for guilty that you used in the previous passage, and remember that guilt is in the Master Glossary.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for testify, or talk about something that you have seen in a court where people are judging if someone is guilty. Translate the idea of testify in the same way you have in other books of the Bible, and refer to the Master Glossary for more information about testify. Pause this audio here.

The second example is when someone touches something that is unclean or ritually dirty. That person becomes ritually dirty and guilty. Unclean does not just mean physically dirty. Yahweh also used the words clean and unclean to talk about being spiritually clean or unclean. In the Bible, a clean person means a person who is fit for service to God—someone who is acceptable to participate in worship to God. A person who is unclean is unfit for service to God. Animals and even objects can also be clean or unclean. In this passage, Yahweh is talking about people who are ritually unclean because they have accidentally sinned.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for unclean when it refers to animals. Look up clean and unclean in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

A person can become ritually dirty if a person touches a ritually dirty animal's carcass. A carcass is the dead body of an animal.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for a carcass. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh talks about three different types of animals: domesticated animals, wild animals, and swarming creatures. These three different types of animals included all the animals that existed. Domesticated animals are animals that people have taught to do what people want the animals to do. Domesticated animals generally live with people, and people use these animals for food or work. Wild animals are animals that do not obey people and that are not used to people. Wild animals generally stay away from people, though these animals might occasionally go near people and cause problems for people. People might hunt wild animals, but people do not stay near wild animals. Finally, swarming creatures are all the small creatures, like insects or really small animals. The Israelites used these three categories of animals to talk about every different kind of animal.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for domesticated animals, wild animals, and swarming creatures. If you have already translated these phrases in another book of the Bible, use the same words that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The third example is when someone touches a human's uncleanness. Even if the person is unaware of what they have done, that person is guilty. A person's uncleanness is a way to refer to something that the human body produces, like poop, blood, or semen, that makes people ritually dirty if someone touches it. It is also a way to refer to a disease a person has, like a skin disease, that makes people ritually dirty when someone touches it or has it. Yahweh will explain later what things specifically will make people ritually dirty if someone touches those things.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will translate the idea of a human's uncleanness. Pause this audio here.

The fourth example law is when a person swears an oath or serious promise without thinking seriously about the oath. When someone swears an oath, that person says, "I will absolutely keep my promise. If I do not, God may punish me."

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for oath. Look up oath in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh says that if someone is guilty because that person did any of the four things Yahweh just talked about, then that person needs to confess that they are guilty. When Yahweh says to confess, Yahweh means that the person needs to say out loud what that person did wrong. Here, the person probably says it to the priest, though Yahweh might mean that the person says it to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for confess. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

A person needs to bring a purification offering to Yahweh because that person is guilty. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. Look up Yahweh in the Master Glossary for more information.

The purification offering needs to be something from the flock; it can be either a sheep or a goat. Use the same words or phrases for sheep and goat that you used in previous passages.

When the person brings the purification offering to the priest, the priest gives the offering for the person. Use the same word or phrase for priest as you used in previous passages. Look up priest in the Master Glossary for more information.

This is how the priest will make atonement for the person's sin. Use the same words or phrases for atonement and for accidental sin that you used in previous passages. Look up atonement and sin in the Master Glossary for more information.

Then Yahweh explains what someone needs to do if that person cannot afford a sheep for the purification offering. That person needs to bring two doves or two pigeons. Some translations say two turtledoves or two pigeons. Doves and pigeons are two different types of birds. Use the same words or phrases for pigeons and doves that you used in the first passage of Leviticus. For more information on dove, look in the Master Glossary.

Stop here and look at a picture of doves and pigeons again as a group. Pause this audio here.

The priest will sacrifice one of the birds as a purification offering, and then the priest will sacrifice one bird as a burnt offering. Use the same word for burnt offering that you used in previous passages, and refer to burnt offering in the Master Glossary if needed.

When the priest offers the first bird as a purification offering, the priest wrings the bird's neck until the bird dies and the head becomes partially detached from the body. Then the priest sprinkles some of the blood onto the altar. Use the same word or phrase for sprinkling blood, and for altar, that you used in previous passages. Look up altar in the Master Glossary for more information. The priest drains the rest of the bird's blood out at the base, or bottom, of the altar.

Then the priest offers the second bird as a burnt offering by following the laws Yahweh gave earlier in Leviticus. Yahweh explains that this process will be how the priest will make atonement for the person's sin. This means that the priest will offer the animal as a purification offering, and then Yahweh will not punish the person for what they did wrong. Yahweh specifically says here that Yahweh will forgive the person. Use the same word or phrase for forgive as you used in previous passages. Look up forgiveness in the Master Glossary for more information.

Then Yahweh explains what someone needs to do if that person cannot afford two doves or two pigeons for a purification offering. Yahweh says the person needs to bring one-tenth of an ephah of good-quality flour to offer as a purification offering. Use the same word or phrase for good-quality flour that you used in previous passages.

An ephah was probably a large basket that people used to carry and measure flour. One tenth of an ephah was about 2.25 liters, and a tenth of an ephah of flour weighed between 1 and 2 kilograms. You may use the actual weight or volume of the flour in your translation, rather than saying "ephah," if you would like.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for one-tenth of an ephah, or for this measurement. Look up ephah in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The person should not add any oil or any frankincense of any kind to the flour. Use the same word or phrase for oil that you used in previous passages. Also, use the same word or phrase for frankincense that you used in previous passages.

Stop here and look at a picture of oil and of frankincense as a group. Pause this audio here.

The person takes the flour to the priest, and the priest takes a handful of the flour and puts it on the altar on top of the other fire offerings to burn. This is the memorial portion. That means it is how the person shows that they remember Yahweh and what Yahweh has told them to do. Use the same words or phrases for fire offerings and memorial portion that you used in previous passages. Fire offerings and memorial portion are in the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says that the person who brought the flour will give the rest of it to the priest, just like people give the flour from the grain offerings to the priests. Use the same word or phrase for grain offering that you used in previous passages. Look up grain offering in the Master Glossary for more information.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 5:14–6:7
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 5:14–6:7 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 5:14–6:7 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 5:14–6:7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh has been giving Moses laws to give to the Israelites that explain when and how the people are supposed to give offerings to Yahweh, so that they can live in good relationship with Yahweh. Yahweh has explained how to offer burnt offerings, grain offerings, peace or fellowship offerings, and sin or purification offerings. Now Yahweh explains the last main type of offering, which most translations call a guilt or reparation offering. It is a guilt offering because a person is guilty when that person does something wrong, and this offering is how Yahweh forgives that person. Reparation is a word that means payment for what someone owes. Since this offering is a way that people pay Yahweh or other people what that person owes, people sometimes call this offering a reparation offering. [This offering is different from the purification offering because a person sacrificed a guilt offering when that person did something that caused]{.mark} Yahweh or other people to lose something valuable. This offering repaid the value to other people or to Yahweh. The sacrifice allowed the priest to make atonement for the person so that Yahweh would forgive the person. Then Yahweh restored Yahweh's relationship with that person and cleansed that person from their guilt.

This passage involves three different situations that would cause someone to need to make a guilt offering, and what that guilt offering must be.

In the first situation, Yahweh tells Moses what the Israelites need to do when someone sins accidentally against any of Yahweh's holy things. Yahweh also says that when a person sins against Yahweh's holy things, that person is being unfaithful to Yahweh. Yahweh's holy things probably mean any of the items in the Tent of Meeting or the Tent of Meeting itself. The holy things are also things that people are supposed to give to Yahweh, such as firstborn animals or money. This probably included things that the priests and the Levites were supposed to get and things that people promised to give to Yahweh. These holy items have a value that people can measure. Yahweh is probably talking about when someone promises to give Yahweh something, but does not give it to Yahweh. Yahweh says that when that person sins, that person needs to bring a ram that is physically perfect from the flock as a guilt offering. A ram was an adult male sheep. Rams were the most valuable type of sheep.

Stop here and look at a picture of a ram as a group. Pause this audio here.

The person must choose a ram they own that has a certain value. The Israelites did not have a set of coins at this time, but used various weights of precious metal for money. A shekel was a weight measurement of about 11 grams. There were different standards for weight measurement at this time, so Yahweh specifies which measurement to use. The person should use the shekel measurement that weighed as much as priests in the holy place decided a shekel should weigh.

Stop here and look at a picture of a shekel as a group. Pause this audio here.

The holy place or sanctuary was another name for the Tent of Meeting, and people used the term later as a name for the temple as well. It is not clear from this passage how many shekels the ram needed to be worth. It is possible that the price of a ram would change over time, so the priests were in charge of determining how expensive the ram should be.

The person who brought the guilt offering also had to pay money to make peace or make up for the holy thing that that person had sinned against. This is probably because the holy thing needed to go through a special ritual for people to be able to use it again. It is also possible that people needed to make a new holy thing to replace the one that someone had sinned against. The person had to pay for the full value of the holy thing. The person also had to pay an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the cost. This person paid that money to the priest.

Then the priest makes atonement with the ram to ask Yahweh to forgive that person and restore the relationship between Yahweh and the person. When the priest makes atonement, Yahweh also cleans the person from the guilt of what that person did wrong and forgives that person. Yahweh does not explain here how the priest is supposed to sacrifice the ram.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Do you have any holy or special things in your culture? What do you do if someone misuses those things or ruins them? How does someone make peace or pay back the value of what that person ruined? Pause this audio here.

In the next situation, Yahweh says that when someone sins by doing anything that Yahweh told the Israelites not to do, that person is guilty. Yahweh specifies that even if the person does not realize they have sinned until later, that person is still guilty. If that person is guilty, Yahweh says that person needs to bring a ram that was physically perfect from the flock, just like in the first situation. This ram also needs to be worth a certain amount of shekels, that weigh the amount the priests in the holy place decided a shekel should weigh. The priest then makes atonement for the wrong thing the person did, and Yahweh will forgive the person. Yahweh wants people to know that even when people do not know that they break Yahweh's laws, those people are still guilty of breaking one of Yahweh's laws.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What do you do in your culture when someone breaks the law accidentally, or without realizing that the person has broken the law? How do people in your culture punish that person, and how do you bring that person back into your community? Pause this audio here.

In the last situation, Yahweh describes several ways someone might take something valuable from their neighbors illegally. Yahweh says that people who do this are being unfaithful to Yahweh. When Yahweh says neighbor, Yahweh means the people who are part of the Israelites' community.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What people do you consider to be part of your community? What are some things you are supposed to do or not do for people in your community? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that anyone who does one of these things is betraying Yahweh. The first thing a person might do is lie about something a neighbor gave the person as a deposit or as a pledge. A deposit is something someone gives to you to keep safe. A pledge is something someone gives you as a sign of a promise that the person will do something. When Yahweh says that someone might lie about it, Yahweh means a person might lie and say their neighbor did not give anything, or the person might lie and say that their neighbor gave the person less than the neighbor actually gave. Another way to translate "deposit or pledge" would be "something a person is supposed to take care of."

Stop here and discuss this as a group: How do people in your culture keep things safe? Do people ever ask neighbors to take care of something for them? What happens if the neighbor steals the thing instead of taking care of the thing? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also says that a person might just steal something from their neighbor. A person might also extort their neighbor, or force their neighbor to give something that the neighbor does not want to give. The last thing a person might do is find something that belongs to someone else and then lie and say they do not have that thing. In these situations, the person has sworn a false oath that they did not have something or did not do something wrong.

Yahweh ends these examples by saying that Yahweh is talking about any kinds of sins that involve taking something valuable from a person and lying about it, since a guilt or reparation sacrifice is about repaying things.

Yahweh says that if someone does any of those things, when that person realizes their guilt, that person needs to make peace, or give back the thing that the person should not have. That means the person needs to give back whatever that person lied about or stole. That would also include whatever someone gave to the person that the person lied about, or the lost thing the person found and swore they did not have. The person needs to give that thing back and pay the other person an extra one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the value of the thing. The person needs to do this on the same day the person gives Yahweh a guilt offering. The person needs to bring a ram from the flock that is physically perfect. This ram also needs to be worth a certain amount of shekels, that weigh the amount the priests in the holy place decided a shekel should weigh. The priest then makes atonement for the wrong thing the person did, and Yahweh will forgive the person for whatever the person did that was a sin.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: What do people in your culture do when someone steals from another member of the community?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 5:14–6:7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains how to offer a guilt offering when a person sins against one of Yahweh's holy things.

In the second scene: Yahweh explains how to offer a guilt offering when a person does something Yahweh commanded the Israelites not to do.

In the third scene: Yahweh explains the situations where a person might steal something from someone in their community. Yahweh then explains how to offer a guilt offering when the person admits their guilt.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • The person who offers the guilt offering because they have sinned
  • The priest
  • And the neighbor whose things someone else stole

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Yahweh has been speaking to Moses and has been giving Moses laws that the Israelites need to obey for offerings. Although we do not know where Moses is when Yahweh gives him the laws in this passage, it is possible that Moses is still on Mount Sinai and that Yahweh gives Moses these laws there. In any case, now Yahweh gives laws for the last type of offering in this part of Leviticus.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives the laws for how someone gives a guilt offering when that person sins against one of Yahweh's holy things without meaning to. This person is unfaithful to Yahweh. In other words, this person betrays Yahweh and shows that he is not loyal to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will say that someone has sinned against Yahweh and is unfaithful to Yahweh. Pause this audio here.

The person must bring a ram that is perfect and worth a certain number of shekels based on the weight of shekels the priests in the holy place used. This person gives the ram to the priest at the Tent of Meeting.

That person needs to make restitution, or peace, with whoever they have wronged. That means that this person also gives the priest money that is equal to the value of the holy thing the person sinned against. The person also gives additional money equal to 20 percent of the value of the holy thing. Then the priest will make atonement for that person, and Yahweh will forgive that person. Yahweh will explain how the priest offers the ram in Leviticus 7.

Stop here and discuss as a group: How will you say that the person who wronged someone else must make restitution, or peace, with whoever they wronged? Pause this audio here.

Stop here and do this activity as a group. Talk about what 20 percent means. Find a group of 10 items. Twenty percent of these 10 items is 2. Therefore, add 2 things to the 10 things. You will have 12 things. If someone takes 10 things away from someone else, that person would have to give back 12 things—the 10 they took and 2 more. Then, come up with things in your society that people all know the value of, such as fish, bread, or houses. What would it be to pay back the value of those things and an additional 20 percent as well? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, Yahweh gives the laws for when someone accidentally does something Yahweh commanded the Israelites not to do, and then the person realizes they sinned. Yahweh says that in these situations, a person is still guilty and deserves punishment. Yahweh says that the person needs to bring a ram that is perfect and worth a certain number of shekels based on the weight of shekels that people use in the holy place. The person gives the ram to the priest. Then the priest will make atonement for that person, and Yahweh will forgive that person. Yahweh repeats that it is a guilt offering for the sin the person did against Yahweh that made the person guilty. Yahweh wants to emphasize that even though the person did not know they did something Yahweh told the Israelites not to do, that person is still guilty of breaking one of Yahweh's laws.

In the third scene, Yahweh gives several examples of how someone might be unfaithful to Yahweh by stealing. First, a person might lie about something the neighbor gave as a pledge or a deposit. A pledge is something someone gives you as a sign of a promise that the person will do something. You are supposed to return a pledge to the person when the person does what they say they will. However, someone could lie and say their neighbor did not give a pledge or that the person has not yet done what they promised. A deposit was something that someone gave someone else to take care of. If a person were going on a trip, the person could protect something valuable if they gave it to someone to keep safe. People often gave valuable things to their neighbors to protect while a person was away. But someone could lie and pretend to have lost the valuable thing or say that the thing had always belonged to that person. Yahweh is saying that that is a sin. Second, a person steals from someone in their community. That means a person would attack and take something from their neighbor. Third, a person might extort their neighbor, or force their neighbor to give something. That usually means a person threatens to do something to the neighbor if the neighbor does not give the thing the person asks for. Or a person might trick their neighbor so the neighbor gives the thing without realizing it. Finally, a person might find something that belongs to someone else and lie about it. If anyone swears a false oath about any of these things, that person sins. Yahweh says that any of these things is something someone might do that is a sin.

Yahweh specifically lists again all the ways someone might be unfaithful to Yahweh by stealing and repeats that people sin when they do these things. You might list these things all again, or you might summarize the things.

As soon as someone realizes that the person has sinned by doing something like this, that person needs to give back what the person stole. The person also gives additional money worth 20 percent of the thing's value. Then that person needs to bring a ram that is perfect and worth a certain number of shekels based on the weight of shekels the priests in the holy place used. The person must give the ram to the priest. Then the priest will make atonement for them. Yahweh will forgive that person for anything that person has done that made the person guilty.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 5:14–6:7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • The person who offers the guilt offering because they have sinned
  • The priest
  • And the neighbor whose things someone else stole

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh tells Moses to tell the Israelites: "If you accidentally sin against any of Yahweh's holy things, then bring a guilt offering to Yahweh. It needs to be a ram that has no problems with it and is worth a certain number of shekels. The priests at the holy place will weigh the shekels according to the sanctuary standard. The person also needs to pay for the holy thing that the person sinned against, plus an additional 20 percent of its value. Then the priest will sacrifice the ram to ask Yahweh to forgive the person, and Yahweh will forgive the person."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who sinned against one of Yahweh's holy things, "What are you thinking or feeling?" The person might answer things like:

  • I feel guilty or ashamed because I sinned against one of Yahweh's holy things; or
  • I am glad Yahweh forgave me when I brought the guilt sacrifice; or
  • I did not do it on purpose, so why am I in trouble?
Continue the drama.

Then Yahweh told Moses to tell the Israelites: "If you accidentally disobey any of the laws that I am giving you, even just one of them, when you realize that you are guilty, you need to make it up to me. Bring a guilt offering to Yahweh. It needs to be a ram that has no problems with it and is worth a certain number of shekels. The priests at the holy place will weigh the shekels according to the sanctuary standard. Then the priest will sacrifice the ram to ask Yahweh to forgive that person for what the person unintentionally did, and Yahweh will forgive that person. The person gave a guilt offering because even though that person did not mean to break one of Yahweh's laws, that person was still guilty."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you thinking or feeling?" The person might answer things like:

  • I forgive this person because I love the person so much; or
  • Even though the person did not realize that they disobeyed my laws, my laws are really important, so I am glad the person realized they were guilty.
Continue the drama.

Then Yahweh told Moses to tell the Israelites: "If you lie about something a neighbor gave you to take care of, or if you rob their neighbor, you are guilty. If you force your neighbor to give you something your neighbor does not want to give you, you are guilty. Also, if you find something that does not belong to you and then swear you do not have it, you are guilty."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person whose things someone stole, "What are you thinking or feeling?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am upset because someone stole something from me; or
  • I thought I could trust my neighbor, but now my neighbor lies about what I gave.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh says, "Any of these things is something someone might do that is a sin. As soon as someone admits that they sinned in something like this, the person needs to give back what the person stole and then also give money worth 20 percent of the thing's value. Then the person needs to bring a ram that is perfect and worth a certain number of shekels. The priests at the holy place will weigh the shekels according to the sanctuary standard. The person must give the ram to the priest. Then the priest will make atonement for that person, and Yahweh will forgive that person for anything the person has done that made the person guilty."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you thinking or feeling?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am glad I can help someone ask Yahweh for forgiveness; or
  • This person did something really bad. I do not like that the person did not get a worse punishment.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 5:14–6:7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Yahweh continues to speak to Moses. Use the same word for Yahweh that you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh tells Moses what to do when an Israelite is unfaithful to Yahweh and sins accidentally against any of Yahweh's holy things. Use the same phrases for sins accidentally as you have used previously, and refer to sin in the Master Glossary for more information.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will talk about being unfaithful to Yahweh. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh's holy things probably refer to any of the things that a person promises to give to Yahweh, and the things that Yahweh told the Israelites to give to Yahweh. That includes firstborn animals, the first crops in a harvest, and the money that the priests and the Levites are supposed to get. It probably also refers to the things in the Tent of Meeting and, later, in the temple. These things are holy because Yahweh said that these items belonged to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for holy things. Look up holy in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

This person who sins needs to bring a ram that was physically perfect from the flock to the priest. A ram was an adult male sheep. Rams were the most valuable type of sheep. Use the same words for priest, ram, and physically perfect that you used in previous passages. For more information on priest and perfect, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Israelites used the ram for a guilt offering. People also sometimes translate this offering as a reparation or repayment offering. People gave the guilt offering when someone did something wrong that took value from someone else, either from Yahweh or from another person. People also gave a guilt offering when someone broke any of Yahweh's laws without meaning to. That is probably because people at that time thought that when you broke a law against a god, you owed the god money or something else valuable to make up for disobeying the god.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for guilt offering. Look up guilt offering in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The ram needs to be worth a certain amount of shekels of silver. A shekel is a unit of measurement for weight. A shekel is about 11 grams.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for shekel. Look up shekel in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

People used different standards for weights, so Yahweh says to use a certain standard—the holy or sanctuary standard. This was a shekel that weighed as much as what the priests in the holy place decided a shekel should weigh. The holy place, or sanctuary, was another name for the Tent of Meeting, and people used it later as a name for the temple as well. Use the same term for sanctuary, or holy place, that you used in previous passages. Sanctuary is in the Master Glossary.

The person who sinned against one of Yahweh's holy things or against someone else had to make restitution, or peace, with the person that they sinned against. The person had to make it right again with Yahweh and with the person that they stole from or harmed.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will say that the person had to make restitution, or peace. For more information about peace, refer to the Master Glossary. In this situation, peace refers to the good relationship between two people or groups when one has harmed the other. Pause this audio here.

The person who brought the guilt offering also had to pay money to make up for the holy thing that the person had sinned against. The person had to pay for the full value of the holy thing, then the person also had to pay an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the cost. The person paid that money to the priest. Then the priest makes atonement. That means that the priest offers the ram as a sacrifice to ask Yahweh to forgive that person and restore the relationship between Yahweh and the person. With atonement, Yahweh also cleans the person from the guilt of what the person did wrong. Use the same word for atonement that you used in previous passages, and remember that atonement is in the Master Glossary.

Yahweh does not explain here how the priest is supposed to sacrifice the ram. Yahweh says Yahweh will forgive this person when the priest makes atonement. Use the same word for forgive that you used in previous passages. For more information on forgiveness, refer to the Master Glossary.

In the next situation, Yahweh talks about when someone accidentally sins and disobeys Yahweh's commandments. Use the same word or phrase for commandment that you used in previous passages. For more information on commandment, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says that even if someone does something wrong without meaning to, that person is guilty. That means that the person is supposed to receive the consequences for what the person did. That person has a debt to Yahweh that the person needs to repay. Use the same word or phrase for guilty that you used in previous passages, and remember that guilt is in the Master Glossary.

In the last situation, Yahweh describes several ways someone might take something valuable from their neighbors illegally. When Yahweh says neighbor, Yahweh means the people who are part of the Israelite community. Sometimes this word just means people in the village, and sometimes it means the people in the country.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for neighbor. Look up neighbor in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that anyone who does one of these things is betraying Yahweh. The first thing the person might do is lie about something a neighbor gave them as a deposit or as a pledge. A deposit is something someone gives to you to keep safe. A pledge is something someone gives you as a sign of a promise that the person will do something. A person may lie and say the neighbor did not give anything, or the person might lie and say that the neighbor gave less than the neighbor actually gave. Another way to translate "deposit or pledge" would be "something a person is supposed to take care of."

Stop here and discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use for deposit and pledge. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also specifies that a person might just steal something from their neighbor. A person also might oppress or extort their neighbor. This means that a person might force their neighbor to give the person something that the neighbor does not want to give.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for oppress or extort.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
