title: Leviticus 6:8–18
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 6:8–18 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:8–18 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:8–18 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this next part of Leviticus, Yahweh gives Moses more instructions about the offerings so that Moses can tell his brother Aaron and Aaron's sons exactly what to do. Aaron and Aaron's sons, as well as all of Aaron's male descendants, were Yahweh's priests. The priests were in charge of giving the offerings of animals and grain to Yahweh. So that is why the priests needed more specific instructions about what to do.

In this section, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about two of the five offerings. These two offerings are the burnt offering and the grain offering. Remember that, for the burnt offering, every part of the animal except for the hide burned up. Remember that the purpose of the grain offering was to honor Yahweh as king or to ask Yahweh for a favor. Yahweh probably talks about these two offerings together because the priests were supposed to offer both a burnt offering and a grain offering, along with a wine offering, every day in the morning and at the time when the sun went down. For the people of Israel, a new day started at night, so every time the sun went down, a new day began. The priests gave these two offerings on behalf of all the Israelites at the beginning of every new day when the sun went down, as well as when the people of Israel woke up in the morning to begin their work.

Yahweh starts by telling Moses to tell Aaron and Aaron's descendants the command for the burnt offering. Yahweh's first instruction is that the priests should burn the burnt offering on the bronze altar every night until the morning. We know from other parts of the Bible that the type of animal that they offered for the daily burnt offering was a year-old lamb. So, these instructions mean that a priest would kill a year-old lamb at the time when the sun went down and place parts of the lamb on the bronze altar. The lamb would burn on the altar all night. The parts of the animal needed to stay on the altar until morning, and the fire on the bronze altar could not go out. The fire had to continually burn from evening until morning.

After the animal had burned up so that all that was left were ashes, the priest needed to put on linen clothes. Linen was a kind of fabric that people made from the flax plant. Linen was lightweight and expensive, so in many countries at this time, usually only kings and wealthy people wore linen. Since the priests were servants of Yahweh, who was both God and king over the people of Israel, people made the priest's uniform out of linen fabric for the priest to wear when the priest did Yahweh's work.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what kind of fabric do different people wear? What kind of fabric do kings, chiefs, and government officials wear? What do people think when people see different kinds of fabric? Pause this audio here.

There were two parts to the linen clothes that the priest needed to wear. First were linen undergarments, and second was a linen tunic that went over the undergarments. No one knows exactly what this clothing looked like, but the tunic was probably long enough to reach the priest's ankles.

Stop here and look at pictures of what the priest's tunic and undergarments might have looked like as a group. Pause this audio here.

When the priest got dressed in the linen clothes, the priest probably put the clothes on in a way so that the priest was never fully without clothes, since Yahweh told the people of Israel that no one could be without clothing near Yahweh's altar. This rule was probably because many other people groups at this time worshiped their gods and goddesses by having sex in the holy area. But Yahweh repeatedly told the people of Israel and the priests not to worship Yahweh that way. So, to avoid being naked near the bronze altar, the priest probably put the linen clothes on in a way that avoided doing that.

After the priest dressed in the linen clothes, the priest was supposed to gather together the ashes from the burnt offering that had been burning all night, and move the ashes from the top of the altar to the side of the altar. The side of the altar was the east side, which is the direction the sun rises in the morning.

Stop here and look at a picture of the bronze altar as a group. Notice where the priest would have put the ashes. Pause this audio here.

After that, the priest needed to take off the linen clothes and put on other clothes. Then, the priest needed to carry the ashes to a ceremonially clean place outside the area where the people of Israel were camping. Nobody knows if there was one clean place that people brought the ashes to, or if people just brought the ashes to any ritually clean place outside of the Israelites' camp.

Stop here and discuss as a group where people in your community might take ashes or other leftovers from a fire outside of people's living spaces. Pause this audio here.

The priests must also keep the fire on the altar burning all day. So, the priest needed to put wood on the fire on the bronze altar every morning. Then the priest would offer another burnt offering on the altar. And the priest would also burn up the fat from the fellowship, or peace, offering as incense. The people of Israel thought that the smell from sacrifices smelled good like incense and that it was one way to honor Yahweh and make Yahweh happy.

Once again, Yahweh made sure to tell Moses to tell the priests that the fire on the altar had to always be burning.

After Yahweh gave Moses the instructions for the daily burnt offering, Yahweh gave Moses the instructions for the grain offering. In general, the purpose of the grain offering was probably to honor Yahweh as king or to ask Yahweh for a favor. In this part, Yahweh focuses on the instructions for eating the grain offering.

The priests were supposed to bring the offering of grain before Yahweh to the bronze altar. Then the priest needed to take a handful of the good-quality flour and oil, along with all of the frankincense that was on top of the mixture of flour and oil. That is the memorial portion. The priest would then burn the memorial portion on the bronze altar, and it would smell good to Yahweh.

Whatever flour and oil were left belonged to any of Aaron's male descendants. Not all of Aaron's descendants could be priests. For example, if one of Aaron's descendants was lame, that man could not be a priest. But that man could still eat the grain offering as long as the man obeyed the requirements for eating it.

Any of Aaron's descendants who ate the grain offering needed to eat it without adding leaven or yeast. Even if the descendants baked the flour, the descendants had to bake the flour without leaven or yeast. And the descendants also needed to eat the grain offering in the holy place of the courtyard that surrounded the Tent of Meeting. This food was a gift from Yahweh to Yahweh's priests. The grain offering was most holy, like the other fire offerings, which were the purification offerings and guilt offerings.

This grain offering was Aaron's descendants' portion of Yahweh's fire gifts, or offerings, throughout every generation forever. And, like in the purification and guilt offerings, anyone and anything that touched these offerings would become holy. If someone or something was holy, then that meant that the person or thing belonged to Yahweh. For people, that meant that there were more strict rules for what that person did. It also meant that only Yahweh could punish that person, so everyone else needed to treat that person with respect and care because that person belonged to Yahweh. For things, that meant that people could not use the things for everyday use since those things belonged to Yahweh. So people needed to treat Yahweh's things with more respect and care than they would treat other things. It is not always a good thing for everything that touches the offering to become holy because it is dangerous when something dirty or common touches something that is holy. The only people who should touch these offerings are the people Yahweh says should touch the offerings.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your culture, what happens to a person if the person touches something that they should not touch because it is very special or dedicated to a divine being?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:8–18 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells Moses the instructions for the burnt offering that the priests were supposed to offer every morning and every evening on behalf of the people of Israel.

In the second scene: Yahweh tells Moses the instructions for the grain offering that the priests were supposed to offer to honor Yahweh as king and to ask Yahweh for favors. This scene specifically focuses on who is allowed to eat the grain offering and all of the requirements for eating it.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron and Aaron's descendants, who are the priests
  • Any of Aaron's male descendants, including the ones who are not priests
  • And a person who touches the grain offering

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Yahweh talks about the offerings priests will burn on the bronze altar in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting, which is the sacred place. The priests will also take ashes to a clean place outside of the Israelites' camp.

The first scene begins when Yahweh tells Moses to give Aaron and Aaron's descendants the command to obey the instructions. The instructions in the first scene are about the burnt offerings that the priests burn every day. The instructions start and say that the burnt offering has to burn on the altar all night. This means that the parts of the animal needed to stay on the altar until morning and that the fire itself had to keep burning.

Stop here and, as an activity, give instructions for how to do something that needs to happen every day. How does the storyteller make it clear that this needs to happen every day? How does the storyteller make it clear what time of day things happened? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh focuses on what the priest needed to do in the morning. First, the priest needed to put on a linen tunic and linen undergarments. Next, the priest needed to take the ashes that were on the bronze altar and put the ashes next to the altar on the side of the altar where the sun rises in the morning. After that, the priest needed to take the linen clothes off and put other clothes on. Finally, the priest needed to take the ashes outside the area where everyone was camping and put the ashes in a clean place.

Then Yahweh reminds the priests that the fire on the bronze altar must not go out. This means that the fire has to stay burning all night and all day.

So, every morning after the priest cleans the ashes off the bronze altar, a priest needs to add wood to the bronze altar. The priest needs to add this wood every morning. After the priest puts the wood on the bronze altar, the priest needs to put the morning burnt offering on the wood, as well as the fat from the peace, or fellowship, offerings.

Once again, Yahweh reminds the priests that the fire on the bronze altar must not go out. The fire has to stay burning on the bronze altar, all day and all night. Yahweh gives these instructions about the fire not going out three times during this scene. This shows how important these instructions are.

Stop here and, as an activity, give instructions about how to do something important. How does the storyteller emphasize the important part of the instructions? Pause this audio here.

The instructions in the second scene are about the grain offering. The focus of this scene is on what priests needed to burn on the bronze altar and what Yahweh allowed the priests to eat. In this scene, the narrator gives more instructions about eating part of the grain offering.

To begin, the priests were supposed to bring the offering of grain before Yahweh to the bronze altar. Then a priest needed to take a handful of good-quality flour and oil, along with all of the frankincense that was on top of the mixture of grain and oil. That was the memorial portion. The priest would then burn the memorial portion on the bronze altar, and the memorial portion would smell good to Yahweh.

Any of Aaron's male descendants were allowed to eat whatever was left over from the good quality flour and oil. The male descendants would probably use the flour and oil to make bread. However, there were two main instructions for how the descendants could eat it. No one may add yeast or leaven. And the male descendants needed to eat the food in the sacred place of the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh says twice that no one may add yeast to the flour.

The grain offering was a gift from Yahweh to Yahweh's priests and was most holy. Like the purification offerings and guilt offerings, the grain offering was very holy. Again, Yahweh says that any male descendant of Aaron could eat the grain offering. The offering was Aaron's male descendants' portion of Yahweh's fire gifts throughout every generation forever.

The instructions end when they say that anyone and anything that touched these offerings would become holy. Remember that in this case, the idea of holy means that the person or thing now belongs to Yahweh, and people cannot use it for anything ordinary.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:8–18 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron and Aaron's descendants, who are the priests
  • Any of Aaron's male descendants, including the ones who are not priests
  • And a person who touches the grain offering

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In scene one, Yahweh tells Moses to give Aaron and his descendants the command to obey these instructions. The instructions in the first scene are about the burnt offerings that the priests were supposed to offer every day. The instructions start by saying that the burnt offering had to burn on the altar all night.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I need to make sure there is enough wood on the altar so that the fire does not go out; or
  • I will take turns with the other priests so that someone is always awake to keep the fire going; or
  • I want to honor Yahweh by making sure the fire does not go out.
Continue the drama.

In the morning, the priest needed to put on a linen tunic and linen undergarments. Then, the priest needed to take the ashes that were on the bronze altar and put the ashes next to the altar on the side of the altar that faces where the sun rises in the morning. After that, the priest needed to take the linen clothes off and put other clothes on. Finally, the priest needed to take the ashes outside the area where everyone was camping and put the ashes in a clean place.

Yahweh then reminds the priests that the fire on the bronze altar must not go out. The fire has to stay burning all night and all day.

Every morning, after the priest cleaned the ashes off the bronze altar, the priest needed to add wood to the bronze altar. Then the priest needed to put the burnt offering on the wood, as well as the fat from the peace offerings.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am glad I get to be the one to offer the burnt offering to Yahweh today; or
  • I need to make sure to add enough wood so that the fire keeps burning all day.
Continue the drama.

Once again, Yahweh reminds the priests that the fire on the bronze altar must not go out. The fire has to stay burning on the bronze altar, all day and all night.

In scene two, Yahweh gives the instructions for the grain offering. The priests needed to bring the offering of grain before Yahweh to the bronze altar. Then the priest needed to take a handful of good-quality flour and oil, along with all of the frankincense that was on top of the mixture of grain and oil. That is the memorial portion. The priest would then burn the memorial portion on the bronze altar, and it would smell good to Yahweh.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so glad my people want to honor me as their king; or
  • I love my people; or
  • This smells good.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh allowed any of Aaron's male descendants to eat whatever was left over from the good quality flour and oil. However, the descendants must not add yeast or leaven, even if the men baked it. Also, the descendants needed to eat what was left over from the grain offering in the sacred place of the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting.

The grain offering was a gift from Yahweh to Yahweh's priests and was very holy, like the purification offering and the guilt offering. The grain offering was Aaron's descendants' portion of Yahweh's fire offerings throughout every generation forever.

The instructions end when they say that anyone and anything that touched these offerings would become holy.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:8–18 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

This section starts when Yahweh tells Moses to command Aaron and Aaron's descendants. This word refers to the way someone with authority tells someone else what to do. Pick a word that emphasizes that Yahweh has authority to tell Aaron and Aaron's descendants what to do. Also, look up the name Yahweh in the Master Glossary. Translate this name the same way as you translated it previously.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for command. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, decide if the same word is appropriate to use here. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells Moses to give Aaron and Aaron's descendants the command to follow the instructions, or law, for the burnt offering. This word for "instructions" refers to wisdom, teaching, or instructions that someone who is older and wiser tells someone who is younger. Parents give instructions to their children, elders give instructions to people who are younger, and Yahweh gives instructions to Yahweh's people. Pick a word that gives the idea of teaching and wisdom that people have to listen to and obey.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for law, or instructions. Refer to law in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, decide if the same word is appropriate to use here. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh's first instruction is that the burnt offering has to burn on the altar all night. Use the same word or phrase for burnt offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on burnt offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

In the morning, the priest needs to put on linen clothes. Linen is a kind of fabric that people make from a flax plant. Linen was lightweight and expensive, so in many countries at this time, only kings, wealthy people, and special people like priests would usually wear this kind of linen. Since the priests were servants of Yahweh, who was both God and king over the people of Israel, Yahweh said to make the priest's uniform out of linen fabric for the priest to wear when the priest did Yahweh's work.

Stop here and look at a picture of linen fabric as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for linen. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The two parts are a linen tunic and linen undergarments. The linen tunic would cover the priest's chest, shoulders, stomach, and legs, probably down to the ankles. The priest would wear the undergarments underneath the tunic around his waist.

Stop here and look at a possible picture of the tunic and undergarments as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use for tunic and undergarments. Refer to tunic in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated these words in another book of the Bible, use the same words that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

After the priest dressed in the linen clothes, the priest needed to take the ashes that were on the bronze altar and put the ashes next to the altar on the east side of the altar. The east side was the side that faces where the sun rises in the morning. Use the same word or phrase for east as you used in previous passages. Look up altar in the Master Glossary for more information. Translate altar the same way that you did in previous passages.

After that, the priest needed to take the linen clothes off and put other clothes on. Finally, the priest needed to take the ashes outside the area where everyone was camping to a ritually clean place. Use the same word or phrase for priest and clean as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest or clean, refer to the Master Glossary.

The instructions then remind the priests that the fire on the bronze altar must not go out. The fire had to stay burning all night and all day.

After the priest cleaned the ashes off the bronze altar, the priest needed to add wood to the bronze altar. This needed to happen every morning. After the priest put the wood on the bronze altar, the priest needed to put the burnt offering on it, as well as the fat from the peace or fellowship offerings. Use the same word or phrase for peace or fellowship offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on fellowship offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Once again, the instructions remind the priests that the fire on the bronze altar must not go out. The fire had to stay burning on the bronze altar, all day and all night.

Once Yahweh finished giving the instructions for the burnt offering, Yahweh gave the instructions, or law, for the grain offering to honor Yahweh as king or to ask Yahweh for a favor. Use the same word or phrase for grain offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on grain offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

The priest needed to bring the offering of grain before Yahweh to the bronze altar. Then the priest needed to take a handful of good-quality flour and oil, along with all of the frankincense that was on top of the mixture of grain and oil. Use the same words or phrases for good-quality flour, oil, and frankincense as you used in previous passages.

That was called the memorial portion. Use the same word or phrase for memorial portion as you used in previous passages, and refer to memorial portion in the Master Glossary for more information.

The priest would then burn the memorial portion on the bronze altar as incense that would smell good to Yahweh. Use the same words or phrases for incense and for a good smell as you used in previous passages.

Yahweh allowed any of Aaron's male descendants to eat whatever was left over from the fine flour and oil. However, the men must not add yeast or leaven, even if the men baked it. Yeast and leaven are two different ways to describe something that people add to dough to help the dough become fluffier after people bake the dough. Use the same word or phrase for yeast or leaven as you used in previous passages.

Also, the men needed to eat what was left over from the grain offering in the sacred, or holy, place of the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. The word "sacred," or "holy," refers to things that belong to a god. Since the people of Israel agreed that Yahweh would be their only God, the word "holy" here refers to the place that was given to Yahweh. In particular, this section is talking about the tent and courtyard that belonged to Yahweh. When something was holy, people needed to be careful and treat it with extra respect because it belonged to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for sacred. Look up holy in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The grain offering was a gift from Yahweh to Yahweh's priests and was most holy. This means that people completely dedicated it to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for most holy as you used in previous passages.

The grain offering, the purification offering, and the guilt offering were all more holy than the other fire gifts. Use the same words or phrases for purification offering and guilt offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on sin or purification offering and guilt offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh gave all three of those offerings to Aaron's male sons, or descendants, to eat. This is a statute for generations to come. Use the same words or phrases for statute and generations as you have used previously, and refer to statute and generation in the Master Glossary for more information. A statute is an instruction especially for the place of worship. A person's descendants are his children, grandchildren, and all future generations from the same family line. Sometimes, storytellers will use the word for "son" or a person's male child to talk about a descendant.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for descendant. If you have translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word here. Refer to descendant in the Master Glossary for more information. Pause this audio here.

This was their portion of Yahweh's fire offerings throughout every generation. Use the same word or phrase for fire offerings as you have used previously, and refer to fire offerings in the Master Glossary for more information.

In the original language, this word for "portion" refers to a boundary. It can refer to a boundary line between one person's land and another person's land. It can refer to the boundaries, or rules, of what people are allowed to do and not allowed to do. It can also refer to the boundary that marks what one person's portion is. In this section, you need to decide if the phrase "this boundary for all generations forever" means "this is the rule that priests get to eat this part of the offering" or "this part of the offering is the priests' portion." Then, translate accordingly.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for portion. If you have already translated this idea in another book of the Bible, decide if the same word is appropriate to use here. Pause this audio here.

The instructions end when they say that anyone and anything that touched these offerings would become holy. In this situation, it is not a good thing for everything that touches the offering to become holy because it is dangerous when something dirty or common touches something that is holy.

Stop here and discuss as a group whether the word or phrase you use for holy or sacred can work for a situation that is not good. If not, discuss how you can communicate that these things become sacred, but that this is a dangerous situation.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 6:19–23
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 6:19–23 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:19–23 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:19–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this passage, the storyteller describes more of the laws that Yahweh gave the Israelites through Moses so that the Israelites could live in good relationship with Yahweh. In the group of laws we heard previously, Yahweh told the priests how the priests should eat or deal with the offerings Yahweh described in the first part of the book of Leviticus after the priests sacrificed the offerings. Earlier, Yahweh told Moses to instruct Aaron and the other priests about how to clean up after the burnt offering and how to eat the grain offering. In this passage, Yahweh tells Moses to instruct Aaron and Aaron's descendants how to offer grain when Yahweh anoints, or chooses, someone to be the next high priest.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What kinds of ceremonies or rituals do people in your culture do when someone becomes a leader? This may be a religious leader, a community leader, or some other kind of leader. Pause this audio here.

Each time a priest became the new high priest, a leader anointed the new high priest with oil. This represented how Yahweh set the priest apart as dedicated to Yahweh and how Yahweh chose this priest as the religious leader of Israel. Exodus 29 and Leviticus 8 both describe this process with more details. When a priest became the high priest, the leader representing Yahweh poured special sacred oil on the new high priest's head.

Stop here and listen to a recording of your translation of Exodus 29, if you have already translated it. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh has just given instructions for how the priests should eat their share of the grain offering. However, the new high priest must also bring a grain offering to Yahweh on the day that Yahweh anoints the new high priest, and the new high priest may not eat any of this special grain offering. In this passage, Yahweh tells Moses what must happen on the day that Yahweh chooses a new high priest. Aaron or any of Aaron's descendants who becomes the high priest should bring flour. Most likely, this flour would have been the ground-up grain or seed of the wheat or barley plant.

Stop here and look at a picture of wheat as a group. Then look at a picture of barley as a group. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh instructed the new high priest to bring one-tenth of an ephah of the flour and to split it in half. An ephah is a unit of measurement that the ancient Israelites used to measure the volume of dry things like grain or flour. An ephah was about 2 liters.

Stop here and find something that is around 2 liters. It can be dry or liquid. Pause this audio here.

The priest would offer one-half of this amount of flour to Yahweh in the morning, and the priest would offer the other half of this amount of flour to Yahweh in the evening. To prepare the flour, the priest would mix the flour with olive oil and use a griddle to cook the dough over a fire. A griddle is a large, flat piece of pottery or metal that people prop up on stones over a fire underneath it. The priest would cook the dough on top of the griddle to make bread.

Stop here and look at a picture of olives and olive oil as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: If people in your culture cook bread, what is the process people use to make bread? If people in your culture do not make bread, what is the process people use to make any food that involves mixing ingredients together to make a dough or paste and then cooking the dough? Pause this audio here.

The new high priest would then bring the bread and offer it to Yahweh in several pieces. It is possible that the priest had baked the bread in multiple pieces and soaked the baked bread in oil. Or the priest had thoroughly mixed the flour and oil together, baked the dough, and then broken the bread into pieces. Either way, the priest would offer the bread to Yahweh by burning it completely on Yahweh's altar. The smoke from the burning bread would make a good smell to please and honor Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: When someone in your culture becomes a religious leader, does the leader bring offerings to a deity or spirit? If yes, what kinds of offerings does the leader bring? How is that similar to or different from the Israelite high priest who offers bread to please and honor Yahweh? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells Moses that this offering must happen every time a priest, who must be one of Aaron's descendants, becomes the new high priest. Each time this happens, the priest must completely burn up the bread. Normally, Aaron's male descendants can eat the rest of a grain offering. But no one can eat this first grain offering that the new high priest gives. The new high priest must completely burn this grain offering to represent that this offering belongs completely to Yahweh.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:19–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells Moses how Aaron should prepare bread from flour and oil and offer it to Yahweh on the day when Aaron becomes the high priest.

In the second scene: Yahweh tells Moses that each of Aaron's descendants who becomes the high priest after Aaron must offer the same special grain offering Aaron did. Yahweh also tells Moses that the priests cannot eat this offering.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron, the first high priest at the time Yahweh gave these instructions to Moses
  • And Aaron's descendants who will become the high priest after Aaron dies

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In this passage, Yahweh is still giving Moses instructions while Moses and the Israelites are camped at Mount Sinai. You will remember that in the previous passage, Yahweh gave Moses instructions for what the priests should do for the normal grain offering. In scene one of this passage, Yahweh gives Moses instructions for what Aaron and each of Aaron's descendants who become the high priest after Aaron must do when Yahweh anoints that person as the new high priest. These instructions are talking about things that have not actually happened yet, but that will happen in the future every time the Israelites get a new high priest.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: Talk about what someone must do to have a wedding or get married in your culture. Listen for words that show that this is what anyone who wants to have a wedding or get married in the future must do. Pause this audio here.

When a leader anoints Aaron or one of Aaron's descendants, which represents that Yahweh chooses that man as the new high priest, Aaron or that descendant must bring an offering to Yahweh. The new high priest will measure out the right amount of flour and divide it in half. On that day, once in the morning and once in the evening, when the other priests give the regular daily offerings, the new high priest will make bread with that flour. To make the bread, the new high priest will mix the flour with olive oil and cook the dough on a griddle over a fire. The new high priest will then break the bread into pieces and offer it to Yahweh by burning it completely on the bronze altar in front of the Tent of Meeting.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: If people in your culture give offerings to gods or spirits, what do people do when they offer things to the gods or spirits? Pause this audio here.

In scene two of this passage, Yahweh tells Moses that each descendant of Aaron who becomes the high priest in the future must offer the same bread offering, because this is a permanent statute, or rule. The Israelite priests must follow this statute forever, so each new high priest must follow these instructions when they become the high priest. Yahweh also reminds Moses that because the new high priest offers all of the bread in this offering to Yahweh by burning the bread, the priests must not eat any of the offering. The new high priest is supposed to burn up all of the offering to please and honor Yahweh.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:19–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron, the first high priest at the time Yahweh gave these instructions to Moses
  • And Aaron's descendants who will become the high priest after Aaron dies

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh gives Moses instructions for what Aaron and Aaron's descendants should do when Aaron or Aaron's descendant becomes the high priest. Have a person playing Aaron act out that Aaron follows Yahweh's instructions.

Yahweh says that the new high priest, Aaron, should get one-tenth of an ephah of flour and divide the flour in half. Aaron should then mix the flour with oil and use a griddle to bake the dough over a fire to make bread. Aaron should then break the bread into pieces and offer the pieces to Yahweh by burning all of the bread at the Tent of Meeting.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am excited to give this offering to Yahweh and become the high priest; or
  • I am nervous to make this offering to Yahweh since I have dishonored Yahweh before; or
  • I am honored that Yahweh has chosen me as the new high priest to help the Israelites worship Yahweh correctly.
Continue the drama.

Now, pretend that Aaron has died, and one of Aaron's descendants will become the new high priest. This descendant must follow the same instructions Yahweh gave Moses for Aaron. Have a person who plays Aaron's descendant act out how that descendant follows Yahweh's instructions.

Yahweh says that the new high priest, Aaron's descendant, should get one-tenth of an ephah of flour and divide it in half. This descendant should then mix the flour with oil and use a griddle to bake the dough over a fire to make bread. This descendant should then break the bread into pieces and offer the pieces to Yahweh by burning all of the bread on the altar in front of the Tent of Meeting.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron's descendant, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am excited to start my new role as high priest; or
  • I am nervous about whether I will perform this ritual offering correctly; or
  • I am honored that Yahweh chose me for the role of high priest, just like Yahweh chose so many of my ancestors.
Continue the drama.

Now Yahweh tells Moses that the high priest must completely burn up this offering. The priests must not eat any part of this offering.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:19–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this section, Yahweh gives Moses instructions for the special offering, called a grain offering, that each new high priest was supposed to make on the day someone anointed the new high priest. Use the same words or phrases for Yahweh and offering as you used in previous passages, and refer to Yahweh and offering in the Master Glossary for more information.

In the original language, people use the same word for the grain offering in Leviticus 2 and for this special grain offering for the new high priest in this passage. However, the way the priest must make the offering in this passage is a little different.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for this special grain offering. For more information on grain offering, refer to the Master Glossary. Discuss whether you should use the same word or phrase in your language for the grain offering in Leviticus 2 and the offering in this passage. Pause this audio here.

Aaron and each one of Aaron's sons, or descendants, who become the high priest later, make this grain offering on the day that Yahweh sets apart, or anoints each one to be the new high priest. Remember that Aaron's sons or descendants here are all of Aaron's male children, grandchildren, and future generations. Use the same words for sons or descendants and anoint that you used previously. For more information on descendants and anointing with oil, refer to the Master Glossary.

Each time Yahweh anoints a new high priest, that high priest must bring one-tenth of an ephah of flour and divide it in half. Flour is the ground-up seeds of a grass plant. The Israelites would have probably ground up the seeds of a wheat or barley plant, specifically. Use the same word or phrase for flour as you used in previous passages. Remember that an ephah is an amount of flour that would take up around the same amount of space as about 2 liters or 3 pints. Use the same word or phrase for one-tenth of an ephah as you used in previous passages, such as Leviticus 5:11. For more information on ephah, see the Master Glossary.

In the morning of the day Yahweh anoints the new high priest, and again in the evening of that day, the new high priest must take half of the flour and mix it with olive oil to make a dough. Use the same word or phrase for olive oil as you used in previous passages. Then the new high priest must cook the dough on a griddle, which is a large flat piece of pottery or metal that people propped up on stones over a fire. Use the same word or phrase for griddle as you used in previous passages, such as Leviticus 2:5.

Stop here and look at a picture of olive oil as a group. Pause this audio here.

The new high priest must then break this bread into pieces and offer the bread to Yahweh by burning the bread on Yahweh's altar. The smoke from the burning bread would make a good smell to honor and please Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase to talk about this good smell to Yahweh as you used in previous passages.

Yahweh then tells Moses that each one of Aaron's descendants who becomes the high priest in the future must make the same special grain offering on the day that Yahweh anoints that man as the new high priest, because this is a permanent statute that must happen forever. Use the same word or phrase for "permanent statute" that you used in previous passages. For more information on statute, see the Master Glossary.

In this passage, Yahweh calls the new high priest the anointed priest, because Yahweh chose this priest and set the priest apart from the rest of the priests as the high priest. This offering belongs completely to Yahweh, so the high priest must burn up the offering entirely. The priests cannot eat the offering. Use the same word for priest, or anointed priest, as you have used previously. For more information about priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 6:24–30
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 6:24–30 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:24–30 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:24–30 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the first few passages in Leviticus, Yahweh gave instructions to Moses about how to offer different types of offerings so that the Israelite people could live in good relationship with Yahweh. In the next section of Leviticus, which includes this passage, Yahweh tells the priests how people should eat or deal with those offerings after the priests sacrifice the offerings.

In the last passage, Yahweh told Moses to instruct Aaron and Aaron's descendants how to offer grain when Yahweh anoints, or chooses, someone to be the next high priest. Now, in this passage, Yahweh is no longer talking about the grain offering. Yahweh gives more instructions to Moses about what the priests are supposed to do after they offer the sin or purification offering. Yahweh previously told Moses about the purification offering in Leviticus 4.

Stop here and listen to your translation of Leviticus 4:1–35 as needed. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells Moses to give Aaron and Aaron's descendants, who will eventually become priests, more instructions, or further rules to follow to do the purification offering properly. Yahweh calls this the "law" about the purification offering. In the Old Testament, a law usually refers to a set of several rules or instructions to follow, so all the instructions in this passage are included in the law about the purification offering.

The first instruction is a reminder that the priests must kill the animal for the purification offering at the same place a priest kills the animal for the burnt offering. In this passage, Yahweh only talks about purification offerings that the priests make when leaders and individual members of the community accidentally sin against Yahweh and become ritually dirty. The priests only kill goats and sheep for these types of purification offerings, so the priests would kill these animals in the same place where the priests would kill the goats and sheep for the burnt offering.

Stop here and look at a picture of goats and sheep as a group. Pause this audio here.

The priests would kill these goats and sheep on the north side of the bronze altar, in Yahweh's presence. The priests did these sacrifices near the Tent of Meeting, where Yahweh lived among Yahweh's people. The bronze altar was right inside the entrance of the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Since the entrance of the courtyard for the Tent of Meeting was on the east side of the courtyard, someone would see the north side of the altar on their right when they entered the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting.

Stop here and look at a diagram of the Tent of Meeting as a group. Find where the bronze altar is. Then find where the north side of the altar is. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also tells Moses that this offering is most holy or most sacred. Yahweh next tells Moses that the priest who offers the sheep or goat to Yahweh may eat the sheep or goat. When a priest offers a purification offering for a leader or for an individual person who is not a priest, the priest only pours out the animal's blood and burns the animal's fat on the altar to honor Yahweh. The priest does not burn the meat, so the meat is available for someone to eat. Yahweh allows the priests to eat that meat, but Yahweh tells Moses that the priests must eat the meat in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. The priests cannot eat the meat in the priests' homes or elsewhere because only the Tent of Meeting is holy and set apart to be a special place where Yahweh is.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: When people in your culture give a sacrifice or offering to a god or spirit, what happens to the things the people have given after the people finish making the sacrifice or giving the offering? Pause this audio here.

This purification offering is so sacred, or holy, that anything and anyone the meat and blood touch will become holy, or special to Yahweh. However, it is bad and dangerous for things that are dirty to come into contact with things that are holy. This is because holy things are things connected with Yahweh, who is very powerful. Only clean things and people could interact with the most sacred things. If the meat and blood touched something or someone that was not clean or holy, it meant that no one could use that thing or person for ordinary things again. That thing or person now belonged completely to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what is holy? What are the rules for when people interact with what is holy? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh then tells Moses to instruct Aaron and the priests on what to do about things that have touched the holy sacrifice, so that dirty things do not keep touching holy things. The priests must wash any clothes that blood from the sacrifice has splashed on or stained. The priests must wash these clothes in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. The priests cannot wash these dirty clothes away from the Tent of Meeting because the priest cannot take the dangerous combination of sacred, or holy, things and dirty things away from the holy place and near the rest of the people.

A priest also has to do something about the pot that the priest cooks the sacrifice in, since the pot has touched the sacred, or holy, meat. If the priest cooks the meat in a bronze pot, which is a mixture of copper and tin metals, the priest must clean the metal pot. The priest does this by scouring the pot, which means scrubbing the pot with something rough like sand or ash, and then washing the pot with water. This was what the priest would normally do, since the pots that the priests were supposed to use in the sacrifices were bronze metal pots. However, if the priest cooks the meat in a clay pot, the priest cannot clean the pot and use the pot again; the priest must break the pot to destroy it. This is because once something has stopped being an everyday object and has become a sacred object, it is dangerous to use the object for everyday activities.

Stop here and look at a picture of a bronze pot and a clay pot. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Can people in your culture take things that people have used to worship deities or spirits and then use those things for everyday activities? Why or why not? Pause this audio here.

Remember that the priest who killed the animal for the purification offering can eat the meat from the offering. But now, Yahweh explains that this priest is not the only one who can eat that meat. Any priest, and any man or boy who is descended from a priest, may eat the meat. However, the meat from the purification offering is most holy, so these men and boys can only eat the meat in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting, which is a holy space.

So far, Yahweh has only told Moses what the priests should do about purification offerings that the priests make for the leaders and individual members of the community. Yahweh gives Moses rules for how the priests have to eat the meat and deal with the pots they cooked the meat in, because meat is leftover after these purification offerings.

The rules were different when the priests made the purification offering for the whole community of Israel or the high priest who sinned. You will remember that as part of those purification offerings, the high priest brought some of the blood into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement, or make amends with Yahweh for what the high priest or the whole community had done.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: If someone in your culture betrays or offends a deity or spirit, how can that person make amends? How is this different from, or similar to, the ways Yahweh told Moses the high priest could make amends to Yahweh? Pause this audio here.

To make atonement, or make amends, the high priest would go into the Tent of Meeting, which was more holy than anywhere else. The high priest would go to the curtain that separated the part of the tent where the ark of the covenant was, where Yahweh's presence was, from the rest of the tent. The high priest would then sprinkle the blood from the purification offering in front of the curtain that separated the high priest from the place where Yahweh was present. The priests could not eat the meat from these types of purification offerings because the high priest had to take the rest of the offering outside the camp and completely burn it up.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:24–30 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh gives Moses instructions for how Aaron and Aaron's descendants should sacrifice and eat the sin or purification offering.

In the second scene: Yahweh gives Moses instructions about what the priests should do if the blood from the purification offering touches something.

In the third scene: Yahweh gives Moses instructions about who may eat the purification offering and which purification offerings those people may eat.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • Aaron's descendants who become priests
  • And Aaron's male descendants, including those who are not priests

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In this passage, Yahweh continues to give Moses instructions while Moses and the Israelites are camped at Mount Sinai. We do not know where Moses is, but Moses may be in the Tent of Meeting, or on Mount Sinai, while Yahweh gives Moses these instructions. You will remember that in the previous passage, Yahweh gave Moses instructions for what Aaron and each of Aaron's descendants who become the high priest after Aaron must do when Yahweh anoints that person as the new high priest. You will also remember that earlier in the book of Leviticus, in chapter 4, Yahweh gave Moses many instructions about how the priests should offer the purification offering.

In scene one of this passage, Yahweh now gives Moses further instructions or laws to follow for what Aaron and Aaron's descendants who become priests must do when the priests sacrifice the purification offering. First, the priest must sacrifice the sin or purification offering in the same place that the priests sacrifice the burnt offering. This is on the north side of the bronze altar in the Tent of Meeting. Second, the priest who sacrifices the animal for the purification offering may eat the meat from the offering, but that priest must eat the meat in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. This is because the purification offering is very holy, so the priests must eat the offering in a very holy place.

Stop here and discuss these questions as a group: What kinds of places are holy, or sacred, in your culture? What things should people do in a holy place? What kinds of things should people not do in a holy place? Pay attention to the words and phrases you use to describe this holy place. Pause this audio here.

The sin or purification offering is so holy that ritually or spiritually dirty things should not touch it. This is why in scene two of this passage, Yahweh gives Moses instructions for what the priests should do if blood from the purification offering touches things. If the blood from the animal gets on clothing, the priests have to wash the clothing in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. The priest also has to clean the pot that the priest uses to cook the meat from the purification offering, because blood has touched the pot. If the pot is a bronze metal pot, the priest must scrub the pot with something rough and then wash the pot with water to clean the pot. The priest must do this in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. If the pot is a clay pot, the priest must not clean the pot and then use the pot for non-holy purposes. Instead, the priest must destroy the clay pot.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What do people in your culture do to wash cooking pots? Are there any differences from how the priests wash the bronze pots in this passage? Pause this audio here.

In scene three of this passage, Yahweh explains to Moses who may eat the meat from the purification offering, and what kind of purification offering those people may eat. First, Yahweh explains that it is not just the priest who sacrificed the animal for the purification offering who may eat the meat from the purification offering. Any male person in a priest's family may eat the meat. So all of Aaron's male descendants may eat meat from purification offerings, even if those descendants are not priests themselves. Second, Yahweh explains that no one may eat meat from a purification offering where the high priest brings the blood into the Tent of Meeting. Before, in Leviticus 4, when Yahweh first explained how the priests should sacrifice the purification offering, Yahweh explained when the high priest should bring the blood into the Tent of Meeting. When the high priest has sinned or when the whole community has sinned, the high priest brings the blood into the tent. The priests must not eat the meat from this kind of purification offering. However, when anyone else has sinned, the priest does not bring the blood into the tent, and any male descendant of Aaron may eat the offering.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In scene one, Yahweh told Moses that the priest who sacrificed the animal for the purification offering could eat the meat from the offering. In this scene, Yahweh explains to Moses that any male person in a priest's family can eat the offering. What are some things in your culture that only leaders can do? Can family members of those leaders do any of those things because those people are related to the leader? How do you talk about those family members? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:24–30 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • Aaron's descendants who become priests
  • And Aaron's male descendants, including those who are not priests

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh gives Moses instructions for what Aaron and Aaron's descendants should do when the priests sacrifice the animal for the sin or purification offering. Have a person who plays Aaron act out how Aaron follows Yahweh's instructions.

Yahweh says that Aaron should sacrifice the animal for the purification offering at the same place that Aaron would sacrifice the animal for the burnt offering. Aaron may then eat the meat leftover from the purification offering.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am honored that I am able to eat the meat from this sacred offering; or
  • I am nervous about eating this meat because this meat is very sacred; or
  • I am relieved that this purification offering has made amends to Yahweh for someone's sin, so I am glad to eat the meat from this offering.
Continue the drama.

Now, pretend that Aaron has died and one of Aaron's descendants is a priest. This priest must follow the same instructions Yahweh gave Moses. Have a person who plays Aaron's descendant act out how that descendant follows Yahweh's instructions.

Next, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about what the priest should do if the blood from the purification offering touches something. Have the people who play Aaron and Aaron's descendants act out the priest's role. First, blood from the purification offering gets on some clothes. Have the priest characters act out washing the clothes in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Then, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about what the priest should do with the pot the priest used to cook the meat from the purification offering. Have one of the priests act out cooking the meat in a bronze pot. Have one of the priests act out cooking the meat in a clay pot. The priest who cooks the meat in the bronze pot must clean the pot by rubbing the pot with sand or something else rough and then washing the pot with water. The priest who cooks the meat in the clay pot must break the clay pot.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest with the bronze pot, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am tired because cleaning the bronze pot was a lot of work; or
  • I am proud that I followed Yahweh's instructions to clean the bronze pot; or
  • I am relieved that the pot is clean so that nothing dirty touches what is sacred.

Ask the person playing the priest with the clay pot, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am disappointed that I had to destroy the pot; or
  • I am proud that I followed Yahweh's instructions to break the clay pot; or
  • I am relieved that I destroyed the pot so that nothing dirty touches what is sacred.
Continue the drama.

Finally, Yahweh tells Moses that any male member of a priest's family can eat the meat from the purification offering. Have the people playing Aaron, Aaron's descendants who become priests, and Aaron's male descendants who are not priests, act out that they all eat the meat together in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. However, no one can eat the meat from the purification offering for the high priest's sin or the whole community's sin.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am glad to share the meat that people offered to me to make amends with the priests who serve me; or
  • I want to make sure that no one eats meat from an offering for the high priest's sin or the whole community's sin because that meat is so holy that it would be dangerous; or
  • I am glad that the priests are following my instructions well.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 6:24–30 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh gives Moses more instructions for Aaron and Aaron's sons, or descendants, about what the priests are supposed to do when the priests sacrifice the sin or purification offering. For more information on Yahweh, descendants, and the purification offering, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words or phrases for Yahweh, descendants, and purification offering as you used in previous passages, like Leviticus 4.

Yahweh calls these instructions the law of the purification offering. For more information on the law, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for law as you used in previous passages.

Yahweh tells Moses that the priests must kill the animal for the purification offering in the same place the priests kill the animal for the burnt offering. Use the same word for killing an animal that you have used in previous passages. For more information about priests and the burnt offering, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for priest and for burnt offering as you used in previous passages. The sin offering that the priest is offering now is most sacred, or most holy. For more information about holy, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for holy or sacred that you used in previous passages.

The priest may eat the meat from the purification offering, but because the offering is so sacred, the priest must eat this meat in a sanctuary or holy place. For more information about sanctuary, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for sanctuary that you used in previous passages. The holy place where the priest may eat the meat is the courtyard of the tabernacle, which people also call the Tent of Meeting. For more information about the tabernacle, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for Tent of Meeting that you used in previous passages.

Everything that touches the meat from the offering becomes sacred or holy. In this situation, it is not a good thing for everything that touches the meat from the offering to become holy because it is dangerous when something dirty or common touches something that is holy. Use the same word or phrase for holy in this case as you used in Leviticus 6:18.

When any of the blood from the purification offering touches clothing, a priest has to wash that clothing in a holy place. This means the priest must wash the clothing in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. When the priest uses a clay pot to cook the meat, the priest must break the clay pot. When the priest uses a bronze pot, the priest has to scour the pot with something rough and then wash the pot with water. For more information about bronze, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for bronze that you used in previous passages.

Every male descendant of Aaron can eat the meat from the purification offering. The meat from the offering is sacred. However, no one can eat the meat from certain kinds of purification offerings where the high priest brings the blood into the Tent of Meeting to atone for the sin, or make amends to Yahweh. For more information about atonement, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for atone that you used in previous passages.

Here, Yahweh again calls the Tent of Meeting "the sanctuary," because it is a holy place. The kinds of purification offerings where the priest does this are those that make amends for the high priest's sin and those that make amends for the whole community's sin. The priest must completely burn up these kinds of purification offerings.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
