title: Leviticus 7:1–10
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 7:1–10 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:1–10 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:1–10 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous passages, Yahweh has been giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai. Here in this passage, Yahweh repeats the instructions to Moses for how the priests are to offer guilt offerings. Yahweh also tells the priests what the priests can take from each kind of offering.

For the guilt offering, the priests would normally sacrifice an adult male sheep. Although the storyteller does not mention this animal here, Yahweh said several times in previous passages that people should give an adult male sheep as the "guilt offering." Therefore, we know that the "guilt offering" that the storyteller mentions here is the adult male sheep.

Stop here and look at a picture of an adult male sheep. Pause this audio here.

For the guilt offering, the priest would kill the adult male sheep on the north side of the altar of burnt offering.

Stop here and look at a map of the Tent of Meeting and a picture of the altar of burnt offering as a group. Pause this audio here.

Although the narrator does not mention it here, we know from previous passages that the priest would also use a container to collect some of the sheep's blood.

Stop here and look at a picture of tabernacle pots and utensils as a group. Pause this audio here.

After the priest sprinkles or splashes the sheep's blood on the sides of the altar, the priest has to remove certain parts of the sheep's dead body. The priest removes all the fat that covers and surrounds the internal organs of the sheep, the sheep's tail, the two kidneys and the fat on them, and the fatty, or best, part of the liver.

Stop here and look at a picture of a sheep's internal organs as a group. Pause this audio here.

The priest takes all of these special pieces of the sheep's dead body and burns the special pieces with fire on the altar of burnt offering. This is how the priest makes atonement for the Israelite person's sin or makes things right between the person and Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Why was it important for the priest to make atonement for the Israelite people's sin? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also gives rules about who can eat the cooked meat from guilt offerings and where those people can eat the meat. The priest and any of the priest's male relatives can eat the guilt offering. However, the priest and the priest's male relatives must eat the offering in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting because the offering is most holy. The priest and his male relatives must follow the same rules for eating the sin or purification offerings.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, is it common for people to eat offerings that people make to a god or idol? Why or why not? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh tells Moses that a priest who makes a burnt offering can keep the animal hide or skin from the sacrifice. This is a special instruction. Why did Yahweh allow the priests to keep the animal skins or hides from the burnt offering? The rule says the priest should burn the whole offering, but this means only the food parts of the offering. The reason why the priest could keep the animal skin of the burnt offerings was that people did not eat the skin. Instead, a person could stretch the animal skin or hide and make something like clothes or a bag out of the skin. It is possible that the priest did burn the animal skin burnt offerings when he offered the burnt offering for the whole community, but kept the animal skin if an Israelite person offered a burnt offering individually. But we do not know.

Then Yahweh says that the priest who offers a cooked grain offering for a person gets to keep the offering. An Israelite person could prepare a cooked grain offering in an oven, a pan, or a griddle. The Israelite people had ovens that they usually made from clay bricks. These kinds of ovens could be shaped like a cup or shaped like a dome. People would use these kinds of ovens to bake flatbreads. You may be familiar with a tabun, tanur, or tandoor, which are different kinds of ovens that people use today and are similar to these ovens. Yahweh does say exactly what kind of pan and griddle to use. The Israelites may cook bread in a covered pan or on an uncovered pan. People probably made these pans and griddles out of clay or from a type of metal. Since the Israelite people were preparing these cooked grain offerings for Yahweh, it is possible that the people used the bronze utensils from the Tent of Meeting to cook or fry the bread.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people typically cook grains? What utensils do people use? What method of cooking, such as baking or frying, do people use? Pause this audio here.

Stop here and look at pictures of what an oven, a pan, and a griddle might have looked like as a group. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh instructs the priests to share the uncooked grain offerings equally among all of Aaron's male descendants.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:1–10 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh repeats the instructions to Moses for how the priests are to offer guilt offerings. Yahweh also mentions the rules about who can eat guilt offerings and where those people can eat the offerings. The priest and any of the male relatives of the priest can eat the guilt offering, but those men must eat the offering in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. This is because this meat is very special.

In the second scene: Yahweh says the same rules apply for who can eat sin or purification offerings. Then Yahweh tells Moses that a priest who makes a burnt offering can keep the animal hide or skin from the sacrifice. Then Yahweh says that the priest who offers a cooked grain offering gets to keep the offering. But the priests must share the uncooked grain offerings equally among all of Aaron's male descendants.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • An Israelite priest
  • And male relatives of the priest

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In previous passages, Yahweh was giving Moses instructions on how the Israelite people can live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai. Note that the narrator does not mention Moses in this passage, but the narrator does mention Moses in the beginning of Leviticus 6, where the narrator says that Yahweh gave these instructions to Moses.

In the first scene, Yahweh repeats the law or instructions to Moses for how the priests are to offer guilt offerings. Israelite people would bring guilt offerings to the Tent of Meeting. A person would do this when a person accidentally sinned or when a person sinned in certain ways, like if the person stole or lied about property. Yahweh says that the guilt offering is most holy. The words "most holy" mean ritually special. Usually, when a person or thing was "most holy" to Yahweh, it meant the Israelite people had to treat that person or thing in a very special or particular way.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how would you describe something extremely sacred or holy? Do you have any words you would use to talk about the most important spiritual things? Pause this audio here.

For a guilt offering, an Israelite person usually brings an adult male sheep. We know this from chapter 5. Even though this passage does not mention adult male sheep, you might need to remember this if it is important in your language to say what the sacrifice was. For the guilt offering, the priest kills the adult male sheep on the north side of the altar of burnt offering.

Stop here and, as a group, again look at a map of the Tent of Meeting and a picture of the altar of burnt offering as needed. Pause this audio here.

Although the storyteller does not mention it in this passage, we know from a previous passage that the priest also uses a container to catch some of the sheep's blood. Then the priest sprinkles or throws the sheep's blood on the sides of the altar.

Then the priest removes certain parts of the sheep's dead body. The priest removes all the fat that covers and surrounds the internal organs of the sheep, the sheep's tail, the two kidneys and the fat on them, and the best part of the liver.

Stop here and look at a picture of these internal organs as a group again as needed. Remind each other what you called these organs in Leviticus 3 and 4. Pause this audio here.

The priest takes all of these special pieces of the sheep's dead body and burns the special pieces with fire on the altar of burnt offering. Here, Yahweh calls this the food offering.

This is how the priest makes atonement for the Israelite person's sin. To make atonement means that Yahweh forgives the Israelite person's sin, and the ritually "dirty" person will be clean again and is able to worship Yahweh again.

Yahweh also talks about the rules about who can eat the cooked meat from guilt offerings and where those people can eat the cooked meat. Because the guilt offering is most holy, there is a very strict rule about who can eat the sacrificed and cooked meat and where those people can eat the meat. The priest and any of the male relatives of the priest can eat the guilt offering. But those men must eat this offering in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. It is important to translate this in a way that makes it clear that there were no women who could eat this meat from the most holy offerings.

In the second scene, Yahweh gives the same rule for who can eat sin or purification offerings. Then Yahweh tells Moses that a priest who makes a burnt offering for a person can keep the animal hide or skin from the sacrifice.

Then Yahweh says that the priest who offers a cooked grain offering gets to keep and eat the grain offering. An Israelite person who gives a cooked grain offering could cook the offering in an oven, on a pan, or on a griddle. The pans might have been bronze, like the other utensils in the Tent of Meeting.

Stop here and, as a group, look again at pictures of what an oven, a pan, and a griddle might have looked like as needed. Pause this audio here.

For the uncooked grain offerings, the priests must share the offering equally among all of Aaron's male descendants.

Stop here and discuss: Talk about sharing something equally in a large group, where every person gets the same amount. Talk about sharing a staple food, such as wheat, corn, or rice, in this way. How would you explain to someone that everyone gets the same amount of uncooked food? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:1–10 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • An Israelite priest
  • And male relatives of the priest

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Note that the storyteller does not mention Moses in this passage, but the storyteller did mention Moses at the beginning of Leviticus 6, where the storyteller said that Yahweh gave these instructions to Moses.

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh repeats the instructions to Moses for how the priests are to offer guilt offerings. Yahweh also mentions the rules about who can eat guilt offerings and where those people can eat the offerings. The priest and any of the male relatives of the priest can eat the guilt offering, but those men must eat the offering in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. This is because this meat is very special.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am happy that people will get to eat the meat and that it will not go to waste; or
  • Why is it that only the priests can eat the meat?

Ask the person playing the priests, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am happy that Yahweh has provided food for us. Because we work at the Tent of Meeting, we may not have time to grow or buy food from somewhere else. or
  • I wonder why my daughters and wife cannot eat this meat. I trust Yahweh, though, and will follow Yahweh's instructions; or
  • These rules about the holy meat remind me how carefully we must treat other holy things. The rules also remind me that I must deeply respect Yahweh, who is very holy!
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh gives the same rule for who can eat purification offerings. Then Yahweh tells Moses that a priest who makes a burnt offering can keep the animal hide or skin from the sacrifice. Then Yahweh says that the priest who offers a cooked grain offering gets to keep the offering. But for the uncooked grain offerings, the priests must share the offering equally among all of Aaron's male descendants.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I want the Israelite people to know that I will provide for them; or
  • I do not want people to be afraid that they will not have enough to make the sacrifices; or
  • The Israelite people need to be careful with the most holy things.

Ask the person playing the male relatives of the priests, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am thankful that I may eat some of the food that Yahweh shares with the priests, even though I did not prepare this offering; or
  • I am happy that our God is kind and provides food for us; or
  • When I eat the food from the offerings, I think about Yahweh, and I remember that Yahweh is the one who keeps us alive.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:1–10 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh gives more laws or rules about how the priests should offer guilt offerings. Yahweh tells Moses what parts of the offerings the priests may keep for themselves. Use the same word for law as you used in previous passages. Use the same word for guilt offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on law and guilt offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says that the guilt offering is most holy. Use the same word or phrase for most holy as you used in previous passages when you talked about an offering being most holy. For more information on holy, refer to the Master Glossary.

The priest sacrifices, or kills, the guilt offering on the same altar where the priest sacrifices burnt offerings. Use the same word for killing an animal and for burnt offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on burnt offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Use the same words and phrases you used previously for the fat that covers the internal organs, the kidneys and fat near the backside of the sheep, and the best part of the liver.

After the priest kills the animal for the guilt offering, the priest sprinkles or throws the blood onto the sides of the altar. Use the same word for sprinkle or throw as you used in previous passages.

The priest sacrifices the guilt offering on the altar of burnt offering. But in this passage, the storyteller just calls it the altar. Use the same word for altar as you used in previous passages. For more information on altar, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and, as a group, look again at a picture of the altar of burnt offering as needed. Pause this audio here.

The priest burns the guilt offering as a fire offering to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for fire offering as you have used previously. Fire offering is in the Master Glossary.

Use the same words for Yahweh and priest as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh also mentions that this law or rule is the same for sin or purification offerings. Use the same word for purification offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on purification offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

The priests would eat the offerings in the holy place or sanctuary. Use the same word for sanctuary as you have used in previous passages. For more information on sanctuary, refer to the Master Glossary.

The purification offering and the guilt offering belong to the priest who makes atonement with those offerings. Use the same word for atonement as you used in previous passages. For more information on atonement, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh allows the priests to keep the grain offerings. Use the same word for grain offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on grain offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

The storyteller mentions three ways that a person can cook or prepare a grain offering. The person can bake the offering in an oven, cook the offering in a pan, or cook the offering on a griddle. In Leviticus 2, when Yahweh gave instructions for the grain offering, Yahweh mentioned all three of these ways of cooking. Use the same words for oven, pan, and griddle as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and, as a group, look again at pictures of an oven, a pan, and a griddle as needed. Pause this audio here.

The dry grain offering belongs equally to all of Aaron's sons, or male descendants. Use the same word or phrase for descendants as you have used previously, and refer to descendants in the Master Glossary for more information.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 7:11–21
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 7:11–21 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:11–21 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:11–21 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

After Yahweh tells Moses how the priests need to eat the meat of the guilt offering, Yahweh gives Moses more instructions about the peace or fellowship offering. This time, Yahweh does not give instructions about how to kill the animal or make the fellowship offering. Instead, Yahweh tells Moses new information about what the Israelites need to bring when the Israelites make the fellowship offering and when the Israelites can eat the meat. Yahweh starts this story by telling Moses specific rules and regulations that people need to follow when someone gives a fellowship offering to Yahweh. These rules are like laws and have serious consequences when people disobey the rules.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time when you told someone specific instructions that the person needed to follow carefully, or there would be serious consequences. Tell a story about a time when someone else told you specific instructions that you needed to follow carefully. What happened? Pause this audio here.

The offerings that Yahweh talks about in this story are the fellowship offerings. It is important to remember that Yahweh gave instructions about how to kill the animal for the fellowship offering in Leviticus 3. In this story, Yahweh explains what other food the Israelites should bring when someone brings an animal as a fellowship offering and also how people should eat the meat of that animal.

One of the reasons an Israelite might give a fellowship offering is because the person wants everyone to know how amazing Yahweh is. Yahweh calls this kind of fellowship offering "a praise or thank offering." A person would give a praise offering if Yahweh saved the person from their enemies or healed the person. A person might also give a praise offering to Yahweh to thank Yahweh for forgiving that person when that person sinned.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time someone did something amazing to help you. What did you do to thank that person? Pause this audio here.

When the Israelite brings the animal to sacrifice for the praise offering, the Israelite also needs to bring four different kinds of bread. The Israelites made the first kind of bread when the Israelites mixed flour and olive oil together and baked the dough into a thick loaf that did not have any yeast in it. The Israelites made the second kind of bread with flour without yeast, baked it into a thin loaf, and then poured olive oil on top. The Israelites made the third kind of bread with even nicer flour that the Israelites mixed carefully with the oil and baked into a thick loaf without yeast. The fourth and last kind of bread was the only one that had yeast in it. The priest would give some of the bread to Yahweh, and then the priest would eat the rest of the bread with the priest's family.

Stop here and look at pictures of the different kinds of bread as a group. Pause this audio here.

An Israelite may also bring an animal to sacrifice and bread for other kinds of fellowship offerings. Sometimes a person would promise Yahweh that the person would bring a fellowship offering if Yahweh answered a prayer. Yahweh calls this kind of fellowship offering "a vow offering." People bring these sacrifices to show Yahweh how thankful those people are that Yahweh answered their prayer.

Stop here and tell a story about a time you promised to give someone a gift if that person helped you. Pause this audio here.

There is one more reason why an Israelite would bring a fellowship offering to Yahweh. Sometimes the Israelites would want to give Yahweh a gift just because the Israelites loved Yahweh. An Israelite would decide that the Israelite wants to show Yahweh how much the Israelite loves Yahweh, and so the Israelite would bring all the bread and the animal to give to Yahweh. This kind of offering is a freewill offering.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time you gave someone a gift because you love that person so much. What did you do? Tell a story about a time you did something for someone because you appreciated that person. What did you do? Pause this audio here.

After the priests sacrifice the animal, the Israelite family that brought the sacrifice would eat the meat that the priests did not burn up on the altar. The fellowship offering was the only kind of offering that any clean Israelite could eat the meat of, so this offering was like a party for the Israelite family and their community. The Israelite family and maybe even their friends and neighbors would eat the meat together and could tell each other how amazing Yahweh is. The Israelites must finish the meat in a certain amount of time, or the meat would not be good to eat anymore, and Yahweh would punish the Israelites. The Israelite had to eat the meat of the praise offering in one day, but the Israelite could take two days to eat the meat for the vow and the freewill offering. If a person ate any of the meat from the vow or freewill offering on the third day, then Yahweh would punish the person.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What rules does your culture have about when people can eat certain foods? What are the punishments if someone breaks those rules? Pause this audio here.

Remember, Leviticus 5:1–13 talked about what people would need to do if someone touched a person or animal that was not ritually clean. If someone touched an animal or a person that was not ritually clean, then the person would not be ritually clean anymore. If someone who is not ritually clean eats any of the meat from the fellowship offering, then Yahweh says the Israelites need to punish that person. The punishment is very strong. The Israelites would make the person leave the community and never return, and the Israelites might even kill the person.

Yahweh punishes a ritually dirty person strongly for eating the fellowship offering because the fellowship offering is special to Yahweh. Only ritually clean people should touch or eat important offerings.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What is the worst punishment in your culture? What does someone need to do in order to get that punishment? Tell a story about someone who had to leave the community and never return. Why did that person have to leave the community? How did the community feel about it? How did you feel about it?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:11–21 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells Moses that Yahweh is going to explain the laws the Israelites need to follow if the Israelites bring different kinds of fellowship offerings to Yahweh.

In the second scene: Yahweh explains what the Israelites should do when the Israelites want to give Yahweh a praise offering, which the Israelites give Yahweh when the Israelites want to praise or thank Yahweh. Yahweh explains what kind of bread the Israelites should bring when the Israelites bring a praise offering and how the Israelites should eat the meat.

In the third scene: Yahweh explains how the Israelites should eat the meat from the fellowship offerings that are vow or freewill offerings. Yahweh also explains what the consequences are if the Israelites disobey.

In the fourth scene: Yahweh describes the consequences if the meat of the peace offering becomes ritually dirty or if a ritually dirty person eats the meat.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The priest who makes the offering
  • The Israelite who brings the offering and their family
  • A disobedient Israelite

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In scene one, Yahweh explains to Moses that Yahweh is about to tell Moses the laws for the fellowship offerings. It is important to remember that Yahweh introduced Yahweh's instructions about the guilt offering in the same way.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Discuss how you introduced the information about the instructions for the guilt offering and whether you could use that same language here. Pause the audio here.

In scene two, Yahweh explains that the person who brings the praise offering, which is a kind of fellowship offering, must also bring different kinds of bread. The Israelite must make three loaves of bread without any yeast and one kind of bread with yeast. The Israelite brings these four kinds of bread to the Tent of Meeting when the Israelite brings the animal that the Israelite is going to sacrifice.

Stop here and look at a picture of the Tent of Meeting as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and talk about how you will describe the four types of bread in your translation. Remember that the Israelites made the first kind of bread when they mixed flour and olive oil together and baked the dough into a thick loaf that did not have any yeast in it. The Israelites made the second kind of bread with flour without yeast, baked it into a thin loaf, and then poured olive oil on top. The Israelites made the third kind of bread with even nicer flour that the Israelites mixed carefully with the oil and baked into a thick loaf without yeast. The fourth and last kind of bread was the only bread that had yeast in it. Pause this audio here.

The priest who sacrifices the animal may eat some of each kind of bread. The story describes this priest as the priest who sprinkles or throws the blood of the fellowship offering against the altar. It is important to remember that earlier, Yahweh told the priest to use a bowl to throw the blood of the fellowship offering against the altar when the priest killed the animal for the fellowship offering. Here, the storyteller describes how the priest throws the blood to show clearly that the priest who killed the animal is the priest who gets to eat the bread that the Israelite brought.

The Israelites who brought the fellowship offering have to eat the meat the same day that the priest kills the animal. The Israelites cannot leave any of the meat to eat the next day. The Israelites have to eat everything on the day the Israelites bring the sacrifice.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how do you tell someone that the person has to do something on the same day you are giving the instructions? Pause this audio here.

In scene three, Yahweh explains how the Israelites should eat the meat for the vow and freewill offerings. The Israelites can eat the meat of the vow and freewill offerings on the day the priest sacrifices the animal and the day after the priest sacrifices the animal. If the Israelites eat the meat on any other day, then Yahweh will not accept the offering.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use to explain what day the Israelites must not eat the meat anymore. Pause this audio here.

If the Israelites eat the meat on the third day after the sacrifice instead of burning the meat like Yahweh says to, then Yahweh will not accept those Israelites. This could mean that Yahweh will reject the Israelite who brought the offering. This could also mean that Yahweh will not accept the Israelite's gift and will ignore the gift, so it will be like the Israelite never gave a gift at all.

The story says that the person who ignores the rules and eats the meat on that third day will receive a punishment, or "take on his own iniquity." In other words, the person has done wrong things against Yahweh and is guilty. The storyteller does not say who will punish the person, but normally the phrase here describes the way Yahweh punishes people and the way people punish other people.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time that God or a spirit punished someone in your culture. Tell a story about a time the community punished a person. Discuss whether you use the same words to talk about both kinds of punishment. Pause this audio here.

In scene four, Yahweh explains what will happen if the meat from the fellowship offering is no longer ritually clean or if someone who is not ritually clean eats the meat. It is important to notice that Yahweh uses the general term "fellowship offering" here instead of any of the names for the specific kinds of fellowship offerings. The rules in scene four apply to all of the fellowship offerings that Yahweh has talked about so far.

If the meat touches anything that is unclean or ritually dirty, then someone must burn up the meat. It is important to remember that if something is ritually dirty, then that thing cannot come close to God. The meat for the offering is a gift to God, so the meat can not touch anything that would make the meat ritually dirty.

If a person touches a ritually dirty animal or something that prevents the person from participating in ritual activities, then the person is ritually dirty and cannot eat the meat. If that person eats the meat, the person's punishment is to not be part of Yahweh's people anymore. Yahweh repeats these instructions twice to show how important the instructions are. First, Yahweh says that if anyone who is ritually dirty eats the meat, then the Israelites will cut that person off from the rest of the people. This could mean that the people kill the ritually dirty person, but it probably means that the Israelites force the ritually dirty person to leave the community and never return. This is one of the strongest punishments that the Israelites had because the ritually dirty person could never become part of the community again.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for "cut off from their people." Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh talks about what happens to the person who touches something ritually dirty and gives a list of ritually dirty things. The list includes things that come from people who are ritually dirty, ritually dirty animals, or any other living thing that is not ritually clean. If the person touches any of those ritually dirty things and eats the meat, then the Israelites must cut the person off from the rest of the people.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What was a time when you wanted someone to understand how serious your instructions were or how bad the consequences would be if the person did not listen to you? What did you say? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:11–21 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The priest who makes the offering
  • The Israelite who brings the offering and their family
  • A disobedient Israelite

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

The story begins with Yahweh talking to Moses and telling Moses that these are the rules that the Israelites need to follow when they bring peace or fellowship offerings to Yahweh.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I know I need to take this seriously; or
  • I should write this down so that everyone else knows what they need to do.
Continue the drama.

The Israelite family that has the kinds of bread and the animal to sacrifice for the praise offering walks over to the priest to bring the sacrifice to Yahweh. The family gives the priest the three kinds of bread that do not have yeast, and then the bread that does have yeast. The priest sacrifices the animal and splashes its blood on the altar, gives the meat to the family, and then takes one of each kind of bread.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing the Israelite family, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people may answer things like:

  • God healed me when I was sick, and I am so thankful! I want everyone to know how amazing God is! or
  • I sinned, and God forgave me. I want to thank God and tell everyone how kind God is; or
  • We have to make sure we eat all this meat today. Maybe we should get our friends to come and eat the meat with us.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person may answer things like:

  • I am so thankful to God for this food for my family! or
  • I am excited to eat this bread!
Continue the drama.

The Israelite family brings the same kinds of bread and animal as they did for the praise offering, but this time the family tells the priest that they are bringing it for a vow offering or a freewill offering. The family members eat some of the meat, sleep, eat some of the meat, and sleep again. If there is any meat left after the family has slept a second time, they burn most of it.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing the family, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people may answer things like:

  • God answered my prayer, so I am bringing this sacrifice to show God how thankful I am; or
  • I wanted to give God this gift, so I am bringing God this sacrifice; or
  • Now that it is the third day, we need to burn all this up so that God does not punish anyone who eats it. I do not want to be punished!
Continue the drama.

The Israelite who disobeys comes and eats some of the meat on the third day. Yahweh shows that he does not accept any of the sacrifice anymore and punishes this Israelite.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the disobedient Israelite, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • Why is Yahweh so mad at me? I only ate some of the meat; or
  • I am so sad that my actions mean that Yahweh will not accept any of my family's sacrifice.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person may answer things like:

  • I am so disappointed that one Israelite disobeyed me and ate the meat; or
  • I am sad I cannot accept this sacrifice anymore; or
  • The meat of the sacrifice is special to me, and I am angry that the disobedient Israelite was so disrespectful and disobedient.
Continue the drama.

One of the Israelites touches the meat to an object that is unclean or drops the meat on the ground. The meat is now unclean, so the Israelite burns it.

Pause the drama.

Ask the actor who burned the meat, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I really wanted to eat this meat, but now that it has touched the ground. This meat is not clean anymore, so I need to burn it; or
  • I do not want to eat something that is unclean! I do not want Yahweh to punish me.
Continue the drama.

The Israelite family eats the clean meat together. The disobedient Israelite says that he is unclean and then eats the meat. The other Israelites chase the disobedient Israelite away. Then another disobedient Israelite touches unclean animals or unclean things and then eats the meat. The other Israelites chase the disobedient Israelite away so that he cannot come back.

Pause the drama.

Ask the disobedient Israelite, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I should not have eaten the meat. Now I cannot return home and be with my family. I am upset that I disobeyed God; or
  • I did not think that it would be a problem if I was not clean and ate the meat. I should have listened to God.

Ask the other Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

  • God's rules are important! The disobedient Israelite should not have eaten the meat. The disobedient Israelite deserved to be punished; or
  • I am sad that we will not see that person again. I wish that person had obeyed Yahweh.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:11–21 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Yahweh tells Moses about the laws the Israelites need to obey when the Israelites give fellowship offerings. The word law is the same word Yahweh used in the last story to talk about very important rules that people need to obey. Use the same word or phrase here that you used in previous passages to talk about laws. For more information on law, refer to the Master Glossary.

These laws that Yahweh tells Moses are about sacrifices for the peace or fellowship offering. Use the same word or phrase for sacrifice and fellowship offering that you did in chapter three to talk about this kind of offering. For more information on this offering, refer to the Master Glossary for sacrifice and for "peace or fellowship offering."

The word offering talks about gifts that people would give to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase here that you used in previous passages. For more information on offerings, refer to the Master Glossary.

In this story, the storyteller uses God's name, Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh that you have in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

The first kind of sacrifice is a praise or thanksgiving offering. This is the offering that people give Yahweh when Yahweh has done something amazing for those people or forgiven those people for something those people did wrong. The Israelites would give this offering to thank Yahweh and to tell everyone else what Yahweh did to help the Israelites.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the praise or thanksgiving offering. Pause this audio here.

There are four kinds of bread that the Israelites are supposed to give to Yahweh. Three of the kinds of bread do not have yeast in them. Yeast is what makes bread fluffy instead of flat.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of the kinds of bread without yeast. Pause this audio here.

People also put olive oil in the bread without yeast. Olive oil is a normal cooking oil that the Israelites used to make food.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of olive oil. Pause this audio here.

One kind of bread uses yeast to make it fluffy.

Stop here and look at pictures of bread with yeast in it. Pause this audio here.

Use the same words or phrases to describe yeast and olive oil that you have used in previous passages.

Stop here and decide as a group how you will describe these four kinds of bread. Pause this audio here.

The Israelites have to eat the meat from the praise offering on the same day that the Israelites offer the animal. The Israelites can not eat any of the meat the next day.

Stop here and discuss how you will describe when the Israelites must not eat the meat anymore. Pause this audio here.

Another kind of fellowship offering is the vow offering. A vow offering is an offering that an Israelite gave Yahweh after Yahweh had answered a prayer. An Israelite would pray and ask Yahweh for something and would promise to give a vow offering if Yahweh answered the prayer.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for vow offering. Look up offering and vow in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated the word vow in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The last kind of praise offering is the freewill offering. A freewill offering is an offering that an Israelite gave Yahweh just because the Israelite wanted to give Yahweh something.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for freewill offering. For more information about the freewill offering, refer to the Master Glossary. Pause this audio here.

If a person eats the meat on the wrong day, Yahweh will not accept it. This might mean that Yahweh does not accept the person who gave the offering, or it might mean that Yahweh will not accept the person's offering, and it will be like the person never brought an offering.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use to explain how Yahweh does not accept the person or offering if the Israelite eats the meat on the wrong day. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh will punish anyone who eats the meat on the wrong day. Yahweh explains that the person who eats the offering on the wrong day will "carry his own iniquity." This phrase describes a punishment, but Yahweh does not say who is punishing the person. Probably, this describes a punishment that only Yahweh gives people who disobey Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss the ways your culture talks about punishment from God. Discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use to translate the phrase "bear his own iniquity, or take the punishment." For more information, refer to iniquity in the Master Glossary. Pause this audio here.

If the meat touches anything that is unclean or ritually dirty, then the Israelites cannot eat it anymore. It is important to remember that something being ritually dirty does not mean that the thing was physically dirty. If something was ritually dirty, then the Israelites could not use it to worship Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase here that you used in previous passages to talk about people, animals, or objects that are ritually dirty. For more information on clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 7:22–27
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 7:22–27 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:22–27 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:22–27 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh has been telling Moses to give all these instructions to Aaron and Aaron's sons. Now, Yahweh tells Moses to give specific instructions to all of the Israelites. Moses is supposed to tell the Israelites that Yahweh does not allow the Israelites to eat any of the fat from certain animals.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of animal fat with and without meat. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh does not allow the Israelites to eat sheep fat, cattle fat, or goat fat. You will remember that the Israelites sacrificed sheep, cattle, and goats to Yahweh, and that those animals' fat belonged to Yahweh. You will remember that cattle is a general word that can include female cows, bulls, and oxen.

Stop here and look at pictures of sheep, cattle, and goats. Then discuss this question as a group: What parts of an animal does your community eat? Are there parts of the animal that you are not allowed to eat? Why? Pause this audio here.

If the sheep, cattle, or goat dies by itself or if another animal kills one of those animals, then that dead animal's fat does not belong to Yahweh anymore.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What does your community do with animals that die because the animals are old or sick, or because another animal has killed the animals? Pause this audio here.

The Israelites could only sacrifice perfect animals, and animals that died by themselves were not perfect anymore. If another animal killed a sheep, cow, or goat, then the sheep, cow, or goat was not perfect anymore, and the Israelites could not sacrifice the animal either. Instead, the Israelites could use the fat of that animal to make things, but the Israelites still could not eat the animal's fat.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you use animal fat in your culture? What kinds of things do you make with animal fat? What rules do you have about what kind of fat people must use for specific purposes? Pause this audio here.

If anyone eats the fat of any of these three kinds of animals, the Israelites will cut that person off from the community. It is important to remember that when the community cuts someone off, the community is severely punishing that person, and that person is no longer a part of the community. Yahweh also says that the Israelites are not supposed to eat the blood of any bird or any animal. It does not matter where the Israelites lived, what kind of house the Israelites had, or how important the Israelites were; Yahweh does not allow the Israelites to eat the blood.

Stop here and discuss this question: What kinds of homes do you have in your community? What rules do you have about what you can eat in certain places? Pause this audio here.

If an Israelite eats any of the blood of any bird or any other animal, then the community would cut that person off. When Yahweh talks about eating the blood, Yahweh is talking about eating meat that still has blood in it. The Israelites have to drain all the blood out of an animal before the Israelites can eat the meat. The Israelites have to make sure the Israelites do not eat any of the animal's blood when the Israelites eat the animal's meat.

Stop here and look at a picture of people draining an animal's blood. Discuss this question: How does your community kill animals for meat? Pause this audio here.

After Yahweh flooded the earth in the book of Genesis, Yahweh told Noah that people must not eat an animal's blood because the animal's blood is where the animal's life is. The animal's blood belongs to Yahweh because Yahweh is the one who creates life.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What rules does your community have about how people should treat blood? Where do you think an animal's life is in its body?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:22–27 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells Moses to talk to the Israelites and tell the Israelites what to do.

In the second scene: Yahweh gives instructions about what Israelites are supposed to do with animal fat.

In the third scene: Yahweh warns the Israelites not to eat any blood.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the Israelites, including the disobedient Israelites

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In scene one, Yahweh gives Moses instructions to tell the Israelites. The instructions about the offerings were instructions that Yahweh told Moses to tell to Aaron and Aaron's sons. But now Yahweh is telling Moses the instructions that all of the Israelites need to hear and understand. It is important to remember that Moses is still just listening to Yahweh's instructions. Moses has not told the Israelites these instructions yet. It is important to remember that the instructions that Yahweh is giving Moses are serious instructions.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you tell your entire community about instructions that people need to follow? How will you tell this story so that it is clear that Yahweh is giving instructions to Moses to tell all of the Israelites and not only Aaron and Aaron's sons? Pause this audio here.

In scene two, Yahweh tells Moses the instructions the Israelites need to follow when the Israelites eat cattle, sheep, or goats as food. When the Israelites eat those animals, the Israelites need to be careful not to eat any of the fat. It is important to remember that the priests burn the fat from cattle, sheep, and goats on the altar as part of an offering to Yahweh. If a person eats that fat, the person is stealing what belongs to Yahweh.

If an animal is already dead or if another animal attacks the animal and kills it, then the Israelites could not offer the animal to Yahweh, so the Israelites could use the fat for other things. Yahweh says again that the Israelites cannot eat the fat, even if the animal died because the animal was old or sick or because another animal had killed it.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time when a wild animal attacked one of the animals in your community. What did the dead animal look like? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says again that the Israelites can never eat the fat of any animal that the Israelites can offer to Yahweh. This is a summary that explains that Yahweh is still talking about the cattle, sheep, and goats that Yahweh talked about at the beginning of the story. Since the priest burns the fat of cattle, sheep, and goats on the altar, everyone knew that the Israelites could sacrifice cattle, sheep, and goats as a fire offering. If a person eats the fat of one of these animals, the community will cut off that person.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will show that in this story, Yahweh is talking about the animals that people can offer to Yahweh in one of the fire offerings, or offerings that priests burn. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and remind each other of how you will say that the community will cut off that person, or remove that person from the Israelite community. Pause this audio here.

In scene three, Yahweh warns the Israelites about what will happen if the Israelites eat any of the blood. It is important to remember that the animal's blood also belonged to Yahweh, so if a person ate the blood, it was like stealing from Yahweh. No matter where an Israelite lives, Yahweh does not allow the Israelites to eat the blood of any bird or other animal. This rule is very serious and important. It is so serious that the community will cut off anyone who breaks the rule, just like the community will cut off anyone who eats the fat of the animals that people sacrificed to Yahweh.

Stop here and look again, as needed, at the picture of the animals hanging so that the blood drains from the animal. Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:22–27 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the Israelites, including the disobedient Israelites

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

It is important to remember that Yahweh is telling Moses to give these instructions to the Israelites, so the Israelites were not actually eating these animals while Yahweh was talking to Moses. You may still act out the Israelites eating or not eating the animals in order to remember the story well.

The story begins as Yahweh tells Moses to tell the Israelites more instructions.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I want Moses to understand how important these instructions are; or
  • I want to make sure all of the Israelites follow these rules.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I need to make sure that all of the Israelites follow these instructions; or
  • Why are these instructions for all of the Israelites and not just for Aaron and Aaron's descendants?
Continue the drama.

Yahweh instructs the Israelites not to eat the fat of cattle, sheep, or goats. Show how some of the animals die from sickness or old age, or because a wild animal attacked the animal.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing the Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people may answer things like:

  • I was planning on sacrificing that animal to Yahweh, but now I cannot; or
  • I am excited that I can use this fat to make things we need in our house.
Continue the drama.

A disobedient Israelite goes to eat some of the fat from the animals, and the rest of the Israelites force the disobedient Israelite to leave the group and not come back.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing the Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people may answer things like:

  • I am so angry that person stole from Yahweh! That person deserves this punishment; or
  • I am sad that the person has to leave the community now, but that person disobeyed Yahweh's rules.
Continue the drama.

The Israelites act out draining the blood from birds and other animals, so the Israelites do not eat any blood. A disobedient Israelite eats some of the blood, and the rest of the Israelites force the disobedient Israelite to leave.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing the Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people may answer things like:

  • The animal's blood belongs to Yahweh! I am so angry that the disobedient Israelite took what belongs to Yahweh! or
  • We are never supposed to eat an animal's blood. Why did the disobedient Israelite think this was a good idea? Now we need to punish that Israelite.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 7:22–27 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this story, the narrator uses the name Yahweh. It is important to remember that Yahweh is God's name. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh as you used in previous passages.

The word Israelites means all of the people who descended from a man whose name was Israel. The Israelites were God's people, and the rules in the Book of Leviticus are about how the Israelites were supposed to live. For more information about the Israelites, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for the Israelites as you used in previous passages.

An animal's fat is the thick white substance on animal meat. Use the same word or phrase for fat as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and look at the pictures of animal fat again as a group as needed. Pause this audio here.

The animals in this story are sheep, goats, and cattle. It is important to remember that these are the animals that people would sacrifice to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase to describe these animals as you used in previous passages. Remember that cattle is a general word that includes female cows, bulls, and oxen.

The phrase "found dead" talks about animals that people and other animals did not kill. The animals might die because the animals are old or because the animals are sick.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for found dead. Pause this audio here.

The phrase wild animals talks about animals that do not work with people. Wild animals do not provide milk, meat, transportation, or any other kind of help. Wild animals attack the animals that belong to people. Wild animals are dangerous.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for wild animals. If you have already translated this phrase in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The Israelites are not supposed to eat the fat of any animal that people can offer as a fire offering. It is important to remember that people can sacrifice cattle, sheep, goats, and birds as fire offerings. Here, this term is not talking about a specific kind of offering, but it is instead talking about every kind of offering that the priests would burn on the altar. The meat would cook on the altar just like how people cook meat on fire for their own food, so sometimes people call this offering an "offering by fire." Use the same word or phrase for fire offering as you used in previous passages.

The phrase cut off from their people either means that the community killed the disobedient person or forced the disobedient person to leave and never come back. This was one of the most severe punishments that the Israelites had. Use the same word or phrase for cut off from their people that you used in previous passages.

The phrase wherever you live is a way to say that this rule applies to every Israelite in every place. It does not matter where the Israelites live or what the Israelites do. Yahweh does not allow the Israelites to eat the blood.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for wherever you live. If you have already translated this phrase in another book of the Bible, use the same word or phrase that you have used there.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
