title: Leviticus 9:1–7
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 9:1–7 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:1–7 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:1–7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In Leviticus, Yahweh has been giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. During this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai. The Israelites recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. In the previous passages, Moses has been doing the ceremony that officially makes Aaron and Aaron's sons into Yahweh's priests. Once Moses finished this ordination ceremony, the priests could start doing their priestly duties and do religious tasks. This passage starts on the eighth day, one week after the start of the ordination ceremony. Here, Moses gives Aaron and the Israelite elders instructions from Yahweh for what sacrifices the priests must offer to complete the ordination ceremony. This is the first time that Aaron actually does the sacrifices that Yahweh had commanded in the previous chapters.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what do you do to officially recognize someone who will do a special task or hold a certain role? Describe the process. Pause this audio here.

In this story, Moses asks Aaron to bring a young male bull for a sin, or purification, offering. A young male bull is an animal that is old enough to become a father, but still young. Some scholars think that this bull would be one year old, like some of the other animals in the passage. Others think that the bull was a three-year-old bull. We do not know, but it is probably a physically mature bull that was still fairly young.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a young male bull. If you have not done so yet, stop and discuss what word you could use for a bull that is between one and three years old. Pause this audio here.

The purification offering is usually for someone who accidentally sins or does something to make themselves ritually unclean. In this case, Yahweh considers the whole assembly or all the Israelite people as ritually dirty. This ceremony is to make all the Israelite people ritually clean so that the Israelites can begin to have a relationship with Yahweh. Yahweh had told Moses that Yahweh would appear to the Israelites on that day, and the sin or purification offering helped the Israelites be prepared for Yahweh to appear to them.

Aaron must also bring a ram, which is an adult male sheep, for a burnt offering. Even though Moses has already purified Aaron and Aaron's sons to be priests, Yahweh still requires Aaron to offer a purification offering and a burnt offering for Aaron. Aaron must make these offerings before Yahweh will allow Aaron to offer sacrifices for the entire Israelite community. When Aaron makes the sacrifices for the Israelite people, Aaron makes atonement for the Israelites, which means Aaron does what is necessary to bring the Israelites back to Yahweh. Aaron makes the purification offering to make sure that Aaron is pure and fit to worship Yahweh. Aaron makes the burnt offering to show that Aaron is fully devoted to Yahweh. Yahweh only wants leaders who are right with Yahweh and fully devoted to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what pressures keep leaders from dealing with their own areas of weakness or sin? How common is it for leaders to admit publicly that the leaders are not right with Yahweh? Pause this audio here.

There is an interesting connection here to things that happened in the past. You will remember that when the Israelite people came out of Egypt, Aaron had made a golden calf idol for the Israelites. Now, before Aaron can take his role as priest to serve Yahweh, Aaron's first sacrifice is of a young male bull. Not only that, but the sacrifice is specifically for Aaron's own sin. In a similar way, the second animal Aaron must sacrifice for Aaron's own burnt offering is a ram or adult male sheep. This adult male sheep might remind the Israelite people of the story of Abraham, when Yahweh provided an animal for Abraham to sacrifice. The young male sheep might remind the Israelite people of the Passover. Just like during the Passover, the blood covers the Israelites' sins and makes Yahweh's anger turn away.

Moses also tells Aaron to tell the Israelite elders, or leaders, to bring animals for offerings. The Israelite leaders must bring a male goat for a sin or purification offering, as well as a calf and a lamb, which is a young male sheep. Both the calf and the lamb must be a year old and physically perfect. The calf and lamb will be burnt offerings for the Israelite people.

The Israelite leaders must also bring animals for fellowship offerings. The assembly or Israelite leaders must bring a ram and an ox. We know from other passages that the ox could be either a male bull, a female cow, or a castrated male bull. A castrated male bull is a male bull that people have changed so that the bull cannot make offspring. Try to use a word that could refer to a male bull or a female cow. However, if you must choose one, use the male form of the word here. In the original language, the storyteller used a word that means larger cattle in general, and it was one of these larger cattle that the people were to use for the fellowship offering.

The Israelite leaders must also bring a grain offering, which is flour that people mix with oil. Aaron and the Israelite leaders bring all these items for the offerings to the front of the Tent of Meeting. There, Moses instructs Aaron to follow Yahweh's instructions so that Yahweh's glory, or majesty, can appear to the people. Aaron must sacrifice Aaron's purification offering and burnt offering. Then Aaron must make the offerings for the Israelites. In this way, Aaron will make atonement for Aaron and the Israelites, just as Yahweh commanded. When Aaron makes atonement for himself and the Israelites, they will be able to have a good relationship with Yahweh, and Yahweh can be close to the people.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:1–7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Moses told Aaron, the priests, and the elders of Israel the instructions for how to do the first offerings. First, Aaron must sacrifice a sin or purification offering and a burnt offering for himself. Then the elders of Israel had to offer four sacrifices: a purification offering, a burnt offering, a fellowship offering, and a grain offering. Then Yahweh would come to the Israelites in a special way.

In the second scene: Moses, Aaron, the priests, and the elders of Israel all came together at the Tent of Meeting with all the animals for the offerings. Then Moses said some important words. Moses told all the people there that Yahweh told these people to make these offerings so that Yahweh could come near to them and show them Yahweh's power. Then Moses told Aaron to make the sacrifices for Aaron and for the people of Israel, so that Aaron could make atonement for everyone.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • The priests, whom people also call the sons of Aaron
  • The elders of Israel
  • Yahweh
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The Israelite people were still camped at the bottom of Mount Sinai. Yahweh was giving Moses and Aaron many laws, instructions, and rules for how the Israelite people could live and please Yahweh. For the last seven days, Moses has been leading the people through the ceremony or ordination of the priests. These ceremonial sacrifices in this passage happen at the end of the ceremony of the ordination service.

In the first scene, Moses told Aaron, the priests, and the elders of Israel the instructions for how to do the first offerings. These events happened on the eighth day of the ordination ceremony. For the last seven days, the Israelites have been celebrating the ordination of the priests. These offerings are part of the ceremony before the priests begin their regular duties around the Tent of Meeting.

Stop here and discuss: Try to think of a story where someone told people what to do, and then the people did what the people were supposed to do. Pay attention to the language you use to describe the instructions, and then how you repeat the instructions as you tell about people doing those things. You will need a similar structure for this passage, where Moses gave instructions, and then everyone followed the instructions. Pause this audio here.

Moses called together Aaron, Aaron's sons, and the elders of Israel. This was a formal way to ask these people to all come together for an important meeting.

Stop here and discuss: Think about a time someone formally invited you to an important event, meeting, or ceremony. In your language, take turns telling each other your stories. Notice what words you use to talk about someone inviting you and to talk about what happened or what people said at the event or meeting. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller uses the phrase "the sons of Aaron" to refer to the priests. Since Yahweh only allowed descendants of Aaron to be priests, this means that all of the priests were related to Aaron. This did not just mean Aaron's sons, but could also refer to Aaron's grandsons, great-grandsons, and later generations. Yahweh only allowed males to be priests.

The elders of Israel were older men in the community whom the community honored due to the elders' age, wisdom, and importance in the families or clans of Israel. The elders met with Moses, Aaron, and the priests in the assembly, which was a special group that met together to make important decisions for all the people of Israel.

Here are the instructions that Moses gave to the assembly. First, Aaron must sacrifice a purification offering and a burnt offering for Aaron. For the purification offering, Aaron must offer a young male bull. The original language says a bull, a son of the herd. This does not tell us how old the bull is, but the bull is probably still young yet old enough to reproduce or to have offspring.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a bull. Pause this audio here.

For the burnt offering, Aaron had to offer an adult male sheep.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of an adult male sheep or ram. Pause this audio here.

All of the animals for these sacrifices needed to be perfect. This means that the animals cannot be sick or have any physical problems, injuries, or unusual features. The priest must sacrifice all the animals "before Yahweh," which means at the altar of burnt offering in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting.

Then the leaders of Israel had to bring four offerings: a purification offering, a burnt offering, a peace or fellowship offering, and a grain offering. For the purification offering for all of Israel, the assembly had to offer a young male goat.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a young male goat. Pause this audio here.

For the burnt offering, the assembly had to offer a young male bull and a young male sheep. These animals were supposed to be about a year old and perfect. For the fellowship offering, the assembly had to offer a ram, or an adult male sheep, and one large ox. We know from other passages that this could be either a male bull, a female cow, or a castrated male bull, which is a male bull that cannot have offspring. Try to use a word that could refer to either a male bull or a female cow. However, if you must choose one, use the male form of the word here.

Stop here and discuss: What words does your language use to make a difference between the males and the females of herding animals? Pause this audio here.

The assembly also had to offer a grain offering of flour that a person had mixed with olive oil.

After these instructions, the leaders of the Israelites followed the instructions. The leaders brought all the animals and the grain and oil mixture to the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting for the offerings. The assembly of Moses, Aaron, the priests, and the elders of Israel, who represented the Israelite families, did this.

Then Moses said two very important things. Moses told the assembly of Israelites that Yahweh told the Israelites to do these things so that Yahweh would appear to the Israelites in Yahweh's glory. In the original language, glory means "weight" or "heaviness." It means "importance" or "honor." Bible narrators often use this word to refer to how a king shows the king's power and greatness.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, describe someone with a lot of importance or wealth. Notice what words you use to describe this person. Pause this audio here.

Moses told the people that Yahweh would appear to the people. This means Yahweh will present himself or make Yahweh known. Yahweh would reveal who Yahweh was to the assembly. People do not just come to know Yahweh; Yahweh must reveal or show himself to people. It may be helpful to talk about Yahweh introducing or presenting himself, or showing Yahweh's greatness.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, how does someone introduce themselves? Are there any important ceremonies, such as at a wedding, where someone presents another person in an important way? What words do you use to describe a person who is making a big entrance? Pause this audio here.

Then Moses told Aaron that Aaron needed to sacrifice the offerings for Aaron's own atonement and the offerings for the Israelite people's atonement. This refers to all the people of Israel.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:1–7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • The priests, whom people also call the sons of Aaron
  • The elders of Israel
  • Yahweh
  • And all of the Israelite people

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Moses tells Aaron, the priests, and the elders of Israel the instructions for how to do the first offerings. First, Aaron must sacrifice a sin or purification offering and a burnt offering for Aaron. Then the leaders of Israel must bring four offerings: a purification offering, a burnt offering, a fellowship offering, and a grain offering. Then Yahweh will come to these people in a special way.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I must offer sacrifices for my own sin before I can atone for other people's sin. I feel sad that we have all disobeyed Yahweh, but thankful that Yahweh has given us a way to have a good relationship with Yahweh again; or
  • As I sacrifice the bull for my offering, I remember how I once led the people in worship of a golden calf idol. I feel ashamed when I remember how I disobeyed and dishonored Yahweh; or
  • Yahweh is so great and mighty. I have a big responsibility to the community and to Yahweh to do what is right.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Moses, Aaron, the priests, and the elders of Israel all come together at the Tent of Meeting with all the animals for the sacrifices. Then Moses says some important words. Moses tells all the people there that Yahweh told those people to make these offerings so that Yahweh could come near to the people and show the people Yahweh's power. Then Moses tells Aaron to make the sacrifices for Aaron and for the people of Israel, so that Aaron could make atonement for everyone.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am excited that I will be close to my people and can show them who I am; or
  • I hope the Israelite leaders understand how important this is; or
  • I am pleased that the Israelites are listening to the instructions that I gave to Moses.

Ask the person playing all the Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am grateful that Aaron and our elders are doing these sacrifices for us! Now I know Yahweh will come to live with us; or
  • I am relieved that there is a way now for us to be close to Yahweh.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:1–7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Moses gave instructions to Aaron, Aaron's sons, and the elders of Israel. The elders of Israel are a group of older men who were the heads of different clans or family groups based on family relationship and family line. These older men represented their families at important religious ceremonies and made important decisions for all the Israelite people. When this group of priests and elders met together for a special purpose, people called it the "assembly." For more information on "elders and Israel," refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same phrases for "elders of Israel" and assembly as you used in previous passages.

Yahweh chose Aaron and Aaron's descendants to be the priests of Israel. Yahweh appointed Aaron and Aaron's sons as priests on this day. Use the same word or phrase for sons as you have used previously, and refer to sons in the Master Glossary for more information.

For Aaron's sin or purification offering, Aaron was supposed to sacrifice a young male bull. A young bull is an animal that is physically mature and able to reproduce offspring, but is still young. This bull should be perfect, or without any problems. Use the same words or phrases for bull, sin or purification offering, and perfect as you used previously. For more information about the purification offering and perfect, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and, as a group, look again at a picture of a young bull as needed. Pause this audio here.

For Aaron's burnt offering, Aaron was supposed to sacrifice a perfect ram, or adult male sheep. Use the same word or phrase for burnt offering as you used previously. Burnt offering is in the Master Glossary.

In this passage, Yahweh commanded the assembly to bring a young male goat for the purification offering for all the people of Israel. The young male goat was probably about a year old, still young but old enough to reproduce. Use the same word for "young male goat" as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a young male goat. Pause this audio here.

Then the assembly was supposed to sacrifice another young male bull and a male lamb, or young sheep, as a burnt offering for all of Israel. Both the bull and the lamb should be one year old and also perfect. Use the same words for "young bull" and "male lamb" or "young male sheep" as you used in previous passages.

For the fellowship offering, the Israelite leaders had to bring an ox and another adult male sheep, or ram, that were perfect. An ox can be any kind of cattle, such as a male bull or a female cow of any age. Use the same word for ox and ram as you used in previous passages. Use the same word for fellowship offering as you have used previously, and refer to peace or fellowship offering in the Master Glossary for more information.

Aaron must bring these animals to sacrifice before Yahweh. Use the same word for sacrifice and for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on sacrifice and Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Israelites must also bring a grain offering mixed with olive oil. Use the same words for grain offering and olive oil as you used in previous passages. For more information on grain offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Use the same word for Tent of Meeting as you used in previous passages. For more information on "Tent of Meeting," refer to tabernacle in the Master Glossary.

Moses says that Aaron and the Israelites must do these things so that Yahweh will show the people Yahweh's glory, or power.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for glory. If you have used this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word here. For more information on glory, refer to the Master Glossary. Pause this audio here.

Moses tells Aaron to make atonement for the Israelite people, which means to restore the relationship between Yahweh and the people. For more information on atonement, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same phrase for atonement as you used in previous passages.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 9:8–14
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 9:8–14 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:8–14 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:8–14 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Through Leviticus, Yahweh has been giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai. The Israelites had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Now the narrator continues the story of when the Israelites celebrated the ordination of Aaron and Aaron's sons as priests.

In the previous passage, Moses told Aaron and the Israelite leaders Yahweh's instructions for how to do the initiation or ordination ceremony so that the priests could start doing priestly duties and perform religious tasks. In the last passage, one week of the ordination ceremony had passed, and Moses gave Aaron Yahweh's instructions on what offerings to make to complete the ordination ceremony for the priests. Now, in this passage, this was the first time that Aaron began doing the sacrifices that Yahweh had commanded in the previous passages. Specifically, we hear in this passage how Aaron did the two sacrifices that Aaron needed to do to make Aaron ritually clean. Aaron had to make a sin or purification offering, and Aaron had to make a burnt offering. Aaron needed to do these offerings first, before Aaron began to make atonement for other people and the whole community.

There is an interesting connection here to things that happened in the past. When the Israelite people came out of Egypt, Aaron had made the Israelites a golden calf idol and told the people to worship the idol. Now, before Aaron could take Aaron's role as priest to serve Yahweh, Aaron's first sacrifice was of a young male bull. This sacrifice showed that Aaron was ritually clean. This sacrifice was also a way for Aaron to recognize Aaron's own sin and failures to obey Yahweh's commands. Perhaps some of the older people remembered the golden calf as the people saw their new priest killing the young bull and offering the bull to Yahweh. Throughout the Israelite people's time in the wilderness, sometimes Aaron made bad leadership decisions. This ceremony was a chance for Aaron to be ritually clean again and to even be an example for the Israelite people to follow. Aaron's priesthood is a reminder that Yahweh's forgiveness can make ritually dirty people clean again. If a person is ritually dirty, it does not mean that person is physically dirty. It means that the person has done something that does not allow the person to worship with the rest of the Israelite people.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Imagine being an ancient Israelite and seeing Aaron kill the young bull, cut it up, and smear the bull's blood on the altar. How would you react? What would you think or say to others? Pause this audio here.

In a similar way, Aaron also must sacrifice a burnt offering for himself. The animal that Aaron must kill is a ram or adult male sheep. This adult male sheep might have reminded the Israelite people of the story of Abraham, when Yahweh provided an animal for Abraham to sacrifice instead of Abraham's son. People in Abraham's time knew that people needed to bring a sacrifice and blood to receive forgiveness from Yahweh. But Yahweh did something surprising, because Yahweh did not require Abraham to bring a sacrifice. Instead, Yahweh gave Abraham exactly what Abraham needed so that Yahweh could forgive Abraham. This was another way that Yahweh had shown that Yahweh was not like the pretend gods or idols that the other people groups worshipped.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what do people believe about forgiveness? When does someone need forgiveness? How does a person ask for that forgiveness? How does someone show that they have forgiven the other people?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:8–14 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Aaron offers the sin or purification offering for himself. Aaron sacrifices the young male bull. Aaron's sons give Aaron the blood of the bull. Aaron dips his finger in the bull's blood and puts the blood on the horns of the altar. Aaron takes certain internal organs from the animal and burns the pieces on the altar. Then Aaron carries the rest of the dead bull's body outside the camp to burn it.

In the second scene: Aaron offers the burnt offering for himself. Aaron kills the ram, or adult male sheep. Aaron's sons give Aaron the blood of the ram. Aaron splashes the ram's blood on the sides of the altar. Aaron's sons give Aaron parts of the body of the dead ram, and Aaron burns the parts one by one. Aaron washes the internal organs and the legs, and also burns those parts.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Aaron
  • Aaron's sons, the priests
  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the assembly of Israelites, though the storyteller does not mention the assembly in this part of the story

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The Israelite people were still camped at the bottom of Mount Sinai. Yahweh has given Moses and Aaron many laws, instructions, and rules for how the Israelite people could live and please Yahweh. For the last seven days, Moses has been leading the people through the process of the ordination of the priests. The purification offering and burnt offerings that Aaron sacrifices in this passage happen at the end of the ordination service, on the eighth day.

The beginning of this passage is a transition. The previous passage gave Moses' instructions and an overview or summary of what would happen next. But this is where Aaron follows the instructions and does what Yahweh wants Aaron to do.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, when you tell a story or narrative, how do you transition from telling information about what should happen and start telling the details of what actually happened? Pause this audio here.

In the first scene, Aaron offers the purification offering for himself. The storyteller says Aaron "comes" to the altar. This means Aaron approaches the altar. The altar that the storyteller mentions here is the altar of burnt offering in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, talk about someone walking close to an important person or an important place. What words do you use to talk about how that person comes close to the important person or place? Pause this audio here.

Aaron kills a young male bull for Aaron's purification offering. The young male bull was probably about a year old. The bull was still young but already old enough to have babies. We know from other passages that when a priest made these sacrifices, someone, probably another priest, would catch the animal's blood in a bowl of some kind. In this passage, Aaron's sons are probably the ones who catch the animal's blood, since Aaron's sons are the ones who give Aaron the container of bull's blood.

Aaron's sons give Aaron the blood of the bull in a bowl. Some translations use a special word to show that Aaron's sons give this container to Aaron in a ceremonial way.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what are the most common ceremonies? What kind of special actions do people do in these ceremonies? What kind of special words do people say in these ceremonies? Pause this audio here.

Aaron dips the index finger of Aaron's right hand in the bull's blood and puts some of the blood on the horns of the altar. Aaron also pours out the rest of the blood at the bottom or base of the altar of burnt offering.

Stop here and look at pictures of the altar of burnt offering as a group. Pause this audio here.

Then Aaron has to remove certain parts of the bull's dead body or carcass. Aaron removes all the fat that covers and surrounds the internal organs of the bull, the two kidneys and the fat on them, and the best part of the liver.

Stop here and look at pictures of the internal organs that Aaron removes for the offering. Pause this audio here.

Aaron burns these pieces on the altar of burnt offering. Then Aaron is probably the person who carries the rest of the dead bull's body through the camp to a certain ritually clean place outside the camp where the priests dump ashes. There, Aaron burns the bull's flesh and hide, which are the rest of the bull's meat and the skin of the bull.

In the second scene, Aaron offers a ram, or adult male sheep, for the burnt offering for himself. Though the storyteller does not say "ram" here, we know it is a ram from previous passages where Moses told Aaron to bring a ram for a burnt offering. Aaron kills the ram. Just like for the other sacrifice, someone must catch the blood of the sacrifice in a container. Again, since the storyteller mentions Aaron's sons earlier in the passage, it is probably Aaron's sons who do this while Aaron kills the ram. Aaron's sons give Aaron the blood of the ram in a special way. Aaron throws the ram's blood on the sides of the altar.

Aaron's sons give Aaron parts of the body of the dead ram, including the head, and Aaron burns each body part one by one. Aaron washes the internal organs and the legs, and also burns those parts on top of the rest of the offering.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:8–14 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Aaron
  • Aaron's sons, the priests
  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the assembly of Israelites, though the storyteller does not mention the assembly in this part of the story

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Aaron offers the sin or purification offering for himself. Aaron sacrifices the young male bull. Aaron's sons give Aaron the blood of the bull. Aaron dips his finger in the bull's blood and puts the blood on the horns of the altar. Aaron takes certain internal organs from the animal and burns the pieces on the altar. Then Aaron may be the person who carries the rest of the dead bull's body outside the camp to burn the body.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am ashamed that I have to carry a bloody carcass through the streets; or
  • Leaders must show people how to become ritually clean again.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Aaron offers the burnt offering for himself. Aaron kills the ram or adult male sheep. Aaron's sons give Aaron the blood of the ram. Aaron splashes the ram's blood on the sides of the altar. Aaron's sons give Aaron parts of the body of the dead ram, and Aaron burns each body part one by one. Aaron washes the internal organs and the legs and also burns those parts.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing one of the sons of Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am humbled to see my father atone for his own ritual dirtiness; or
  • I am honored to be part of this ceremony; or
  • I wonder what it will be like doing this every day.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:8–14 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Aaron must sacrifice at an altar. This is the altar of the burnt offering. This altar has horns. Use the same words for altar, burnt offering, and horns as you used in previous passages. For more information on altar and burnt offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and, as a group, look again at a picture of the altar of burnt offering as needed. Pause this audio here.

The first offering that Aaron had to make was a sin or purification offering for himself. Use the same word or phrase for purification offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on "purification offering," refer to the Master Glossary.

For Aaron's purification offering, Aaron had to kill a young male bull. This word refers to an animal that is physically mature and able to have babies, but still young. Use the same word for bull and for killing an animal as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and, as a group, look again at a picture of a bull as needed. Pause this audio here.

Aaron had to dip or put his finger into the blood so Aaron could smear the blood on the horns of the altar. Use the same words or phrases for dip and smear, and for the horns of the altar, as you used in previous passages.

Aaron also had to pour the rest of the blood out of a container onto the base, or bottom, of the altar. Use the same description for pouring the blood onto the base of the altar that you have used in previous passages.

Aaron burned the fat, the kidneys and their fat, and the best part of the liver from the bull for the purification offering on top of the altar. Then Aaron burned the hide or skin, and the flesh of the animal outside the camp. Use the same words and phrases for these parts of the animal, and for the Israelite camp, as you have used previously.

Aaron did the things that Yahweh commanded Moses to do. Use the same word for Yahweh that you have used previously, and remember that Yahweh is in the Master Glossary.

For the burnt offering, Aaron had to sacrifice a ram, which is an adult male sheep. The narrator does not mention the ram in this passage, but if it is necessary in your language, you can include it. Use the same word for adult male sheep as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and look at a picture of an adult male sheep or ram as a group. Pause this audio here.

Aaron had to sprinkle or throw the blood from the burnt offering onto the sides of the altar. Use the same word for sprinkle or throw blood on the side of the altar as you used in previous passages.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 9:15–24
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 9:15–24 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:15–24 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:15–24 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

At this part of the story, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai. The Israelites had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. In the last passage, Aaron began to offer the sacrifices for the ordination ceremony so that the priests could start doing their priestly duties and perform religious tasks. This part of the story starts right after Aaron presented the offerings for Aaron in the last passage. This ceremony is the first time that Aaron does the sacrifices that Yahweh had commanded the priests to do. The people who are present at this ceremony are the assembly, which in this case is probably a special gathering of the priests and all the elders of Israel who represent all the people. The elders of Israel were usually older men, who represented the different family lines and groups within the people of Israel.

Aaron offers the sin or purification offering, the burnt offering, the grain offering, and the fellowship offering for the people of Israel. Aaron offers these on top of the morning burnt offering. Remember that the morning burnt offering was one of the two burnt offerings that Yahweh told the priests to offer every day. Notice that for Aaron's first day as a priest, Aaron offers most of the different kinds of offerings, and several kinds of ritually clean animals. The purpose of this ceremony is to make the whole community of Israel ritually clean. The focus right now is not on the ritual cleansing of individual sins, but of the whole community's sins. These offerings also dedicate the people of Israel to relationship with Yahweh and to worship of Yahweh. Lastly, the offerings allow a special way for the people of Israel to receive Yahweh's blessing.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what do people think is different between the sin that one person might commit and the sin of the whole community? In your culture, when do you ritually clean yourself only, and when do you ritually clean yourselves as a community? Which is more common? How do you and your community make yourselves ritually clean? Pause this audio here.

After Aaron gives the purification offering, the burnt offering, and the grain offering, Aaron kills the ox and the ram for the fellowship offering. Aaron's sons give Aaron the animals' blood and Aaron sprinkles or throws the sacrificed animal's blood on the sides of the altar. Aaron cuts certain internal organs out of the dead animals. Aaron removes the fatty part of the tail and all the fat that covers and surrounds the internal organs. Aaron removes the two kidneys and the fat on the kidneys. Aaron also removes the fatty part of the liver. Aaron's sons place these parts on the animal's breast pieces and then Aaron burns the fatty pieces on the altar.

Aaron probably only had to offer the fatty part of the tail of the ram, not of the ox. Aaron also offers a wave offering by moving the breasts and the right thigh in a certain way before Yahweh. This is not really a separate offering; it is a part of the ceremonial process.

Aaron blesses the people of Israel after Aaron finishes offering the sacrifices. When a person blesses another person, it means that the person asks Yahweh for safety, health, wisdom, or to provide what the other person needs. Sometimes, people talked about blessing as "asking for peace." In the Old Testament, people often use the word "peace" to refer to a life of wholeness, calm, and safety.

Then Moses and Aaron go into the Tent of Meeting. This is a reminder to the rest of the assembly. Even though the purpose of all the laws and rules is so that the people can be close to Yahweh, there is still a separation between Yahweh and the people. The only people who can go between Yahweh and the people in this special way are the priests.

When Moses and Aaron come out of the Tent of Meeting, Moses and Aaron bless the people of Israel again.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What does peace mean in your culture? What do people think would be the perfect life? How is this the same or different from the peace that Yahweh offers us? Pause this audio here.

After Moses and Aaron give the second blessing, Yahweh shows his glory to the Israelites. Yahweh's presence makes fire that comes down and completely burns up the burnt offering and the pieces of fat. In response, the people of Israel shout all together. It is unclear whether the Israelites shout as part of the ceremony, as a celebration, or if the Israelites are terrified or very scared of what Yahweh had done. The Israelites fall on their faces, which means the Israelites bow to show respect, honor, and worship. When the people bowed in this way, their faces touched the ground. This is how the Israelite people would worship Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you show great respect and honor in your culture?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:15–24 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Aaron offers the purification offering, the burnt offering, and the grain offering for the people of Israel. Then Aaron kills the ox and the ram for the fellowship offering. Then Aaron sprinkles or throws the sacrificed animal's blood on the sides of the altar. Aaron cuts certain internal organs out of the dead animals and burns those pieces on the altar. Aaron also offers a wave offering by moving some of the pieces of meat in a certain way before Yahweh.

In the second scene: Aaron blesses the people of Israel. Then Moses and Aaron go into the Tent of Meeting. When Moses and Aaron come out of the tent, Moses and Aaron bless the people of Israel again. Then Yahweh's presence makes fire that comes down and burns the burnt offering and the pieces of fat. Then the people of Israel worship Yahweh.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Aaron the priest
  • The people of Israel
  • The assembly of people who represent the Israelites
  • Aaron's sons, the priests
  • Moses
  • And Yahweh

The storyteller also mentions how Aaron gives the burnt offering, which requires a young male bull and a young male sheep, but the storyteller does not mention the animals in this passage.

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The Israelite people are still camped at the bottom of Mount Sinai. Yahweh was giving Moses and Aaron many laws, instructions, and rules for how the Israelite people should live and please Yahweh. For the last seven days, Moses has been leading the people through the ordination of the priests. Aaron makes the sacrifices in this passage at the end of the ordination ceremony.

In the first scene, Aaron offers the purification offering, the burnt offering, and the grain offering for the people of Israel. Aaron offers these on top of the normal morning burnt offering.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your language, how do you talk about order of events? Every time you listen to the passage, think about ways that you can talk about the order of the offerings in a way that will make sense to the listener. As you listen, tell each other what you notice in the story. Pause this audio here.

First, Aaron kills the goat for the purification offering for the Israelite people. Aaron does this right after Aaron offers the purification offering and the burnt offering for himself. You may want to use language that makes it clear that Aaron does this immediately after the other two offerings. The storyteller says that Aaron offers this purification offering in a similar way to how Aaron offered a purification offering for himself.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your language, what information about the offering process is helpful to repeat? What is the best way to compare this purification offering to Aaron's purification offering? Pause this audio here.

For the people's purification offering, Aaron offers a young male goat. Aaron slaughters or kills the goat in the proper way and follows the proper instructions for how to sprinkle or splash the animal's blood and burn certain internal organs of the dead animal.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a young male goat. Pause this audio here.

Next, Aaron offers the burnt offering for the people of Israel, which is a young male bull and a young male sheep. These animals are supposed to be about a year old. Some translations say Aaron brings or presents these animals. This means that Aaron ceremonially brings the animals forward before Aaron kills the animals. Although the storyteller does not mention the animals in the passage, you may want to mention that Aaron kills the young male bull and the young male sheep for the burnt offering.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a young male bull and a young male sheep. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says Aaron offers the burnt offering according to Yahweh's "ordinance," or instructions. This means that Aaron follows Yahweh's instructions or rules that Yahweh gave earlier in Leviticus.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your language, talk about a process or a cultural ceremony that is familiar to anyone from your culture. Notice the words, phrases, and patterns of speech you use when you talk about the process or ceremony the first time, and how you talk about it in a similar way or a different way when you talk about it again. Pause this audio here.

Next, Aaron takes a handful of the grain offering and burns the grain in the fire on the same altar as the burnt offering. For this grain offering, a person had to grind wheat into a fine flour and mix it with oil.

For the people of Israel's fellowship offering, Aaron offers an adult male sheep, or ram, and one large ox. We know from other passages that this ox could be either a male bull, a female cow, or a castrated male bull, which is a male bull that cannot have babies.

Aaron kills the ox and the ram for the fellowship offering. We know from other passages that when a priest made these sacrifices, someone, probably another priest, would catch the animal's blood in a bowl. In this passage, Aaron's sons are probably the ones who caught the animal's blood, since Aaron's sons give Aaron the container of bull's blood.

Aaron's sons give Aaron some of the animal blood in a container. Some translations use a special word to show that Aaron's sons give this container to Aaron in a ceremonial way.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how do you describe someone doing something in a ceremonial way? In this passage, Aaron does many things in a special way: Aaron presents the animals for sacrifice, Aaron blesses the people in a certain way, Aaron holds up parts of the fellowship offering as a wave offering, and Aaron's sons give Aaron the bowl of blood in a special way. Discuss here what kind of language you can use to show that people do things in a special way. Pause this audio here.

Then Aaron sprinkles or throws the dead animal's blood on the sides of the altar. Either Aaron or Aaron's sons cuts certain internal organs out of the dead animals to burn those pieces on the altar. Aaron removes the fatty part of the tail, as well as all the fat that covers and surrounds the internal organs. Aaron removes the two kidneys and the fat on the kidneys. Aaron also removes the best part of the liver.

Aaron probably only had to take the fatty part of the tail of the ram, not of the ox. Either Aaron or Aaron's sons places these parts on the animal's breast pieces, and then Aaron burns the fatty pieces on the altar.

Aaron also offers a wave offering by moving some of the pieces of meat in a certain way before Yahweh. Aaron waves the breast meat and the right back leg of the ox and the adult male sheep. Sometimes these pieces of meat have special names.

Stop here and, as a group, look at diagrams of bull meat and sheep meat. Discuss what words in your language refer to these cuts of meat. Pause this audio here.

We know that Aaron would do a special motion while Aaron held the breast meat and the right back leg of the ox and the sheep. Aaron would move in a special, ceremonial way. We are not sure exactly how Aaron waved the meat, but Aaron may have held the meat in his hands and then raised and lowered Aaron's arms several times. This was the wave offering.

In the second scene, Aaron blesses the people of Israel. To do this, Aaron lifts his hands. For ancient Israelites, this showed that the person was praying and blessing other people. Then Aaron steps down. Aaron was standing at the altar of burnt offering in front of everyone. It is possible that there were steps or something around the altar of burnt offering, so that the area where Aaron was standing was higher than the areas around it. Aaron steps down out of people's view or away from the altar in some way. But we do not know exactly what it means.

Then Moses and Aaron go into the Tent of Meeting. The storyteller does not tell us what Moses and Aaron do inside. When Moses and Aaron come back out, Moses and Aaron bless the people of Israel again. We do not know if Moses and Aaron did a special gesture or hand motion here, as Aaron did before, because the storyteller does not mention it.

Then Yahweh shows Yahweh's glory to the Israelites. Yahweh's presence makes fire that comes down and completely burns up the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar of burnt offering. Some translations use a word like "suddenly" to show that Yahweh sent fire that appeared out of nowhere and was possibly even loud. Some scholars think that maybe the fire was lightning. It is important that the translation shows that Yahweh sent this fire, but the fire was not Yahweh himself.

Then the people of Israel shout all together. It is unclear whether the Israelites shouted as part of the ceremony, as a celebration, or if the Israelites were terrified or very scared of what Yahweh had done. The Israelites fall on their faces, which means the Israelites bow to show respect and worship to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will describe the way the Israelites shout in your language. Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:15–24 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Aaron the priest
  • The people of Israel
  • The assembly of people who represent the Israelites
  • Aaron's sons, the priests
  • Moses
  • And Yahweh

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Aaron offers the purification offering, the burnt offering, and the grain offering for the people of Israel around the same time as the priests made the daily morning burnt offerings. Then Aaron kills the ox and the ram for the fellowship offering. Aaron's sons give Aaron the dead animal's blood, and then Aaron sprinkles or throws the sacrificed animal's blood on the sides of the altar. Aaron burns certain internal organs from the dead animals on the altar. Aaron also offers a wave offering by moving some of the pieces of meat in a certain way before Yahweh.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing a son of Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I think about how our lives will be different as we begin to do all the things Yahweh has commanded us to do; or
  • It is exciting to think that we are going to be close to Yahweh; or
  • I know the sacrifices purify us before Yahweh, but it still makes me sad that our ritual dirtiness causes so much death.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Aaron lifts his hands and blesses the people of Israel. Then Moses and Aaron go into the Tent of Meeting. When Moses and Aaron come back out, Moses and Aaron bless the people of Israel again. Then Yahweh's presence makes fire that comes down and completely burns up the burnt offering and the pieces of fat. Then the people of Israel shout and fall with their faces to the ground to worship Yahweh.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing a person from the assembly, either a priest or elder, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • Yahweh is incredibly powerful; or
  • Seeing Yahweh's fire makes me very afraid; or
  • If Yahweh blesses us, who can fight against us and win?

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 9:15–24 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh commanded the people of Israel to bring a young male goat for the purification offering. The young male goat was probably about a year old, still young but old enough to have babies. Use the same word or phrase for "young male goat" as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a young male goat. Pause this audio here.

Aaron had to make an offering for the people. The first offering Aaron made was the sin or purification offering for the people of Israel. Use the same words or phrases for a general offering and for the purification offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on offering and purification offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Aaron also had to make a burnt offering for the people of Israel. Use the same word for burnt offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on burnt offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Aaron offered the burnt offering according to Yahweh's ordinance, or Yahweh's instruction. Use the same word or phrase for ordinance as you used in previous passages. For more information about ordinance, refer to the Master Glossary.

Use the same word or phrase for grain offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on grain offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Aaron slaughters, or kills, the animals for the offerings. Use the same word for slaughter or kill as you used in previous passages.

In this passage, Aaron must sacrifice at an altar. This is the altar of the burnt offering. Use the same word for altar as you used in previous passages. For more information on altar, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of the altar of burnt offering. Pause this audio here.

For the fellowship offering, Aaron had to sacrifice another ox. An ox could be a male bull, or it could be a female cow, or it could be a male castrated bull that worked in the fields. Use the same word for ox as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of an ox. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Aaron must sacrifice a ram, which is an adult male sheep, as a fellowship offering. Use the same word for ram or adult male sheep as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of an adult male sheep or ram. Pause this audio here.

Use the same word for peace or fellowship offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on peace or fellowship offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Aaron would sprinkle or throw the blood onto the horns of the altar. Use the same word for sprinkle or throw that you used in previous passages.

Use the same words for the fatty tail, the fat portions, the kidneys and their fat, the best part of the liver, and the breast and thighs of the animals as you used in previous passages.

Aaron took the breast and thighs of the fellowship offering and moved the pieces in a special way before Yahweh. This is a wave offering. Use the same word for wave offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on "wave offering," refer to the Master Glossary.

Aaron lifted his hands and blessed the Israelites. When a person blesses other people, the person is praying that God will do good things for the people.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for bless. Look up bless in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Aaron and Moses went into the Tent of Meeting. Use the same word for "Tent of Meeting" as you used in previous passages. For more information on the Tent of Meeting, refer to tabernacle in the Master Glossary.

Yahweh shows his glory. The glory of Yahweh is something amazing that goes with or shows Yahweh's presence. Sometimes, Yahweh sends a bright light or a big storm. Here, Yahweh sends fire that completely burns up the burnt offering and pieces of fat. Use the same words for Yahweh and glory as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will translate the way that Yahweh shows his glory. Look up glory in the Master Glossary for more information.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
