title: Leviticus 10:1–11
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 10:1–11 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 10:1–11 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 10:1–11 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this section of Leviticus, Moses dedicates Aaron and Aaron's sons as priests, as Yahweh instructed Moses, and the priests start offering sacrifices at the Tent of Meeting. But in this passage, something goes wrong. Just before this, Aaron and Aaron's sons offered sin offerings, burnt offerings, a grain offering, and a peace offering to Yahweh for the people of Israel. Then fire came from Yahweh and burnt up what was left on the altar, which showed that Yahweh approved of the offerings the priests had sacrificed to Yahweh. But then in this passage, Aaron's two oldest sons, Nadab and Abihu, did something wrong.

Nadab and Abihu took their censers, which are pans that people use to carry burning coals or incense when people burn incense as an offering to Yahweh. Nadab and Abihu took these pans and put fire and incense on the pans. Then Nadab and Abihu used these pans to offer what the narrator calls "strange or unauthorized fire" to Yahweh.

Stop here and look at a picture of a censer. Pause this audio here.

Now, no one is sure exactly what offering unauthorized fire means. It is possible that Nadab and Abihu offered the wrong kind of incense instead of following Yahweh's instructions from Exodus 39 about how to prepare incense correctly. Or Nadab and Abihu could have offered incense at the wrong time of day. Or Nadab and Abihu may have burned the incense like people in another foreign religion did, instead of how Yahweh commanded. Most likely, though, Nadab and Abihu were trying to go into the most holy part of the Tent of Meeting, where Yahweh's presence was. Nadab and Abihu probably went when Nadab and Abihu wanted, instead of waiting for the time Yahweh wanted the priests to burn incense. But whatever the problem was, the point is that Nadab and Abihu offered incense in a way that Yahweh had not instructed Nadab and Abihu to offer it.

Stop here and, as an activity, try to think of at least three reasons it would be a bad thing for the priests to serve Yahweh without following Yahweh's instructions for how the priests should serve Yahweh. Pause this audio here.

When Nadab and Abihu did this thing that Yahweh had not commanded Nadab and Abihu to do, fire came from Yahweh and burned Nadab and Abihu to death. Then Moses told Aaron something that Yahweh had said earlier to Moses. Even though this previous conversation between Yahweh and Moses is not in the Bible, Yahweh had apparently told Moses two things earlier. The first was probably about the people who were nearby Yahweh, which means the priests who went close to Yahweh's presence in the Tent of Meeting. These people near Yahweh had to treat Yahweh as holy. But it could possibly mean that Yahweh would prove to those people that Yahweh is holy. And the second thing Yahweh told Moses was that all the people of Israel would honor and respect Yahweh because of how holy and powerful Yahweh is. Basically, Moses was explaining to Aaron that what Yahweh had said before had been a warning. Yahweh was so holy and powerful that the priests could not just do whatever the priests wanted when the priests were serving Yahweh, especially since serving brought the priests very close to Yahweh's presence. The priests had to serve Yahweh exactly how Yahweh had said, especially because the priests had the privilege of being close to Yahweh. Yahweh had given the priests instructions about how the priests could interact with Yahweh without danger. Yahweh is so holy that it is dangerous for a person to interact with Yahweh without following Yahweh's instructions. When Aaron heard Moses's explanation, Aaron stayed silent and did not say anything.

Stop here and discuss as a group: We do not know why Aaron stayed silent. Possibly Aaron was very sad, or possibly Aaron was afraid. In your culture, why do people stay silent in situations like these? Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss these questions as a group: Think about places or things that are holy in your culture. What special things do people have to do to go to those holy places or interact with those holy things? Are there things that are dangerous to do in the holy places or before interacting with those holy things? Pause this audio here.

Moses then called Moses' and Aaron's cousins, Mishael and Elzaphan, to come help. Mishael and Elzaphan were the sons of Moses and Aaron's father's brother. Moses asked Mishael and Elzaphan to carry the bodies of Nadab and Abihu out of the camp where the Israelites were staying. Mishael and Elzaphan needed to remove the bodies from the sanctuary, or holy place, in and around the Tent of Meeting so that the bodies would not make the Tent of Meeting unclean, or ritually dirty. Aaron could not bury Aaron's own sons because Yahweh did not allow the high priest to make himself ritually dirty by touching a dead body, even if it was the body of a close relative. It is unclear why Aaron's cousins had to take care of the bodies instead of Aaron's other sons. It is possible that Aaron's remaining sons had to remain ritually clean so that Aaron's other sons could keep serving Yahweh in the Tent of Meeting. In any case, the cousins, Mishael and Elzaphan, did what Moses asked. Mishael and Elzaphan carried the bodies of Nadab and Abihu by holding onto the tunics Nadab and Abihu were wearing, probably so that Mishael and Elzaphan did not have to directly touch the bodies. Mishael and Elzaphan carried the bodies outside the Israelite camp. Mishael and Elzaphan likely wrapped the bodies in cloth and buried the bodies, based on what Israelites normally did with dead bodies, but the storyteller does not talk about that part.

Stop here and discuss these questions as a group: When somebody dies in your culture, who takes care of the body? Is there anything that person has to do or that the person cannot do because that person has touched a dead body? Pause this audio here.

Next, Moses told Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, not to mourn their dead relatives. Moses said, "Do not let your hair be messy or take off your priestly hats. Do not tear your clothes." These were things that Israelites would have normally done to mourn someone who died. If Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons did not listen to Yahweh and publicly mourned Nadab and Abihu anyway, Aaron and Aaron's sons would die. Yahweh would be angry with the whole Israelite community because of Aaron and Aaron's sons. The rest of the Israelites could mourn for Nadab and Abihu, but if Aaron or Aaron's sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, did, Aaron and Aaron's sons would die. Moses also told Aaron and Aaron's sons not to leave the Tent of Meeting. If Aaron and Aaron's sons left, Aaron and Aaron's sons would die, because the holy oil that Moses had poured on Aaron and Aaron's sons to show that Yahweh had chosen these men as Yahweh's priests was still on these men's bodies. Clearly, Aaron and Aaron's sons did not have to stay in the Tent of Meeting forever, since the priests did not live in the Tent of Meeting. And the priests moved the tent itself every time the Israelites moved camp. However, Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons apparently could not leave the Tent of Meeting early to mourn their relatives. Aaron and Aaron's sons had to stay at the tent and serve Yahweh as long as Aaron and Aaron's sons had planned to. So Aaron and Aaron's sons did just what Moses said. Aaron and Aaron's sons did not leave the Tent of Meeting or mourn for Nadab and Abihu.

Stop here and discuss these questions as a group: When somebody dies in your culture, what do people do to mourn the person who died? What would you think if a close relative of the person who died did not do these things to mourn? Pause this audio here.

Then, Yahweh spoke to Aaron directly. Every other time in Leviticus, Yahweh gave instructions to Aaron by telling the instructions first to Moses. Then Moses would tell the instructions to Aaron. Or Yahweh would talk to Moses and Aaron together. But here, Yahweh spoke directly to Aaron. Yahweh told Aaron that Aaron and Aaron's descendants should never drink wine or any other kind of alcoholic or fermented drink when Aaron or Aaron's descendants came into the Tent of Meeting. Wine is an alcoholic drink that people make from fermented grapes.

If these men came to serve Yahweh after drinking alcohol, these men would die. It is not clear why Yahweh gave this instruction about alcohol right after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu. Possibly, alcohol was part of the reason that Nadab and Abihu had made the bad decision to ignore Yahweh's commands and offer incense the wrong way. Possibly, the Israelites would often drink alcohol when they mourned dead relatives. Whatever the reason, though, Yahweh made sure that Aaron and all of Aaron's descendants would follow this instruction. Yahweh made this instruction a rule for all the generations of priests who would come after Aaron.

The priests had to be sober and alert when the priests came to serve Yahweh at the Tent of Meeting. Then the priests could properly tell the difference between what people had devoted to Yahweh and what people had not devoted to Yahweh. The priests could also tell the difference between what was ritually clean and could be in Yahweh's sanctuary and what was ritually dirty and could not be in Yahweh's sanctuary. For a person to serve Yahweh as a priest involved being really close to Yahweh's presence, which was dangerous because Yahweh was so holy. Alcohol dulls people's senses, and the priests needed to be alert so that the priests could properly follow the instructions Yahweh gave the priests for how to safely serve Yahweh. Then the priests could also make sure that ritually dirty things never came close to holy things.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: If some people in your culture drink alcoholic drinks, how can drinking alcohol affect people's behavior? Are there things people should not do after those people drink because it is not safe? Pause this audio here.

The priests also needed to be alert so that the priests could teach the Israelites all the statutes, or rules, that Yahweh had given the priests through Moses.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 10:1–11 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Aaron's sons, Nadab and Abihu, offer incense to Yahweh the wrong way and Yahweh kills Nadab and Abihu for doing so.

In the second scene: Moses calls Aaron's cousins to bury Nadab and Abihu. Then Moses tells Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons how to respond to Nadab and Abihu's deaths.

In the third scene: Yahweh gives Aaron permanent instructions for Israel's priests about alcohol.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Nadab
  • Abihu
  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • Aaron's cousins Mishael and Elzaphan
  • Aaron's remaining sons, Eleazar and Ithamar
  • Aaron's descendants who would become priests after Aaron
  • And the assembly of people who represent the Israelites, although the storyteller does not mention them in this story

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Remember that Moses has dedicated the Tent of Meeting and all its things to Yahweh, and has just spent seven days dedicating Aaron and Aaron's sons as Yahweh's priests. On the eighth day, Aaron offered a sin or purification offering, a burnt offering, a grain offering, and a fellowship offering to Yahweh for the people of Israel. Then fire from Yahweh totally burned up the burnt offering, which showed that Yahweh was with the people of Israel and accepted Aaron's offerings.

But then, on that same day, in scene one of this story, Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offer incense in some way that Yahweh did not say to do. Then, fire from Yahweh comes out from where Yahweh is present in the Tent of Meeting, and the fire burns Nadab and Abihu to death. After that, Moses remembers a warning that Yahweh gave earlier. We do not know when Yahweh said this warning, since it is not in the Bible before this. Sometime before the story in this passage happens, Yahweh warned that the priests would have to treat Yahweh as holy and sacred. Yahweh said that the people of Israel would honor and respect Yahweh because of how powerful Yahweh is. Nadab and Abihu did not listen to this warning, since Nadab and Abihu disobeyed Yahweh's instructions on Nadab and Abihu's very first day as Yahweh's priests. So when Moses remembers this warning and tells Aaron, Aaron stays silent and does not say anything. Aaron probably realizes that Yahweh's warning was clear and that Aaron's sons should have known to treat Yahweh as holy and sacred.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: Think about a time that you did something your parent, guardian, or an elder in your community warned you not to do, and something bad happened because of it. Now imagine that afterward, you are remembering their warning. How would you talk about this? Pay attention to how you talk about the warning, since it happened before what you did. Pause this audio here.

In scene two of this passage, Moses tells Nadab and Abihu's relatives how to respond to Nadab and Abihu's deaths. First, someone had to remove the bodies from the sanctuary, which is the entire area in and around the Tent of Meeting. To take care of this, Moses calls Moses and Aaron's cousins, Mishael and Elzaphan, and instructs Mishael and Elzaphan to carry the bodies of Nadab and Abihu outside the Israelite camp, away from the sanctuary. Mishael and Elzaphan grab onto Nadab and Abihu's tunics to lift the dead bodies and obey Moses.

Next, Moses instructs Nadab and Abihu's direct relatives—their father Aaron and their two brothers Eleazar and Ithamar—not to do the normal customs to mourn for Nadab and Abihu. Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar should not let their hair be messy or uncovered, tear their clothes, or end their time of priestly service to Yahweh in the Tent of Meeting early by leaving the courtyard or sanctuary around the tent. In fact, if Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar disobey and mourn for Nadab and Abihu while serving Yahweh as priests, Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar will die, and Yahweh will be angry with the whole community. The rest of the Israelites will be able to mourn for Nadab and Abihu, but Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar cannot, because there is still oil on Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Moses poured this oil during the dedication ceremony to dedicate Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar to Yahweh.

Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar obey Moses' instructions and do not mourn for Nadab and Abihu.

In the last scene, scene three, Yahweh gives Aaron a new instruction. All the other times in Leviticus when Yahweh has told Aaron to do something, Yahweh has talked to Moses first or to Moses and Aaron at the same time. But now, Yahweh talks to Aaron alone. Yahweh instructs Aaron and all Aaron's descendants who will become priests after Aaron not to drink wine or any other fermented or alcoholic drinks so that the priests can stay alert when serving Yahweh.

Stop here and do this exercise as a group: Try to come up with a list of all the fermented or alcoholic drinks that some people in your culture drink. How would you talk about this whole group of drinks? Pause this audio here.

The priests have to be aware enough to tell the difference between holy things, or what people have devoted to Yahweh, and what is not something people have devoted to Yahweh. The priests also have to tell the difference between what is ritually clean and what ritually dirty. If the priests are aware enough to recognize how to follow Yahweh's instructions correctly, then the priests will be able to teach the rest of the Israelites all the instructions and statutes that Yahweh gave Moses for the Israelites.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: If you start talking to someone about something new, like a new topic or a new instruction, but that new thing is related to what the two of you have been doing, what kinds of words do you use to change what your conversation is about? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 10:1–11 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Nadab
  • Abihu
  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • Aaron's cousins Mishael and Elzaphan
  • Aaron's remaining sons, Eleazar and Ithamar
  • Aaron's descendants who would become priests after Aaron
  • And the assembly of people who represent the Israelites, although the storyteller does not mention them in this story

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Aaron's oldest sons, Nadab and Abihu, offer incense to Yahweh in some way that Yahweh did not instruct. Have the people playing Nadab and Abihu take pans and act out putting coals and incense in the pans. Then fire comes from Yahweh and kills Nadab and Abihu. Then Moses tells Aaron something that Yahweh has said before. Earlier, Yahweh said, "The people who are near me must treat me as holy, and all the people of Israel will honor me because of how holy and powerful I am." Have the person playing Moses tell this to the person playing Aaron. Aaron does not say anything.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am afraid because I have just started serving Yahweh as a priest, and now this happened because Yahweh is so holy; or
  • I am grieving for my sons; or
  • I am angry at Moses for reminding me of what Yahweh said instead of grieving for my sons.
Continue the drama.

Then, Moses calls Moses and Aaron's cousins, Mishael and Elzaphan, and instructs Mishael and Elzaphan to carry the bodies of Nadab and Abihu away from the holy place and outside the Israelite camp. Have the people playing Mishael and Elzaphan act out carrying away the bodies. Mishael and Elzaphan carry the bodies by holding onto the clothes because Mishael and Elzaphan do not want to touch the dead bodies directly.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Mishael or Elzaphan, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am honored that my relative Moses trusts me to help in this situation; or
  • I am horrified at what has happened to my relatives, and I do not want to do anything wrong, so that nothing happens to me; or
  • I am grieving for my relatives, Nadab and Abihu.
Continue the drama.

Meanwhile, Moses tells Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, not to do anything to mourn for Nadab and Abihu. Moses says Aaron and Aaron's sons must not leave the Tent of Meeting, so that Aaron and Aaron's sons will not die. Instead, the people of Israel will mourn for Nadab and Abihu. So Aaron and Aaron's sons Eleazar and Ithamar obey Moses. Have the people playing Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar act out serving Yahweh in the Tent of Meeting instead of mourning.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Eleazar or Ithamar, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am upset because of what has happened to my relatives; or
  • I am sad because of my brothers, and I am trying not to show it because of what Moses said; or
  • I am afraid to keep serving Yahweh in the Tent of Meeting after what happened to my brothers.
Continue the drama.

Then Yahweh tells Aaron that Aaron, Aaron's sons, and Aaron's descendants who will become priests after Aaron must not drink alcohol when the priests serve Yahweh in the Tent of Meeting. The priests must not do this because the priests need to be able to clearly tell the difference between what is holy and what is not holy, and between what is ritually clean and what is not ritually clean. Have the people playing Aaron, Eleazar, Ithamar, and Aaron's descendants who will become priests after Aaron act out serving Yahweh carefully. These priests must also teach the people of Israel everything that Yahweh has taught the priests.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 10:1–11 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu use a censer to offer incense to Yahweh in some way that Yahweh has not instructed these men to do. Use the same words or phrases for incense and Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and look at a picture of a censer as a group. Discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for censer. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Then, fire comes from Yahweh and kills Nadab and Abihu. Moses then tells Aaron about something Yahweh said before. Yahweh said that the people who are near to Yahweh must treat Yahweh as holy or sacred, and the people of Israel would glorify Yahweh, or praise Yahweh, because of how powerful and holy Yahweh is. For more information about what it means to be holy or what it means to glorify, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words or phrases for holy and glorify as you used in previous passages. Aaron does not say anything back to Moses.

Then, Moses calls in Aaron's cousins Mishael and Elzaphan, and Moses asks these men to carry Nadab and Abihu's bodies outside the Israelite camp and away from the holy place or sanctuary. For more information on sanctuary, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for sanctuary as you used in previous passages.

After Moses asks, Mishael and Elzaphan obey Moses and carry the bodies outside the camp by grabbing onto the dead men's clothes instead of touching the bodies directly. You may use the general word for clothing, or your word for tunic. For more information about tunic, refer to the Master Glossary.

Moses tells Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, not to do mourning rituals for Nadab and Abihu, or Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons will die. Instead, the people of Israel will mourn for Nadab and Abihu. Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons also must not leave the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, or Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons will die. This means that Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons must stay inside the sanctuary or courtyard that surrounds the Tent of Meeting, because everything inside that area is holy space. Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons must not leave because Yahweh anointed or chose Aaron and Aaron's sons to be priests. Moses had poured oil on Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons to show that Yahweh had chosen these men. The oil was still on Aaron and Aaron's sons because Yahweh had just anointed these men the week before. For more information on the Tent of Meeting and anoint, refer to tabernacle and anoint in the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for tabernacle and anoint as you used in previous passages. Aaron and Aaron's sons obey the instructions Moses gives.

Then Yahweh gives Aaron an instruction or statute for Aaron and all of Aaron's descendants to follow. For more information on statute, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for statute as you used in previous passages. The instruction is that when Aaron and Aaron's descendants come to the tabernacle, or Tent of Meeting, to serve Yahweh, Aaron and Aaron's descendants must not drink wine or any other alcoholic drinks.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for wine. Look up wine in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for other alcoholic drinks, based on your discussion in the "Defining the Scenes" step for this passage. If you have already translated this concept in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh wants the priests not to drink wine or alcoholic drinks so that the priests can stay aware and be able to tell the difference between what is holy or sacred and what is not holy. It is also so that the priest will be able to tell the difference between what is ritually clean and what is ritually unclean. For more information about clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words or phrases for clean and unclean as you used in previous passages. The priests must be able to teach the people of Israel everything that Yahweh instructed the priests through Moses.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 10:12–20
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 10:12–20 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 10:12–20 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 10:12–20 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this section of Leviticus, Moses has dedicated Aaron and Aaron's sons as priests, as Yahweh instructed Moses, and the priests started offering sacrifices at the Tent of Meeting. But in the last passage, Aaron's two oldest sons, Nadab and Abihu, offered incense to Yahweh in the wrong way. Because Nadab and Abihu disobeyed Yahweh, fire came from Yahweh and killed Nadab and Abihu. Moses told Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons not to mourn for their relatives or stop serving Yahweh at the Tent of Meeting before the time to stop. Otherwise, Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons would die.

This passage takes place right after what happened to Nadab and Abihu. In this passage, Moses gives Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons some instructions about how to properly serve Yahweh at the Tent of Meeting. Aaron's two remaining sons do not completely follow the instructions, which makes Moses angry, but Aaron responds in a way Moses approves of.

After the disaster of Nadab and Abihu's deaths, it seems that Aaron and Aaron's surviving sons did not eat the parts of the offerings that Yahweh had instructed the priests to eat. So Moses reminds Aaron and Aaron's sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, about the instructions for which things the priests should eat from the offerings. The priests should eat the grain left over from what the priests offered to Yahweh in the grain offering. As Yahweh told Moses in Leviticus 6, the priests must eat the offering unleavened, so the priests must prepare the grain without yeast. The priests also must eat the grain in the sanctuary, so the priests must eat the grain inside the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting, beside the altar. The priests must eat grain there because the priests cannot eat food that is holy outside the holy space of the sanctuary. Aaron and Aaron's sons are supposed to eat the grain because the grain is the part of the offering that Yahweh chose for the priests to have, just as Yahweh commanded Moses earlier.

Aaron and Aaron's family are also supposed to eat the animal breast and thigh from the peace or fellowship offering. Yahweh commanded in Leviticus 7 that Aaron, Aaron's sons, and the rest of the priests should receive these parts of the fellowship offering. The priests' families, including family members who are not priests themselves, like daughters and young sons, can eat these animal breasts and thighs. But the priests' families do not have to eat the meat in the sanctuary, because not all of those family members can enter the sanctuary. However, Moses reminds Aaron and Aaron's sons that the priests and their families still have to eat the meat in a place that is ritually clean. When an Israelite brings a fellowship offering to Yahweh, the Israelite must bring the animal's fat and breast to the priest, and the priest must wave those parts in front of Yahweh's presence to symbolically offer those parts to Yahweh. The priest may then have the breast that the priest waved. The Israelite who brings a fellowship offering must also give the right thigh of the animal to the priests. Yahweh explained all this to Moses in Leviticus 7, but now Moses reminds Aaron of what Yahweh commanded then. After the priest waves these animal parts in front of Yahweh's presence to symbolize offering the parts to Yahweh, these parts of the fellowship offering will be the priests' share every time in the future. In other words, Aaron and all of Aaron's descendants who will become priests after Aaron all have the privilege and responsibility to eat these parts of the fellowship offering.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what are some things that leaders get to do or have the right to do? What are some of the leaders' responsibilities? What kinds of things might be both privileges and responsibilities? Pause this audio here.

Then Moses asks someone what happened to the goat that Aaron and Aaron's sons sacrificed as a sin or purification offering earlier that day. It is not clear who Moses asked, or if Moses just looked around to find out what happened. According to Yahweh's instructions in Leviticus 6, the priests were supposed to eat the meat from the purification offering in the sanctuary, so in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. However, when Moses asks about the goat Aaron and Aaron's sons just sacrificed, Moses finds out that the priests completely burned up the goat. But the priests were supposed to leave the meat to eat instead of burning up all the meat. This makes Moses very angry at Aaron's surviving sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, so Moses asks why Eleazar and Ithamar did not eat the meat in the sanctuary. Moses tells Eleazar and Ithamar that the meat is very holy because the Israelites gave the animal to the priests so that the priests could make atonement for the Israelites' sin or make amends to Yahweh for what the Israelites had done. There were different instructions for purification offerings depending on who had sinned. In some purification offerings, the priests were supposed to take the animal blood into the Tent of Meeting, and in some offerings, the priests were not supposed to do this. The priests could only eat the leftover animal meat when the priests did not take the blood into the Tent of Meeting. Eleazar and Ithamar had not taken the goat's blood into the Tent of Meeting, so the priests were supposed to eat the goat's meat in the sanctuary area, inside the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Aaron and Aaron's sons should have done this because Moses had commanded the priests to do so in Leviticus 6.

Even though Moses confronts Aaron's sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, because Eleazar and Ithamar failed to obey Yahweh's instructions, Aaron is the one who answers Moses. Aaron explains that earlier that day, Aaron's sons had sacrificed the purification offering and burnt offering to Yahweh, but such things happened to Aaron. Aaron means that even though Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offered the sacrifices to Yahweh earlier that day, terrible things had happened to Aaron's family, and Aaron had lost Aaron's two older sons. Aaron then asks Moses, "Would Yahweh have been happy if I ate the purification offering today?" Aaron did not ask Moses this question to get information; Aaron used the question to tell Moses something. It is not clear exactly what Aaron meant, but there are two main options. Possibly, Aaron meant that Aaron's sons had disobeyed Yahweh while Aaron was in charge of the sons. Because Yahweh had punished Aaron's sons, Aaron believed that Aaron was guilty too, and it would not be right for Aaron to eat holy food. More likely, though, Aaron meant that since bad things happened to Aaron's sons when Aaron's sons incorrectly served Yahweh, Aaron was afraid to eat the purification offering that day. Either way, Aaron's answer satisfied Moses, and Yahweh did not punish Aaron and Aaron's surviving sons for not eating the meat from the offerings.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How is the way Nadab and Abihu disobeyed Yahweh in the last passage similar to or different from the way Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar disobeyed Yahweh in this passage?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 10:12–20 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Moses reminds Aaron and Aaron's remaining sons about Yahweh's instructions to eat grain and meat leftover from what the priests sacrificed to Yahweh.

In the second scene: Moses confronts Aaron's sons about how the sons did not eat the meat left from the offerings to Yahweh. Aaron defends the decision not to eat, and Aaron's answer satisfies Moses.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • Aaron's surviving sons, Eleazar and Ithamar
  • The priests' families, who may also eat the meat
  • And Yahweh

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Remember that Moses has just dedicated the Tent of Meeting and all its things to Yahweh. Moses has also just spent seven days dedicating Aaron and Aaron's sons as Yahweh's priests. On the eighth day, Aaron offered many sacrifices to Yahweh, and Yahweh accepted Aaron's offerings. But then, on that same day, Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offered incense in some way that Yahweh did not instruct Nadab and Abihu to offer, so fire from Yahweh came out from where Yahweh is present in the Tent of Meeting, and the fire killed Nadab and Abihu.

This passage happens on the same day that Yahweh's fire killed Nadab and Abihu, so it takes place on the eighth day after Moses started dedicating Aaron and Aaron's sons as Yahweh's priests. In scene one, Moses reminds Aaron and Aaron's surviving sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, of what Yahweh said the priests could eat from the sacrifices the priests made to Yahweh. Yahweh had already given these instructions to Moses earlier in Leviticus, and Moses had told these instructions to Aaron. Now, however, Moses tells these instructions to Aaron and Aaron's sons again.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: In your culture, if you need to remind your children of something you previously told your children to do, what do you say? How is this different from or similar to what you say the first time you tell your children to do something? Pause this audio here.

First, Moses reminds Aaron and Aaron's sons to eat the grain left over from what the priests offer to Yahweh in the grain offering. Aaron and Aaron's sons must eat the grain without adding yeast. Aaron and Aaron's sons must eat the grain in the sanctuary, or inside the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Moses also says that this is what Yahweh instructed Moses earlier.

Next, Moses reminds Aaron and Aaron's sons that the priests and their families should eat the animal breast and thigh left over from what the priests offered to Yahweh in the fellowship offering. The priests and their families can eat outside the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting, in any ritually clean place. Before the priests can eat this meat, the priests must bring the animal breast and thigh and the fatty parts of the animal to Yahweh. Then the priests must wave the parts in front of Yahweh's presence in the Tent of Meeting to symbolically offer the parts to Yahweh. Then the priests and the priests' families can eat the meat. Moses says that this part of the animal from the fellowship offering is the priests' portion forever. In other words, Aaron and Aaron's sons and all of Aaron's descendants will be able to eat this part of the animals the priests sacrifice every time the priests sacrifice a fellowship offering.

In scene two, Moses finds out that Aaron and Aaron's surviving sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, have not eaten the meat from the goat of the purification offering. Moses is angry with Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar, so Moses asks why Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar did not eat the goat meat. Moses reminds Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar that the meat is very holy. The meat is holy because the Israelite people gave the animal to the priests so that the priests could offer the animal to Yahweh to make amends for the Israelites' sins and take away the Israelites' guilt. Moses says that Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar were supposed to eat the meat because the meat was left from a purification offering where the priests did not take the blood from the animal inside the Tent of Meeting. When the purification offering does not involve that, the priests are supposed to eat the meat leftover after the sacrifice, just like Yahweh commanded Moses earlier in Leviticus.

Moses asks this question and tells these things to Eleazar and Ithamar, but Aaron is the one who answers Moses. Aaron explains that earlier that day, Aaron's sons sacrificed burnt offerings and purification offerings to Yahweh, but terrible things still happened to Aaron. Aaron is talking about how Aaron's two older sons, Nadab and Abihu, died earlier in the day because Nadab and Abihu disobeyed Yahweh and did not treat Yahweh as holy. Aaron then asks Moses if Yahweh would have been happy if Aaron had eaten the meat left from the purification offering. Aaron may mean that Yahweh would not be happy because Aaron is guilty because of what Aaron's sons did earlier in the day. More likely, Aaron means that Aaron is afraid to eat the purification offering because Aaron is not sure Yahweh would be happy for Aaron to eat the meat. Either way, Aaron's answer satisfies Moses.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: In what kinds of situations might you say a question when you do not actually want to know more information? What kinds of things can you say with a question instead of a statement? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 10:12–20 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • Aaron's surviving sons, Eleazar and Ithamar
  • The priests' families, who may also eat the meat
  • And Yahweh

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Moses gives Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar instructions. Have the person playing Moses tell these things to Aaron and Aaron's sons, and have the people playing Aaron and Aaron's sons act out how they follow the instructions. Moses says that Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar should eat the grain leftover from the grain offering. The priests must prepare the grain without using yeast, and the priests have to eat the grain in a holy place. So the priests have to eat the grain in the sanctuary—that is, inside the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting.

Moses also says that Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar should eat the animal breast and thigh leftover from the fellowship offering. The priests and the priests' families, including people who were not priests, such as daughters, should eat those pieces of meat in a ritually clean place, though this does not have to be inside the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Moses reminds Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar that when an Israelite brings an animal to the priests for a fellowship offering, the priest must bring the breast and the fatty parts of the animal and wave these pieces in front of Yahweh's presence to symbolically offer the pieces to Yahweh. Then the priest can have the animal's breast and thigh. Moses then says that these parts leftover from the fellowship offering belong to the priests as the priests' perpetual share, so all Aaron's descendants who become priests after Aaron will do the same thing.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am happy to explain Yahweh's instructions again so Aaron and Aaron's sons can follow the instructions well; or
  • I am worried that Aaron or Aaron's sons might mess up again as the priests try to obey Yahweh's instructions; or
  • I am frustrated with Aaron and Aaron's sons because they need to hear these instructions again.
Continue the drama.

Then Moses tries to figure out what happened to the goat that Aaron and Aaron's sons sacrificed as a purification offering earlier that day. Have the person playing Moses look around for the goat or ask anybody who is standing nearby what happened to the goat. Moses realizes that Aaron and Aaron's sons did not eat the meat leftover from the offering, but instead burned it all up. Have the person playing Moses confront the people playing Aaron's sons Eleazar and Ithamar and say the following things. Moses first asks why Eleazar and Ithamar did not eat the meat, as Eleazar and Ithamar were supposed to. Moses then says why Eleazar and Ithamar should have eaten the meat. Moses says that the Israelites gave the animal for the purification offering to the priests so the priests could sacrifice the animal to atone for the people's sins or make amends with Yahweh for what the people had done wrong. This meant that the meat leftover from the sacrifice was very holy. Because of the type of purification offering the priests sacrificed that day, Aaron and Aaron's sons should have eaten the leftover meat in the sanctuary area.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing Eleazar and Ithamar, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

  • I am scared because I made a mistake and my brothers just died for their disobedience to Yahweh; or
  • I am sorry for not eating the meat that Yahweh instructed us to eat; or
  • I am angry that my uncle Moses is confronting us because we are doing our best.
Continue the drama.

Have the person playing Aaron step in and answer Moses' question. Aaron asks a question and says, "Would Yahweh have been happy if I ate the purification offering today?"

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am afraid to eat the holy meat because I feel guilty about how my older sons, Nadab and Abihu, disobeyed Yahweh; or
  • I am scared to eat the holy meat because Yahweh is so powerful, and I just saw Yahweh kill my sons; or
  • I am confused about what the right way to obey Yahweh is.
Continue the drama.

Aaron's answer satisfies Moses, so have the person playing Moses do or say something that shows Moses approves of Aaron's answer.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 10:12–20 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Moses reminds Aaron and Aaron's sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, of the instructions for what things the priests could eat after the priests gave offerings to Yahweh. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word for Yahweh as you used in previous passages.

Aaron and Aaron's sons should eat the grain left over from what the priests offered to Yahweh in the grain offering, but the priests must prepare the grain without yeast. For more information on the grain offering, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for grain offering as you used in previous passages.

Aaron and Aaron's sons also must eat the offering in the sanctuary, inside the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting or tabernacle, beside the altar. For more information on sanctuary or altar, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words or phrases for sanctuary and altar as you used in previous passages. Aaron and Aaron's sons are supposed to eat the grain because the grain is the part of the offering that Yahweh chose for the priest to have. Earlier in Leviticus, Yahweh had commanded Moses that the priests should eat this part.

Aaron and Aaron's family are also supposed to eat the animal breast and thigh from the peace or fellowship offering. For more information on the fellowship offering, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for fellowship offering as you used in previous passages.

Since the priests' family, including family members who are not priests themselves, such as daughters and young sons, can eat these animal breasts and thighs, the families do not have to eat these parts in the sanctuary. The priests and their families can eat the meat in any place that is ritually clean. For more information on clean, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for clean as you used in previous passages.

When an Israelite brings a fellowship offering to Yahweh, the Israelite must bring the animal's fat and breast to the priest. The priest must wave these parts in front of Yahweh's presence to symbolically offer these parts to Yahweh in a wave offering. The priest and his family may then eat the breast that the priest waved. Use the same word or phrase for wave offering as you have used previously, and refer to wave offering in the Master Glossary for more information.

The Israelite who brings a fellowship offering must also give the right thigh of the animal to the priests. For all of the priests, now and in the future, these parts of the fellowship offering will be the priests' families' portion. Use the same word or phrase for portion as you have used in previous passages.

Then Moses tries to figure out what happened to the goat that Aaron and Aaron's sons offered to Yahweh as a sin or purification offering earlier that day. Moses learns that the priests completely burned up the goat instead of eating the meat. For more information on the purification offering, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for purification offering as you used in previous passages.

Moses becomes very angry at Aaron's surviving sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, so Moses asks why Eleazar and Ithamar did not eat the meat in the sanctuary. Moses tells Eleazar and Ithamar that the meat is very holy because the Israelites gave the animal to the priests so that the priests could offer the animal to Yahweh to make atonement for the Israelites' iniquity. Remember that when someone continues to do something wrong against Yahweh, or disobeys Yahweh, that person becomes guilty. In other words, that person is no longer in a right relationship with Yahweh. The priests have to atone for the person, or help restore the person's relationship with Yahweh. For more information on atonement and iniquity, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words or phrases for atonement and iniquity as you used in previous passages.

Because of the type of purification offering, Aaron and Aaron's sons had not taken the goat's blood into the holy place, or inner part of the sanctuary, of the Tent of Meeting. In cases like this, the priests were supposed to eat the meat in the sanctuary area, inside the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting. Moses confronts Eleazar and Ithamar, but Aaron is the one who answers Moses's question. Aaron explains that earlier that day, Aaron's sons had sacrificed the purification offering and the burnt offering to Yahweh, but bad things had happened to Aaron's oldest sons. For more information on holy place, or the inside of the tabernacle, and burnt offering, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for holy place and burnt offering as you used in previous passages. Aaron then asks Moses, "Would Yahweh have been happy if I ate the purification offering today?" Moses approves of Aaron's answer.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 11:1–8
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 11:1–8 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:1–8 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Note: You may choose to go through step five before this step. In step five, you will discuss all the animals in the passage and also what the phrases "divided hoofs" and "chew the cud" mean.

In this passage, Yahweh talks to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh gives instructions and tells Moses and Aaron to say the same words to the Israelite people. Yahweh gave the Israelite people many rules about how the Israelites should live, what the Israelites should do, and what the Israelites should not do. Yahweh wants the Israelite people to understand that Yahweh is not like the idols and false gods that the Egyptians worshipped. Yahweh also wants the Israelite people to be different from all the other people groups.

In this passage, Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron what animals the Israelite people can eat for food. Remember, at this time, the Israelite people still live in the wilderness. There is not a lot of food or water in the wilderness where the Israelites are. Many times, the Israelite people worry about what the Israelites can eat. But Yahweh always provides food for the Israelites. All the animals that Yahweh mentions in this passage are animals that the Israelite people would see in the wilderness. Perhaps an Israelite person would see another people group eat one of these foods and want to eat the food too. But the Israelite people are not supposed to eat these animals. The Israelites must trust Yahweh and follow Yahweh's rules.

Yahweh's rules put the animals into two groups: ritually clean animals and ritually dirty animals. If the Israelite people eat ritually clean animals, then the people also stay ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats an unclean or ritually dirty animal, then the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty. When an Israelite person is ritually dirty, that person is not able to worship Yahweh and make sacrifices to Yahweh or go into the tabernacle area.

In this passage, Yahweh talks about land animals, which are animals that run on the ground with four legs. Yahweh said Israelite people can eat land animals that both chew the cud and have divided hoofs. An animal with divided hoofs is an animal with a hard covering on the animal's toes. This covering, which people call a hoof, is in two parts, all the way down the foot. If you look at a footprint of an animal like this, you will see two completely separate marks in the ground.

Stop here and look at pictures of divided hoofs as a group. Pause this audio here.

An animal that chews the cud is an animal that eats lots of green plants. These animals chew and chew and chew. Even after these animals swallow, these animals will burp up their food and chew the food again.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a video of an animal chewing the cud. Pause this audio here.

Examples of ritually clean animals that Israelite people could eat are cattle, goats, and sheep. In this passage, Yahweh explains why four different animals are ritually dirty animals.

First, Yahweh mentions the camel. Camels are ritually dirty. Even though camels chew the cud, camels are ritually dirty because camels do not have divided hoofs.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the pictures of the camels and the camels' feet. Pause this audio here.

Next, Yahweh mentions the rock hyrax. Rock hyraxes are ritually dirty. Even though rock hyraxes chew the cud, rock hyraxes are ritually dirty because rock hyraxes do not have divided hoofs.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a rock hyrax. Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh mentions the wild rabbit. Wild rabbits are ritually dirty. Even though wild rabbits chew the cud, wild rabbits are ritually dirty because wild rabbits do not have divided hoofs.

Stop here and look at a picture of a wild rabbit as a group. Pause this audio here.

Last Yahweh mentions the wild pig or boar. These wild pigs, or boars, are ritually dirty. Even though wild pigs have divided hooves, wild pigs are ritually dirty because wild pigs do not chew the cud.

Stop here and look at a picture of a wild pig as a group. Pause this audio here.

At the end, Yahweh warns the Israelite people that even touching the dead body of one of these animals would make the people ritually dirty.

Why did Yahweh tell the Israelite people not to eat these animals? Why were cattle and sheep and goats ritually clean animals but not these other four animals? Was it because cattle, sheep, and goats were more healthy for the Israelite people to eat? Maybe. Was it because some of these ritually dirty animals, like the wild rabbit, would have reminded the Israelite people of the Egyptian people's idol worship? Maybe. We do not know why Yahweh made some animals ritually clean and other animals ritually dirty. Yahweh did not say why Yahweh made these rules this way.

But we know that Yahweh wants Yahweh's people to be different from other people. We know Yahweh wants Yahweh's people to know that Yahweh is not like other idols or false gods that other people worship. We know that Yahweh wants other people to think about what is so special about Yahweh and Yahweh's people.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What do people in your culture who do not worship Yahweh think about Yahweh? How do the people who follow Yahweh act differently from the people who do not follow Yahweh in your community?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has one scene.

In the first scene: Yahweh is talking to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh is giving instructions to Moses and Aaron for the Israelite people. In this passage, Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron rules about what food the Israelite people can eat. If the Israelite people eat ritually clean animals, then the people also stay ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats an unclean or ritually dirty animal, then the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty. Israelite people were only supposed to eat animals with divided hoofs that chew the cud. In this passage, Yahweh explains why four different animals are ritually dirty animals.

Note: You may choose to go through script five before this script. In script five, you will discuss all the animals in the passage and also what the phrases "divided hoofs" and "chew the cud" mean.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Remember that the Israelite people are living in the wilderness at this time. An Israelite person might see one of these animals in the wild and want to eat that animal. The Israelite people probably knew that other people groups ate these animals.

You can act out this passage in different ways. You might choose to have a person represent Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron. The person who is representing Yahweh would be explaining the rules to Moses and Aaron. If you act out the passage in this way, you might want to use the pictures of the animals to show while you talk about the different animals. It may also be helpful to use the pictures of the animal's feet to show the difference.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the pictures of the different animals. Pause this audio here.

If you want, you might decide to act out Moses and Aaron retelling Yahweh's words to the people of Israel.

Another way to act out this passage would be to imagine situations where an Israelite person sees one of the dirty animals. You can show the person trying to decide whether or not to eat the dirty animal. Maybe show that people from another people group offer ritually dirty food to the Israelite people. The Israelite people must tell the other people why the Israelites cannot eat the food. Please remember, the storyteller does not mention other people groups in the passage, but it may be helpful to imagine what the scene is like.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will act out this passage. Pause this audio here.

In scene one, Yahweh uses special words to talk about what Yahweh allows the Israelite people to eat and what Yahweh does not allow the Israelite people to eat. Yahweh's words describe situations that will happen in the future. Yahweh uses words to say what the Israelite people should do and should not do.

Stop here and discuss how someone would give permission to eat something in your language and culture. Think about a situation where you tell someone that that person can do something. You are happy if the person does that thing, and you are happy if the person does not do that thing. Discuss how you would talk to the person. Take turns telling a person that the person can eat something. Pause this audio here.

Now stop here and discuss how someone would warn someone not to eat something in your language and culture. Think about a situation where you tell someone not to do something, not even one time. Discuss how you would talk to the person. Take turns telling a person not to eat something. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron the main rule: the Israelite people should only eat animals with divided hoofs that chew the cud. "Divided hoofs" might be hard to translate. You may want to translate this idea with something like "feet split in two parts" or "two hard toes on each foot."

If you have not done so yet, stop here and discuss how you will translate "divided hoofs." Pause this audio here.

It may also be difficult to translate "chew the cud." Some languages need to say something like "animals that eat their food twice" or "animals that chew and chew green plants."

If you have not done so yet, stop here and discuss how you will translate "chew the cud." Pause this audio here.

If the Israelite people follow this rule, the Israelites will be ritually clean. Then Yahweh gives examples of ritually dirty animals and explains why if a person eats one of these animals, that person is breaking the rule. A rule is one idea that applies to many different situations. When the Israelite people understood the rule, the Israelites could see a new animal and know whether or not the new animal was a ritually clean or ritually dirty animal.

Stop here and discuss how someone would give a rule in your language and culture. Try to think of a rule that is true in lots of different situations. Pause this audio here.

After Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron the rule, Yahweh gives examples of ritually dirty animals that the Israelite people would see. First, Yahweh mentions the camel. Camels are ritually dirty. Even though camels chew the cud, camels are ritually dirty because camels do not have divided hoofs.

Next, Yahweh mentions the rock hyrax. Rock hyraxes are ritually dirty. Even though rock hyraxes chew the cud, rock hyraxes are ritually dirty because rock hyraxes do not have divided hoofs.

Then Yahweh mentions the wild rabbit. Wild rabbits are ritually dirty. Even though wild rabbits chew the cud, wild rabbits are ritually dirty because wild rabbits do not have divided hoofs.

Last, Yahweh mentions the wild pig or boar. Wild pigs are ritually dirty. Even though pigs have divided hooves, pigs are ritually dirty because pigs do not chew the cud.

At the end, Yahweh warns the Israelite people that even touching the dead body of one of these animals would make the people ritually dirty.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has one scene.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh is talking to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron rules about what food the Israelite people can eat. If the Israelite people eat ritually clean animals, then the people also stay ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats an unclean or ritually dirty animal, then the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing Moses and Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

  • The Israelite people ate many animals when the Israelites lived in Egypt. I do not think the Israelites will like the new rules; or
  • Other people eat these foods. Why can we not eat these foods? What if there is not enough food for the people? or
  • Yahweh always provides food for us in the wilderness. I trust Yahweh to feed us.
Continue the drama.

Israelite people are only supposed to eat animals with divided hoofs that chew the cud. In this passage, Yahweh explains why four different animals are ritually dirty animals. Those four kinds of animals are the camel, the rock hyrax, the wild rabbit, and the pig.

If you want, you can act out Moses and Aaron telling Yahweh's words to the people of Israel. In that case, you may want to include this.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

  • I am confused why Yahweh does not let us eat these animals; or
  • I am sad because I like to eat pig; or
  • Yahweh has many rules. I understand some of Yahweh's rules. I do not understand some of Yahweh's other rules. But I know Yahweh wants the best for us.
Continue the drama.

You may want to include some people who are not Israelites. These people could be Egyptian people, Midian people, or other people. These people are not in the passage. But you can ask these people what they think of the Israelite people's food rules.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the other people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • The Israelite people are not like us. The Israelites are not like any other people group; or
  • I am curious why Yahweh gave the Israelite people this rule.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Yahweh told Moses and Aaron to talk to the people of Israel. Use the same words or phrases for Yahweh and "people of Israel" or Israelite people as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and Israelite, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Israelite people were only supposed to eat animals with divided hoofs that chew the cud. An animal with divided hoofs has special feet or hoofs that split into two separate toes. Like human toes, these animals' toes can move a little bit to help the animals as the animals walk over hills and mountains.

Stop here and, as a group, look again at pictures of divided hoofs as needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for divided hoofs. If you have already translated this idea in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Some animals that eat lots of grass and plants, like cattle, sheep, and goats, have a special eating process. These animals chew their food in their mouths for a very long time. Then these animals swallow the food in their mouths, but later, the animals burp the food back into their mouths and chew on the food again. People who work with these animals call this process "chewing the cud."

Stop here and, as a group, look again at a video of an animal as the animal chews the cud as needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for chew the cud. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The Israelites must not eat camels. A camel is a large animal with long, slender legs and a long neck. A camel's body has shaggy, light brown hair all over. Camels can go a long time without drinking water and are good at traveling long distances. Today, camels are usually 2 meters tall at their hump and can weigh 500 to 1,000 kilograms. The Israelites would have known two different kinds of camels. The Israelites would know camels with two humps, because Abraham, their ancestor, owned camels with two humps. People would use this kind of camel to travel long distances and to carry heavy loads. The Israelites also would have known camels with one hump, which are wild camels that could swim in the water. Israelites were not supposed to eat either kind of camel.

Stop here and look at pictures of the two kinds of camels as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for camel. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Yahweh uses the words clean and unclean or dirty to talk about what foods the Israelite people should and should not eat. In this passage, these words do not refer to physical cleanliness. When an Israelite person eats clean food, the person stays ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats dirty food, then the Israelite person becomes ritually dirty, and that person cannot worship Yahweh. Use the same words or phrases throughout for ritually clean and ritually dirty as you used in previous passages.

A rock hyrax is a small, round animal that uses all four legs to climb and walk. A rock hyrax has short legs and no tail. Rock hyrax fur is long, thick, and soft. This animal lives in rocky areas in the Middle East. A rock hyrax weighs around 3 or 4 kilograms and measures 30 to 50 centimeters long.

Stop here and, as a group, look again at a picture of a rock hyrax as needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for rock hyrax. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

A wild rabbit or hare is an animal with long, big ears. A wild rabbit has thin front legs with small feet and strong, big back legs with big feet. Wild rabbits can run and jump quickly using these big back feet. A wild rabbit has soft brown or gray hair on its body. A wild rabbit's ears can be 10 centimeters long. A wild rabbit's body can be between 40 and 70 centimeters long, and a wild rabbit weighs between 1 and 5 kilograms.

Stop here and, as a group, look again at a picture of a wild rabbit as needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for wild rabbit. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

A wild pig or boar is a big, strong animal with a thick body and short legs. The wild pig has rough, dark hair. The wild pig has thick hair on its back and neck. The wild pig has a large head with little eyes. The wild pig can run very fast.

Stop here and, as a group, look again at a picture of a wild pig as needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for pig. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

Yahweh says that the Israelites will be unclean if they even touch the dead body of one of these animals. Use the same word or phrase for dead body of an animal that you have used in previous passages.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
