title: Leviticus 11:9–12
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 11:9–12 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:9–12 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:9–12 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the book of Leviticus, Yahweh was talking to Moses and Aaron and giving the Israelite people many rules about how the Israelites should live, what the Israelites should do, and what the Israelites should not do. In this passage, Yahweh still talks to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh gives instructions to Moses and Aaron and tells Moses and Aaron to say the same words to the Israelite people. Just like Yahweh did in the previous passage, Yahweh gives Moses and Aaron rules about what foods a ritually clean person could eat.

In this passage, Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron what water creatures the Israelite people can eat for food. Remember, at this time, the Israelite people still live in the wilderness. Many times, the Israelite people have been worried about what the Israelites can eat. But Yahweh always provides food for the Israelites. Perhaps an Israelite person would see another people group eat one of these water creatures and want to eat the creature too. Or perhaps an Israelite person would find a new creature in the water. If the Israelites knew Yahweh's rule, the Israelite person could always know if the Israelite was obeying Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss: How do you know what Yahweh wants? How does it make you feel to know that Yahweh tells us exactly what Yahweh wants from us? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh's rules put the animals into two groups: ritually clean animals and ritually dirty animals. If the Israelite people eat ritually clean animals, then the people also stay ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats an unclean or ritually dirty animal, then the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty.

In this passage, Yahweh talks about water creatures, which people can find in salt water or in fresh water. The rule is this: all water creatures that have both fins and scales are ritually clean. Any water creatures that only have fins or only have scales, or do not have scales or fins, are ritually dirty. A fin is a thin, flat body part that sticks out from the animal's body and helps the animal move through the water. A scale is a small, hard piece that grows on the skin of certain sea creatures. These scales overlap and create a protective layer for the creature.

Stop here and look at pictures of fins and scales as a group. Pause this audio here.

At the end of this passage, Yahweh warns the Israelite people that to even touch the dead body of one of these ritually dirty water creatures would make the people ritually dirty. Yahweh makes Yahweh's rules simple and clear for the Israelite people. After the Israelite people hear these rules, the Israelites would know which water creatures are good to eat and which water creatures are bad to eat.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Is seafood a regular part of the diet in your culture? Is it surprising to you that Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to only eat water creatures with fins and scales?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:9–12 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has one scene.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells the eating rule for water creatures. The rule is that the Israelite people can eat water creatures that have both fins and scales. This rule applies to creatures that live in the saltwater and also to creatures that live in the freshwater.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The background information is that Yahweh gave eating rules to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh also told Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelite people the eating rules. In this passage, the storyteller does not mention Yahweh, Moses, or Aaron by name, but remember that Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron are having this conversation.

You can act out this passage in different ways. You might choose to have people represent Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron. The person who is representing Yahweh would be explaining the rules to Moses and Aaron. If you do it this way, you might want to use the pictures of fins and scales to show the difference between clean and dirty animals.

If you want, you might decide to act out how Moses and Aaron retell Yahweh's words to the people of Israel.

Another way to act out this passage would be to imagine situations where an Israelite person sees a water creature, either while the person is fishing or maybe in a market. You can show the person trying to decide whether or not to eat the water creature. Maybe show how people from another people group offer ritually dirty food to the Israelite people. The Israelite people must tell the other people why the Israelite people cannot eat the food. Please remember, the storyteller does not mention other people groups in the passage, but it may be helpful to imagine what the scene is like.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will act out this passage. Pause this audio here.

In scene one, Yahweh is giving a rule about what foods the Israelite people can eat and should not eat. Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron the main rule about water creatures: the Israelite people should only eat water creatures that have both fins and scales. The Israelite people should not eat any water creatures that only have fins or only have scales, or do not have any fins or scales.

Stop here and look at the pictures of fins and scales. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says this rule is for water creatures that live in saltwater and for water creatures that live in freshwater, such as rivers or streams. Yahweh also says that this rule applies to big water creatures but also to little water creatures that "swarm," or swim around in big groups.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a group of fish. Discuss as a group what words you can use in your language to refer to creatures that live in groups like that. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that the Israelites can eat the water creatures that have fins and scales. In other words, these animals are ritually clean. This means the Israelite people can eat those creatures and remain ritually clean. The water creatures that do not have fins or do not have scales, or do not have either fins or scales, are detestable to the people. This is a strong way to say that these animals are ritually dirty for the Israelites to eat. When something is detestable, it is disgusting—people really do not want to eat that thing. If an Israelite person eats one of those creatures, that person becomes ritually dirty too. Even if an Israelite person touches the dead body of one of the dirty water creatures, that person will become dirty too. Yahweh very much does not want the Israelites to have contact with these creatures.

In this passage, the storyteller says many things in the same way as the storyteller did earlier in Leviticus. It is a good idea to talk about ritually clean and ritually dirty foods in similar ways. Remember that in this passage, Yahweh uses strong language to talk about how these water creatures are ritually dirty.

Stop here and discuss: What words do Yahweh and the storyteller use over and over again in Leviticus 11? What is the same in this passage as Leviticus 11:1–8? What is different in this passage from Leviticus 11:1–8? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:9–12 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has one scene.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh is talking to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron rules about what food the Israelite people can eat. If the Israelite people eat ritually clean animals, then the people also stay ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats an unclean or ritually dirty animal, then the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty. In this passage, Yahweh says the rule for saltwater creatures and freshwater creatures: the only water creatures that the Israelites can eat are creatures that have scales and fins.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I hope the Israelite people will stay ritually clean; or
  • The Israelite people will be different from all other peoples.
Continue the drama.

If you want, you can act out Moses and Aaron telling Yahweh's words to the people of Israel. In that case, you may want to include this.

Ask the people playing Moses and Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

  • These rules will be good for the Israelite people; or
  • I am glad that we can still eat fish!
Continue the drama.

You may want to include some people who are not Israelites. These people are not in the passage. These people could be Egyptian people, Midian people, or other people. Maybe a person tries to sell water creatures to the Israelite people. But you can ask these other people groups what they think of the Israelite people's food rules.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the other people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I want the Israelites to buy my food; or
  • I am curious why the Israelite people have these rules.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:9–12 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh talks about ritually unclean or dirty animals to talk about what foods the Israelite people should not eat. Yahweh uses very strong language. Yahweh says that these animals are detestable, or disgusting, for the Israelites to eat. You may also need to use the word clean to talk about what foods the Israelites could eat. In this passage, these words do not refer to physical cleanliness. When an Israelite person eats clean food, the person stays ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats dirty food, then the Israelite person becomes ritually dirty. You may either use a word for detestable, or disgusting, or you may use words for ritually dirty in this passage. If you use the words for ritually clean and dirty, use the same words or phrases throughout for ritually clean and ritually dirty as you used in previous passages. See the Master Glossary for more information about clean and unclean.

Some translations make it clear that Yahweh really does not want Yahweh's people to eat things that are ritually dirty, and so the translations say that the Israelites must consider the animals without fins and scales to be detestable. This means that Yahweh does not want the Israelites to interact with those animals at all.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will translate the idea of someone strongly disliking something. Will you use the term for ritually dirty, or for detestable? Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Yahweh refers to the seas. Here, the sea or ocean can refer to any big amount of salt water. The Israelite people could use the rule about fins and scales to determine whether any sea creature was ritually clean or ritually dirty.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of the ocean. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also refers to streams and wadis. A wadi is a deep valley between hills or mountains that sometimes fills with rainwater. Yahweh was referring to freshwater sources of water. Freshwater sources of water are streams and rivers that have water that is not saltwater. The Israelite people could also use the rule about fins and scales to decide whether any creature that lived in a river or stream was ritually clean or ritually dirty.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a wadi. Pause this audio here.

Many creatures that live in the water have fins. A fin is a thin, flat body part that sticks out from the animal's body and helps the animal move through the water. For example, a fish has different kinds of fins, including a big fin on its back and a tail fin.

Stop here and look at the picture of a fish as a group. Look at the different kinds of fins that the fish has. Pause this audio here.

A scale is a small, hard piece that grows on the skin of certain sea creatures. For example, many fish have lots of flat scales. These scales overlap and create a protective layer for the creature.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the pictures of fish scales.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 11:13–19
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 11:13–19 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:13–19 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:13–19 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the book of Leviticus, Yahweh was talking to Moses and Aaron and giving the Israelite people many rules about how the Israelite people should live, what the Israelite people should do, and what the Israelite people should not do. In this passage, Yahweh still talks to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh gives instructions to Moses and Aaron to give to the Israelite people.

In this passage, Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron what flying creatures are ritually dirty for the Israelites. Remember, at this time, the Israelite people still live in the wilderness. Many times, the Israelite people have been worried about what the Israelites can eat. But Yahweh always provides food for the Israelites. The Israelite people have just set up the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh gives instructions for how the Israelite people are supposed to be ritually clean.

What kind of birds does Yahweh say are ritually dirty? Most of these ritually dirty birds are hunters that eat small animals or even old, dead animals. These birds eat the blood too, as the birds eat the raw meat. In Leviticus, Yahweh's rules show how both people and animals near the Israelite people need to be ritually clean. It is probable that the reason Yahweh says these birds are ritually dirty to eat is that these birds eat things that are ritually dirty.

Some of these birds are also water birds, but these birds live near water that might be dirty and eat dirty things out of that water. Similarly, if these birds eat things that make the birds dirty, it seems that this is one of the reasons that Yahweh does not want the Israelite people to eat these birds.

Although sometimes it is difficult to know exactly what birds Yahweh is talking about in this passage, it seems that several of these birds were birds that the Egyptian people honored, worshiped, or considered symbolic. Think of what it is like for the Israelite people. In Egypt, the people saw the way the Egyptians honored these birds. But now Yahweh says these birds are ritually dirty. Maybe this was another way that Yahweh wants Yahweh's people to be different from all the other people groups.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In what ways does Yahweh want us to be different from other people? Pause this audio here.

Because the list of birds is so long, it is likely that this list was a complete list of all the ritually dirty birds. That means that any other bird would be ritually clean. Here is the complete list of birds that Yahweh talks about in this passage: Eagle, vulture, black vulture, red kite, all kinds of black kite, all kinds of raven, horned owl, screech owl, gull, all kinds of hawk, little owl, cormorant, great owl, white owl, desert owl, carrion vulture, storks, all kinds of herons, hoopoe, and bat.

Stop here and look at photos of all these kinds of birds as a group.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:13–19 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has one scene.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells what flying creatures, mostly birds, are ritually dirty. Remember, Yahweh is telling this list to Moses and Aaron, who will tell the Israelite people what birds are ritually dirty. If the Israelite people eat ritually clean birds, then the people also stay ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats an unclean or ritually dirty bird, then the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty.

Note: You may choose to go through step five before this step. In step five, you will discuss the names for the different kinds of birds.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The background information is that Yahweh gave eating rules to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh also told Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelite people the eating rules. This passage does not mention Yahweh, Moses, or Aaron by name, but remember that Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron are having this conversation.

You can act out this passage in different ways. You might choose to have people represent Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron. The person who is representing Yahweh can tell Moses and Aaron which birds are ritually dirty. If you do it this way, you might want to use the pictures from step five to show the ritually dirty birds while you talk.

If you want, you might decide to act out Moses and Aaron retelling Yahweh's words to the people of Israel.

Another way to act out this passage would be to imagine situations where an Israelite person sees a flying creature, either while hunting or maybe in a market. You can show the person trying to decide whether or not to eat the flying creature. Maybe show how people from another people group offer ritually dirty food to the Israelite people. The Israelite people must tell the other people why the Israelites cannot eat the food. Please remember, Yahweh does not mention other people groups in the passage, but it may be helpful to imagine what the scene is like.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will act out this passage. Pause this audio here.

Remember, the Israelite people have been wandering in the wilderness. There have been times when the Israelites were worried about having enough food. But Yahweh always gave the Israelites food to eat. The birds in this passage are birds that the Israelite people would see in the wilderness.

In scene one, Yahweh talks about all the different birds that are ritually dirty. Yahweh again uses a strong word to talk about these birds. Yahweh says that these birds are detestable, or disgusting, to the Israelites. Most of these birds are "birds of prey." This means that these are hunting birds that kill and eat other animals. Most of the birds in the list also look for already dead animals and eat the rotten animal meat. Other birds on the list are birds that live near dirty water. These birds also eat many things that are not clean. This is the list of flying creatures in the passage: eagle, vulture, black vulture, red kite, black kite, raven, horned owl, screech owl, gull, hawk, little owl, cormorant, great owl, white owl, desert owl, carrion vulture, storks, herons, hoopoe, and bat. The birds in this list that are birds of prey are: eagle, vulture, black vulture, red kite, black kite, horned owl, screech owl, hawk, little owl, great owl, white owl, desert owl, and carrion vulture. The birds in this list that are water birds are: cormorant, storks, and herons. The raven is also a scavenger bird that eats dead meat that the raven finds. The reason Yahweh includes the hoopoe and the bat in this list is less clear, but it is probably because the hoopoe and the bat ate ritually dirty animals too. If you do not have names for all these kinds of birds, you may want to put the birds in groups based on the kind of bird or based on what the birds do. For example, you could say, "many different kinds of owls" or "birds that eat other animals."

Stop here and look at photos of all these kinds of birds as a group as needed. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group the most natural way to group these birds in your language. Pause this audio here.

You may need to use words from other languages for some of the birds' names. If your language has words for birds that eat old, dead animals, you might want to explain what kind of birds these are in a general way. For example, "any kind of bird that ate animals or old dead animals."

Stop here and discuss as a group the most natural way to translate the names of the birds and how you will describe the birds. Pause this audio here.

In step five, you will hear more about each kind of bird. Sometimes we do not know exactly what kinds of birds Yahweh talks about in the passage. Some of these birds refer to groups of birds. Yahweh says, "any kind of black kite... any kind of raven... any kind of hawk... any kind of heron." That means that the Israelite people knew about different kinds of birds that the Israelites called black kites, and all of those birds were ritually dirty. This is true for all four kinds of birds Yahweh mentions: black kites, ravens, hawks, and herons.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your language, how do you refer to groups of birds that are similar or have the same name? Pause this audio here.

The pictures should give you some idea of what these birds looked like. Ancient people highly praised or valued many of these birds. Egyptians used several of these birds to worship the Egyptian gods and for symbolism in Egyptian art and language.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language and culture, are there any birds that have special meaning? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:13–19 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has one scene.

Note: You may choose to go through step five before this script. In step five, you will discuss the names for the different kinds of birds.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh is talking to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron rules about what food the Israelite people can eat and cannot eat. If an Israelite person eats an unclean or ritually dirty animal, then the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty. In this passage, Yahweh says which flying creatures are detestable, or ritually dirty.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing Moses and Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

  • What if we do not have enough food? or
  • I am thankful that Yahweh gives us good food to eat; or
  • Yahweh is really different from the Egyptian gods.
Continue the drama.

If you want, you can act out Moses and Aaron telling Yahweh's words to the people of Israel. In that case, you may want to include this.

Ask the people playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

  • Why is Yahweh giving us so many rules? or
  • I wonder why Yahweh says we cannot eat those birds.
Continue the drama.

You may want to include some people who are not Israelites. These people are not in the passage. These people could be Egyptian people, Midian people, or other people. Maybe a person tries to sell flying creatures or their meat to the Israelite people. But you can ask these other people what they think of the Israelite people's food rules.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the other people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • In Egypt, we like these birds; or
  • I am curious why the Israelite people have these rules.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:13–19 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, the storyteller uses the word unclean or ritually dirty to talk about what foods the Israelite people should not eat. In this passage, these words do not refer to physical dirtiness. When an Israelite person eats clean food, the Israelite stays ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats dirty food, then the Israelite person becomes ritually dirty. Use the same word or phrase throughout for ritually dirty as you used in previous passages. Refer to the Master Glossary for more information about clean and unclean.

If you also use a stronger word for ritually dirty, like detestable, use the same word here as you used in previous passages.

Eagles are large, powerful birds. An eagle has a strong beak and sharp claws for hunting. This kind of bird flies high in the sky and can see very well. Eagles hunt and eat many kinds of animals. The Israelite people knew about eagles that had light brown feathers. This kind of eagle lives in mountains and dry areas.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of an eagle. Pause this audio here.

Vultures are large birds with long necks. Most vultures have no feathers on their heads. Vultures find and eat animals that are already dead. This passage mentions three kinds of vultures: vultures, black vultures, and carrion vultures.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the three pictures of vultures. Pause this audio here.

Kites are birds with long wings and thin bodies. Kites have strong, curved beaks and sharp claws that are good for hunting. Kites fly very carefully and glide smoothly in the sky. Kites also eat small animals and sometimes eat dead animals that the kites find.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the two pictures of kites. Pause this audio here.

The kind of raven in this passage has shiny black feathers and a short tail. Ravens can live in hot, dry places and rocky areas. Ravens can eat fruits, berries, and seeds, as well as dead animals that the ravens find.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the picture of a raven. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Yahweh mentions many kinds of owls. Yahweh mentions the horned owl, the screech owl, the little owl, the great owl, the white owl, and the desert owl. Owls sleep during the day and hunt at night. Owls have round faces and large eyes. Owls can fly very quietly, without making any noise. Owls catch and eat small animals.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of owls. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the different kinds of owls. Pause this audio here.

Gulls are birds that live near the ocean and sometimes other water sources. Gulls have pointed wings and can fly over the water for a long time. Gulls are good at catching fish and finding dead things to eat.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of gulls. Pause this audio here.

Hawks are another kind of bird that have sharp claws and sharp beaks. Hawks can also see very well and hunt for small animals. It is possible that hawks referred to different kinds of birds that ancient people used to help people hunt animals.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of a shikra, which is one type of hawk. Pause this audio here.

Cormorants are a kind of bird that also lives by the ocean. Cormorants have shiny black feathers and large beaks that help the cormorants catch fish.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of a cormorant. Pause this audio here.

Storks are very tall birds with long legs and a long neck. Storks have long beaks. Storks like to walk through water and look for fish, insects, and frogs to eat.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of a stork. Pause this audio here.

Herons are tall birds with long legs and long beaks. Herons can fly slowly. Herons like to walk and stand in water and look for fish, insects, and frogs to eat. Herons like to live near water.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of a heron. Pause this audio here.

Hoopoes are small birds that have fancy orange feathers with black spots on their head. Hoopoes also have stripes of white and black feathers on the hoopoes' wings. Hoopoes like to live near the ground and eat insects.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of a hoopoe. Pause this audio here.

Bats are small animals with very large, thin ears. Bats hunt at nighttime and use their big ears to help the bats find insects to eat. Bats have wings and can fly like birds, but bats have fur or hair on their bodies. Bats do not have feathers like birds.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of a bat. Pause this audio here.

Now that you have looked at all the flying creatures, stop here and discuss as a group: Which birds are similar to birds that would be familiar to your people? What birds would be unfamiliar? Discuss how you would order these birds in a list.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 11:20–23
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 11:20–23 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:20–23 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:20–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the book of Leviticus, Yahweh was talking to Moses and Aaron and giving the Israelite people many rules about how the Israelites should live, what the Israelites should do, and what the Israelites should not do. In this passage, Yahweh still talks to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh gives instructions to Moses and Aaron to give to the Israelite people.

In this passage, Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron what insects are ritually clean for the Israelites. Remember, at this time, the Israelite people still live in the wilderness. Many times, the Israelite people have been worried about what the Israelites can eat. But Yahweh always provides food for the Israelites. The Israelite people had recently set up the Tent of Meeting, and now Yahweh gives instructions for how the Israelite people are supposed to be and stay ritually clean.

First, Yahweh says that almost all insects are unclean or ritually dirty. Then Yahweh explains that a few insects are ritually clean. This is the rule for what insects are good to eat: the insect has to be a flying insect that jumps. Yahweh also gives the names of the insects that are ritually clean: the locust, the destroying locust, the cricket, and the grasshopper. The Israelites were probably familiar with several kinds of locust, and the grasshopper was probably also a type of locust.

Stop here and look at the pictures of the locusts and crickets as a group. Pause this audio here.

In that time, it was common for people to eat locusts. People might cook the locusts over a fire or cook the locusts in water. The people may even preserve and dry the locusts in salt. We do not know exactly why Yahweh allowed the Israelite people to eat these insects, but not other insects. Is it because Yahweh wanted to protect the Israelite people from eating an insect that could hurt someone? Maybe. Is it because Yahweh wanted to see if the Israelite people would listen to and obey Yahweh? Maybe. Sometimes Yahweh commands something, and Yahweh's people must listen and obey, even when the people do not know the reason why Yahweh says to do it.

Stop here and discuss: Sometimes, we do not know why Yahweh asks us to do something. Do you listen to Yahweh even when you do not understand Yahweh's rules? What makes it easy to listen? What makes it hard to listen?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:20–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has one scene.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains what insects are ritually clean. Remember, Yahweh is telling this list to Moses and Aaron, who will tell the Israelite people what insects are ritually clean. If the Israelite people eat ritually clean insects, then the people also stay ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats an unclean or ritually dirty insect, then the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty.

Note: You may choose to go through step five before this step. In step five, you will discuss the names for the different kinds of locusts.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The background information is that Yahweh gave eating rules to Moses and Aaron to tell to the Israelite people. This passage does not mention Yahweh, Moses, or Aaron by name, but remember that Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron are having this conversation.

You can act out this passage in different ways. You might choose to have people represent Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron. The person who is representing Yahweh can tell Moses and Aaron which insects are ritually clean. If you do it this way, you might want to use the pictures from step five to show the ritually clean insects while you talk.

If you want, you might decide to act out Moses and Aaron retelling Yahweh's words to the people of Israel.

Another way to act out this passage would be to imagine situations where an Israelite person sees an insect, either while hunting or while traveling. You can show the Israelite person trying to decide whether or not to eat the insect. Maybe show how people from another people group offer ritually dirty food with dirty insects to the Israelite people. The Israelite people must tell the other people why the Israelites cannot eat the food. Please remember, the storyteller does not mention other people groups in the passage, but it may be helpful to imagine what the scene is like.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will act out this passage. Pause audio here.

The Israelite people have been wandering in the wilderness. There have been times when the Israelites were worried about having enough food. But Yahweh always gave the Israelites food to eat. The insects in this passage are insects that the Israelite people might see in the wilderness.

In Leviticus 11:10, Yahweh talked about "swarming things" to mean animals in the water that live and travel in a big group.

In this passage, Yahweh uses the same term "swarming and flying creatures" as Yahweh used in Leviticus 11:10, but this time Yahweh is referring to a certain kind of insect. In some languages, creatures that travel in such groups have names that only refer to the whole group, rather than to the individual creatures.

Stop here and, as a group, watch the video of swarming locusts. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Does your language have any special words for any animal that lives and travels in big groups? Does your language have any special words for insects that live and travel like this? Pause audio here.

In scene one, Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron that almost all insects are ritually dirty. Yahweh again uses a strong word to talk about these insects. Yahweh says that these insects are detestable, or disgusting, to the Israelites.

Then Yahweh talks about the few insects that are ritually clean. This is the rule for what insects are good to eat: the insect has to be a flying and swarming insect. Yahweh says that these insects must jump on four legs. But all the insects in this passage have six legs. Yahweh probably chose this language to show that Yahweh was no longer talking about flying creatures with two legs, like birds or bats. If this is confusing, you may want to translate with a phrase such as "insects with legs and wings" or "insects with sets of legs."

Stop here and discuss the best way to translate this in your language. Pause audio here.

Yahweh is talking about which insects are ritually clean. Although Yahweh gives the general rule, Yahweh does clarify the specific insects that the Israelite people may eat: the locust, the destroying locust, the cricket, and the grasshopper.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Is it common for people to eat bugs in your culture? Pause audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:20–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has one scene.

Note: You may choose to go through step five before this script. In script five, you can see some pictures of different kinds of locust.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh is talking to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron rules about what food the Israelite people can eat and cannot eat. If an Israelite person eats an unclean or ritually dirty creature, then the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty. In this passage, Yahweh says which insects are ritually clean: the locust, the destroying locust, the cricket, and the grasshopper.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing Moses and Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

  • At least there are lots of locusts for us to eat; or
  • I am overwhelmed by all these rules; or
  • I hope the Israelite people will listen to Yahweh.
Continue the drama.

If you want, you can act out Moses and Aaron telling Yahweh's words to the people of Israel. In that case, you may want to include this:

Ask the people playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

  • I am happy that I can still eat locusts because I like to eat locusts; or
  • I am worried I will not remember all these rules.
Continue the drama.

You may want to include some people who are not Israelites. These people are not in the passage. These people could be Egyptian people, Midian people, or other people. Maybe a person tries to sell insects or offer food with ritually dirty insects to the Israelite people. You can ask these people what they think of the Israelite people's food rules.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the other people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I think that is a good rule; or
  • What if the Israelites accidentally eat one of the insects that the Israelites' God said not to eat?

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:20–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, the storyteller uses the word unclean or ritually dirty to talk about what foods the Israelite people should not eat. You may also need to use the word clean to talk about what foods the Israelites could eat. In this passage, these words do not refer to physical cleanliness. When an Israelite person eats clean food, the person stays ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats dirty food, then the Israelite person becomes ritually dirty. Then the Israelite person needs to go through a cleansing process to become ritually clean again. Use the same words or phrases throughout for ritually clean and ritually dirty as you used in previous passages. Refer to the Master Glossary for more information about clean and unclean.

If you also use a stronger word for ritually dirty, like detestable, use the same word here as you used in previous passages.

In this passage, Yahweh gives rules about creatures that fly in big groups and have lots of legs. We call this kind of creature "insects." The rule says insects are ritually dirty, except for a few kinds of hopping insects.

The four kinds of insects in this text are the locust, the destroying locust, the cricket, and the grasshopper. These insects have strong back legs, which the insects use for jumping. We do not know exactly which name goes with which insect. But here are some pictures of different kinds of locust that would be familiar to the Israelite people. These pictures will show you what kind of insects were ritually clean and good to eat:

Stop here and look at the pictures of kinds of locust as a group. Discuss what you will call each type of insect.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 11:24–28
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 11:24–28 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:24–28 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:24–28 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the book of Leviticus, Yahweh was talking to Moses and Aaron and giving the Israelite people many rules about how the Israelites should live, what the Israelites should do, and what the Israelites should not do. In this passage, Yahweh still talks to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh gives instructions to Moses and Aaron to give to the Israelite people. Remember, at this time, the Israelite people still live in the wilderness. The Israelite people have recently set up the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh gives instructions for how the Israelite people are supposed to be, and stay, ritually clean.

In Leviticus 11, Yahweh has been giving rules about which animals are ritually clean and which animals are ritually dirty. The Israelite people could eat the ritually clean animals. But the Israelite people became ritually dirty if the Israelites ate or even touched the dead body of a ritually dirty animal. In the first part of this passage, Yahweh emphasizes that the Israelites could not touch the body of a ritually dirty animal. Some scholars believe that this rule is referring back to the last passage, which spoke about which insects were ritually clean and which insects were ritually dirty. Other scholars believe that this statement is for this passage, which talks about three kinds of ritually dirty animals. Either way, Leviticus 11 clearly states that the Israelite people are not supposed to touch or carry the dead body of any kind of the ritually dirty animals. If an Israelite person does become ritually dirty by touching one of these animals, that person needs to wash their clothes and will be ritually dirty until sunset. That means that the person cannot participate in any form of worship to Yahweh until the day is over.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Do you think verses 24 and 25 go with the last passage or with this passage? Pause this audio here.

The next part of the passage repeats three kinds of animals that are ritually dirty: animals that do not have divided hoofs, animals that do not chew the cud, and animals that have paws.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of hoofs that are not divided and animals with paws. Pause this audio here.

The rule is the same for any person who touches the dead body of one of these ritually dirty animals. If an Israelite person becomes ritually dirty in this way, that person must also wash their clothes. This washing was not to clean the person's body. It was a ceremonial washing to ritually clean the person.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What kind of ceremonial washings do people do in your culture? How do you think people in your culture will respond to the idea of ceremonial washings? Pause this audio here.

After the Israelite person ceremonially washed, the person still had to wait until the sun went down before the person was ritually clean again.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:24–28 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh states a rule here. The rule is that an Israelite person becomes ritually dirty when that person touches the dead body of a ritually dirty animal. The ritually dirty person must wash their clothes. The person remains ritually dirty until the sun sets.

In the second scene: Yahweh mentions three kinds of animals that are ritually dirty: animals that do not have divided hoofs, animals that do not chew the cud, and animals that walk on their paws. The Israelite person who touches a dead body of one of these types of animals becomes ritually dirty. The ritually dirty person must wash their clothes. The person remains ritually dirty until the sun sets.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • The people of Israel
  • And an Israelite person who is ritually dirty because that person touched a dead animal's body

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Remember that Yahweh is giving this set of rules to Moses and Aaron. Moses and Aaron would then tell these words to the people of Israel. Even though the storyteller does not mention Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron in this passage, Yahweh, Moses and Aaron are the people who are having this conversation.

In the first scene, Yahweh says what happens if an Israelite person touches the dead body of a ritually dirty animal. If an Israelite person touches the dead body of a ritually dirty animal, the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty. The Israelite person must wash their clothes. But even after that, the Israelite person stays ritually dirty until the sun sets.

An Israelite person could become ritually dirty either because that person touched the dead animal's body or because that person carried the dead animal's body. This refers both to the Israelite person who accidentally touches a ritually dirty dead animal and also to the Israelite person who purposefully touches a ritually dirty dead animal. In both situations, the Israelite person would be ritually dirty for the rest of the day.

Stop here and discuss: In your own language, describe a time when you accidentally touched something that you should not have touched. Pay attention to the words that you use. Pause the audio here.

In the second scene, Yahweh mentions three kinds of animals that are ritually dirty, all of which Yahweh has mentioned before. First, Yahweh mentions animals that do not have divided hoofs. Then Yahweh mentions animals that do not chew the cud. Notice that in this passage, this refers to two separate groups of animals. Yahweh is referring to the animals that have one quality but not the other quality required to be a ritually clean kind of animal. An animal needs to both have divided hoofs and chew the cud in order to be ritually clean. If an Israelite person touches the dead body of either kind of ritually dirty animal, that person also becomes ritually dirty. Lastly, Yahweh says that animals that walk on four feet and have paws are also ritually dirty. This refers to animals like dogs and cats and other animals that have paws.

Stop here and discuss: Does your language have any specific words or phrases for animals that walk or move on their four legs and have paws? Pause the audio here.

Yahweh repeats the same rule as before for these ritually dirty animals. If an Israelite person touches the dead body of one of these animals, that person also must wash their clothes and wait until the sun sets to become ritually clean again.

Stop here and discuss: Think of a riddle, rule, or saying that people repeatedly say in your language. Talk about how to repeat these instructions in a way that makes sense in your own language. Pause the audio here.

The passage ends when it repeats the statement that these animals are ritually dirty.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:24–28 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • The people of Israel
  • And an Israelite person who is ritually dirty because that person touched a dead animal's body

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In scene one, Yahweh states a rule. The rule is that an Israelite person becomes ritually unclean if that person touches the dead body of a ritually dirty animal. The Israelite person who touches the dead body becomes ritually dirty. The ritually dirty person must wash their clothes. The person remains ritually dirty until the sun sets.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the ritually dirty Israelite person, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I wish I had not touched the dead body of the animal; or
  • I am worried about what other people will think of me; or
  • I am glad that I will be ritually clean soon.
Continue the drama.

In scene two, Yahweh mentions three kinds of animals that are ritually dirty: animals that do not have divided hoofs, animals that do not chew the cud, and animals that walk on their paws. The Israelite person who touches a dead body of one of these types of animals becomes ritually dirty. The ritually dirty person must wash their clothes. The person remains ritually dirty until the sun sets. This person cannot join in any worship or ceremony while the person is ritually dirty.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the ritually dirty Israelite person who could not go to worship, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am sad that I do not get to go to worship Yahweh; or
  • This is to protect me. If I try to come close to Yahweh right now, I might die. The rule is good; or
  • I do not want people to know that I am ritually dirty.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:24–28 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh uses the word unclean or ritually dirty to talk about the animals the Israelites should not eat as food or touch if those animals have died. In this passage, these words do not refer to physical cleanliness. If an Israelite person picks up the dead body of an unclean animal, then the Israelite person becomes ritually dirty. Then the Israelite person needs to go through a cleansing process to become ritually clean again. Use the same word or phrase for dead bodies of animals that you have used previously. Use the same word or phrase throughout for ritually clean and ritually dirty as you used in previous passages. For more information about clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Israelite people were only supposed to eat animals with divided hoofs that also chew the cud.

An animal with divided hoofs has special feet or hoofs that split into two separate toes. Like human toes, these animals' toes can move a little bit to help the animals as the animals walk over hills and mountains. Use the same word or phrase for divided hoofs as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of divided hoofs. Pause this audio here.

Some animals that eat lots of grass and plants, like cattle, sheep, and goats, have a special eating process. These animals chew their food in their mouths for a very long time. Then these animals swallow the food in their mouths. But later, the animals burp the food back into their mouths and chew on the food again. People who work with these animals call this process "chewing the cud." Use the same word or phrase for "chew the cud" as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a video of an animal as it chews the cud. Pause this audio here.

The Israelite people were not supposed to eat or pick up the dead bodies of animals that have four legs and walk on paws. Paws are the rough spots on the bottom of furry animals' feet that help the animals walk and balance.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of an animal paw.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
