title: Leviticus 11:29–38
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 11:29–38 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:29–38 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:29–38 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the book of Leviticus, Yahweh has been talking to Moses and Aaron and giving the Israelite people many rules about how the Israelites should live, what the Israelites should do, and what the Israelites should not do. In this passage, Yahweh still talks to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh gives instructions to Moses and Aaron to give to the Israelite people. Remember, at this time, the Israelite people still live in the wilderness. The Israelite people have recently set up the Tent of Meeting, and Yahweh gives instructions for how the Israelite people are supposed to be and stay ritually clean.

In Leviticus 11, Yahweh has been talking about different kinds of animals and whether those animals are ritually clean or ritually dirty. First, Yahweh talked about "cattle" or land animals, then water creatures, then birds, then insects. Now, in this passage, Yahweh explains what crawling animals are ritually dirty. We do not know exactly why Yahweh made a separate category for these animals, but it might be because these were animals that often came into the Israelite people's tents and homes. Because of this, people would have more questions about how these animals made other things dirty. These animals would likely climb into things and touch many things in the house because it was hard to catch these animals. From this passage, we learn that the ritually dirty animal does not seem to make anyone or anything dirty while it is alive. However, once the ritually dirty animal dies, the animal's body makes everything the body touches ritually dirty.

First, Yahweh gives the list of ritually dirty crawling creatures: mole, mouse, great lizard, gecko, monitor lizard, wall lizard, skink, and chameleon.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the pictures of these creatures. Pause this audio here.

All of these animals stay close to the ground, and many of these animals live in the ground too. Many of these animals are also great climbers, and some can even climb walls. The list of animals is primarily of lizards and lizard-like animals, although there are also small mammals on the list, too. In step five, we will discuss more about what these animals might actually look like. But the importance of these animals seems to be that the animals can all climb or dig into the Israelite people's tents and homes. These animals are another category of swarming creatures, [like the insects that Yahweh talked about previously.]{.mark} [These animals, like the swarming insects, move chaotically. These animals do not move in straight lines. These animals also climb into both dirty places and clean places.]{.mark} Again, even though these animals are ritually dirty, these animals do not defile a person if the animal is alive. However, once the animal dies, any person who touches the dead body becomes ritually dirty. However, the person is only ritually dirty until the sun goes down and it is evening time.

Then Yahweh talks about what to do in four situations when one of these ritually dirty animals touches something and dies. First, if one of these animals dies and touches something, an item like a tool, bag, or clothing, then a person could clean the item if the item is wood, cloth, animal hide, or sackcloth. When an Israelite person finds a dirty item, the person must put the item in water. Then, at sunset, the item becomes clean again.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what do people believe about sunset and nighttime? Why do you think these objects became clean again at sunset? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh talks about the second situation. In this case, the crawling creature dies and touches a cooking pot, a water pot, or another kind of cooking space like an oven. People made these cooking vessels out of clay, which is mud that the sun hardens or that people cook to make hard. Clay pots have a texture that absorbs whatever the clay pot touches. This is probably the reason why the Israelite people must break and destroy these pots when the pots are ritually dirty.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What do you think of the difference between how the Israelite people should treat ritually dirty clay pots compared to items that people made from other materials? [Why do you think Yahweh made this rule? What kinds of rules do you have, like this, in which the type of material of the vessel matters?]{.mark} Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh talks about the third situation. The crawling creature dies in a cistern, well, or another source of water. In this situation, the crawling creature does not make the water source ritually dirty. However, if someone picks the dead animal's body out of the water and touches the body, then that person is ritually dirty until evening.

In the last situation, the crawling creature dies while touching the plant seeds for the Israelite's fields. If the crawling creature dies and touches the seeds when the Israelites are saving the seeds, the seeds are still ritually clean, and a person can still plant the seeds. But if the crawling creature dies when the seeds are wet, and people are planting the seeds, then the seeds become ritually dirty.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:29–38 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has five scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains what crawling animals are ritually dirty. Remember, Yahweh is telling this list to Moses and Aaron, who will tell the Israelite people what crawling animals are ritually dirty. If an Israelite person eats or touches the dead body of an unclean or ritually dirty crawling animal, then the Israelite person also becomes ritually dirty.

In the second scene: Yahweh describes four situations. In the first situation, one of the ritually dirty animals falls onto a tool or onto clothes that people made from wood, cloth, animal hide, or sackcloth.

In the third scene: Yahweh gives instructions for the second situation, which describes what to do if one of the ritually dirty animals falls into a cooking pot or other clay pots.

In the fourth scene: Yahweh gives instructions for what the people should do if one of the ritually dirty animals falls into a water source.

In the fifth scene: Yahweh gives instructions for what the people should do if one of the ritually dirty animals falls on plant seeds.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The background information is that Yahweh gave eating rules to Moses and Aaron. Yahweh also told Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelite people the eating rules. This passage does not mention Yahweh, Moses, or Aaron by name, but remember that Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron are the people who are having the conversation.

You can act out this passage in different ways. You might choose to have people represent Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron. The person who is representing Yahweh can tell Moses and Aaron which crawling animals are ritually dirty. If you do it this way, you might want to use the pictures from script five to show the ritually dirty crawling animals while you talk.

If you want, you might decide to act out Moses and Aaron retelling Yahweh's words to the people of Israel.

For scenes two through five, act out the situations where one of the ritually dirty crawling animals falls on something. Have an Israelite person follow the instructions for what to do in each situation.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will act out this passage. Pause this audio here.

The Israelite people have been wandering in the wilderness. There have been times when the Israelis have been worried about having enough food. But Yahweh always gave the Israelites food to eat. The crawling animals in this passage are ones that the Israelite people might see in the wilderness.

In Leviticus 11:10, swarming things refer to animals in the water that live and travel in big groups. In Leviticus 11:20, swarming things refer to insects that fly. In this passage, the same word refers to creeping animals or animals that crawl along the ground.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your language, how do you describe animals that crawl on the ground? Pause this audio here.

In the first scene, Yahweh talks about the ritually dirty crawling animals: mole, mouse, great lizard, gecko, monitor lizard, wall lizard, skink, and chameleon. Even touching the dead body of one of these animals makes an Israelite person ritually dirty until evening.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the pictures of these creatures. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh mentions that "any kind" of great lizard is ritually dirty. The Israelite people probably knew several different kinds of lizards that fit into this category. The picture of the great lizard in step five gives just one example of the kind of lizard that the Israelite people might recognize.

In scene two, Yahweh describes the first situation. Most of the ritually dirty crawling creatures are creatures that the Israelite people might find inside the Israelites' tents or homes. Many of these animals can climb up walls. What happens if one of these ritually dirty animals dies and falls on something like a tool or a kind of cloth? Yahweh mentions things that people make out of four kinds of materials: wooden things, such as tools and bowls; cloth fabrics, such as wool, linen, or cotton; leather things that a person made out of animal hide; and sackcloth, which people made from coarse material such as goat or camel hair. If this happens, an Israelite person must put the item in water. The item would be ritually dirty during the day, but when the sun goes down, the item becomes clean again.

In scene three, Yahweh describes the second situation. What happens if the ritually dirty crawling animal falls into a cooking vessel or a water jug? Any clay pot for food or drink becomes ritually dirty, and people must break that clay pot into pieces. The Israelite people also must be careful that water from that clay pot does not get into any of the Israelites' other food.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what are some common rules to keep your food safe and clean? What makes food "dirty"? Pause the audio here.

In scene four, Yahweh describes the third situation. What happens if the ritually dirty crawling animal dies and falls into a water cistern or water source? The water source remains clean, but if an Israelite person touches the dead animal's body, then that person is ritually dirty.

Stop here and look at a picture of a cistern. Pause the audio here.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, how do people collect water and save it for later? Pause the audio here.

In scene five, Yahweh describes the fourth situation. What happens if a ritually dirty animal dies and falls onto plant seeds that the Israelite people are storing somewhere? The seeds remain clean, and a person can plant the seeds. But what if the animal falls on seeds that are wet and ready to grow? Those seeds are ritually dirty.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:29–38 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has five scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives the list of ritually dirty crawling animals: mole, mouse, great lizard, gecko, monitor lizard, wall lizard, skink, and chameleon. Even touching the dead body of one of these animals makes an Israelite person ritually dirty until evening.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the pictures of these creatures. Pause this audio here.

[In scene two, Yahweh describes the first situation. One of these ritually dirty animals could die and fall on an item. If people made that item out of wood, cloth, animal skin, or sackcloth, that item becomes ritually dirty, too. The Israelites must put that item in water.]{.mark} The item would be ritually dirty during the day, but when the sun goes down, the item becomes clean again.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am frustrated that I cannot use my tool; or
  • Why do I need to put the item in water?
Continue the drama.

In scene three, Yahweh gives the second situation. What happens if the ritually dirty crawling animal falls into a cooking vessel or a water jug? Any clay pot for food or drink becomes ritually dirty, and a person must break the clay pot into pieces. The Israelite people also must be careful that water from that clay pot does not get into any of the Israelites' other food.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • At least I can have my tool tomorrow, but why do I need to break the clay pot? or
  • I am sad to lose my cooking pot; or
  • I am thankful that Yahweh wants us to have clean food; or
  • Even the water from the pot can make our food not clean.
Continue the drama.

In scene four, Yahweh gives the third situation. What happens if the ritually dirty crawling animal dies and falls into a water cistern or water source? The water source remains clean, but if an Israelite person touches the dead animal's body, then that person is ritually dirty.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am relieved that our water sources stay clean; or
  • I am sad to lose my cooking pot; or
  • I am thankful that Yahweh wants us to have clean food.
Continue the drama.

In scene five, Yahweh gives the fourth situation. What happens if a ritually dirty animal dies and falls onto plant seeds that the Israelite people are storing somewhere? The seeds remain clean, and a person can still plant the seeds. But what if the animal falls on seeds that are wet and ready to grow? Those seeds are ritually dirty.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am relieved that our seeds stay clean while we store the seeds; or
  • We could never keep such animals out of the store bins; or
  • I hope this does not happen because it would be a waste to lose seeds this way.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:29–38 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh uses the word unclean or ritually dirty to talk about what animals the Israelite people should not touch. You may also need to use the word clean to talk about what things were ritually clean. In this passage, these words do not refer to physical cleanliness. An Israelite person who was ritually clean was able to participate in religious ceremonies and worship. An Israelite person who was ritually dirty, often from touching or eating something that was ritually dirty, had to go through a cleansing process to become ritually clean again. Use the same words or phrases throughout for ritually clean and ritually dirty as you used in previous passages.

A mole is a round, hairy animal that lives underground. A mole has big paws that help the mole dig underground. A mole has very small eyes and does not see well. This kind of mole weighs between 20 and 70 grams.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a mole. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for mole. Pause this audio here.

A mouse is a rodent with fur that is usually brown or gray. A mouse has big ears and big eyes. A mouse has a long tail that does not have any fur. This kind of mouse is about 10 centimeters long and usually weighs between 40 and 85 grams.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a mouse. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for mouse. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

A great lizard is a large reptile that lives in deserts. A lizard can be light brown or a darker brown. A great lizard has tough, dry scales that cover its body. A great lizard has a flat body and a large tail with scaly horns on the tail. A lizard eats plants. A lizard is usually about 75 centimeters long and can weigh up to one kilogram.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a spiny-tailed lizard, which is a type of great lizard. Pause this audio here.

There are several kinds of lizards in this passage. You will need to decide as a group what you want to call these lizards in your language or whether to refer to the lizards as a group.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for lizard. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

A gecko is a kind of small lizard that makes sounds that might sound like sighs, chirps, or clicks. A gecko has smooth skin and very big eyes that help the gecko see at night. A gecko's toes are sticky, which allows the gecko to crawl on walls and trees. This kind of gecko is usually 11 or 12 centimeters long.

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a gecko. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for gecko. Pause this audio here.

A monitor lizard has a long body and strong legs, which the monitor lizard uses to dig and climb. This type of monitor lizard is light brown with dark brown stripes. A monitor lizard has a long tongue that the lizard sticks out of its mouth. This helps the monitor lizard look for food. In Hebrew, people called this lizard the "strong lizard."

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of a monitor lizard. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for monitor lizard. Pause this audio here.

A wall lizard, which people also call an agama, is a kind of lizard. An Agama's body has scales, with pointed scales on its back and down its tail. Agamas are very good at climbing. Agamas can grow up to 30 centimeters long and weigh 20 grams, 50 grams, or sometimes even 70 grams! In Hebrew, people call this animal the "wandering lizard."

Stop here and, as a group, look at a picture of an agama lizard. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for wall lizard or agama. Pause this audio here.

A skink is a kind of lizard that has a long body that is round and thin. A skink has a thick neck, so it is hard to see where the head ends and the body begins. The kind of skink that lives in this area has a special way of traveling through the sand gracefully.

Stop here and look at a picture of a skink as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for skink. Pause this audio here.

A chameleon is a reptile with very large eyes. A chameleon has a large bump on its head. A chameleon has a large body and small, skinny legs that help the chameleon climb. A chameleon is often green or brown but has the ability to change its color. In Hebrew, people call this animal the "low to the ground" lizard.

Stop here and look at a picture of a chameleon as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for chameleon. Pause this audio here.

If anyone touches the dead body of one of these animals, that person will be unclean until the sun sets. Use the same word or phrase for "dead body" as you have used previously.

Yahweh talks about items that people made out of different kinds of material. A hide is the skin of an animal that a person has cleaned and stretched into leather. The Israelite people would make cloth from plants such as cotton or flax, or out of sheep's hair, which people call wool. But the Israelites would make sackcloth from goat hair or camel hair. Sackcloth was scratchy and uncomfortable. Ancient Israelites often wore sackcloth when the Israelites were grieving. Sackcloth was also a symbol of extreme poverty or hardship.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for sackcloth. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

A spring was a place in the ground where fresh water would naturally come up to the surface, and people could collect the water to drink.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for a spring of water. Pause this audio here.

A cistern was a large underground cave or well that ancient people used to collect rainwater. Because the rain comes quickly and in large amounts in the desert, it is important that extra water has a place to go. The cisterns would collect that water so that people could use the water when there was not much rain.

Stop here and look at a picture of a cistern as a group. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for cistern. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

If the dead body of an animal falls on seeds that someone will plant in their fields, the seeds remain ritually clean. But if there is water on the seeds, the seeds become ritually dirty.

Stop here and decide as a group what word or phrase you will use for seeds. Refer to the Master Glossary for more information about seeds, and use the same word for seeds that you have used in previous books of the Bible.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 11:39–47
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 11:39–47 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:39–47 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:39–47 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In Leviticus 11, Yahweh has been giving Moses and Aaron rules about what animals the Israelite people should consider ritually clean and what animals the Israelite people should consider ritually dirty. Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron to tell these rules to the Israelite people so that the Israelites can be ritually clean and be close to Yahweh. Ritually clean animals are animals that the Israelite people can eat and stay ritually clean. But if an Israelite person eats or touches the dead body of a ritually dirty animal, that Israelite person will also be ritually dirty.

In the first part of this passage, Yahweh says something that may surprise people. Even the bodies of ritually clean animals that die from old age or because of an accident are ritually dirty. An Israelite person who touches, carries, or eats the dead animal's body becomes ritually dirty too. The person must wash their clothes, and the person must wait until the sun sets. Then the person becomes ritually clean again.

Stop here and discuss: Why do you think that the ritually clean animals also become ritually dirty if the animal dies naturally from sickness, an accident, or old age? Pause the audio here.

Next, Yahweh restates a general rule about what animals are ritually dirty. The rule is this: swarming animals are ritually dirty. In Leviticus 11:10, the swarming creatures refer to certain animals that live in the water, many of which travel in big groups and move in odd ways through the water. In Leviticus 11:20, swarming things refer to insects that fly in large groups. In Leviticus 11:29, swarming things refer to animals that creep and crawl along the ground. Some scholars believe that one reason these animals are ritually dirty is that there is something unnatural or chaotic about how these animals move.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what kinds of animals do people not like or will not touch? Why do people in your culture not like those animals? Pay attention to what words you use to describe these animals. Pause the audio here.

Why do the Israelite people need to follow these rules about what to eat and not eat? The reason is that Yahweh is holy. Yahweh is pure and good. Yahweh asks the Israelite people to be holy because Yahweh is holy. This means the Israelite people need to live in a way that is clean and good. In this passage, Yahweh talks about ritually clean animals in a different way than Yahweh talks about ritually dirty animals. In the same way, Yahweh talks about the Israelite people, Yahweh's people, in a different way than how Yahweh talks about all the other people groups on the earth. Yahweh wants the Israelite people to live differently from all the other people groups because the Israelite people know Yahweh and what is important to Yahweh. Yahweh also wants the Israelite people to show other people groups what Yahweh is like and to show other people how to worship Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss: What kind of actions can a person do that are important to Yahweh? What do you do differently in your life to show others what is important to Yahweh? Pause the audio here.

These rules, which are about eating animals and remaining ritually clean and not becoming ritually dirty, are supposed to remind the Israelite people of something very important. When the Israelites think of these rules, the Israelite people are supposed to remember Yahweh's love and the blessing of having a special relationship with Yahweh. When the Israelite people were slaves in Egypt, Yahweh brought the Israelites out of slavery and promised to be with the Israelites and to protect the Israelites. Yahweh also gave these rules to the Israelite people to teach the Israelites something about what is important to Yahweh.

As Yahweh finishes this section of Leviticus, Yahweh reminds us of the purpose of all the rules in this section. These rules help the Israelite people know which animals are ritually clean and ritually dirty.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:39–47 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains that even ritually clean animals become ritually dirty when the clean animals die because the animals are old or because an accident happens. In this situation, an Israelite person who touches the dead animal's body, whether by mistake or intentionally, is ritually dirty. An Israelite person who is ritually dirty in this way must wash their clothes and is ritually dirty until the sun sets.

In the second scene: Yahweh restates what animals are ritually dirty. This is a reminder of all the rules in Leviticus 11. Swarming animals are ritually dirty, whether the animals are land animals, water creatures, insects, or creatures that live in the ground. Yahweh reminds the Israelite people why the Israelites must follow these rules: Yahweh is holy, and the Israelites are to be like Yahweh. Then Yahweh gives a final summary statement. These are the rules to help the Israelite people know which animals are ritually clean and which are ritually dirty.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • The people of Israel
  • And an Israelite person who is ritually dirty

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Remember that Yahweh is giving this set of rules to Moses and Aaron. Moses and Aaron would then tell these words to the people of Israel. Even though Moses and Aaron's names are not in this passage, Moses and Aaron were the original people Yahweh spoke these words to.

Stop here and discuss: Does your language have special words or phrases that you use when you are telling a person someone else's words? Pause the audio here.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains something that Yahweh had not said yet. Even a ritually clean animal can become ritually dirty, depending on how the animal dies. If a person kills the ritually clean animal in the right way, the animal is ritually clean and good to eat. But if the animal dies, whether from old age or because of an accident, the dead animal's body is ritually dirty. An Israelite person who eats, touches, or carries the dead animal's body becomes ritually dirty too. It does not matter if the Israelite person accidentally touches the dead body or purposefully moves the body. In either case, the Israelite person becomes ritually dirty. Sometimes an Israelite person might need to move the dead body, if, for example, the animal dies while the animal is in a pen with other animals. But the person still becomes ritually dirty. The person must wash their clothes and wait until the sun sets. Then the person becomes ritually clean again.

Stop here and discuss: Do you make a difference in your language between something that a person does on purpose and something that a person does accidentally? Pause the audio here.

In the second scene, Yahweh reminds the Israelite people of the main food rule. Swarming animals are detestable, which is a strong way to say that these animals are ritually dirty. That includes swarming creatures in the water, insects, and swarming animals that creep on the ground. This rule also talks about any other "creeping" animals that Yahweh has not yet talked about. Remember that the idea of swarming may mean that these animals move around in a chaotic way. The rule about swarming creatures is a general rule to help the Israelite people remember which animals are ritually clean and which animals are ritually dirty.

Stop here and discuss: What are the different words in your language that you might need to use to explain the idea of "swarming animals"? Pause the audio here.

Why do the Israelite people need to follow these dietary rules? The reason is that Yahweh is holy. Yahweh is pure and whole and good. Yahweh asks the Israelite people to be holy because he, Yahweh, is holy. The Israelite people needed to change their eating habits so that the Israelites could be close to Yahweh. It was another sign to all the people in the world that the Israelite people were Yahweh's special people. This statement, "be holy because Yahweh is holy," is a very important one in Leviticus. You will hear this statement many times in Leviticus.

Stop here and discuss: What are some ways in your language that you might emphasize a very special message? How can you translate "be holy because Yahweh is holy" in a way that people can remember and that shows that it is very important? Pause the audio here.

When the Israelite people were slaves in Egypt, Yahweh brought the Israelites out of slavery and promised to be with the Israelites and to protect the Israelites. Yahweh wants a relationship with the Israelite people that is special. Yahweh shows the Israelites many times that Yahweh is not like the false gods that the Egyptian people worshipped.

The last thing Yahweh says is really just a summary, that the Israelite people should use these rules to know what animals are ritually clean and ritually dirty.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:39–47 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • The people of Israel
  • And an Israelite person who is ritually dirty

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Remember that Yahweh is the one giving this set of rules to Moses and Aaron. Moses and Aaron would then tell these words to the people of Israel. Even though the storyteller does not mention Moses and Aaron in this passage, Moses and Aaron were the original people Yahweh spoke these words to.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains how a ritually clean animal can become a ritually dirty animal. If people kill the animal the right way, the animal is ritually clean and good to eat. But if the animal dies, whether from old age or because of an accident, the dead animal's body is ritually dirty. An Israelite person who touches, eats from, or carries the dead animal's body becomes ritually dirty too and must wash their clothes and wait until the sun sets to be ritually clean again.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person who is ritually dirty, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I think it is a waste of meat to not be able to eat it; or
  • I am ritually dirty, but I did not even cause my animal to die; or
  • I really want to do what Yahweh commands us to do.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh reminds the Israelite people of some main rules for the food the Israelites may eat. For example, swarming creatures are detestable, or ritually dirty, whether in the water, on land, or in the ground. Why do the Israelite people need to follow these special eating rules? Yahweh is holy, and the Israelites are to be holy like Yahweh is.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I want my people to be close to me; or
  • I brought my people out of slavery so that my people could live good and clean lives.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh explains that Yahweh is the God of the people of Israel. Yahweh freed the Israelites from being slaves in Egypt. Again, Yahweh says to be holy like Yahweh is holy. Then Yahweh reminds the Israelites that the Israelite people should use these rules to know what animals are ritually clean and ritually dirty.

Pause the drama.

Ask the people playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The people might answer things like:

  • I am thankful that Yahweh chose us; or
  • When people make rules, the rules can be difficult. But Yahweh's rules are for our good; or
  • I am happy that we get to eat good things.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 11:39–47 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh uses the word unclean or dirty to talk about what dead animals the Israelite people should not touch. In this passage, these words do not refer to physical dirtiness. If an Israelite person touches the dead body of a ritually dirty animal, then the Israelite person becomes ritually dirty. Then the Israelite person needs to go through a cleansing process to become ritually clean again. Use the same words or phrases throughout for bodies of dead animals, and ritually clean and ritually dirty, as you used in previous passages, and refer to the Master Glossary for more information about clean and unclean. If you use a word that means very dirty, or detestable, use the same word as you have used previously.

Yahweh tells his people to not make themselves unclean or detestable, or to not defile themselves.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will talk about people making themselves unclean or detestable. Look up defile in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already described this idea in another book of the Bible, discuss if you want to talk about it in the same way here. Pause this audio here.

Use the same word for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh told the Israelite people to consecrate themselves, or make themselves holy. The Israelite people would take special baths, change their clothes, and not have sex for a time to consecrate themselves. In this passage, Yahweh generally wanted the Israelite people to be holy, or different from all the other groups of people. Use the same word or phrase for consecrate as you used in previous passages. Look up consecrate in the Master Glossary for more information.

Yahweh said the Israelite people were to be holy because Yahweh is holy. Yahweh is pure and complete and good. Yahweh chose Yahweh's people to have a special purpose. Yahweh wants Yahweh's people to be ritually clean so Yahweh's people can be close to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for holy as you used in previous passages. Look up holy in the Master Glossary for more information.

Yahweh says that this is the law, or rule, about eating or touching unclean animals. Look up law in the Master Glossary for more information. Use the same word for law as you used in previous passages.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 13:1–8
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 13:1–8 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:1–8 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh has been giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai. The Israelites had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Here, in this passage, Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron instructions for the priests on how to determine whether a person with a skin problem is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

Remember, for an Israelite person, to be ritually clean or ritually dirty was not actually about physical cleanliness. In the same way, just because an Israelite person had a defiling skin problem, it did not necessarily mean that the person had a serious medical disease. Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to be ritually clean so that the Israelites could be near to Yahweh and worship Yahweh. The main concern was whether the Israelite people were ready spiritually to obey and follow Yahweh.

In the past, translators have translated the phrase "defiling skin disease" as leprosy. However, scholars agree that most likely, the modern disease of leprosy did not exist in that region at that time. Also, Yahweh instructed the priests to look for certain symptoms that do not seem to describe modern leprosy at all. Similarly, Yahweh does not mention certain symptoms that are extremely common in leprosy. So it seems unlikely that the defiling skin disease refers to leprosy. Instead, it likely refers to an entire group or category of skin diseases.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how do you talk about different kinds of skin diseases? What skin diseases do you consider normal? What skin diseases do you consider a problem? How do people talk about someone who has a bad skin disease? Pause this audio here.

The question remains, why did Yahweh consider some human skin problems to be defiling or something that makes a person ritually dirty, and not other human skin problems? It does seem likely that one of the reasons why Yahweh said that an Israelite person with a defiling skin disease should live apart from others was to keep other people from getting the same skin disease. We know from other passages that a ritually clean Israelite person could become ritually dirty by touching another Israelite person who was ritually dirty. Again, the focus seems to be more on a person being ritually clean and spiritually ready than on someone spreading a disease to someone else.

Yahweh gives three kinds of human skin problems or three kinds of sores that cause an Israelite person to go to see the priest for examination. An Israelite must go to a priest if their skin has swelling, rashes or scabs, or bright spots. Scholars believe that these descriptions also include scaly and flaky skin, which could also be symptoms of a defiling skin disease.

If an Israelite person has one of these three skin conditions, that person must go see a priest for examination. The priest must check for two characteristics when the priest checks the Israelite's skin. First, the priest must determine if the hair around the skin sore has turned white. This requirement causes another problem for scholars. According to modern medicine, skin diseases do not normally cause hair to turn white. However, some scholars have suggested that this refers to psoriasis or even infections, such as fungal infections, which could cause the hair to appear white.

Stop here and, as a group, look at pictures of possible defiling skin diseases. Pause audio here.

Then the priest must determine whether the sore is deeper than the skin around it.

If the priest decides that the hair has turned white and the sore is deep in the skin, then the priest must declare the person to have a defiling skin disease. This means that the Israelite person is a ritually dirty person. This means that until the person heals, the person cannot participate in worship at the Tent of Meeting or in other communal activities with the people of Israel. We know from later in Leviticus that the ritually dirty Israelite person with a defiling skin disease had to live separately from all the other people of Israel. Not only that, but the person with the defiling skin disease must wear torn clothes and keep messy hair, which were signs of mourning. Lastly, the person had to cover their face and warn people that the person was ritually dirty, so that no one would accidentally become ritually dirty by touching the person.

[However, if the sore is not deeper than the skin around it, and the hair does not turn white, then the person has to live alone for seven days. Then the priest will check that person's skin again. If the sore or rash did not spread, the person has to live alone for seven more days. If the sore or rash still has not spread, then the priest will declare that the person is ritually clean. The person just needs to wash their clothes, and the person will be ritually clean again. However, if the sore or rash spreads after the priest declares the person ritually clean, then the person has to come back to the priest again. If the rash continues to spread, then the priest will declare that person ritually dirty.]{.mark}

When a priest declares that an Israelite person is ritually clean or ritually dirty from a skin condition, this is probably a sort of public proclamation. It is important for other Israelite people to know when someone is ritually dirty, because other people could become ritually dirty by being in contact with the ritually dirty person.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, if the community rejects someone or calls someone taboo, how is that person supposed to act? How are other people supposed to treat the person?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh gives Moses and Aaron instructions for the priests on how to determine whether a person with a skin problem is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

In the second scene: If an Israelite person has a concerning skin problem, the person must go to the priest. If the priest determines that the Israelite person has a defiling skin disease, the priest will declare the person to be ritually dirty.

In the third scene: If the priest determines that the Israelite person's skin disease does not look bad, the priest will isolate the Israelite person for seven days. Then the priest must check the person's skin for a second time. If the rash is the same and has not gotten worse, the priest will isolate the Israelite person for another seven days. If the rash has faded, the priest will declare the Israelite person to be ritually clean. The person must wash their clothes and is then ritually clean.

In the fourth scene: Yahweh explains what to do if the priest has announced that an Israelite person is ritually clean but the rash returns. If, after the Israelite person leaves the priest, the person's rash gets worse, the person must go back to the priest. The priest must examine the person again, and if the rash is worse, the priest must declare that the Israelite person is ritually dirty because of the defiling skin disease.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person with a concerning skin problem
  • An Israelite person who comes with the person with a concerning skin problem
  • And the priest who examines the skin problem

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, Yahweh starts giving a new set of rules. These rules teach the priests how to decide whether an Israelite person with a skin problem is ritually clean or ritually dirty. Moses wrote the rules. Moses and Aaron also told the Israelite people what Yahweh had said.

Stop here and discuss: Imagine an important person tells you something. After that, you go and tell a new person the same words. What words would you use to re-tell someone else's words? Pause the audio here.

In the past, people translated the defiling skin disease in this passage with the word "leprosy." However, most scholars agree that the skin diseases in this passage are not the same as modern-day leprosy.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Is there an accepted Bible in your region, perhaps in another language? If so, how does that Bible translate the defiling skin disease? If it uses a term such as leprosy, discuss whether it would be helpful to follow that translation in your own translation. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Yahweh gives the priest specific instructions for what to look for in a skin disease. None of those descriptions matches a description of modern-day leprosy. Most scholars think that the defiling skin disease probably refers to a big category that includes many different skin diseases. Yahweh gives instructions so that the priests could look at any skin problem and determine whether or not it was a defiling skin disease.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how do you talk about different kinds of skin diseases? What skin diseases do you consider normal? What skin diseases do you consider a problem? How do people talk about someone who has a bad skin disease? Pause the audio here.

Yahweh says that someone must bring the Israelite person with the skin problem to the priest. Who brings the person? Probably a close relative will go with the person with the skin problem and be present when the priest looks carefully at the person's skin. However, in some languages, it may be easier to simply say, "If a person has a skin problem, that person must go to the priest."

In scene two, Yahweh gives three kinds of human skin problems or three kinds of sores that will cause an Israelite person to go to see the priest for examination. There is some disagreement between scholars about exactly what these different words mean, but here are some likely descriptions of what each skin problem refers to.

The first human skin problem is swelling. A person with swelling in their skin probably refers to a person whose skin is swollen and inflamed. The person's skin looks puffed up and bigger than it should, and it may be sensitive when a person touches the skin.

The second human skin problem is a rash. This might refer to a raised bump on the skin, such as a scab or a boil. It could also refer to a lot of little bumps on a person's skin, which people often call a rash.

The third human skin problem is a bright spot. This probably refers to white spots on human skin. However, it may refer to any human skin that is an unusual color for that person.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, do you have words for any of these skin problems? How would you talk about or group the skin problems? Pause the audio here.

If an Israelite person has one of these three skin problems, that person must go see a priest so the priest can examine the person. The priest must answer two questions when the priest looks carefully at that person's skin. First, the priest must determine if the hair around the sore has turned white. Then the priest must determine whether the sore is deeper than the skin around the sore. It is unclear whether this means that the sore is an actual hole or dent in the skin or if the sore is deep in the skin down to the flesh of the person, which likely shows infection. If possible, try to translate this phrase in a way that allows for both meanings.

Stop here and discuss. First, listen to this statement: "His sore is deeper than the skin of his body." When you hear this statement, what do you think it means? In your language, how would you describe a human sore that is deep in a person's skin? Pause the audio here.

In this passage, the word "hair" does not refer to a singular strand of hair, but rather to many hairs that might be around the human's sore.

If the priest decides that the hair has turned white and the sore is deep in the skin, then the priest must declare that the person has a defiling skin disease. This means that the Israelite person is a ritually dirty person. This means that until the person heals, the person cannot participate in worship at the Tent of Meeting or other community activities with the people of Israel.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what term will you use for "defiling skin disease"? Pause this audio here.

In the third scene, Yahweh tells what the priest should do if the person does not have a defiling skin disease. The Israelite person may have a skin sore that is white. But the priest may see that the sore is not deeper than the rest of the person's skin and that the sore is not turning the person's hair white. If so, then the priest must instruct the Israelite person with the skin sore to live by himself or herself, away from anyone else. After one week, the priest must look carefully at the person's sore a second time. If the person's sore has not changed, the priest instructs the person with the skin sore to live in isolation for another seven days. Then the priest re-examines the person's skin sore a third time. If the person's skin sore has not spread or has become smaller, then the priest can announce that the person is ritually clean. The Israelite person must wash their clothes, and then the person can act like a ritually clean person again.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will describe someone living by themselves. How will you also describe the person coming back to the priest three times for the priest to look at the person's skin? Pause this audio here.

In the fourth scene, Yahweh talks about what to do if the sore returns. After a priest declares the Israelite person with a skin sore to be ritually clean, the Israelite person can go back to normal life. But if the person's skin sore spreads or gets worse, then that person must go back to the priest again. If the priest also agrees that the person's skin sore has spread, then the priest declares that person to be ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person with a concerning skin problem
  • An Israelite person who comes with the person with a concerning skin problem
  • And the priest who examines the skin problem

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron instructions for the priests on how to determine whether a person with a skin problem is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I feel bad because I do not want to be around people who have bad diseases; or
  • How will I know how to help these people? or
  • If I am with the person who is ritually dirty, do I become ritually dirty too?
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh explains that if an Israelite person has a concerning skin problem, the person must go to the priest. The priest may determine that the Israelite person has a defiling skin disease and will declare the person ritually dirty.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person with the skin disease, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I feel embarrassed; or
  • I am upset that I will not be able to be with my family; or
  • I would do anything for someone to heal me! or
  • Did Yahweh forget me? Does Yahweh still love me?
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh explains what to do if the priest determines that the Israelite person's skin disease does not look bad. The priest must isolate the Israelite person for seven days and then look carefully at the person's skin for a second time. If the rash is the same and has not gotten worse, the priest will isolate the Israelite person for another seven days. If the rash has not gotten worse, the priest will declare the Israelite person ritually clean. The person must wash their clothes and then can act ritually clean.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am relieved that this person's rash is not worse; or
  • I do not want to make a mistake, because it will be bad for someone who is contagious to be around other people.
Continue the drama.

In the fourth scene, Yahweh explains what to do if a rash returns. The priest may announce that an Israelite person is ritually clean, even though the person had a rash. But if after the Israelite person leaves the priest, the person's rash gets worse, the Israelite person must go back to the priest. The priest must examine the person again, and if the rash is worse, the priest must declare that the Israelite person is ritually dirty because of the defiling skin disease.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am frustrated because I thought I was still ritually clean; or
  • I do not understand why this happened to me; or
  • People will think badly of me, but I did not do anything bad to cause this skin disease.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Use the same word for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh instructs the priests to determine whether an Israelite person has a defiling skin disease. If the person has a defiling skin disease, the person is ritually dirty. For more information on leprosy, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the pictures of possible defiling skin diseases. Pause this audio here.

title: Leviticus 13:9–17
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 13:9–17 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:9–17 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:9–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh has been giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai and had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Here, in this passage, Yahweh continues to give Moses and Aaron instructions for the priests on how to determine whether a person with a skin condition is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

Remember, for an Israelite person, being ritually clean or ritually dirty was not actually about physical cleanliness. In the same way, just because an Israelite person had a defiling skin problem, it did not necessarily mean that the person had a serious medical disease. Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to be ritually clean so that the Israelites could be near to Yahweh and worship Yahweh. The main concern was whether the Israelite people were ready spiritually to obey and follow Yahweh.

In the past, people have translated the phrase "defiling skin disease" as leprosy. You will remember from the previous passage that scholars believe that it is very unlikely that the skin diseases in this passage are modern leprosy. Instead, the phrase "defiling skin disease" likely refers to an entire group or category of skin diseases.

In this passage, Yahweh gives the priests three characteristics of human skin sores to determine if an Israelite person has a chronic skin disease, which is one of the defiling skin diseases. The three characteristics are: white swelling, white hair, and raw flesh.

Stop here and, as a group, look at the pictures of possible defiling skin diseases. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, the priest looks for the presence of raw flesh as a definite sign of defiling skin disease. If a person has all three characteristics—white swelling, white hair, and raw flesh—around their skin sores, the priest will declare the person to have a long-term skin disease.

Stop here and discuss: What do people think and say about people with long-term illness in your culture? How do other people treat people with long-term illness? Pause this audio here.

Sometimes a person can recover from a defiling skin disease. In these cases, the priests will again look for signs of raw flesh to decide whether a person's skin is white because it is healing or a person's skin is white because the person has a defiling skin disease.

When a priest declared that an Israelite person was ritually clean or ritually dirty from a skin disease, this was probably a sort of public proclamation. It was important for other Israelite people to know when someone was ritually dirty, because other people could become ritually dirty by being in contact with the ritually dirty person. An Israelite person who was ritually dirty had to behave in certain ways. You will remember that we know from later in Leviticus that the ritually dirty Israelite person with a defiling skin disease had to live separately from all the other people of Israel. Not only that, but the person with the defiling skin disease must wear torn clothes and keep messy hair, which were signs of mourning. Lastly, the person had to cover their face and warn people that the person was ritually dirty, so that no one would accidentally become ritually dirty by touching the person.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Imagine having to live as a ritually dirty Israelite person with a defiling disease. What do you think it would be like to live that way? What do you think you would think or feel? Pause this audio here.

Even though the storyteller does not mention it in this passage, there is a certain custom for a person whom the priest declared is ritually clean after having a defiling skin disease. Even though the priest already declared that the person is ritually clean, the person still needs to go and wash their clothes. Then the person could go back to living with other Israelite people, attending worship ceremonies, or being a part of other parts of life in the community.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:9–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: If an Israelite person has a defiling skin disease with white swelling and raw flesh, then another Israelite person should take the Israelite person with the skin problem to the priest. If the priest decides that the Israelite person has a defiling skin disease, the priest will declare the person ritually dirty.

In the second scene: An Israelite person may have a defiling skin disease that spreads and covers their whole body. The priest will examine the person's body and may declare the person is ritually clean. But any time the person with the concerning skin problem has raw flesh, the person becomes ritually dirty. If the person's raw flesh turns white, the person can go back to the priest. If the priest determines that the raw flesh has turned to white skin, the priest can declare the person ritually clean again.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person with a concerning skin problem
  • An Israelite person who comes with the person with a concerning skin problem
  • And the priest who examines the skin problem

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Yahweh was giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai. The Israelites have recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Note that the storyteller does not mention Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron in this passage, but at the beginning of Leviticus 13, the storyteller says that Yahweh first gave these instructions to Moses and Aaron.

In the first scene, Yahweh talks about what to do if an Israelite person has a defiling skin disease. Yahweh says that someone must bring the Israelite person with the skin problem to the priest. Who brings the person? Probably a close relative will go with the person with the skin problem and be present when the priest looks carefully at the person's skin. However, in some languages, it may be easier to simply say, "If a person has a defiling skin disease, that person must go to the priest."

Notice that throughout this passage, Yahweh's instructions for the priests are how to treat someone after a priest has already declared that person ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease. The priest looks for three characteristics this time.

First, the priest looks for white swelling. A person with white swelling in their skin probably refers to a person whose skin is swollen and inflamed as well as white. The person's skin might look puffed up and bigger than it should, and may be sensitive when a person touches the skin. White swelling could also refer to scaly or flaky skin.

Next, the priest sees if the hair is white. Again, we do not know exactly what this means. But it is most likely that the skin sore either causes the skin to flake or that there is an infection in such a way that changes the appearance of the hair around the sore.

Next, the priest looks for raw flesh. This means that the human skin sores are deep into the part of the skin that does not always heal on its own. When a person has a skin sore this deep, the person feels hurt when someone touches the sore because the skin is sensitive. When a person has a sore that deep, the sore is also likely to become infected.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what words would you use to describe these skin characteristics? Pause this audio here.

If the priest sees these skin characteristics, it means the person with the defiling skin disease has a chronic, or long-lasting, disease. This can also mean that the defiling skin disease has advanced into a worse stage. Another way to say this is that the person's skin disease is established, which means that it will take the person a very long time to heal.

Then the priest will declare the person to be ritually dirty. But the priest does not tell the person to live in isolation for a short time period to test whether the skin heals. The reason the priest does not do this is that the priest had already declared the person ritually dirty before. The priest's examination is, in this case, a confirmation that the person with the defiling skin disease is still ritually dirty.

In the second scene, Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a skin condition or rash that spreads and covers the person's whole body. This likely also means that the rash on the skin spreads very quickly or that the rash is an intense kind of rash. This passage says that the rash covers the person from the person's head to the person's feet. In your language, you may have another phrase that you use to refer to a body condition that is all over a person's body.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how would you describe a rash that spreads quickly? How would you describe a rash that covers a person's whole body? Pause this audio here.

This person with the skin problem or rash all over their body must also go to the priest. The priest must examine the person with the skin problem. The priest may see that the rash has spread all over the person's body and turned white. This means that the skin problem is not serious, because the person did not get infected raw skin from the rash. It is possible that this person had the defiling skin disease, but the disease is now cured. Even though the marks of the disease are still on the person's body, the person is no longer at risk of getting infection from it.

In a situation like this, the priest declares the person ritually clean.

However, any time the person with the rash has raw flesh, the priest must declare the person with the rash to be ritually dirty and tell that person that the person has a defiling skin disease.

If the person has a defiling skin disease, but the person's raw flesh becomes white, the person with the skin problem must go back to the priest. In this case, the raw flesh becoming white probably means that skin is growing again where the skin sore was before. If the priest sees that the person's sores have turned white, the priest can declare the person to be ritually clean. If it is confusing to use the term "white" here, you might simply want to say that the priest sees that the person's raw flesh is healed.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:9–17 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person with a concerning skin problem
  • An Israelite person who comes with the person with a concerning skin problem
  • And the priest who examines the skin problem

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a defiling skin disease with white swelling and raw flesh. Another Israelite person will take the Israelite person with the skin problem to the priest. If the priest determines that the Israelite person has a defiling skin disease, the priest will declare the person ritually dirty.

Pause the drama.

After the priest declares that the person with the concerning skin problem is still ritually dirty, ask the person playing the Israelite who went with that person to see the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I was hoping that the person I love would be healed; or
  • My friend is still ritually dirty. We must wait longer; or
  • I will pray for healing.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a defiling skin disease that spreads and covers their whole body. The priest will examine the person's body, and if the skin is white, the priest will declare the person is ritually clean. But any time the person with the concerning skin disease has raw flesh, the person becomes ritually dirty. If the person's raw flesh turns white, the person can go back to the priest. If the priest determines that the raw flesh has turned to white skin, the priest can declare the person ritually clean again.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person after the priest declared that person to be ritually clean again, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so excited! or
  • I cannot wait to eat with my family and friends again; or
  • I will go wash right away so I can go to the Tent of Meeting to thank Yahweh.

Filling the Gaps

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Use the same word or phrase for "defiling skin disease" as you used in previous passages. For more information on leprosy, an old term for a defiling skin disease, refer to the Master Glossary. Talk about the swelling, the white color, and all the other words you used for the skin conditions in the same way as previous passages.

In this passage, the priests are the ones who look at the person's skin to decide if a person with a skin disease is ritually dirty or not. Use the same word for priest as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

In this passage, Yahweh gives instructions to the priests to determine whether or not an Israelite person was ritually dirty because of their skin disease. Use the same word or phrase throughout for ritually clean and ritually dirty as you used in previous passages. For more information, refer to the Master Glossary for clean and unclean.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.
