Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 13:18–28
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 13:18–28 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:18–28 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:18–28 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh has been giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai. The Israelites recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Here, in this passage, Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron instructions for the priests on how to determine whether a person with a skin problem is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

Remember, for an Israelite person, to be ritually clean or ritually dirty was not actually about physical cleanliness. In the same way, just because an Israelite person had a defiling skin problem, it did not necessarily mean that the person had a serious medical disease. Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to be ritually clean so that the Israelites could be near to Yahweh and worship Yahweh. The main concern was whether the Israelite people were ready spiritually to obey and follow Yahweh.

In the past, translators have called the "defiling skin disease" leprosy. You will remember from the previous passage that scholars believe that it is very unlikely that the skin diseases in this passage are modern leprosy. Instead, the phrase "defiling skin disease" likely refers to an entire group or category of skin diseases.

In this passage, Yahweh gives instructions for how a priest will determine a defiling skin disease of two specific kinds: boils and burns. So far in Leviticus 13, the skin problems have been big skin diseases that can cover a person's whole body. But the two skin problems in this passage do not cover the whole body. Boils are usually small, and even though sometimes there will be whole groups of boils, boils usually come in small groups. A burn from a fire can happen anywhere on a person's body, but only the skin that the fire touches is burned.

Stop here and look at the pictures of human skin boils and human skin burns. Pause this audio here.

An Israelite person must go to a priest for the priest to examine the boil or burn if the person's skin has one of two characteristics. If the person has white swelling in the boil or burn, the person must go to the priest. Or, if the person has a white, red, or pink spot in the boil or burn, the person must go to the priest.

Yahweh gives the priest two things to look for in boils or burns. If the boil or burn has these characteristics, it is a defiling disease. If the sore is deeper than the skin, and if the hair around the sore is white, then the priest must declare that the person has a defiling skin disease and is ritually dirty. The hair turning white is another problem for scholars. According to modern medicine, skin diseases do not normally cause hair to turn white. However, some scholars have suggested that this refers to psoriasis or even infections, such as fungal infections that could cause the hair to appear white.

If these skin characteristics are not present, the priest must tell the person with the boil or burn to live alone for seven days. This means that the person must live outside the camp, away from other people. After seven days, the priest will look carefully at the person's skin again. The same priest must look again so that the priest can compare how the boil or burn looked before to what the priest sees now. If the white swelling or the bright spot in the sore has spread, the priest will say to the person with the skin problem, "You are ritually dirty. You have a defiling skin disease." But if the white swelling or bright spot in the sore has not spread, the priest will say to the person with the skin problem, "You are ritually clean. It is only a scar." Then the priest will allow the person to return to the person's home.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what do people think or say about scars? Pause the audio here.

When a priest declares that an Israelite person is ritually clean or ritually dirty from a skin disease, this is probably a sort of public proclamation. It was important for other Israelite people to know when someone was ritually dirty, because other people could become ritually dirty by being in contact with the ritually dirty person. An Israelite person who was ritually dirty had to behave in certain ways. We know from later in Leviticus that the ritually dirty Israelite person with a defiling skin disease had to live separately from all the other people of Israel. The person could not visit with or touch their family. Not only that, but the person with the defiling skin disease must wear torn clothes and keep messy hair, which were signs of mourning. Lastly, the person had to cover their face and warn people that the person was ritually dirty, so that no one would accidentally become ritually dirty by touching the person.

Stop here and discuss this question in your language as a group: Imagine someone told you that a family member that you love has to live isolated, far away from everyone else in the community. What would you think? How would you feel? What would you do? Pause the audio here.

Even though the storyteller does not mention it in this passage, there was a certain custom for a person when the priest declared the person was ritually clean after the person had a defiling skin disease. Even though the priest already declared that the person was ritually clean, the person still had to go and wash their clothes. Then the person could go back to live with other Israelite people, attend worship ceremonies, or be a part of other parts of life in the community.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:18–28 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a boil on their skin that has healed, but now a new, concerning skin problem appears where the boil was on the skin. This person must go to the priest and show the priest the new, concerning skin problem. The priest will determine if the person is ritually dirty from a defiling skin disease. If the priest is not certain whether the person has a defiling skin disease, the priest will tell the person to go and live alone for seven days. Then the priest must examine the person with the concerning skin problem again. If the person's skin problem has spread in their skin, the priest will declare that the person is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease. But if the person's skin problem is the same or is smaller and healing, the priest will declare that the person is ritually clean.

In the second scene: Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a burn on their skin. As the person's burn heals, a new spot may appear in the raw flesh that is either white, red, or pink. The priest must examine the new skin spot or sore. If the priest determines the person has a defiling skin disease, the priest will tell the person that the person is ritually dirty. If the priest is not certain whether the person has a defiling skin disease, the priest will tell the person to go and live alone for seven days. Then the priest must examine the person with the concerning skin problem again. If the person's skin problem has spread in their skin, the priest will declare that the person is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease. But if the person's skin problem is the same or is smaller and healing, the priest will declare that the person is ritually clean.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person with a boil on their skin
  • A priest who examines the skin problem
  • And an Israelite person with a burn on their skin

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Yahweh was giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai. The Israelites recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Note that Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron's names are not in this passage, but at the beginning of Leviticus 13, the storyteller says that Yahweh first gave these instructions to Moses and Aaron.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a boil on their skin that heals. People also call a boil a sore. These are the same kind of skin sores that the Egyptians had during the 10 plagues in Exodus. If you have already translated the passage with the 10 plagues of Egypt, you will want to use the same word here.

These boils often get infected with pus. Sometimes people call these "eruptions" because the pus sometimes bursts out of the skin.

In this situation, the Israelite person had a boil that healed, but now, in the same place, there is a new kind of concerning skin problem. Yahweh mentions two kinds of concerning skin problems that the Israelite person must go to the priest to examine.

The first concerning skin problem is white swelling of the sore. A person's skin sore with white swelling probably refers to a sore that is swollen and inflamed as well as white. The person's skin around the sore might look puffed up and bigger than it should, and may be sensitive when a person touches it. White swelling could also refer to scaly or flaky skin around or in the sore.

The second concerning skin problem is a bright spot in the sore that is either white or reddish. It is probable that this refers to any bright spots in the sore that are white, red, or pink.

Stop here and look at the pictures of human skin boils. Discuss what words you use to describe skin problems, such as boils, in your language. Pause the audio here.

If the Israelite person with a boil has either of these concerning skin problems in or around their sore, that person must go to a priest for examination. The priest will look for two characteristics of the skin sore. One thing the priest must do is determine whether the skin sore is deeper than the skin around it. It is unclear whether this phrase means that the sore is an actual dent or sunken area in the skin or if the sore is deep in the skin down to the inner flesh of the person, which likely means the skin is infected. If possible, try to translate this phrase in a way that allows for both meanings. The priest must also determine if the hair around the sore has turned white. This does not refer to one specific hair, but any hairs that are around the skin sore. If the person's concerning skin problem is both deep in the skin and has white hairs around it, the priest declares the person is ritually dirty because the person has a defiling skin disease.

If the person with the concerning skin disease does not have white hair around their skin sore and the sore is not deep in the skin, and if the sore looks like it is fading, then the priest must tell the person to live alone and separate for seven days. A skin sore is fading if the sore looks like it is healing, is going away, and is smaller and less noticeable than before.

After seven days, the priest must examine the person with the skin sore again. If the person's skin sore has spread, or gotten worse or bigger, then the priest will declare the person is ritually dirty because the person has a defiling skin disease. But if the person's skin sore has not gotten worse, the priest will declare that the person is ritually clean.

In scene two, Yahweh gives a very similar process for a person with a burn. A burn is when fire touches a person and hurts the person's skin.

If an Israelite person has a burn, and a white, red, or pink bright spot appears in the raw flesh, the person must go to the priest so the priest can look at the burn.

Stop here and look at the pictures of human skin burns. Discuss what words you use to describe burns in your language. Pause the audio here.

The priest looks for the same two characteristics of the skin burn. One thing the priest must do is determine whether the skin sore is deeper than the skin around it. The priest must also determine if the hair around the sore has turned white. If the person's concerning skin problem is both deep in the skin and has white hairs around it, the priest will declare the person is ritually dirty because the person has a defiling skin disease.

If the person with the burn does not have white hair around their skin sore and the sore is not deep in the skin, and if the sore looks like it is fading or healing, then the priest must tell the person to live alone and separate for seven days.

After seven days, the priest must examine the person with the skin sore again. If the person's skin sore has spread, or gotten worse or bigger, then the priest will declare the person is ritually dirty because the person has a defiling skin disease. But if the person's skin sore has not gotten worse, the priest will declare that the person is ritually clean.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:18–28 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person with a boil on their skin
  • A priest who examines the skin problem
  • And an Israelite person with a burn on their skin

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person had a boil on their skin that healed, but then a new, concerning skin problem appears where the boil was on the skin. This person must go to the priest and show the priest the new, concerning skin problem. The priest determines that the person is ritually dirty from a defiling skin disease.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person with the boil, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I do not understand why this happened to me; or
  • I wonder if Yahweh still loves me; or
  • I worry about whether I will ever get better.
Continue the drama.

If the priest is not certain whether the person has a defiling skin disease, because of the characteristics of the skin problem, the priest will tell the person to go and live alone for seven days. Then the priest must examine the person with the concerning skin problem again. If the person's skin problem has spread in their skin, the priest will declare that the person is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease. But if the person's skin problem is the same or is smaller and healing, the priest will declare that the person is ritually clean.

In the second scene, Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a burn on their skin. As the person's burn heals, a new spot may appear in the raw flesh that is either white, red, or pink. The priest must examine the new skin spot or sore. If the priest determines the person has a defiling skin disease, the priest will tell the person that the person is ritually dirty. If the priest is not certain whether the person has a defiling skin disease, because of the characteristics of the skin problem, the priest will tell the person to go and live alone for seven days.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I will pray that Yahweh heals this person; or
  • I really hope that this person is better when I examine the person again.
Continue the drama.

Then the priest must examine the person with the concerning skin problem again. If the person's skin problem has spread in their skin, the priest will declare that the person is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease. But if the person's skin problem is the same or is smaller and healing, the priest will declare that the person is ritually clean.

Remember, Yahweh gave these original instructions to Moses and Aaron.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • This is a big responsibility for the priests; or
  • What will the people say when the people hear these rules? or
  • How will we be able to take care of every person with a skin disease?

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:18–28 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, the priests examine a person to decide if a person with a skin disease is ritually dirty or not. Use the same word for priest as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh gives instructions to the priests to determine whether or not an Israelite person is ritually dirty because of a skin disease. Use the same word or phrase throughout for ritually clean and ritually dirty as you used in previous passages. For more information about clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh instructs the priests to determine whether an Israelite person has a defiling skin disease. If the person has a defiling skin disease, the person is ritually dirty. Use the same word or phrase for defiling skin disease as you used in previous passages. For more information on leprosy, an old term that people sometimes use for "defiling skin disease," refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and look at the pictures of human skin boils and burns.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 13:29–37
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 13:29–37 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:29–37 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:29–37 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh was giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai. The Israelites recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Here, in this passage, Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron instructions for the priests on how to determine whether a person with a concerning skin problem is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

Remember, for an Israelite person to be ritually clean or ritually dirty was not actually about physical cleanliness. In the same way, just because an Israelite person had a defiling skin problem, it did not necessarily mean that the person had a serious medical disease. Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to be ritually clean so that the Israelites could be near to Yahweh and worship Yahweh. The main concern was whether the Israelite people were ready spiritually to obey and follow Yahweh. In biblical times, it was common for Israelite people to assume that a person had a physical disease because Yahweh wanted to punish that person.

Stop here and discuss: What do people in your culture believe is the main cause of sickness? How do people assume that spiritual things influence someone becoming sick? Pause the audio here.

In the past, translators have translated "defiling skin disease" as leprosy. You will remember from the previous passage that scholars believe that it is very unlikely that the skin diseases in this passage are modern leprosy. Instead, the phrase "defiling skin disease" likely refers to an entire group or category of skin diseases.

In this passage, Yahweh gives instructions for how a priest will decide whether or not a person with a head sore—either in the person's hair or on the person's face or beard—has a defiling skin disease. This passage describes these head sores as scabs that cause the person to lose hair in those places. For this reason, some scholars think that some likely skin conditions in this passage are ringworm and favus.

Stop here and look at the pictures of ringworm and favus as possible defiling diseases in this passage. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh gives the priest two characteristics to determine if a person with a skin sore or scab on their head has a defiling skin disease. The priest looks to see if the skin sore is deep in the skin and if the skin sore has thin, yellow hairs in it. In other examinations in Leviticus 13 about defiling skin diseases, the priest looks for white hair. We do not know exactly why here the priests look for yellow, thin hair instead. It may be that because these are areas on the body where Israelite people had thick, dark hair, the hair would look different. Or it may be because this refers to a different kind of defiling skin disease. In modern medicine, doctors connect yellow hair with bacterial infections. No matter the reason, it is worth noticing that in this passage, Yahweh gives different instructions to the priests.

If the priest sees these characteristics—a sore deep in the skin with yellow, sparse hairs growing in it—then the priest declares the person ritually dirty because the person has an "itching" defiling skin disease.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how do you describe something that is extremely itchy on the skin? Pause the audio here.

If the priest sees that the skin sore does not look deep in the skin and the skin does not have black hair in it, the priest tells the person to isolate or live alone for seven days, probably somewhere outside the camp and definitely away from other people. This probably means that it is too early to tell whether the person's skin sore will be a defiling skin disease or not.

After seven days, the priest examines the head sore again. The same priest must examine the person again so that the priest can compare how the person's head skin sore has changed. This time, the priest looks for three things. First, the priest looks to see if the skin sore has not spread or gotten worse. The priest also makes sure there are no yellow hairs in the skin sore. The priest also makes sure that the skin sore does not look deep in the skin. If these three things are true, the priest will tell the person with the head skin sore to shave their hair all around the skin sore. To shave means to cut or remove all the hair. This will help the priest see if the sore has spread later. Then the priest will tell the person with the head skin sore to isolate or live alone for seven more days.

In this passage, Yahweh does not mention what the priest should do if the person's head skin sore has spread. However, based on the pattern in the passage, it is almost certain that if the priest sees the skin sore spread at this point, then the priest will declare the person with the skin sore as ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease.

If the person does a second period of isolation for seven days, at the end of that period, the person must come back to the priest. The same priest must examine the person a third time. This time, the priest looks to see if the person's head skin sore has spread. If the person's head skin sore has not spread and does not look deep in the skin, the priest says to the person, "You are ritually clean," and the person can go wash their clothes and go home.

But even after the priest tells the person with the head skin sore that the person is ritually clean, the person can still become ritually dirty again. If the person with the skin sore goes away and then their skin sore spreads, the person with the skin sore must come back to the priest again for another examination. If the priest sees that the skin sore has spread, even if there are no yellow hairs, the priest still declares that the person with the head skin sore is ritually dirty.

But if the priest thinks the person's head skin sore is the same, and if black hair is growing in the person's head skin sore, the priest declares the person with the healed skin sore as ritually clean. The priest looks for the black hair as a sign that the person's head skin sore is healed.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, who looks at people's infections? How does that person decide if a person is healed or still sick? Pause the audio here.

When a priest declared that an Israelite person is ritually clean or ritually dirty from a skin condition, this was probably a sort of public proclamation. It was important for other Israelite people to know when someone was ritually dirty, because other people could become ritually dirty by being in contact with the ritually dirty person. An Israelite person who was ritually dirty had to behave in certain ways. We know from later in Leviticus that the ritually dirty Israelite person with a defiling skin disease had to live separately from all the other people of Israel. The person could not visit with or touch their family. Not only that, but the person with the defiling skin disease must wear torn clothes and keep messy hair, which were signs of mourning. Lastly, the person had to cover their face and warn people that the person was ritually dirty, so that no one would accidentally become ritually dirty by touching the person.

After a priest declares that an Israelite person is ritually clean after having a defiling skin disease, the person must go and wash their clothes. The person must do this before the person could go back to live with other Israelite people, attend worship ceremonies, or be part of other parts of life in the community.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:29–37 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a sore on their scalp or on their face. That person must go to the priest, and the priest must examine the sore. If the person's skin sore has two characteristics, then the priest declares the person ritually dirty because the person has a defiling skin disease. If the priest decides the sore does not look bad or that it is too early to tell, the priest tells the Israelite person with the skin sore to live alone for seven days or one week.

In the second scene: After seven days, the priest will examine the person's skin sore a second time. If the person's skin sore has not spread, the person is supposed to shave or take off the hair around the scab. Then the person with the skin sore has to live alone for another seven days or one week.

In the third scene: After another seven days or one week, the priest will examine the person's skin sore for a third time. If the person's skin sore has not spread, the priest can declare the person ritually clean. The person must go and wash their clothes. But even after this, the person with the healing skin sore might need to come back for the priest to look at their skin sore again. If the person's skin sore spreads, the priest will declare the person ritually dirty. But if the person's skin sore has not changed and has normal, black hair growing in it, the priest will declare the person as ritually clean.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person with a sore on their head or face
  • And a priest who examines the skin problem

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Note that the storyteller does not mention Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron in this passage. But at the beginning of Leviticus 13, the storyteller says that Yahweh first gave these instructions to Moses and Aaron.

In scene one, Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a sore on their scalp or on their face. The original words are "in the head or in the beard." Many translations choose a word for "chin" rather than beard, since Yahweh mentions that both men and women can have this kind of sore. So this probably means a sore that appears in the part of a person's face where some people can grow a beard.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what words do you use to talk about different parts of the head or face? How do you refer to head hair? How do you refer to beard hair? Pause the audio here.

People also call this kind of sore "a scab." The person with the sore on their scalp or face must go to the priest, and the priest must examine the sore. The priest will look for two skin characteristics. If the person's skin sore looks deeper than the skin and the hair in the sore is yellow and thin, the priest will declare the person with the skin sore as ritually dirty with the defiling skin disease.

It is unclear whether the sore being "deeper than the skin" refers to an actual dent in the skin or to a sore deep in the skin down to the flesh of the person, which shows that there is an infection. If possible, try to translate this phrase in a way that allows for both meanings.

The priest also looks to see if the hair that is in or around the sore is "yellow and thin." This means there is less hair than normal, and that the hair looks unhealthy and brittle.

In this passage, the word "hair" does not refer to a singular strand of hair, but rather to many hairs that might be around or in the human skin sore.

If the priest decides that the hair has turned yellow and the sore is deep in the skin, then the priest must declare that the person has a defiling skin disease. This means that the Israelite person is a ritually dirty person. Until the person heals, this person cannot join in worship at the Tent of Meeting or other communal activities with the people of Israel.

This time, when it says "defiling skin disease," the original language mentions that this is a "tearing off" disease. That probably means that it is a skin disease that itches so badly that a person wants to scratch the skin. Some scholars think this defiling skin disease refers to diseases such as ringworm or favus.

Stop here and look at pictures of possible defiling skin diseases, ringworm and favus. Pause this audio here.

If the priest sees that the person's skin sore is not deep in the skin and that there is no black hair in the person's skin sore, the priest will tell the Israelite person with the skin sore to live alone for seven days or one week.

Some translations say "no black hair" here, while others say "no yellow hair." If there is no hair in the sore, it is likely that the priest will decide that the sore is too new to know whether or not the sore will become a defiling skin disease. Ways to avoid this issue are to translate this phrase as "no healthy hair," or "no normal hair," or simply "no hair."

Stop here and discuss: How do the Bible versions you use talk about the hair here? Discuss the best way to translate the phrase "no black hair" in your own language. Pause the audio here.

If the priest decides the sore does not look bad or that it is too early to tell, the priest will tell the Israelite person with the skin sore to live alone for seven days.

In the second scene, after seven days, the priest will examine the person's skin sore a second time. The priest looks for three characteristics of the skin sore: the person's skin sore has not spread, there are no yellow hairs in the skin sore, and the skin sore is not deep in the skin. If the person's skin sore is like this, the person must shave the hair around the sore, but not the sore itself. Most likely, the person just shaves the hair in the area around the sore, or all the hair on their head. To shave means to remove, cut, or take off the hair that is all around the sore. This is the same whether the person's skin sore is on the head or on the beard. Then the person with the skin sore has to live alone for another seven days or one week.

In the third scene, after another seven days or one week, the priest will examine the person's skin sore for a third time. If the person's skin sore has not spread and the skin sore is not deep in the skin, the priest can declare the person ritually clean. The person must go and wash their clothes.

But even after this, the person with the healing skin sore might need to come back for the priest to look at the skin sore again. If the person's skin sore spreads, the priest will declare the person ritually dirty. But if the person's skin sore has not changed and has normal, black hair growing in it, the priest will declare the person as ritually clean "as far as the priest can see." In other words, in the priest's opinion, the person is ritually clean.

Stop here and discuss: In this passage, the priest examines someone three times. The storyteller repeats Yahweh's instructions. Discuss in your language what information or instructions you should repeat. Discuss if there is any information that you should shorten or imply. Pause the audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:29–37 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person with a sore on their head or face
  • And a priest who examines the skin problem

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a sore on their scalp or on their face. That person must go to the priest, and the priest must examine the sore.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person with a sore on their head, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am nervous about what the priest will say; or
  • I might have to live alone for a while, so I will say goodbye to my family before I go; or
  • I am worried about what people might think.
Continue the drama.

If the person's skin sore has two characteristics, the priest will declare the person is ritually dirty because the person has a defiling skin disease. If the priest decides the sore does not look bad or that it is too early to tell, the priest will tell the Israelite person with the skin sore to live alone for seven days or one week.

In the second scene, after seven days, the priest will examine the person's skin sore a second time. If the person's skin sore has not spread, the person must shave or take off the hair around the scab. Then the person with the skin sore has to live alone for another seven days or one week.

In the third scene, after another seven days, the priest will examine the person's skin sore for a third time. If the person's skin sore has not spread, the priest can declare the person ritually clean. The person must go and wash their clothes.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • After three examinations, the person is finally healed! Hurray! or
  • I am amazed. Yahweh made our bodies to be so good at healing; or
  • The person will be so happy to go back and see their family after such a long time.
Continue the drama.

Even after this, the person with the healing skin sore might need to come back for the priest to look at the person's skin sore again. If the person's skin sore spreads, the priest will declare the person ritually dirty. But if the person's skin sore has not changed and has normal, black hair growing in it, the priest will declare the person as ritually clean.

Remember, Yahweh originally gave these instructions to Aaron and Moses. You may want to act that out as well and ask people what they are feeling or thinking.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I want my people to know that taking time to heal is a good thing to do. It is not shameful to stop and heal; or
  • I want the person who is ritually dirty to have hope that I can heal that person; or
  • I am Yahweh who heals. I will show the people my miracles, and my people will praise me.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:29–37 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, the priests examine a person to decide if a person with a skin disease is ritually dirty or not. Use the same word for priest as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh gives instructions to the priests to determine whether or not an Israelite person is ritually dirty because of their skin disease. Use the same word or phrase throughout for "ritually clean" and "ritually dirty" as you used in previous passages. For more information on clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh instructs the priests to determine whether an Israelite person has a defiling skin disease. If the person has a defiling skin disease, the person is ritually dirty. Use the same word or phrase for defiling skin disease as you used in previous passages. For more information on leprosy, an old term for "defiling skin disease," refer to the Master Glossary. Remember that Yahweh specifically calls these skin problems "itching" defiling skin diseases.

Stop here and look at the pictures of possible defiling skin diseases. How will you describe these "itching" defiling skin diseases?

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
