title: Leviticus 13:38–46
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 13:38–46 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:38–46 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:38–46 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh was giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai, where the people had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Here, in this passage, Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron instructions for the priests on how to decide whether a person with a concerning skin problem is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

Remember, an Israelite person being ritually clean or ritually dirty was not actually about physical cleanliness. In the same way, just because an Israelite person had a defiling skin problem, it did not necessarily mean that the person had a serious medical disease. Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to be ritually clean so that the Israelites could be near to Yahweh and worship Yahweh. The main concern was whether the Israelite people were ready spiritually to obey and follow Yahweh. In biblical times, it was common for Israelite people to assume that a person had a physical disease because Yahweh wanted to punish that person.

In the past, translators have often translated the idea of "defiling skin disease" as leprosy. You will remember from the previous passage that scholars believe that it is very unlikely that the skin diseases in this passage are modern leprosy. Instead, the phrase "defiling skin disease" likely refers to an entire group or category of skin diseases. In this passage, Yahweh talks about a person with a defiling skin disease.

In this passage, Yahweh explains that an Israelite person who has a white spot on their skin must go to the priest for an examination. If the priest looks at the person's skin and sees that the white spot on the person's skin is a dull white color, the priest will declare the person to be ritually clean. Many scholars think this refers to a common skin disease.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a person with this common skin disease, called vitiligo. Pause the audio here.

In this passage, Yahweh also gives instructions for how a priest will determine whether or not a man who is balding, or losing his hair, is ritually clean or ritually dirty. In the last passage, Leviticus 13:29–37, Yahweh gave instructions to the priests on how to know if a person's head sore was a defiling skin disease. In that passage, Yahweh says the priest will look for areas of the head and beard that were not growing normal hair. Yahweh clarifies in this passage that the way a man loses his hair as the man grows older does not make the man ritually dirty. However, if the man is losing hair in his face or beard due to a skin sore, then the priest should use the same rules as before. If the person has a skin sore that is red, white, or pink, or in the same way as the ones Yahweh described in the last passage, the person is ritually dirty.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a man who is balding. Pause the audio here.

Stop here and look at the pictures of the same types of skin sores we talked about in the previous passage, ringworm and favus. These are the possible defiling diseases in this passage. Pause the audio here.

At the end of this passage, Yahweh gives instructions for how a person who is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease should act. The person with the defiling skin disease must wear torn clothes and have messy hair. Israelite people did these two actions when the people were mourning. The person with the defiling skin disease must rip their clothes and not comb their hair to show that the person is distressed and very sad because the person is ritually dirty.

Yahweh also says that the person with the defiling skin disease must cover their mustache, mouth, or the lower part of their face. This is another sign of mourning. Israelites do these actions to mourn the death of a family member or to show sadness because Yahweh had punished someone who sinned. The emphasis is that the person is very sad.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, how do people mourn or show extreme sadness? For what reasons do people mourn in your culture? Pause the audio here.

The person with the defiling skin disease must also say, "ritually dirty," or "I am ritually dirty!" to any people who come near. These words are a warning so that other people stay away and do not accidentally become ritually dirty by touching the ritually dirty person.

The person also must live alone, outside the camp, as long as that person is ritually dirty. That person must not join in any community events or celebrations. That person must not visit or touch their family members. A person would be very upset if they must live in isolation, away from their family, friends, and everyone the person knows.

Probably one of the reasons why an Israelite person would mourn when the person had a defiling skin disease is that the person would lose everything and everyone in their life. The person would mourn as if a person were dead. In a way, the person with a defiling skin disease mourned as if they themselves were dead, because that person had lost everything that person had. The person lost their relationships, their family members, and their way of life. For ancient Israelites, if a person lost their family, that person had lost all safety and protection, that person had lost their status, and that person had lost their dignity.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, can the community reject someone and force that person out of the community? When does this happen? How would you feel if your community rejected you? Pause this audio here.

When a priest declares that an Israelite person is ritually dirty from a skin disease, this is probably a sort of public proclamation. It is important for other Israelite people to know when someone is ritually dirty, because other people can become ritually dirty by being in contact with the ritually dirty person.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:38–46 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a white spot on their skin. The person with the white spot must go to the priest for an examination. If the priest looks at the person's skin and sees that the white spot on the person's skin is a dull white color, the priest will declare the person to be ritually clean.

In the second scene: Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite man has balding on his head, which means the man has a spot on his head where no hair will grow. An Israelite man with normal balding is ritually clean. However, if the Israelite man has a bald spot because the man has a red, pink, or white sore on his head, then the man is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease. The priest must look at the man's head and decide whether or not the man with the bald spot on his head is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

In the third scene: Yahweh gives instructions for how a person who is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease should act. The person with the defiling skin disease must wear torn clothes and have messy hair. The person with the defiling skin disease must also cover the lower part of their face and say, "I am ritually dirty!" to any people who come near. The person must live this way as long as the person is ritually dirty. The person also must live alone, outside of the camp, and away from ritually clean people.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person with a dull white spot on their skin
  • A priest who examines people with concerning skin problems
  • An Israelite man who is balding
  • And an Israelite person with a defiling skin disease

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Note that the storyteller does not mention Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron in this passage. But at the beginning of Leviticus 13, the storyteller says that Yahweh first gave these instructions to Moses and Aaron.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a white spot on their skin. In the original language, it says something similar to "white bright-spots bright-spots." Yahweh says the word "bright spots" two times to emphasize it. This probably means white blotches, or large areas of discolored skin.

So the person with the white spots must go to the priest for an examination. The priest will look at the person's skin and may see that the white spot on the person's skin is a dull white color. In this case, the word dull refers to a faint change in color. Sometimes people translate the phrase "harmless rash" as "rash," but what it means is a skin condition that is harmless and not deep in the skin. Many scholars think this refers to a common human skin condition.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a person with vitiligo. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: Have you seen this skin condition before? In your language, how do you talk about a person who has this skin condition? Pause this audio here.

In a situation like this, the priest declares the person to be ritually clean.

In the second scene, Yahweh talks about when an Israelite man has balding on his head, which means the man has a spot on his head where no hair will grow. People who speak different languages might use different phrases to refer to a man who is balding. One person might say, "The man's hair has fallen out of his head." Another person might say, "The man is losing his hair," and another, "The man's hair is bare." In this passage, Yahweh specifies that the baldness is on the front of the man's head, above the man's forehead.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a man who is balding. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what words do you use to describe a man who is balding or losing his hair? Pause this audio here.

An Israelite man with typical balding is ritually clean. However, if the Israelite man has a bald spot because the man has a red, pink, or white sore on his head, then the man is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease. The priest must look at the man's head and decide whether or not the man with the bald spot on his head is ritually clean or ritually dirty. If the man has a sore on his head, the priest will declare that the man is ritually dirty.

In the third scene, Yahweh gives instructions for how a person who is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease should act. In this passage, Yahweh mentions something that any person with a defiling skin disease must do. Some translations use the term "leper," however, this is likely to give the wrong impression, since the defiling skin disease is not the same thing as modern-day leprosy. Because of this, it is better to translate this phrase as "any person with a defiling skin disease."

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what is the phrase you use for "defiling skin disease"? In your language, what is the simplest way to refer to a person who has a defiling skin disease? Is there a name you can call that person that will make sense to people who are listening to the passage for the first time? Pause this audio here.

The person with the defiling skin disease must wear torn clothes and have messy hair. Israelite people did these two actions when the people were mourning. The person with the defiling skin disease must rip their clothes and not comb their hair to show that the person is distressed and very sad because the person is ritually dirty. Also, a person would be very upset if the person must live in isolation, away from their family, friends, and everyone they know.

Stop here and discuss: Imagine that someone told you that you must live away from everyone you know. No one can touch you or come close to you. In your language, describe how you would feel. How would you tell your family? What would you do? Pause the audio here.

Stop here and discuss: Now imagine that a family member that you love told you they must live away from all people. No one can touch that person or come close to that person. In your language, what would you tell your family member? How would you tell the rest of your family? Pause the audio here.

Yahweh also says that the person with the defiling skin disease must cover their mustache. This was another sign of mourning. Since this instruction was for men and women, it may be helpful to translate this as "mouth" or "the lower part of their face." The emphasis is that the person is very sad.

The person with the defiling skin disease must also say, "ritually dirty" or, "I am ritually dirty!" to any people who come near. These words are a warning so that other people stay away and do not become ritually dirty.

Stop here and discuss: How do you warn someone in your language? How would you tell someone to stay away from something or someone that people must not go near? Pause the audio here.

The person must do these things—wear torn clothes, have messy hair, cover the lower part of their face, and shout "I am ritually dirty!"—as long as the person is ritually dirty. The person also must live alone, outside the camp and away from ritually clean people, as long as that person is ritually dirty.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:38–46 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person with a dull white spot on their skin
  • A priest who examines people with concerning skin problems
  • An Israelite man who is balding
  • And an Israelite person with a defiling skin disease

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains what to do if an Israelite person has a white spot on their skin. The person with the white spot must go to the priest for an examination. If the priest looks at the person's skin and sees that the white spot on the person's skin is a dull white color, the priest will declare the person to be ritually clean.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing the Israelite person with the dull white spot, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so relieved that I am still ritually clean; or
  • I worry that people will think I am ritually dirty; or
  • I wonder why Yahweh made me this way.

Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh talks about when an Israelite man has balding on his head, which means the man has a spot on his head where no hair will grow. An Israelite man with typical balding is ritually clean.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing the Israelite bald man who is ritually clean, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am sad that I do not have hair; or
  • I am envious of others who are not bald; or
  • I am grateful that I have lived long enough to become bald.

Continue the drama.

However, if the Israelite man has a bald spot because the man has a red, pink, or white sore on his head, then the man is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease. The priest must look at the man's head and decide whether or not the man with the bald spot on his head is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

In the third scene, Yahweh gives instructions for how a person who is ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease should act. The person with the defiling skin disease must wear torn clothes and have messy hair. The person with the defiling skin disease must also cover the lower part of their face and say, "I am ritually dirty!" to any people who come near. The person must live this way as long as the person is ritually dirty. The person also must live alone, outside of the camp, and away from ritually clean people.

Pause the drama. Ask the person playing the Israelite person with the defiling skin disease, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so sad! I can never see my family or friends; or
  • I am scared others will mock me; or
  • I do not know how I will be able to live in the wilderness by myself;
  • What if I never get better?

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:38–46 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, the priests will decide if a person with a skin disease is ritually dirty or not. Use the same word for priest as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh gives instructions to the priests to determine whether or not an Israelite person was ritually dirty because of their skin disease. Use the same word or phrase throughout for ritually clean and ritually dirty as you used in previous passages. For more information on clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh instructs the priests to determine whether an Israelite person has a defiling skin disease. If the person has a defiling skin disease, the person is ritually dirty. Use the same word or phrase for "defiling skin disease" as you used in previous passages. For more information on leprosy, an old term for defiling skin disease, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and look at the pictures of possible defiling skin diseases. Pause this audio here.

A person with a defiling skin disease must live outside the Israelite camp, or the group of tents where all the Israelites lived. Use the same word or phrase for camp as you have used in previous passages.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 13:47–59
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 13:47–59 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:47–59 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:47–59 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh was giving Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai, where the people had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Here, in this passage, Yahweh is giving Moses and Aaron instructions for the priests on how to determine what to do if a person's moldy garment is ritually dirty. The priests must decide whether a person may clean the garment or not.

Remember, to be ritually clean or ritually dirty was not actually about physical cleanliness. Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to be ritually clean so that the Israelites could be near to Yahweh and worship Yahweh. The main concern was whether the Israelite people were ready spiritually to obey and follow Yahweh. Even the animals and things around the Israelite people needed to be ritually clean.

In this passage, Yahweh explains how an Israelite person with a moldy garment of wool, linen, or leather must bring the garment to the priest so the priest can examine it. The word "garment" means clothing, covering, or fabric.

Stop here and discuss: Describe the kinds of clothes that people commonly wear in your culture. Pay attention to the words you use to describe clothing. Pause this audio here.

It is unlikely that Yahweh's rules in this passage are only for clothes. These rules are probably for anything that people make from wool, linen, or leather. A person makes woolen garments out of a sheep's coat or fur. A person makes linen garments out of the stems of the flax plant. A person makes leather garments out of animal skins. These rules are for the materials. It does not matter what people made with the materials.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of wool, linen, and leather. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: There are three main materials in this passage: wool, linen, and leather. In your culture, what materials do people use to make clothes or fabrics? How do people use these materials to make other items besides clothes? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh talks about mold in the "warp or woof" of the woven fabric. Weavers use these terms to talk about the different threads that weavers use to make fabric. These are the threads that go in different directions. But many scholars do not think this is what these words mean. Many scholars think that Yahweh is talking about any kind of woven fabric. This means that this rule is for any fabric that a person weaves, no matter what method the person uses to weave or create the fabric.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of ancient weaving techniques. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what are common ways that people weave fabric? If people in your culture do not weave fabric, discuss your own process for making cloth and fabric. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Yahweh mentions two kinds of molds that can be present in garments: greenish mold and reddish mold. The term for "reddish" is actually "reddish-white." It is likely that this refers to pink mold, which is bacteria that often grows on damp fabric and leather.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of green and red mold in fabric and leather. Pause this audio here.

For the Israelite people, being ritually clean was also about being whole or complete. Many of these rules might have seemed inconvenient or perhaps sometimes unnecessary. There may have been times when the Israelite people heard Yahweh's rules and thought, "Why is Yahweh asking us to do so much?" Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to fully commit to being Yahweh's people. The Israelite people needed to decide that being close to Yahweh was more important than anything else. The Israelites also needed to trust Yahweh to tell the Israelites what to do and to believe Yahweh enough to do it, even when the Israelites did not like or understand the instructions.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Talk about a time when you had to do something hard or inconvenient in order to obey Yahweh.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:47–59 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains how an Israelite person with a moldy garment of wool, linen, or leather must bring the garment to the priest so the priest can examine the garment. This is the first examination. If green or red mold is present, the priest will isolate the garment for seven days.

In the second scene: The priest will examine the garment for the second time. If the mold has spread or gotten worse in the garment, it is an active defiling mold, and the garment is ritually dirty. So someone must destroy the garment with fire. But if the mold has not spread or not gotten worse, then the priest will tell the person to wash the garment. Then the priest will isolate the garment for another seven days.

In the third scene: After another seven days, the priest will tell the person to wash the garment again. Then the priest must examine the garment for a third time. If the mold has not changed in the garment, even though the mold did not spread, the garment is ritually dirty, and the person must burn the garment. If the mold faded, the priest must tear off the part of the garment that has the mold. If the mold reappears, a person must burn the garment. If a priest declares that a garment that was ritually dirty has become ritually clean again, a person must wash the garment another time, even though the person had already washed the garment for the examinations.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person who has a moldy garment
  • And an Israelite priest who examines the moldy garment

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Note that the storyteller does not mention Yahweh, Moses, and Aaron in this passage. But at the beginning of Leviticus 13, the storyteller says that Yahweh first gave these instructions to Moses and Aaron.

In the first scene, Yahweh says that an Israelite person with a moldy garment of wool, linen, or leather must bring the garment to the priest so the priest can examine the garment. The word "garment" can mean any type of clothing. However, the focus of this passage is mainly about Yahweh's rule for the kind of material. So people probably use these same rules for anything that a person made from wool, linen, or leather. You may wish to use a broader term in your language, perhaps one that means "cloth" or "fabric." The original word meant something like "covering," which can be another word for many kinds of woven things.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what words can you use for the word "garment"? Is there a word that can describe things that people make out of wool, linen, or leather? Pause the audio here.

So far in Leviticus 13, Yahweh has instructed the priests to determine what to do if an Israelite person has a defiling skin disease. In this passage, Yahweh uses similar language for defiling marks of mold and mildew in fabric and leather. Later, in Leviticus 14, Yahweh uses similar language for defiling marks of mold or mildew that grows on walls in houses. Most languages cannot use the same words for each of these kinds of defiling problems.

Stop here and discuss: Describe a person who has a skin disease. Then describe a person who has moldy clothes. Then describe a person who has a home or shelter with mold. Pay attention to what words you use to describe each of these situations. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh mentions three kinds of garments. People make woolen garments out of a sheep's coat or fur. People make linen garments out of the stems of the flax plant. People make leather garments by stretching out animal skins and drying the skins. There might still be hair on the animal skins, or the person might take the hair off the animal skin.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of wool, linen, and leather. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what do you call each of these types of materials? What do you call things that people make out of these materials? Pause this audio here.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of ancient weaving techniques. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how do you talk about the different ways that people make fabrics? Pause this audio here.

The priest will look at the moldy garment. This is the first examination. If green or red mold is present, the priest will isolate the garment for seven days.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of green and red mold in fabric and leather. Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, the priest will examine the garment for the second time. If the mold has spread or gotten worse in the garment, it is an active defiling mold. An active defiling mold can mean "persistent" because the mold keeps coming back. It can mean "destructive" or "rotting" because it ruins the clothes. It can mean that no person can make the mold go away. Since the garment is ritually dirty in such a bad way, the priest must order that a person should destroy the garment in fire.

But if the mold has not spread or not gotten worse, then the priest will tell the person to wash the garment. Then the priest will isolate the garment for another seven days.

In the third scene, after another seven days, it is likely that the priest tells the person to wash the garment again. Then the priest will examine the garment for a third time. If the mold has not changed in the garment, even though the mold did not spread, the garment is ritually dirty, and the person must burn the garment. There is a phrase here that means something like "on the front or back." Other ways to say this would be "it does not matter if the mold is on one side or the other side" or "whether the mold is on the inside or outside."

If the mold has faded after the person washed the garment, the priest must tear off the part of the garment that has the mold. If the mold reappears, a person must burn the garment. If a priest declares that a garment that was ritually dirty has become ritually clean again, a person must wash the garment another time, even though the person had already washed the garment for the examinations.

Yahweh ends this section with a summary statement that these are the rules for how priests should declare moldy clothes as ritually clean or ritually dirty.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:47–59 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • An Israelite person who has a moldy garment
  • And an Israelite priest who examines the moldy garment

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh says that an Israelite person with a moldy garment of wool, linen, or leather must bring the garment to the priest so the priest can examine the garment. This is the first examination. If green or red mold is present, the priest will isolate the garment for seven days.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person with the moldy garment, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • That garment is special to me. I hope I do not need to destroy the garment; or
  • I blame my brother for ruining my garment; or
  • I do not like mold.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, the priest will examine the garment for the second time. If the mold has spread or gotten worse in the garment, the mold is an active defiling mold, and the garment is ritually dirty. So someone must destroy the garment with fire. But if the mold has not spread or not gotten worse, then the priest will tell the person to wash the garment. Then the priest will isolate the garment for another seven days.

In the third scene, after another seven days, the priest most likely tells the person to wash the garment again. Then the priest will examine the garment for a third time. If the mold has not changed in the garment, even though the mold did not spread, the garment is ritually dirty, and the person must burn the garment. If the mold has faded after the person washed the garment, the priest must tear off the part of the garment that has the mold. If the mold reappears, a person must burn the garment. If a priest declares that a garment that was ritually dirty has become ritually clean again, a person must wash the garment another time, even though the person had already washed the garment for the examinations.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person with the moldy garment that is now ritually clean again, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am happy; or
  • I need to go wash the garment; or
  • I will not lend this to my brother again. My brother caused the garment to become moldy, and someone spent a lot of time to make this garment!

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 13:47–59 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh instructs the priests on what to do if a person's garment, clothing, or cloth has mold. Yahweh mentions three kinds of garments. People make woolen garments out of a sheep's coat or fur. People make linen garments out of the stems of the flax plant. Use the same word or phrase for linen as you used in previous passages. People also weave pieces of wool and flax together to make woven cloth. People make leather garments out of animal skins or pelts. Use the same word or phrase throughout for woolen garment, linen garment, and leather garment.

Stop here and look at pictures of wool, linen, and leather as a group. Discuss what words you will use for wool and linen garments, woven wool and linen garments, and leather. Pause this audio here.

So far in Leviticus 13, Yahweh has instructed the priests to determine what to do if an Israelite person had a defiling skin disease. In this passage, Yahweh uses similar language for defiling marks of mold or mildew in cloth and leather.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of moldy fabric and moldy leather. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for defiling marks or defiling mold. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, the priests must look closely at a moldy piece of fabric or a moldy piece of leather to determine if the garment is ritually dirty or not. Use the same word for priest as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh gives instructions to the priests to determine whether or not a moldy piece of fabric or a moldy piece of leather is ritually dirty. Use the same word or phrase throughout for ritually clean and ritually dirty as you used in previous passages. For more information about clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 14:1–9
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 14:1–9 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:1–9 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:1–9 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh was giving Moses instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this point in time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai, where people had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Here, in this passage, Yahweh gives Moses instructions for the priests to perform ceremonial cleansings for people, or purify people whose defiling skin disease has healed. The person must go through the ceremonial cleansing before the person is ritually clean again.

Please remember that the ceremonial cleansings do not heal the person. The priest does not do the ceremonial cleansing until after the person with the defiling skin disease is already healed. Remember, for an Israelite person to be ritually clean or ritually dirty was not actually about physical cleanliness. In the same way, just because an Israelite person had a defiling skin problem did not necessarily mean that the person had a serious medical disease. Before the priest agrees to do the ceremonial cleansing, the priest visits the ritually dirty person to make sure that the person is healed and ready for cleansing.

Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to be ritually clean so that the Israelites could be near to Yahweh and worship Yahweh. The main concern was whether the Israelite people were ready spiritually to obey and follow Yahweh. The priest did the ceremonial cleansing so that the person could be ritually clean again and be part of the community again. Yahweh gave the Israelites this process of ceremonial cleansing so that a person who used to be separate from the community had a way to come back into the community.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what kind of person does the community reject? What do people say and think about these people? How can that person become a part of the community again? Pause this audio here.

The ceremonial cleansing must take place outside the camp or away from the area where people live. This is because the person who was ritually dirty is not allowed to be in the areas where people live. So the priest and anyone else who was part of the ceremony have to come outside the camp to the ritually dirty person.

The priest will tell someone to bring two birds, cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop plant. The two birds must be alive and must be ritually clean birds.

The priest must use three items to sprinkle the blood and water onto the person who is going through ceremonial cleansing: cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop.

Cedar wood is a strong-smelling wood that has a reddish-brown or sometimes tan color. Since ancient times, people have used cedar wood for its ability to preserve things, to purify, and even to keep away bugs. Many people think cedar wood smells nice.

Many scholars think the scarlet thread is a thread or string that a person dyed red. To do this, a person would collect a certain kind of red insect. The person would make the red dye from this insect, and then would put threads and fabrics in the dye to make the threads and fabrics red. The person would already have made and dried the scarlet threads. So the priest will tell someone to go get some of the scarlet thread for the ceremonial cleansing.

Hyssop is a plant that has woody stems and green leaves. People used this plant in the ancient world for purification and for medicine. The priest probably uses the hyssop to sprinkle the blood. Remember, the Israelite people used hyssop to put the lamb's blood on their doors for the Passover in Exodus. It is possible that when the priest would use the hyssop to sprinkle the blood, the priest or the other Israelites would think of the Passover.

Someone will kill one of the birds and catch its blood in a clay pot of spring water. Spring water is water that comes from a flowing or moving water source, like a river or spring.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a clay pot. Pause this audio here.

The priest must dip the live bird in the blood and water mixture in the clay pot. The priest also dips the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop plant in the bird's blood and water mixture. The priest must use the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop plant to sprinkle the bird's blood and water mixture on the ritually dirty person. Then the priest will tell the person, "You are ritually clean again!"

Then the priest must release the live bird and let the bird fly away in an open field. That probably just means that the bird flies away from the Israelite people's tents and living areas. Later in Leviticus, Yahweh will give instructions to the priests about the scapegoat, which a person would also release in the wilderness. It is possible that when the priest releases the bird into the wilderness, the bird reminds the Israelite people of when a person releases the scapegoat into the wilderness.

Then the person must shave or take all the hair off their head and all the hair off their body. The person also must wash their clothes and their body in water.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, do people regularly shave or remove their head hair? If so, what does it mean when a person does that? Why do you think the Israelite person had to shave their head? Pause this audio here.

After shaving and washing, the person can go inside the camp, but the person must wait seven more days before they can go back and live in their own tent again. After the seven days, the person must shave or remove all the hair from their body again. The person must wash their clothes and take a bath again. In the next parts of the chapter, Yahweh also gives instructions for the sacrifices that the priest must make on the eighth day as part of the ceremonial cleansing. Then the person will be fully ritually clean.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:1–9 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh gives Moses instructions about how a person whose defiling skin disease has healed can become ritually clean again.

In the second scene: Yahweh says the priest must examine the person with the defiling skin disease to determine that the person is healed. Then, people must prepare for the ceremonial cleansing. Someone must bring two ritually clean birds and kill one of the birds. The priest must dip the live bird in the dead bird's blood and water mixture. The priest also dips the special items in the bird's blood and water mixture. The priest will sprinkle the bird's blood and water mixture on the ritually dirty person with special items. Then the priest will declare that the person is ritually clean again. Then the priest will release the live bird and let the bird fly away.

In the third scene: After the priest tells the person, "You are ritually clean again!" the person must wash their clothes and shave or remove all the hair from their body. Then the person will be ritually clean and can come into the camp or area where people live. But the person must wait seven more days before the person can go back and live in their own tent again. After the seven days, the person must shave or remove all the hair from their body again. The person must wash their clothes and take a bath. Then the person is fully ritually clean.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The healed Israelite person who needs ceremonial cleansing
  • And an Israelite priest

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, Yahweh gives Moses the law about how a person whose defiling skin disease has healed can become ritually clean again. Yahweh's laws are special sets of instructions or rules. In this passage, Yahweh says these words to Moses. Then Moses will tell everyone else Yahweh's words. Moses also writes these words down so the Israelite people will always know Yahweh's instructions.

If a person with a defiling skin disease has healed and is ready to be ritually clean again, the person has to go through a ceremonial cleansing before the person is ritually clean again. This ceremony is for ritual cleansing for spiritual purposes, not to heal the person or physically clean the person. Sometimes people call this process a purification process. Use a word in your language that shows that this process is for spiritual cleansing. This original phrase means "day of cleansing," but the ceremonial cleansing actually took a whole week to complete.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what will you call the ceremonial cleansing? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, Yahweh says the priest must examine the person with the concerning skin disease or problem to determine that the person is healed. The priest only does the ceremonial cleansing for people who are already healthy, not to try to heal people from their disease. Once the priest determines that the person is healed, the priest will prepare for the ceremonial cleansing.

The priest will tell someone to bring two birds, cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop plant. The two birds must be alive and must be ritually clean birds. The word in the original language for bird means "sparrow," but here it probably means any kind of small bird.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a sparrow. Pause this audio here.

The priest will use three items to sprinkle the blood and water onto the person who is going through ceremonial cleansing: cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop.

Cedar wood is a strong-smelling wood that is reddish-brown or sometimes tan-colored. Someone probably cut this cedar wood into a small enough piece for a person to hold easily in one hand.

Many scholars think the scarlet thread is a thread or string that a person dyed red. The priest would probably use the scarlet thread to tie the cedar wood and the hyssop together.

Hyssop is a plant that has woody stems and green leaves. People used this plant in the ancient world for purification and for medicine.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop. Pause this audio here.

Someone must also bring a clay pot full of spring water. Spring water is water that comes from a flowing or moving water source. The priest will tell someone to kill one of the birds over the clay pot of water, so that the bird's blood falls into the pot too. The priest will use the bird's blood and water mixture in this process a few times. We will call this the bird's blood and water mixture. You will need to decide what to call this in your language.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what will you call this bird's blood and water mixture? Pause this audio here.

The priest must dip the live bird in the blood and water mixture. The priest also dips the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop plant in the bird's blood and water mixture. The priest probably dips all these things together into the blood and water mixture.

The priest must use the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop plant to sprinkle the bird's blood and water mixture on the ritually dirty person. Then the priest will tell the person, "You are ritually clean again!" Notice this is only the first step of the person becoming ritually clean again. The person will have to wait seven more days and do more things before the person will be fully ritually clean again and ready to go home.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, talk about a process, ceremony, or ritual that takes days to complete. Notice the language you use to talk about things that happen at different times or different parts of the process. Pause this audio here.

Then the priest must release the live bird and let the bird fly away in an open field. That probably just means away from the Israelite people's tents and living areas.

Then the person must shave or take all the hair off their head and all the hair off their body. The person also must wash their clothes and their body in water.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, how do people usually remove head hair and body hair? Pause this audio here.

The person will then be clean enough to enter the camp and to be around people again. But the person cannot go back to live in their tent with their family yet.

After seven days or one week of living in the camp among people, the person must shave or take all the hair off their head and all the hair off their body again. Yahweh lists the hair on a person's head: the person must shave off the hair on their head, beard, and even eyebrows! Then the person must wash their clothes and their bodies with water again.

In the next parts of the chapter, Yahweh will give instructions for the sacrifices that the priest must make on the eighth day as part of the ceremonial cleansing. Then the person will be fully ritually clean and can go back to live in their tent with their family.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:1–9 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The healed Israelite person who needs ceremonial cleansing
  • And an Israelite priest

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh is giving Moses instructions about how a person whose defiling skin disease has healed can become ritually clean again.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so happy that people can become ritually clean again! or
  • The priests will be happy to perform this ceremony.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh says the priest must examine the person with the defiling skin condition to determine that the person has healed. Then, people must prepare for the ceremonial cleansing. Someone must bring two ritually clean birds and kill one of the birds. The priest must dip the live bird in the dead bird's blood and water mixture. The priest must also dip the special items in the bird's blood and water mixture. The priest must sprinkle the bird's blood and water mixture on the ritually dirty person with special items. Then the priest will declare that the person is ritually clean again. Then the priest will release the live bird and let the bird fly away.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person having the ceremonial cleansing, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so excited to see my family. It has been a long time; or
  • I am nervous about what people will say about me; or
  • I want the week to be over so I can go home.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, after the priest tells the person, "You are ritually clean again!" the person must wash their clothes and shave or remove all the hair from their body. Then the person will be ritually clean and can come into the camp or area where people live. But the person must wait seven more days before the person can go back and live in their own tent again. After the seven days, the person must shave or remove all the hair from their body again. The person must wash their clothes and take a bath. Then the person will be fully ritually clean.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person having the ceremonial cleansing, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I want to go celebrate! or
  • I have waited for so long to be healed, and now I do not have to wait anymore! or
  • I am so happy and content.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:1–9 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Yahweh is giving Moses instructions about how a person who is healed from a defiling skin disease can become ritually clean again. Use the same word for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

These special instructions are Yahweh's laws, which can mean rules or instructions. Use the same word for Yahweh's laws that you have used in previous passages. Look up law in the Master Glossary for more information.

Yahweh instructs the priests to help an Israelite person who had a defiling skin disease. If the person had a defiling skin disease, the person was ritually dirty. For more information on leprosy, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for "defiling skin disease" as you have in previous passages.

Stop here and look at pictures of possible defiling skin diseases as a group. Pause this audio here.

The priest must meet the person outside the camp for this ceremony. A camp is a settlement of tents or temporary shelters for people to live in. Use the same word for camp as you used in previous passages.

If a person whose defiling skin disease has healed is ready to be ritually clean again, the person has to go through a ceremonial cleansing, or purification ceremony, before the person is ritually clean again. In this passage, Yahweh gives instructions for how to do a ceremonial cleansing.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for ceremonial cleansing. For more information, refer to purification ceremony in the Master Glossary. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, the priests do the ceremony for the person who has healed. Use the same word for priest as you have used previously, and for more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

In this passage, Yahweh gives instructions to the priests to do a ceremony for an Israelite person who was ritually dirty because of their skin disease. Use the same word or phrase throughout for ritually clean and ritually dirty as you used in previous passages. For more information on clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary.

People bring birds for the ceremonial cleansings. In the original language, the word means "sparrow," but here it probably means any kind of small bird. These birds must be ritually clean birds.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a sparrow. Pause this audio here.

The priest uses three items to sprinkle the blood and water onto the person who is going through ceremonial cleansing: cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop.

Cedar wood is a strong-smelling wood that is reddish-brown or sometimes tan-colored. Since ancient times, people have used cedar wood for its ability to preserve things, to purify, and even to keep away bugs. Many people think cedar wood smells nice. Someone probably cut this cedar wood into a small enough piece for a person to hold easily in one hand. If you have already translated a word for cedar wood in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

Many scholars think the scarlet thread is a thread or string that a person dyed red. The person would make the dye from a certain kind of insect. The priest would probably use the scarlet thread to tie the cedar wood and the hyssop together. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

Hyssop is a plant that has woody stems and green leaves. People used this plant in the ancient world for purification and medicinal purposes. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop. Discuss what words you will use for these items. Pause this audio here.

The priest has to dip the live bird in the dead bird's blood and the water mixture. The priest also has to dip the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop into the bird's blood and water mixture. This means the priest puts these things in the bird's blood and water mixture and brings the items out quickly. Use the same word for this motion that you used earlier in Leviticus 4.

The priest had to sprinkle or splash the water with the blood of the sacrifice onto the person who was ritually dirty with a defiling skin disease. Use the same word or phrase for sprinkle as you used in previous passages.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
