title: Leviticus 14:10–20
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 14:10–20 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:10–20 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:10–20 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh has been giving Moses instructions on how the Israelite people are supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai, where people had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Here, in this passage, Yahweh is giving Moses instructions for the priests to perform ceremonial cleansings, or purification, for people whose defiling skin disease has healed. The person must go through the ceremonial cleansing before the person is ritually clean again.

Please note that the ceremonial cleansings did not heal the person. The priest did not do the ceremonial cleansing until after the person with the defiling skin disease had already healed. Remember, for an Israelite person to be ritually clean or ritually dirty was not actually about physical cleanliness. In the same way, just because an Israelite person had a defiling skin problem did not necessarily mean that the person had a serious medical disease. Before the priest agreed to do the ceremonial cleansing, the priest would go visit the ritually dirty person to make sure that the person was healed and ready for cleansing.

Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to be ritually clean so that the Israelites could be near to Yahweh and worship Yahweh. The main concern was whether the Israelite people were ready spiritually to obey and follow Yahweh. The priest did the ceremonial cleansing so that the person could be ritually clean again and be part of the community again. Yahweh gave the Israelite person this process of ceremonial cleansing so that a person who used to be separate from the community had a way to come back into the community.

The first part of the ceremonial cleansing would happen outside the camp, away from the area where people lived. But the second part of the ceremonial cleansing would happen a week later at the Tent of Meeting. This passage is about the second part of the ceremonial cleansing. The person had to offer all the main kinds of sacrifices: a burnt offering, a sin or purification offering, a guilt offering, which included the wave offering, and a grain offering. The only offering that the person did not need to include was the fellowship or peace offering, which was usually an offering that a person gave on their own because the person wanted to give the offering. This means that Yahweh did not require the fellowship offering from people.

Here is a reminder of the process that the priest went through to make the guilt offering. Usually, the person brought an animal to the Tent of Meeting and laid their hands on the animal's head. The person also usually publicly confessed their sin. In cases of defiling skin diseases, it is unclear whether or not the person confessed something. In ancient times, people thought that disease was a direct result of a god's punishment. Although there are times in the Bible when it says Yahweh punishes someone with a skin disease, such as when Yahweh gave Miriam leprosy, the Bible also encourages people not to assume that disease or disaster was a result of someone's sin. So we do not know whether ancient Israelites would confess a sin when someone made this sacrifice for a defiling skin disease. Then the priest would kill the animal, and someone would catch the blood in a bowl. Although the storyteller does not say this information here, we know that the priest would throw some of the blood on the altar. For this ceremony, the priest would also put the blood on the person's right earlobe, on the thumb of the person's right hand, and on the big toe of the person's right foot. The priest does a similar thing with the one-third liter of oil that the person would bring. In this way, the priest makes atonement for the person who has been healed.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, are there any rituals that involve marking a person's body with a liquid? If so, describe what is similar or different in your rituals compared to the ritual for this kind of guilt offering. If not, talk about what you think people in your culture would think about this kind of ritual. Pause this audio here.

The priest also offered a wave offering of the sheep for the guilt offering and the container of olive oil. The wave offering was not a separate offering but more of a special movement that the priests did with some of the offerings.

Here is a reminder of the full process that the priest went through to make the purification offering, although in this passage the storyteller does not state everything the priest did: First, the priest would sacrifice the young female sheep for the purification offering. The person who was part of the cleansing ceremony had to place their hand on the head of the young female sheep. After the priest killed the sheep, the priest would collect the sheep's blood in a bowl. The priest would then put the blood on the horns of the altar. The priest also had to take some of the sacrificed animal's fat and organs and burn those parts on the altar.

Here is a reminder of the process that the priest went through to make the whole burnt offering: First, the priest would kill the other young male sheep for the burnt offering. The person who was part of the ritual cleansing ceremony had to put their hand on the head of this sheep, too. Like for the purification offering, the priest had to collect the blood during the sacrifice so that the priest could sprinkle or throw the blood on the altar. The priest then had to skin the dead animal's body and cut the body into pieces. The priest also had to wash the animal's internal organs with water. The priest would put the dead animal's head, fat, and organs on the altar, and the priest would burn the whole sacrifice.

Here is a reminder of the process that the priest went through to make the grain offering: First, the person would present the grain offering to the priest. The priest would take a handful of the wheat flour and oil mixture. The priest would burn the handful of wheat flour mixture on the altar for Yahweh. Then the priest would keep the rest of the flour and oil mixture. For this sacrifice in this passage, the person had to bring three times the normal amount of flour and oil. Some scholars think this might be because the person who was becoming ritually clean was offering three sheep.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:10–20 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh says that the person who is going through ceremonial cleansing has to bring three sheep—two young male sheep and one young female sheep—to the Tent of Meeting. The person also has to bring a grain offering and a container full of olive oil. The priest who pronounced the person ready to be ritually clean must bring the person and their offerings before Yahweh, that is, in front of the Tent of Meeting.

In the second scene: The priest must offer a guilt offering and a wave offering. The priest will kill one of the young male sheep and collect the blood. The priest must put the sacrificed sheep's blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb of the person's right hand, and the big toe of the person's right foot. Then the priest must sprinkle the olive oil before Yahweh. The priest also has to put olive oil over the blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb of the person's right hand, and the big toe of the person's right foot. The priest also must pour the rest of the olive oil on the person's head.

In the third scene: The priest must give the purification offering and the burnt offering using the two other young sheep. The priest must also offer the grain offering. This is how the priest makes atonement for the person who is going through the ceremonial cleansing. After all of this, the person will be fully ritually clean.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The person who needs to complete the ceremonial cleansing
  • And the Israelite priest

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Note that the storyteller does not mention Moses in this passage. But at the beginning of Leviticus 14, the storyteller says that Yahweh first gave these instructions to Moses.

In the first scene, Yahweh says the person who is going through ceremonial cleansing must bring three sheep—two young male sheep and one young female sheep. The person must bring these animals on the eighth day after the priest has examined the person outside the camp and first declared that they are clean. For the seven days in between, the person has been in the camp, but not living in their tent. The sheep the person brings must be physically perfect. The sheep could not be sick, hurt, or physically maimed. The person must take these sheep to the Tent of Meeting. Throughout this passage, the storyteller refers to "the person who needs to become ritually clean."

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your language, what word or phrase do you use to refer to people who are ritually dirty? What about people who are ritually clean? What words do you use to refer to the ceremonial cleansing? Talk about what words or phrases you would like to use for a person who is going through ceremonial cleansing. Pause this audio here.

The person also has to bring a grain offering of three-tenths of an ephah of flour mixed with olive oil. An ephah was probably a container that people used to carry and measure flour. It is unclear how much three-tenths of an ephah would weigh. It was possibly about 7 liters and weighed about 5 kilograms. You can use whatever measuring system people normally use to measure dry substances like flour.

Ancient Israelites would usually bring wheat or sometimes barley grain for sacrifices. For the ceremonial cleansing, the Israelite person needs to bring fine flour, which probably refers to wheat flour. Fine flour also means the best quality of flour. If necessary, you can use a more general word for seeds of cultivated grasses that people use to make flour.

The person also needs to bring a container full of olive oil. It is possible that a log of oil was about three-tenths of a liter.

So the person who needs to become ritually clean needs to bring three sheep, three-tenths of an ephah of flour, and a container of oil. The priest who pronounced the person ready to be ritually clean must bring the person and their offerings before Yahweh, that is, in front of the Tent of Meeting.

Next, the priest must offer a guilt offering and a wave offering. First, the priest has to kill one of the young male sheep at the altar of burnt offering. The meat from this offering is "most holy." That means that the only people Yahweh allows to eat the meat from this sacrifice are the priests.

When the priest kills the first young male sheep for the guilt offering, the priest must collect the blood in a bowl or cup. The priest must put the sacrificed sheep's blood on the person's right ear lobe, the thumb on their right hand, and the big toe on their right foot.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of a person's right ear lobe, right thumb, and right big toe. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what words do you use for these human body parts? Describe a person putting a liquid on these body parts in a ceremonial way. What would you call this action? If helpful, have a person act out the process so you can talk about each step in your language. Pause this audio here.

At some point in the process, the priest also offers a wave offering of the animal or of some of the animal's body parts and the container of olive oil. These body parts are probably the same or similar to the animal's body parts that the priests removed for the wave offering in Exodus 29:19–22. The wave offering is not a separate offering but more of a special movement that the priests do with some of the offerings. The priest will lift the offering up in the air in a special way.

We do not know exactly when the wave offering happens, since Yahweh only mentions the wave offering in the summary statement. The priests usually did wave offerings with the meat or fat portions of the animal, which means the priest would do this offering after the priest killed the animal and before the priest burned the animal fat and animal organs on the altar. However, it is possible the priest did these wave offerings before the priest killed the animal. The next passage suggests that the priest does the wave offering for these offerings before the priest kills the animals.

Then the priest has to sprinkle the olive oil before Yahweh. First, the priest will pour some of the olive oil into the palm of his left hand. Then the priest dips his right forefinger into the olive oil. Then the priest sprinkles the oil seven times before Yahweh.

The priest also has to put olive oil over the blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb of the person's right hand, and the big toe of the person's right foot. The priest puts the oil on top of the marks of sheep's blood that the priest made on the person's body. The priest must also pour the rest of the olive oil on the head of the person who is becoming ritually clean.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a person dipping their finger in oil. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: First, as a group, copy the actions that the priest must do with the oil. Make sure to use the left hand to hold the oil and the right hand to sprinkle the oil. Talk about how you would describe this process in your language. Pause this audio here.

The priest makes atonement for the person who is going through the ceremonial cleansing. This means that the priest reconciles the person to Yahweh, and Yahweh covers the person's bad actions.

In the third scene, the priest has to give the purification offering and the burnt offering using the two other young sheep. The priest also has to offer the grain offering. This is how the priest makes atonement for the person who is going through the ceremonial cleansing. After all of this, the person will be fully ritually clean.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:10–20 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The person who needs to complete the ceremonial cleansing
  • And the Israelite priest

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh says the person who is going through ceremonial cleansing must bring three sheep—two young male sheep and one young female sheep—to the Tent of Meeting. The person must also bring a grain offering and a container full of olive oil. The priest who pronounced the person ready to be ritually clean must bring the person and the person's offerings before Yahweh, that is, in front of the Tent of Meeting.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I must make many sacrifices today for the person who wants to be ritually clean; or
  • I am happy that this person will finally be able to be in the community again; or
  • Yahweh requires much from us. But we learn so much by following Yahweh's rules.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh says the priest must offer a guilt offering and a wave offering. The priest has to kill one of the young male sheep and collect the blood. The priest must put the sacrificed sheep's blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb of the person's right hand, and the big toe of the person's right foot. Then the priest will sprinkle the olive oil before Yahweh. The priest will also put olive oil over the blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb of the person's right hand, and the big toe of the person's right foot. The priest will also pour the rest of the olive oil on the person's head.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who is becoming ritually clean again, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so excited to be ritually clean again! or
  • I cannot wait to live with my family again; or
  • I wonder if Yahweh will accept me.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh says the priest must give the purification offering and the burnt offering using the two other young sheep. The priest must also offer the grain offering. This is how the priest makes atonement for the person who is going through the ceremonial cleansing. After all of this, the person will be fully ritually clean.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am satisfied with the sacrifices; or
  • This person has waited a long time for me to heal them, but the person never stopped praying to me; or
  • Well done, my servants. Today, you remembered my instructions and obeyed.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:10–20 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

The person who offers the ceremonial cleansing sacrifice must bring two young male sheep. This means a male sheep that was young, but old enough to have babies. Use the same word for "young male sheep" as you used in previous passages.

The Israelite person must also bring a young female sheep for the offering. Use the same word for "young female sheep" as you used in previous passages.

Yahweh told the Israelites that when a person chose any animal for sacrifice, the animal must be healthy. That meant that the animal had no physical defects or was physically perfect or blameless. The animal could not be blind or deformed. The animal could not have any injuries or bruises. Use the same word for "physically perfect" that you used in previous passages. For more information, refer to perfect in the Master Glossary.

The Israelite person bringing the sacrifice also needed to bring three-tenths of an ephah of flour for a grain offering. Use the same word or phrase for "grain offering" that you used in previous passages. For more information on grain offering, look in the Master Glossary.

An ephah was probably a large basket that people used to carry flour. Three-tenths of an ephah probably weighed about 5 kilograms. Use the same word or phrase for ephah that you used in previous passages. For more information on ephah, look in the Master Glossary.

Use the same word for flour that you used in previous passages. Remember, this probably refers to wheat flour.

The Israelite person also had to bring a log of olive oil for the grain offering. A "log of oil" was probably about one-third of a quart or three-tenths of a liter. Use the same word or phrase for oil that you used in previous passages.

In this passage, the priest who declared the person clean in the first part of the ceremonial cleansing was the one who was supposed to kill the animals for the offerings to Yahweh to finish the ceremonial cleansing. Use the same words or phrases for "kill an animal," priest, and Yahweh that you have used previously. For more information on priest and Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

In this passage, Yahweh gave instructions to the priests for a ceremony for the Israelite person who was no longer ritually dirty because of their skin disease. Use the same words or phrases throughout for "ritually clean" and "ritually dirty" as you used in previous passages, and refer to clean and unclean in the Master Glossary for more information.

Use the same phrases for Tent of Meeting and sanctuary, or holy place, as you used in previous passages. For more information on tabernacle and sanctuary, refer to the Master Glossary.

The priest brought the animals for the offerings and the person to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. This was probably the courtyard area of the tabernacle, around the bronze altar. Use the same words or phrases for offerings and "entrance of the Tent of Meeting" as you have used previously. The general word for offerings is in the Master Glossary.

Use the same phrases for guilt offering, wave offering, sin or purification offering, and burnt offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on these offerings, refer to the Master Glossary.

The guilt offering is most holy. Use the same word or phrase for "most holy" as you have used previously. Holy is in the Master Glossary.

The priest had to put the blood of the sacrificed sheep on the right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe of the person.

Stop here as a group and look again at a picture of a person's right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe as needed. Pause this audio here.

The priest had to pour oil into the palm of his left hand and dip his right forefinger into the sacrificed sheep's blood. Use the same word for this motion that you used earlier in Leviticus 4.

Stop here as a group and look again at a picture of a person dipping their finger in oil as needed. Pause this audio here.

The priest had to sprinkle, or throw, the blood of the sacrifice in front of Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for sprinkle as you used in previous passages.

The priest must sacrifice the offering on the altar of the burnt offering. Use the same word for altar that you used in previous passages. For more information on altar, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of the altar of the burnt offering. Pause this audio here.

The priest makes atonement for the person who needs to be clean. Use the same word or phrase for atonement that you have used previously, and refer to atonement in the Master Glossary for more information.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 14:21–32
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 14:21–32 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:21–32 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:21–32 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh has been giving Moses instructions on how the Israelite people are supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people are still camping at Mount Sinai, where people had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. Here, in this passage, Yahweh gives Moses instructions for the priests to perform ceremonial cleansings for people whose defiling skin disease has healed. The person must go through the ceremonial cleansing, or purification ceremony, before the person is ritually clean again.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of possibly defiling skin diseases. Pause this audio here.

Please note that the ceremonial cleansings did not heal the person. The priest did not do the ceremonial cleansing until after the person with the defiling skin disease had already healed. Remember, for an Israelite person to be ritually clean or ritually dirty was not actually about physical cleanliness. Before the priest agreed to do the ceremonial cleansing, the priest would go visit the ritually dirty person to make sure that the person had healed and was ready for cleansing.

Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to be ritually clean so that the Israelites could be near to Yahweh and worship Yahweh. The main concern was whether the Israelite people were ready spiritually to obey and follow Yahweh. The priest did the ceremonial cleansing so that the person could be ritually clean again and be part of the community again. Yahweh gave the Israelites this process of ceremonial cleansing so that a person who was separate from the community had a way to come back into the community.

The first part of the ceremonial cleansing happened outside the camp, away from the area where people lived. But the second part of the ceremonial cleansing happens one week later at the Tent of Meeting. This passage is about the second part of the ceremonial cleansing. In the last passage, Yahweh said that the person has to offer all the main kinds of sacrifices: a burnt offering, a sin or purification offering, a guilt offering, which includes the wave offering, and a grain offering. The only offering that the person does not need to include is the fellowship or peace offering, which was usually an offering that a person gave on their own. Yahweh did not require the Israelites to give Yahweh a fellowship offering.

In this passage, Yahweh gives instructions for the ceremonial cleansing of a person who is poor. This person does not own very much and cannot afford three sheep, one for each offering. Instead, a poor person can bring one sheep and two birds for their offerings.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, how do people talk about and treat poor people? What do you think about the way Yahweh treats poor people? Pause this audio here.

This passage is very similar to the last passage because both are instructions on how to do the ceremonial cleansing for a person whose defiling skin disease has healed. The only difference is that these instructions are for the poor person. You may need to decide the best way to repeat this information.

Stop here and discuss: What is the same in this passage and the last passage? What is different in this passage? In your language, what information do you need to include in this passage? Pause this audio here.

Here is a quick reminder of the process that the priest went through to make the guilt offering. Usually, the person brought the animal to the Tent of Meeting and laid their hand on the head of the animal. The person also usually publicly confessed their sin. In cases of defiling skin diseases, it is unclear whether or not the person confessed something. Then the person would kill the animal and let the blood fall into a bowl. The priest would throw the blood on the altar. In this case, the priest would also put the blood on the person's right earlobe, on the thumb of the person's right hand, and on the big toe of the person's right foot. The priest does a similar thing with the one-third liter of oil that the person would bring. In this way, the priest makes atonement for the person who has been healed.

For this cleansing ceremony, the priest also offers a wave offering of some of the animal's body parts and the container of olive oil. The wave offering was not a separate offering, but more of a special movement that the priests did with some of the offerings.

Here is a quick reminder of the process that the priest went through to make the purification offering. When a person brought a bird for this sacrifice, the priest offered the bird by twisting the bird's neck until it died and then pulled until the head started to come off the body. The priest had to make sure the head was still partially attached to the body. As the blood poured out of the dead bird's body, the priest had to collect some of the bird's blood in a bowl. Then the priest had to sprinkle or throw some of the blood on the side of the altar. The priest drained the rest of the bird's blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering.

Here is a quick reminder of the process that the priest went through to make the burnt offering: First, when the person brought a bird for this sacrifice, the priest had to bring the bird to the bronze altar. Then the priest had to wring off the bird's head and burn up the head on the altar. After that, the priest had to drain the blood on the side of the altar. Then, the priest had to remove the inside part of the bird that digests food. After the priest removed the inside part of the bird and feathers, the priest had to throw both things on the east side of the altar in the same place where the priest would put the ashes that were left behind after the fat from a sacrifice burned up. People called this place the place where the fat ashes went.

Stop here and look at a picture of the bronze altar. Note the east side, where the fat ashes were. Pause this audio here.

Here is a quick reminder of the process that the priest went through to make the grain offering: First, the person would present the grain offering to the priest. The priest would take a handful of the wheat flour and oil mixture. The priest would burn the handful of wheat flour mixture on the altar for Yahweh. Then the priest would keep the rest of the flour and oil mixture. In the last passage, Yahweh said a person had to bring three-tenths of an ephah of flour for the grain offering for the ceremonial cleansing. In this passage, Yahweh says the poor person only had to bring one-tenth of an ephah of flour for the grain offering. Some scholars think this might be because the poor person who was becoming ritually clean was only offering one sheep, rather than the three sheep.

In these offerings, the priest would make atonement for the poor person who had been healed of a defiling skin disease.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:21–32 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains what to do when an Israelite person is poor and cannot afford three sheep for the cleansing ceremony. This person can bring one sheep and two doves or pigeons instead. The person also only brings one-tenth of an ephah of flour. In all, the person must bring: one young male sheep, one-tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with olive oil, a log of olive oil, and either two doves or two pigeons.

In the second scene: The person must bring everything for the sacrifices for the ceremonial cleansing to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. The Israelite priest will present the wave offering and kill the young male sheep for the guilt offering. The priest must put the sheep's blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb on the person's right hand, and the big toe of the person's right foot. Then the priest will sprinkle the olive oil before Yahweh. The priest must also put olive oil over the blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb of the person's right hand, and the big toe of the person's right foot. Then the priest will pour the rest of the olive oil on the person's head.

In the third scene: The priest must give the purification offering and the burnt offering using the two doves or pigeons. The priest must also offer the grain offering. This is how the priest makes atonement for the person who is going through the ceremonial cleansing. After all of this, the person will be fully ritually clean. The storyteller ends this scene with a summary statement that these are the instructions for a person who has healed from a defiling skin disease, who cannot afford three sheep.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • A poor person who is going through ceremonial cleansing
  • And an Israelite priest

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Note that the storyteller does not mention Moses in this passage. But the storyteller mentions Moses at the beginning of Leviticus 14, where the storyteller says that Yahweh first gave these instructions to Moses.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains what an Israelite person who is poor needs to do to go through ceremonial cleansing. Yahweh gives a special version of the ceremonial cleansing for people who do not have enough money or resources to get three sheep for the sacrifices.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how do you say that someone is poor or does not have enough? Pause this audio here.

The poor Israelite person still must bring one young male sheep for the guilt offering. The person must also bring one-tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with olive oil for a grain offering. An ephah was probably a container that people used to carry and measure flour. It is unclear how much one-tenth of an ephah would weigh. It was possibly about 2 liters and weighed about 1.5 kilograms. The flour must be finely ground flour, which probably refers to wheat flour. Fine flour also means the best quality of flour. The person also must bring a "log" or container of olive oil. It is possible that a log of oil was about three-tenths of a liter. Since this person is poor, the person can bring two doves or two pigeons instead of bringing a second young male sheep and a young female sheep for the purification offering and the burnt offering.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of doves and pigeons. Pause this audio here.

So in all, the poor person must bring all the same things for the ceremonial cleansing, except that the person may bring two birds instead of two sheep and only bring one-tenth of an ephah of flour rather than three-tenths of an ephah of flour.

In the second scene, the person must bring everything for the offerings for their ceremonial cleansing to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. The priest must hold the young male sheep and the container of oil and move those things in a special way as a wave offering.

Then the priest has to kill the young male sheep for the guilt offering and collect the blood in a bowl. The priest must put the dead sheep's blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb of the person's right hand, and the big toe of the person's right foot.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a person's right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe. Pause this audio here.

Then the priest has to pour the olive oil into his left hand and dip his right forefinger into the olive oil.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a person dipping their finger in oil. Pause this audio here.

The priest will sprinkle the olive oil seven times before Yahweh. This probably will happen at the altar of the burnt offering.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of the altar of the burnt offering. Pause this audio here.

The priest must also put olive oil over the blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb on their right hand, and the big toe on their right foot. The priest must put the oil on top of the marks of sheep's blood that the priest made on the person's body. The priest must also pour the rest of the olive oil on the person's head.

The priest makes atonement for the person who is going through the ceremonial cleansing. This means that the priest reconciles the person to Yahweh and covers the person's bad actions. The storyteller uses this phrase throughout the passage to describe how the priest uses the offerings to make the person ritually clean again.

In the third scene, the priest must give the purification offering and the burnt offering using the two doves or two pigeons. The priest must also offer the grain offering. This is how the priest makes atonement for the person who is going through the ceremonial cleansing. After all of this, the person will be fully ritually clean.

The storyteller ends this passage with a summary statement: This is Yahweh's law for a person who has healed from a defiling skin disease and who does not have enough wealth to get three sheep for the ceremonial cleansing.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:21–32 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • A poor person who is going through ceremonial cleansing
  • And an Israelite priest

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh talks about what to do if an Israelite person is poor and cannot afford three sheep for the sacrifice. This person can bring one sheep and two doves or two pigeons instead of the other two sheep. The person also only brings one-tenth of an ephah of flour. In all, the person must bring: one young male sheep, one-tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with olive oil, a log of olive oil, and either two doves or two pigeons.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who is going through ceremonial cleansing, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am relieved that Yahweh provided a way for me to make these offerings; or
  • I am thankful my relative helped me get these animals so that I can go through ceremonial cleansing; or
  • What if people talk badly about me because I had to bring a poor person's offering?
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, the person must bring everything for the offerings for their ceremonial cleansing to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. The Israelite priest will present the wave offering and kill the young male sheep for the guilt offering. The priest must put the sacrificed sheep's blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb on their right hand, and the big toe on their right foot. Then the priest sprinkles the olive oil before Yahweh. The priest must also put olive oil over the blood on the person's right earlobe, the thumb on their right hand, and the big toe on their right foot. The priest will then pour the rest of the olive oil on the person's head.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • This ceremony reminds me of the ceremony that we did for Aaron and Aaron's sons when Aaron and Aaron's sons became priests; or
  • I am surprised. The community rejected this person, but now Yahweh commands us to treat this person with honor.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, the priest must give the purification offering and the burnt offering using the two doves or pigeons. The priest must also offer the grain offering. This is how the priest makes atonement for the person who is going through the ceremonial cleansing. After all of this, the person will be fully ritually clean. The storyteller ends this scene with a summary statement that these are the instructions for a person who has healed from a defiling skin disease and who cannot afford three sheep.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I want every person to be able to come back to me; or
  • This person is ritually clean, just as much as any other person; or
  • I will care for and help people who are poor.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:21–32 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh gave instructions for becoming ceremonially clean, or pure. For more information about how someone can purify themselves, refer to the Master Glossary for purify and for purification ceremony.

Even if the person going through the ceremonial cleansing was poor, the person must still bring a young male sheep for the guilt offering. This means a male sheep that was young, but old enough to have babies. Use the same word for young male sheep as you used in previous passages.

Use the same phrase for guilt offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on guilt offering, refer to guilt offering in the Master Glossary.

The Israelite person must bring one-tenth of an ephah of finest flour for the grain offering. Remember, this probably refers to wheat flour. An ephah was probably a large basket that people used to carry flour. One-tenth of an ephah probably weighed about 1.5 kilograms. Use the same words or phrases for ephah, flour, and grain offering that you used in previous passages. For more information on ephah and grain offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Israelite person also had to bring olive oil for the sacrifices. Use the same word or phrase for oil that you used in previous passages. A log of oil was probably about one-third quart or three-tenths of a liter. Use the same phrase for "log of oil" as you used in previous passages.

If the Israelite person was poor, the person could bring two doves or two pigeons for the sin or purification offering and the whole burnt offering instead of a young male sheep and a young female sheep. Use the same words for doves and pigeons that you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of doves and pigeons again as needed. Pause this audio here.

Use the same phrases for purification offering and for burnt offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on purification offering and burnt offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

In this passage, the priest who declared the person clean in the first part of the ceremonial cleansing was the one who was supposed to kill the animals for the offerings to finish the ceremonial cleansing. Use the same words for priest and for killing an animal as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

Use the same phrase for Tent of Meeting as you used in previous passages. For more information on the Tent of Meeting, refer to tabernacle in the Master Glossary. Use the same phrase for "entrance to the Tent of Meeting" that you used previously. Remember that the entrance was probably the courtyard area around the altar of burnt offering.

Use the same word for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Use the same phrase for wave offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on wave offering, refer to wave offering in the Master Glossary.

The priest had to put the blood of the dead sheep on the right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe of the person.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a person's right earlobe, right thumb, and right big toe again as needed. Pause this audio here.

The priest had to pour oil into the palm of his left hand and dip his right forefinger into the sacrificed sheep's blood. The priest was making atonement for the person. Use the same word or phrase for atonement as you have used previously, and see atonement in the Master Glossary for more information.

Stop here as a group and look again at a picture of a person dipping their finger on their right hand in oil as needed. Pause this audio here.

The priest had to sprinkle or throw the blood of the sacrifice in front of Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for sprinkle or throw as you used in previous passages.

Yahweh's law is Yahweh's rules and instructions for the Israelite people. Use the same word for law as you used in previous passages. For more information on law, refer to the Master Glossary.

An Israelite person had to go through ceremonial cleansing after the person had healed from a defiling skin disease. Before the ceremonial cleansing, the healed Israelite person would be ritually dirty, and after the ceremonial cleansing, the healed Israelite person would be ritually clean. For more information on leprosy, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word for "defiling skin disease" as you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and look again at pictures of possible defiling skin diseases as needed.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 14:33–42
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 14:33–42 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:33–42 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:33–42 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh gives Moses and Aaron instructions on how the Israelite people are supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people are still camping at Mount Sinai, where people had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions.

Yahweh gives instructions to Moses and Aaron to prepare the Israelites for when the Israelite people move into the Canaan people's land. In the wilderness, the Israelite people live in tents or small shelters that a person lives in for a short amount of time. But when the Israelite people move into the Canaan people's land, the Israelites will have houses to live in. People make these houses by making bricks or building stones out of clay. Then the people make the bricks into a house. In this passage, Yahweh uses the word "stones" for these clay bricks. But depending on your language, using a word like "stones" might be confusing for something that a person makes out of clay. Some people had houses that people built with both stones or rocks and also clay bricks. While some Canaan people probably did build houses out of rocks and stone, in this passage, Yahweh talks about houses that people had built out of clay bricks. A person cannot move these houses like a person can move a tent. Sometimes ancient people would also mix lime, sand, and water together to create a plaster to put on the walls.

Yahweh gives instructions to Moses and Aaron for what a priest should do if a person has a house with a defiling mold in the clay walls.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of mold on clay walls. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what kinds of houses do people typically live in? What could be wrong with a house that would make it impossible to live in? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh had promised to give the Canaan people's land and houses to the Israelite people. Yahweh calls the Canaan people's land "the land that I am giving you." This means Yahweh is planning to give the Israelite people the Canaan people's land, houses, and their possessions if the Israelite people obey Yahweh. Yahweh says this will be the Israelite people's possession. This is a phrase that Yahweh often uses when Yahweh talks about the land that Yahweh promised to give to Abraham. This means that the Israelite people will live in that land and own the houses that the Canaan people used to own.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Why do you think Yahweh promised to give the Israelite people the land and houses that the Canaan people owned? Pause this audio here.

When you listened to this passage, did it remind you of another passage? The instructions that Yahweh gives to the priests for defiling mold in houses are similar to the instructions Yahweh gave earlier about defiling mold in cloth or leather.

Stop here and listen to your translation of Leviticus 13:47–59 to remember Yahweh's instructions for how to deal with mold on cloth. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Yahweh gives instructions for what to do when a person who owns a house finds defiling mold in the clay walls. The person who owns the house must go to a priest and tell the priest that the person thinks their house or shelter has defiling mold. Then the priest will tell the person to take all the people and things out of the house or shelter before the priest comes to look at the walls. The person will remove the things from the house before the priest comes, so that if the priest declares the house ritually dirty, the priest will not have to declare the people and their things ritually dirty, since nothing is in the house. If the priest looks at the walls and sees that the mold looks to be deep in the walls, the priest must close the doors to the house or shelter. No person may go into the house for seven days or one week.

After seven days, the priest will come back to examine the house again. If the mold has spread on the walls, the priest must tell the owner that someone must tear all the moldy bricks out of the house or shelter. Someone must carry all the moldy bricks outside the camp to an area that is ritually dirty. Someone also must scrape all the inside bricks of the house or shelter. Someone also must take all the dust that the person scrapes off and carry it outside the camp to an area that is ritually dirty. Then someone must put new clay bricks and plaster in the place where the old, moldy bricks were.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What do you do when parts of your home have problems? How do you carefully repair your home so that the damaged parts of your home do not affect the people and things in your home?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:33–42 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh gives instructions to Moses and Aaron for what people should do if a person has a house with a defiling mold in the clay walls.

In the second scene: Yahweh explains what to do when a person who owns a house or shelter finds defiling mold in the clay walls. The person must go to a priest and tell the priest that their house or shelter may have defiling mold. Then the priest will tell the person to take all the people and things out of the house or shelter before the priest comes to look at the walls. If the priest looks at the walls and sees that the mold looks to be deep in the walls, the priest must close the doors to the house or shelter. No person is allowed to go into the house for seven days or one week.

In the third scene: Yahweh says the priest must come back after one week to examine the house again. If the mold has spread on the walls, the priest will tell the owner that someone must tear all the moldy bricks out of the house or shelter. Someone must carry all the moldy bricks outside the camp to an area that is ritually dirty. Someone also must scrape all the inside bricks of the house or shelter. Someone also must take all the dust that comes off the wall and carry the dust outside the camp to an area that is ritually dirty. Then the person must put new clay bricks and plaster in the place where the old, moldy bricks were.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • A person who owns a house with a defiling mold in their house or shelter
  • The people who tear out the moldy parts of the house and replace them with new bricks and plaster
  • And an Israelite priest

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the first scene, Yahweh gives instructions to Moses and Aaron to prepare the Israelites for when the Israelite people moved into the Canaan people's land. In the wilderness, the Israelite people lived in tents or small shelters that people live in for short amounts of time. But in the Canaan people's land, people made houses out of clay bricks. The Israelite people will live in these houses. Yahweh had promised to give the Canaan people's land and houses to the Israelite people. Yahweh calls the Canaan people's land "the land that I am giving you." This means Yahweh was planning to give the Israelite people the Canaan people's land, houses, and their possessions if the Israelite people obeyed Yahweh. Yahweh says this will be the Israelite people's possession. This is a phrase that Yahweh often uses when Yahweh talks about the land that Yahweh promised to give to Abraham. This means that the Israelite people will live in that land and own the houses and everything that the Canaan people used to own.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, talk about giving a person a gift. Talk about how you would say that a person gave another person some land. How would you say that Yahweh was going to give the Canaan land to the Israelite people? How would you say that the Israelite people will own the land? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh gives these instructions to Moses and Aaron about what a person and a priest should do if a person has a house or shelter with a defiling mold in the clay walls. Yahweh uses the word "stones" for these clay bricks. But depending on your language, using a word like "stones" might be confusing for something that a person makes out of clay. Some people built houses with both stones or rocks and also clay bricks. Some Canaan people probably did build houses out of rocks and stone. Some Canaan people probably built houses out of clay bricks on foundations of stones. In this passage, Yahweh talks about houses that people had built out of clay bricks.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What will you call these clay "stones" in your language? Pause this audio here.

In an earlier passage, Yahweh gave Moses many rules about how the priests should treat a person with a defiling skin disease. In the original language, Yahweh uses the same words to refer both to the person who has this defiling condition, a cloth or leather garment that has this defiling condition, and a shelter that has this defiling condition. Yahweh uses the word for both red mold that grows on buildings and green mold that grows on buildings.

Stop here and look at pictures of red mold and green mold as a group. In your area, what kinds of molds do you have? Discuss what you will call the kinds of mold in these pictures in your language. Pause audio here.

In the second scene, Yahweh explains what to do if a person who owns a house or shelter finds defiling mold in the clay walls. The person must go to a priest and tell the priest that their house or shelter may have defiling mold. Then the priest will tell the person to take all the people and things out of the house or shelter before the priest comes to look at the walls.

Then the priest must come to look at the mark or spot of mold on the clay walls of the house. When the priest looks at the walls, the priest will look for two things. First, the priest will look to see if the mold is either a greenish color or a reddish color. Second, the priest will look to see if the mold looks to be deep in the walls. The words here are like the words that Yahweh uses to talk about the defiling skin disease being deep in the skin of the person. This probably means that mold is making a hole in the clay bricks or spreading in a way where the mold is destroying the clay bricks.

Stop here and discuss: Remind each other what words you used in your language to talk about how the defiling skin disease was deep in the skin of the person. What words will you use to talk about how the mold is deep in the wall? Pause this audio here.

If the priest looks at the walls and sees that the mold is green or red and that the mold looks deep in the walls, the priest must close the doors to the house or shelter. No person may go into the house for seven days or one week.

In the third scene, Yahweh says the priest must come back after one week to examine the house again. You may want to say that the priest re-examines the mold or that the priest examines the walls a second time. The priest will look to see if the mold has spread on the clay brick walls. "The mold has spread" can mean that the mold is getting bigger and is now on more bricks. "The mold has spread" can also mean that the mold has gotten deeper in the bricks and is making bigger holes in the bricks.

If the mold has spread on the walls, the priest must tell the owner that someone must tear or take all the moldy bricks out of the house or shelter. Someone must carry all the moldy bricks outside the camp to an area that is ritually dirty. This was a place away from where the Israelite people lived. People could leave ritually dirty things in this place so that the people did not become ritually dirty too.

Someone also must scrape all the inside bricks of the house or shelter. The priest will probably tell the person or people who live in the house to scrape the bricks. The people must do this to all the clay bricks on the inside or interior of the house. Someone also must take all the dust that people scrape off the walls and carry the dust outside the camp to an area that is ritually dirty. This word for dust sometimes means mud or can even mean "dry earth." This might refer to the mortar or mud that a person uses to hold the clay bricks together. Or it may mean the surface of all the bricks. Either way, try to use a word like mud or plaster. Sometimes ancient people would also mix lime, sand, and water together to create a plaster to put on the walls.

Stop here and look at the pictures of the mold on the brick wall again. In your language, what words do you use to talk about how people build houses or shelters? Talk about someone building a shelter with clay bricks. Notice what words you use for things like "bricks," "taking away bricks," "putting in new bricks," and "mortar." Pause this audio here.

Then the person must put new clay bricks and plaster in the place where the old, moldy bricks were.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:33–42 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • A person who owns a house with a defiling mold in their house or shelter
  • The people who tear out the moldy parts of the house and replace them with new bricks and plaster
  • And an Israelite priest

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives instructions to Moses and Aaron for what a person and a priest should do if a person has a house with a defiling mold in the clay walls.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • The priests are responsible for making sure all Israelite things are ritually clean, even houses; or
  • If I come into a house with a defiling mold and there are things or people in the house, are those people or things ritually dirty too? or
  • Yahweh has promised to give us the Canaan people's houses. I will be happy when we can live in houses instead of the tents we live in now.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, a person who owns a house or shelter may find defiling mold in the clay walls. The person must go to a priest and tell the priest that the person's house or shelter may have defiling mold. Then the priest will tell the person to take all the people and things out of the house or shelter before the priest comes to look at the walls. If the priest looks at the walls and sees that the mold looks to be deep in the walls, the priest must close the doors to the house or shelter. No person may go into the house for seven days or one week.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person who owns the house, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • Where will we stay for the next seven days? or
  • I am grateful that we are not ritually dirty, even though our house is.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, the priest must come back after one week to examine the house again. If the mold has spread on the walls, the priest will tell the owner that someone must tear all the moldy bricks out of the house or shelter. Someone must carry all the moldy bricks outside the camp to an area that is ritually dirty. Someone also must scrape all the inside bricks of the house or shelter. Someone also must take all the dust that came off the walls and carry the dust outside the camp to an area that is ritually dirty. Then the person must put new clay bricks and plaster in the place where the old, moldy bricks were.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite person who owns the house, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • The priest comes and tells us what to do, but we must do all the work; or
  • It is a long way to carry the bricks to the ritually dirty place outside the camp; or
  • We will do what the priest says because we know it will make Yahweh happy.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:33–42 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Yahweh talks about what to do when the people live in houses in the land of Canaan. Ancient people normally made these houses from clay or mud bricks. Sometimes people also used rocks or stones to build these houses. Use the same words for Yahweh and Canaan as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and Canaan, refer to the Master Glossary.

In previous passages, Yahweh gave Moses rules about how the priests should treat a person with a defiling skin disease. In this passage, Yahweh tells Moses how the priests should treat a house or dwelling that has a defiling mold in it. Yahweh uses the same words to refer both to the person who has this defiling condition and the building that has this defiling condition. Remember that at the end of Leviticus 13, you also used a word for defiling marks of mold or mildew in fabric and leather.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of defiling mold. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for defiling mold in a house. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, an Israelite priest is the one who must examine a house for a defiling mold. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for priest as you have used in previous passages.

The priest tells the person to take everything and everyone out of the house, so that those things will not be unclean or ritually dirty. Use the same words or phrases for unclean as you have used previously. For more information, refer to clean and unclean in the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
