title: Leviticus 14:43–57
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 14:43–57 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:43–57 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:43–57 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh was giving Moses instructions on how the Israelite people were supposed to live in good relationship with Yahweh. At this time, the Israelite people were still camping at Mount Sinai, where people had recently built the Tent of Meeting according to Yahweh's instructions. In this passage, Yahweh gives instructions for the priests. The priests were the spiritual leaders who taught the people what Yahweh wanted. The priests were also the experts who decided whether a skin disease was a defiling skin disease and whether a mold was a defiling mold or a persistent defiling mold.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, who are the spiritual leaders? What do these leaders teach people? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh wanted the Israelite people to be ritually clean so that the Israelites could be near to Yahweh and worship Yahweh. The main concern was whether the Israelite people were ready spiritually to obey and follow Yahweh. In this passage, Yahweh says the priest is responsible for making the building or home ritually clean. Even the Israelites' animals, clothes, and buildings needed to be ritually clean so that the Israelite people could be close to Yahweh.

Notice that in the passage, Yahweh never says that skin disease or mold defilement is a punishment for people's sin. Sometimes, the Israelites did see a connection between Yahweh's punishment of sin and skin problems, such as Miriam's defiling skin disease in Exodus. However, the Bible does not say a person who has a defiling skin disease or a person who has a house, or fabric, or leather with a defiling mold has done something bad to deserve it.

Here, in this passage, Yahweh gives Moses and Aaron final instructions about what to do if a house has had a defiling mold in it. Yahweh explains what to do if the mold comes back into the house that someone has cleaned out. Then Yahweh says what to do if a person goes into a defiled house that someone has closed for a period of isolation. Then Yahweh says how to perform ceremonial cleansings for houses that no longer have a defiling mold. After the ceremony, the house will be ritually clean again.

This is what the priest does to ceremonially cleanse a house that no longer has mold. As we review the cleansing ceremony, think about how the process is similar to and different from the ceremonial cleansing that the priest does for a person whom Yahweh healed from a defiling skin disease. For example, notice that in this process the priest kills the bird, but when the priest is performing ceremonial cleansing for a person, it is another person who kills the bird.

For this process, the priest must first bring two birds, cedar wood, scarlet thread, and a hyssop plant to the house that is ready to be ritually clean again. The two birds must be alive and ritually clean small birds. We do not know for sure what size or type of birds these were, but we do know that the birds had to be ritually clean.

Stop here and look at a picture of a sparrow as a group. Pause this audio here.

Next, the priest must use three items to sprinkle blood and water onto the house that needs ceremonial cleansing: cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop. Remember that cedar wood is a strong-smelling wood that is reddish-brown or sometimes tan-colored. Since ancient times, people have used cedar wood for its ability to preserve things, to purify, and even to keep bugs away. Many people think cedar wood smells nice.

Many scholars think the scarlet thread is a thread or string that a person dyed red. A person would collect a certain kind of red insect. A person would make red dye from this insect and then put threads and fabrics in the dye to make the threads and fabrics red.

Hyssop is a plant that has woody stems and green leaves. People used this plant in the ancient world for purification and for medicine. Remember, the Israelite people used hyssop to put the lamb's blood on their doors for the Passover in Exodus. It is possible that when the priest used the hyssop to sprinkle the blood during the ceremonial cleansing, the priest and the other Israelites would remember the Passover.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop. Pause this audio here.

The priest must also have a clay pot full of fresh spring water. Spring water is water that comes from a flowing or moving water source. The priest must kill one of the birds over the clay pot of water, so that the bird's blood falls into the pot and mixes with the water.

The priest must dip the remaining live bird into the blood and water mixture in the clay pot. The priest must also dip the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop plant in the blood and water mixture.

The priest must sprinkle the bird's blood and water mixture on the ritually dirty house seven times using the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop plant. Then the priest must take the live bird into a field or the wilderness, a place away from where people live, and let the bird go. Later in Leviticus, Yahweh gives instructions to the priests about the scapegoat, which a person releases in the wilderness. It is possible that when the priest releases the bird into the wilderness, it reminds the Israelite people of the scapegoat that people also release into the wilderness.

The priest makes atonement for the house in this way. This is atonement for an object rather than for a person. When a priest makes atonement for an object, the priest makes that object ready for people to use in the right and proper way again. After the priest completes this ceremony, the house is ritually clean again.

Stop here and discuss: What parts of the ceremonial cleansing for a house are similar to the ceremonial cleansing for a person who has healed from a defiling skin disease? Pause this audio here.

This passage is the last of Yahweh's instructions for the priests on defiling skin diseases and defiling molds.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:43–57 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains what to do if mold starts to grow again in a house that a person cleaned to get rid of the mold. The priest must come back and see that the mold has spread or gotten bigger or worse in the house. Then the priest will declare that it is a persistent defiling mold. The house is ritually dirty, and people must destroy the house and take all the material from the house out of the camp to a ritually dirty place.

In the second scene: Yahweh explains that if a person goes into a house after the priest closes the house up, the person is ritually dirty until the sun sets that day. If a person eats or sleeps in the house, that person also must wash their clothes.

In the third scene: The priest must come to see a house where the people have cleared away all the moldy clay bricks, scraped away all the mold, and rebuilt that part of the house. If the mold is gone, the priest will say that the house is ritually clean. The priest must do the ceremony to make the house ritually clean again.

In the fourth scene: The storyteller ends this passage by explaining that these are the rules for defiling conditions, whether defiling skin diseases, defiling molds in fabric or leather, or defiling molds in houses. These are the instructions for how the priests decide whether or not someone or something is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • A priest
  • The owner of the house
  • The people who tear down the house
  • A person who goes into the closed house
  • And a person who sleeps or eats in the closed house

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Note that the storyteller does not mention Moses or Aaron in this passage. But at the beginning of Leviticus 14, the storyteller says that Yahweh first gave these instructions to Moses and Aaron.

The first scene is about what to do if someone has already cleaned defiling mold from a house, but the defiling mold comes back or grows back.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, what words do you use to talk about things like plants or molds growing back again? Pause this audio here.

If the mold starts growing again in the house, the priest must come back and see that the mold has spread. Other ways to say "spread" might be that the mold has gotten bigger or the mold has gotten worse in the house.

Then the priest will declare that the house has a persistent defiling mold. Yahweh uses a similar word about persistent defiling skin disease in a previous passage. It means that this is a condition that will not go away quickly. Some people say that a persistent defiling mold means a destructive mold that causes things to fall apart or rot away.

Because the house has a persistent defiling mold, the house is ritually dirty. The priest must instruct people, probably the people who lived in the house, to destroy the house and take all the building material out of the camp to a ritually dirty place.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how would you describe how someone destroys or knocks down a building or house? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, Yahweh gives extra information about what happens if a person goes into a house that has a defiling mold. If the priest has closed up a house, and the person goes into that house anyway, the person is ritually dirty until the sun sets that evening. If a person eats or sleeps in that house, that person also must wash their clothes.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how would you talk about a house or shelter if someone closed the door to that house or shelter and told no one to go into it? Pause this audio here.

In the third scene, Yahweh explains what to do if the mold is gone after the people have cleared away all the moldy clay bricks and scraped away all the mold. The priest must come and look at the house. If the mold is gone, the priest says the house is ritually clean. Then the priest must do a ceremonial cleansing, or purification ceremony, to make the house ritually clean again. This process is similar to the ceremonial cleansing that the priest does for a person who has healed from a defiling skin disease so that the person can be ritually clean again.

The priest brings two birds, cedar wood, scarlet thread, and a hyssop plant to the house that is ready to be ritually clean again. The two birds must be alive and must be ritually clean birds. The word for birds means "sparrow," but here it probably means any kind of small bird.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a sparrow. Pause this audio here.

Someone also must bring a clay pot full of spring water. Spring water is water that comes from a flowing or moving water source. The priest kills one of the birds over the clay pot of water, so that the bird's blood falls into the pot too.

The priest uses three items to sprinkle the blood and water onto the house or shelter that needs ceremonial cleansing: cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop.

Cedar wood is a strong-smelling wood that is reddish-brown or sometimes tan-colored. Someone probably cut this cedar wood into a small enough piece for a person to hold easily in one hand.

Many scholars think the scarlet thread is a thread or string that a person dyed red. The priest would probably use the scarlet thread to tie the cedar wood and the hyssop together.

Hyssop is a plant that has woody stems and green leaves. People used this plant in the ancient world for purification and for medicine.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop. Pause this audio here.

The priest must dip the live bird in the blood and water mixture. The priest also dips the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop plant in the blood and water mixture. The priest probably dips all these things in the blood and water mixture together at the same time.

The priest must sprinkle the blood and water mixture on the ritually dirty house seven times using the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop plant. Then the priest must take the other bird into a field or a place away from where people live and let the bird go.

The priest makes atonement for the house in this way. After this, the house is ritually clean again.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: When are some times when you would have a ceremony before someone can use something, such as when someone cleans or prepares a place so people can use the place again? How would you talk about what happens during that kind of ceremony? Now discuss how you want to talk about the way that a priest makes atonement for the house so that people can use the house again. Pause this audio here.

In the fourth scene, the storyteller ends this passage by summarizing the laws in this section of Leviticus. The storyteller says these are the rules for defiling problems, whether defiling skin diseases, defiling molds in cloth or leather, or defiling molds in houses.

The storyteller also mentions the three skin problems that priests need to look at for defiling skin disease: swelling, rash, and shiny spots.

The first human skin problem is swelling. A person with swelling in their skin probably means that the person's skin is swollen and inflamed. The person's skin looks puffed up and bigger than it should, and may be painful when a person touches the skin.

The second human skin problem is a rash. This might mean a raised bump on the skin, such as a scab or a boil. It could also mean a lot of little bumps on a person's skin.

The third human skin problem is a shiny spot. This probably means white spots on the skin. However, it may mean any human skin that is an unusual color for that person.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of possible skin defiling disease. Remember how you translated the names of these skin defiling diseases in previous passages. Pause this audio here.

All of these are the instructions for how the priests decide whether or not someone or something is ritually clean or ritually dirty from a defiling skin disease or a defiling mold.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:43–57 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • A priest
  • The owner of the house
  • The people who tear down the house
  • A person who goes into the closed house
  • And a person who sleeps or eats in the closed house

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains what to do if the mold starts growing again in the house that a person cleaned to get rid of the mold. The priest must come back and see that the mold has spread or gotten bigger or worse in the house. Then the priest will declare that it is a persistent defiling mold. The house is ritually dirty, and people must destroy the house and take all the building material out of the camp to a ritually dirty place.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who owns the house, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am sad that we will have to destroy my house; or
  • My community and family will help me carry the blocks away and build a new house; or
  • I am thankful that no one in my family has to be ritually dirty because of this.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh says that if a person goes into a house after the priest closes up the house, the person is ritually dirty until the sun sets that day. If a person eats or sleeps in the house, that person also must wash their clothes.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who is ritually dirty until evening, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I had nowhere else to sleep; or
  • At least I do not need to make offerings to be clean again; or
  • Every person is ritually dirty sometimes.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh talks about what to do when the priest comes to see a house where the people have cleared away all the moldy clay bricks and scraped away all the mold. If the mold is gone, the priest says the house is ritually clean. The priest must do the purification ceremony to make the house ritually clean again.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • This ceremony is like the ceremony to make people ritually clean after a defiling skin disease; or
  • Even our buildings need atonement so people can be ritually clean before Yahweh.
Continue the drama.

In the fourth scene, the storyteller ends this passage with summary statements. The storyteller says these are the rules for defiling problems, whether defiling skin diseases, defiling molds in fabric or leather, or defiling molds in houses. These are the instructions for how the priests decide whether or not someone or something is ritually clean or ritually dirty.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • Most of our jobs and duties are in the Tent of Meeting. But Yahweh wants us to go to people and help the people when the people are ritually dirty. Why should the priests be the ones to help people who are ritually dirty? or
  • I am thankful that Yahweh gave us ways to become ritually clean again; or
  • I hope the people of Israel will understand how important it is to be ritually clean.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 14:43–57 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh tells Moses how the priests should treat a house or shelter that has a defiling mold in it. Mold or mildew is a fungus that can look like a thin layer of fuzz or fur. Usually, damp or wet weather causes mold, and mold can slowly break down things like clay bricks or food. Mold can also cause people to become sick sometimes. Use the same word or phrase for defiling mold as you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of defiling mold. Pause this audio here.

In this passage, an Israelite priest is the one who must examine a house for a defiling mold. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for priest as you used in previous passages.

The priest may find that the defiling mold is persistent, or that the mold will not go away easily. Use the same word or phrase for "persistent defiling mold" as you have used in previous passages.

If the house has persistent defiling mold, the house is ritually dirty. Use the same word or phrase for ritually dirty and ritually clean as you have used in previous passages. Refer to the Master Glossary for clean and unclean for more information if needed.

The priest must use birds in the ceremony to make the house ritually clean again. The word means "sparrow," but here it probably means any kind of small bird. These birds must be ritually clean birds.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a sparrow. Pause this audio here.

The priest must use three items to sprinkle the blood and water on the house that needs ceremonial cleansing: cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop.

Cedar wood is a strong-smelling wood that is reddish-brown or sometimes tan-colored. Since ancient times, people have used cedar wood for its ability to preserve things, to purify, and even to keep bugs away. Many people think cedar wood smells nice. Someone probably cut this cedar wood into a small enough piece for a person to hold easily in one hand. Use the same word or phrase for cedar wood as you used in previous passages.

Many scholars think the scarlet thread is a thread or string that a person dyed red. The person would make the dye from a certain kind of insect. The priest probably uses the scarlet thread to tie the cedar wood and the hyssop together. Use the same word or phrase for scarlet thread as you used in previous passages.

Hyssop is a plant that has woody stems and green leaves. People used this plant in the ancient world for purification and for medicine. Use the same word or phrase for hyssop as you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and look again at a picture of cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop as needed. Pause this audio here.

The priest must dip the live bird in the dead bird's blood and water mixture. The priest also has to dip the cedar wood, the scarlet thread, and the hyssop into the bird's blood and water mixture. This means the priest puts these things in the bird's blood and water mixture and brings them out quickly. Use the same word for this motion that you used in earlier passages.

The priest must sprinkle, or throw, the water mixed with the bird's blood onto the ritually dirty house. Use the same word or phrase for sprinkle as you used in previous passages.

This ceremony is how the priest makes atonement for the house. This atonement is for an object rather than for a person. When a priest makes atonement for an object, the priest makes that object ready for people to use in the right and proper way again.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you want to translate the way that the priest makes atonement for the house. For more information on atonement, refer to the Master Glossary. Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that Yahweh has been giving the priests instructions, or laws, for an Israelite person who has a defiling skin disease. If the person has a defiling skin disease, that person is ritually dirty. For more information on defiling skin diseases, refer to leprosy in the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for defiling skin disease as you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and look again at pictures of possible defiling skin diseases as needed. Pause this audio here.

Use the same word or phrase for laws as you have used previously, and refer to law in the Master Glossary for more information.

In the last few chapters of Leviticus, Yahweh has instructed the priests about what to do if an Israelite person had a defiling skin disease. Yahweh uses similar language for defiling marks of mold in cloth and leather. Use the same word or phrase for "defiling marks of mold" in cloth or leather as you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and look again at pictures of moldy fabric and moldy leather as needed.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 15:1–12
content:
Hear and Heart

NOTE: This passage talks about subjects that you may want to discuss in groups of only men and only women. Stop here and discuss as a group if you will listen to this passage in groups of only men and only women. Pause this audio here.

In this step, hear Leviticus 15:1–12 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 15:1–12 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 15:1–12 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

NOTE: This passage talks about subjects that you may want to discuss in groups of only men and only women. Stop here and discuss as a group if you will listen to this passage in groups of only men and only women. Pause this audio here.

Earlier in Leviticus, Yahweh told Moses how to deal with diseases that affect skin, cloth, and houses. All of these laws are about whether a person is ritually clean or ritually unclean or dirty. A ritually dirty person cannot touch anything holy, which means that person cannot worship in the Tent of Meeting. In this section of Leviticus, Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelites what the Israelites need to do when someone has issues concerning the reproductive parts of their bodies. This first passage is about when men have anything coming out of their penis that is not urine or semen. People call this a discharge or pus. Israelites do not normally talk directly about the sexual parts of a male and female body, so Yahweh calls a man's penis "flesh." You may also want to use a more general word here if it is more appropriate in your language.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do you talk about the reproductive or sexual parts of your bodies? How do you talk about these parts of the body differently if there are different types of people around? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that the discharge is ritually dirty. Yahweh also says that the man who has the discharge is ritually dirty. The man is ritually dirty, whether the discharge is flowing out of the man's penis or whether the discharge clogs up the man's penis.

Then Yahweh explains what happens when the man who has a discharge from his penis touches other things. The Israelites believed that if a person was ritually dirty for certain reasons, that person could make other things ritually dirty. Here, Yahweh explains what a man makes ritually dirty when the man has a discharge from his penis. Anything the man lies on or sits on becomes ritually dirty. Anyone who touches what the man lies on or sits on needs to wash their body and their clothes, and that person is ritually dirty until evening. For the ancient Israelites, the day started in the evening, so Yahweh is telling the Israelites that the person will be ritually dirty until the next day. The person specifically needs to wash in water. This probably means that the person needs to find a pool of water and go completely underwater for a brief time.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people wash their bodies? Describe the different ways people wash in different situations. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also says that anyone who touches the man who has a discharge from his penis needs to wash their clothes and their body with water, and that person who touched the man will be ritually dirty until evening. Anyone who the man with the discharge spits on needs to wash their clothes and their body with water, and the person the man spits on is ritually dirty until evening. Anything the man rides on becomes ritually dirty. This could refer to a saddle, or the cloth people laid on animals when a person rode on an animal, or the seat of a chariot.

Stop here as a group and look at this picture of a person riding on a horse with a cloth across the horse's back. Pause this audio here.

Also, stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what animals or things do people ride on? What do people use to make riding more comfortable? Pause this audio here.

If anyone carries what the man with the discharge sat on while the man rode, that person needs to wash their clothes and their bodies in water, and the person who carried the item will be ritually dirty until evening. The man with a discharge needs to wash his hands before the man touches someone. When Yahweh tells the Israelites to wash their hands, Yahweh is probably telling the Israelites to pour water on their hands so the Israelites can remove anything dirty from their hands.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people clean their hands? When do people clean their hands? Pause this audio here.

If the man with a discharge touches someone without washing his hands, then the person the man touched needs to wash their clothes and their body with water. The person the man touched will also be ritually dirty until evening, like in the other situations.

If the man with the discharge touches any pottery, the man with the discharge or someone else needs to break the pottery. Pottery is pots, dishes, or other containers that people make from clay. When pottery was ritually dirty, Yahweh did not allow the Israelites to wash the pottery. So when pottery was ritually dirty, the Israelites had to break the pottery.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a clay pot. Pause this audio here.

If the man with a discharge touches any wooden container, then the man or someone else needs to wash the wooden container with water. Like with the hands, Yahweh is probably telling the Israelites to pour water on and into the wooden containers to remove anything dirty from the containers.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a wooden bowl.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 15:1–12 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelites that a man who has pus coming out of his penis is unclean or ritually dirty.

In the second scene: Yahweh explains what happens to people and things the man who has a discharge from his penis touches.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • The Israelites
  • A man who has a discharge from his penis
  • Anyone who touches what the man with a discharge laid on
  • Anyone who sits on what the man with a discharge sits on
  • Anyone who touches the man with a discharge
  • Anyone whom the man with a discharge spits on
  • Anyone who carries or touches what the man with a discharge rode on
  • And anyone whom the man with a discharge touches without washing his hands

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Earlier in Leviticus, Yahweh told Moses how to deal with diseases that affect skin, cloth, and houses. All of these laws concern whether a person is ritually clean or ritually dirty. In this section of Leviticus, Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelites what the Israelites need to do when a person has issues concerning the reproductive or sexual parts of their bodies. The storyteller says that Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron. The storyteller says this to separate the next passages from the previous passage about diseases that affect houses. This passage is about when men have anything coming out of their penis that is not urine or semen. People call this a discharge or pus. Israelites do not normally talk directly about the sexual parts of a male and female body, so Yahweh calls a man's penis "flesh."

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How will you translate "flesh" or "penis" in a way that is appropriate for your culture? Pause the audio here.

In the first scene, Yahweh says that any discharge, or pus, that comes out of a man's penis is ritually dirty. Yahweh also says that the man who has the discharge is ritually dirty. The man is ritually dirty, whether the discharge is flowing out of the man's penis or whether the discharge clogs up the man's penis.

In the second scene, Yahweh gives instructions for when the man who has a discharge from his penis touches other things. Yahweh explains for each situation that the person who touches the man who has a discharge or something the man who has a discharge touches needs to wash their body and their clothes with water, and that person is ritually dirty until the evening. When Yahweh repeats this, Yahweh makes it easier for the Israelites to remember what Yahweh is telling the Israelites to do.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Think about important lists of rules in your culture. How do you help people remember these rules? Pause the audio here.

When Yahweh gives these instructions, Yahweh is not talking about a specific time when these situations happen. Yahweh is giving instructions so that any time in the future that these situations happened, the Israelites would know what to do.

Yahweh says that anything the man lies on or sits on becomes ritually dirty. Anyone who touches what the man lies on or sits on needs to wash their body and their clothes, and that person is ritually dirty until the sun sets. Most people probably lie on a mat on the floor that they use as a bed. You should use a word for something that people regularly lie on to sleep, or just say that it is any object that a person lies on.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will talk about the thing that the man lies on. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also says that anyone who touches the man who has a discharge from his penis needs to wash their clothes and their body with water, and the person who touches the man will be ritually dirty until evening. Anyone who the man with the discharge spits on needs to wash their clothes and their body with water, and the person the man spits on is ritually dirty until evening. Anything the man rides on becomes ritually dirty. Anyone who carries or touches what the man with the discharge sat on while the man rode needs to wash their clothes and their bodies in water, and the person will be ritually dirty until evening. The man with a discharge needs to wash his hands before the man touches someone.

Stop here and do this activity as a group: Take some water and pour it over your hands to remove anything dirty from your hands. How is this different from how you normally would clean your hands? Pause the audio here.

If the man with a discharge touches someone without washing his hands, then the person the man touched needs to wash their clothes and their body with water. The person the man touched will also be ritually dirty until evening, like in the other situations.

If the man with the discharge touches any clay pottery, the man with the discharge or someone else needs to break the pottery. Yahweh does not say who needs to break the pottery because the important thing is that someone destroys the pottery so that no one can use the pottery again.

If the man with a discharge touches any wooden container, then the man or someone else needs to wash the wooden container with water. Like with the hands, Yahweh is probably telling the Israelites to pour water on and into the wooden containers to remove anything dirty from the containers. Yahweh also does not say who needs to wash the wooden container because the important thing is that someone washes the wooden container before someone uses it again.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 15:1–12 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • The Israelites
  • A man who has a discharge from his penis
  • Anyone who touches what the man with a discharge laid on
  • Anyone who sits on what the man with a discharge sits on
  • Anyone who touches the man with a discharge
  • Anyone whom the man with a discharge spits on
  • Anyone who carries what the man with a discharge rode on
  • And anyone whom the man with a discharge touches without washing his hands

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelites what to do when a man has a discharge, or pus, coming out of the man's penis.

In the first scene, Yahweh says that any discharge, or pus, that comes out of a man's penis is ritually dirty. Yahweh also says that the man who has the discharge is ritually dirty. The man is ritually dirty, whether the discharge is flowing out of the man's penis or whether the discharge clogs up the man's penis.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the man with a discharge from his penis, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am feeling a lot of pain because something is wrong with my body; or
  • I am sad that I am ritually dirty because I cannot go to the tabernacle now; or
  • This is embarrassing to have something wrong with my penis.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh gives instructions for when the man who has a discharge from his penis touches other things. Yahweh says that anything the man lies on or sits on becomes ritually dirty. Anyone who touches what the man lies on or sits on needs to wash their body and their clothes, and that person is ritually dirty until evening.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the person who touches what the man with a discharge laid on, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am upset because I am ritually dirty now; or
  • I feel disgusted and dirty because I touched something ritually dirty; or
  • I am glad I only have to be ritually dirty until tomorrow. Yahweh is so nice to give me a way to become ritually clean again.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh also says that anyone who touches the man who has a discharge from his penis needs to wash their clothes and their body with water, and the person who touches the man will be ritually dirty until evening. Anyone who the man with the discharge spits on needs to wash their clothes and their body with water, and the person the man spits on is ritually dirty until evening. Anything the man rides on becomes ritually dirty. Anyone who carries or touches what the man with the discharge sat on while the man rode on something needs to wash their clothes and their bodies in water, and that person will be ritually dirty until evening.

Yahweh also says that anyone the man with a discharge touches needs to wash their clothes and their body with water. And the person the man touched will be ritually dirty until evening, if the man with the discharge did not wash his hands before the man touched the person.

If the man with the discharge touches any clay pottery, the man with the discharge or someone else needs to break the pottery.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the man with a discharge from his penis, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am feeling sad because I had to break the pottery I touched; or
  • I know that I need to destroy the pottery so that it does not make other people ritually dirty.
Continue the drama.

If the man with a discharge touches any wooden container, then the man or someone else needs to wash the wooden container with water.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 15:1–12 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Earlier in Leviticus, Yahweh told Moses how to deal with diseases that affect skin, cloth, and houses. All of these laws concern whether a person is ritually clean or unclean. In this section of Leviticus, Yahweh tells Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelites what to do when someone has issues concerning the reproductive or sexual parts of their bodies. Yahweh is God's personal name that Yahweh told the Israelites to call Yahweh. Use the same words or phrases for Yahweh and Israelites as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and Israelites, refer to the Master Glossary.

This first passage is about when men have anything coming out of their penis that is not urine or semen. People call this a discharge or pus. In this passage, Yahweh calls the penis "flesh." "Flesh" is an indirect word for "penis," because the Israelites did not like to talk directly about these parts of their bodies.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for penis. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for discharge. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that the discharge is unclean or ritually dirty. Yahweh also says that the man who has the discharge is ritually dirty. The man is ritually dirty whether the discharge flows out of the man's penis or clogs up the man's penis. When a person is ritually dirty, the person is not able to touch anything holy, and so the person cannot go to the tabernacle to worship God. Use the same word or phrase for unclean or ritually dirty as you used in previous passages. For more information on clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary.

Then Yahweh explains what happens when the man who has a discharge from his penis touches other things. The Israelites believed that if a person was ritually dirty for certain reasons, the person could make other things ritually dirty. Here, Yahweh explains what a man makes ritually dirty when the man has a discharge from his penis. Anything the man lies on or sits on becomes ritually dirty, and anyone who touches what the man lies on or sits on needs to wash their body and their clothes, and that person is ritually dirty until evening. For the ancient Israelites, the day started in the evening, so Yahweh is telling the Israelites that the person will be ritually dirty until the next day. The person specifically needed to wash in water. This probably meant the person needed to find a pool of water and go completely underwater for a brief time. Use the same word or phrase for wash as you used in previous passages. For more information on wash, refer to purify in the Master Glossary.

Yahweh also says that anyone who touches the man who has a discharge from his penis needs to wash their clothes and their body with water, and that person will be ritually dirty until evening. Anyone who the man with the discharge spits on needs to wash their clothes and their body with water, and that person is ritually dirty until evening. Anything the man rides on becomes ritually dirty. This could refer to cloth people laid on animals when a person rode an animal or the seat of a chariot. Some translations call this a saddle.

Stop here as a group and look at this picture of a person riding a horse with a cloth across the horse's back. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for saddle. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

If the man with the discharge touches any pottery, the man with the discharge or someone else needs to break the pottery. Pottery is pots and dishes that people make out of clay. When pottery was ritually dirty, Yahweh did not allow the Israelites to wash the pottery. So when pottery was ritually dirty, the Israelites had to break the pottery.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a clay pot. Pause this audio here.

If the man with a discharge touches any wooden container, then the man or someone else needs to wash the wooden container or dish with water. Like with the hands, Yahweh is probably telling the Israelites to pour water on and into the wooden containers to remove anything dirty from the containers.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a wooden bowl.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 15:13–18
content:
Hear and Heart

NOTE: This passage talks about subjects that you may want to discuss in groups of only men and only women. Stop here and discuss as a group if you will listen to this passage in groups of only men and only women. Pause this audio here.

In this step, hear Leviticus 15:13–18 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 15:13–18 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 15:13–18 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

NOTE: This passage talks about subjects that you may want to discuss in groups of only men and only women. Stop here and discuss as a group if you will listen to this passage in groups of only men and only women. Pause this audio here.

In this part of Leviticus, Yahweh is talking about things that make people ritually clean and ritually unclean or ritually dirty. In the previous passage, Yahweh told Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelites what happens when a man has pus coming out of the man's penis. People also call that a discharge. In this passage, Yahweh explains what happens when pus stops coming out of a man's penis, as well as what happens when semen comes out of a man's penis.

At the beginning of this passage, Yahweh explains that when a man with a discharge stops having the discharge, the man needs to wait seven days before the man can become ritually clean. On the seventh day, the man needs to wash the man's clothes and the man's body in fresh water. When Yahweh says fresh water, Yahweh means water that comes from a source of water that is flowing or moving. The Israelites considered still, or unmoving, water unsafe, so the Israelites used running water for important purification. When the man who has the discharge waits seven days and then washes his clothes and washes himself, the man will be ritually clean. Then, on the eighth day, the man who had the discharge needs to take two turtledoves or two pigeons to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. Turtledoves and pigeons are two different kinds of birds that Israelites sacrificed to Yahweh. The difference between the two birds is sometimes unclear.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of doves and pigeons. Pause this audio here.

The Tent of Meeting is another name for the tabernacle. Israelites made their sacrifices to Yahweh on the altar at the Tent of Meeting. When the man who had the discharge takes the two birds to the Tent of Meeting, the man gives the birds to the priest there. The priests were in charge of helping Israelites make offerings to Yahweh. The priest will use one bird to make a sin or purification offering and one bird to make a burnt offering. That is how the priest will make atonement for the man who had the discharge. Sometimes the Israelites thought that when a person became sick, Yahweh had made the person sick because the person had sinned. It is possible that the man had to make an offering to get atonement because the man had sinned. The man also might need to make an offering because the man was not able to worship Yahweh while the man had the discharge. Atonement restores a person to full fellowship with Yahweh again when the relationship was broken because the person sinned or was ritually dirty. The two birds were the least expensive animal offering a person could make, so it seems that Yahweh did not consider a discharge as serious as something like a skin disease.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, why do people think people get sick? Pause this audio here.

Next, Yahweh says that if semen comes out of a man's penis, the man needs to bathe his whole body in water, and the man will be ritually dirty until evening. In Israel, the new day starts in the evening, so the man is ritually dirty until the next day. Yahweh also says that if the semen touches any piece of clothing or leather item, the man or someone else needs to wash the item with water, and the item is ritually dirty until evening. Leather is any material that people make from animal skins. People clean the skin and turn it into a flexible material that people use for clothes, tents, and bags.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a leather bag as an example of something people make with leather. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh does not say who needs to wash the garment or the leather item because Yahweh does not need any specific person to wash the garment or the leather item that becomes ritually dirty. When Yahweh says "wash," Yahweh means that Yahweh wants someone to thoroughly scrub the cloth or leather item in water.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people wash clothes? When do people wash clothes? Pause this audio here.

Next, Yahweh says that if a man lies with a woman and semen comes out of his penis, then both the man and the woman need to bathe in water. Both the man and the woman will be ritually dirty until evening. In ancient Israel, the Israelites used the phrase "lie with" to talk about when people have sex. The Israelites did that because the Israelites were sometimes uncomfortable talking about sex directly, so the Israelites talked about it indirectly with this phrase and other phrases. Here, Yahweh is clearly talking about sex because Yahweh talks about when semen comes out of the man's penis.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What rituals or rules does your culture have for men and women after a man and woman have sex?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 15:13–18 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh explains what a man who has a discharge from his penis needs to do when the discharge stops.

In the second scene: Yahweh explains what the man needs to do when semen comes out of a man's penis.

In the third scene: Yahweh explains what a man and woman need to do when the man and woman have sex.

The characters in this passage are:

  • The man who has a discharge from his penis
  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • The Israelites
  • The priest
  • The man whose semen comes out of his penis
  • A man who has sex
  • And a woman who has sex with the man

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In this part of Leviticus, Yahweh is talking about things that make people ritually clean and ritually dirty. In the previous passage, Yahweh told Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelites what happens when a man has pus coming out of the man's penis. People also call this a discharge. In this passage, Yahweh continues to explain what happens when pus stops coming out of a man's penis, as well as what happens when a man has semen come out of the man's penis.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains that when a man with a discharge stops having the discharge, the man needs to wait seven days before the man can become ritually clean. The man needs to wash the man's clothes and the man's body in fresh water. You will remember that this is water that comes from a source of moving water, like a spring from the ground or running stream.

Stop here and remember how you translated the idea of fresh water in previous passages when someone had to wash with water to become ritually clean again. Pause this audio here.

Probably the man needs to both wash the man's clothes and wash the man's body during the seven days that the man is waiting to become ritually clean. Then, on the eighth day, the man who had the discharge needs to take two turtledoves or two pigeons to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. There in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting, near the bronze altar, the man gives the birds to a priest. The priest will use one bird to make a purification offering and one bird to make a burnt offering. When the priest makes the two offerings, the priest atones for the man. This means that Yahweh will restore Yahweh's relationship with the man, and the man will be able to worship Yahweh again.

In the next two scenes, Yahweh talks about when semen comes out of a man's penis. So Yahweh first talked about when bad things, like pus, came out of a man's penis, and now Yahweh is talking about when good and normal things, like semen, come out of a man's penis. These situations Yahweh describes are not about a specific event. Instead, Yahweh is giving instructions for any time these things happen.

In the second scene of this passage, Yahweh says that if semen comes out of a man's penis, the man needs to bathe his whole body in water, and that the man will be ritually dirty until evening, which is the next day. Yahweh also says that if the semen touches any piece of clothing or leather item, the man or someone else needs to wash the item with water, and the item is ritually dirty until evening. Yahweh does not say who needs to wash the garment or the leather item because Yahweh does not need any specific person to wash the garment or the leather item that becomes ritually dirty. When Yahweh says "wash," Yahweh means that Yahweh wants someone to thoroughly scrub the cloth in water.

In the final scene, Yahweh says that if a man lies with a woman and semen comes out of the man's penis, then both the man and the woman need to bathe in water. Both the man and the woman will be ritually dirty until evening. In ancient Israel, people used the phrase "lie with" to talk about when people have sex. People did that because people were sometimes uncomfortable talking about sex directly, so people talked about sex indirectly with this phrase and other phrases. Here, Yahweh is clearly talking about sex because Yahweh talks about when semen comes out of the man's penis.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what are some phrases people use to talk indirectly about sex? When do people use those phrases? Pause this audio here.

In the last passage, Yahweh talked about what to do when a man is ritually dirty. In this passage, Yahweh first talks about what to do when a man is ritually dirty. At the end of this passage, Yahweh talks about what to do when men and women who have sex become ritually dirty. In the next passage, Yahweh will begin to talk about when women are ritually dirty because of things that happen with their vagina. The last scene in this passage talks about both men and women, so Yahweh put it between the section about men and the section about women.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 15:13–18 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • The man who has a discharge from his penis
  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • The Israelites
  • The priest
  • The man whose semen comes out of his penis
  • A man who has sex
  • And a woman who has sex with the man

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains that when a man with a discharge stops having the discharge, the man needs to wait seven days before the man can become ritually clean. The man needs to wash the man's clothes and the man's body in fresh water. Then, on the eighth day, the man who had the discharge needs to take two turtledoves or two pigeons to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. There at the Tent of Meeting, the man gives the birds to a priest. The priest will use one bird to make a purification offering and one bird to make a burnt offering. When the priest makes the two offerings, Yahweh will restore Yahweh's relationship with the man.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the man who had the discharge from his penis, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so glad that I am healed and that Yahweh restored my relationship with Yahweh; or
  • I am embarrassed that I had this discharge from my penis.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene of this passage, Yahweh says that if semen comes out of a man's penis, the man needs to bathe his whole body in water, and that the man will be ritually dirty until evening, which is the next day. Yahweh also says that if the semen touches any piece of clothing or leather item, the man or someone else needs to wash the item with water, and the item is ritually dirty until evening.

In the final scene, Yahweh says that if a man has sex with a woman and semen comes out of the man's penis, then both the man and woman need to bathe in water. Both the man and the woman will be ritually dirty until evening.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the man who had sex, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • It is a little annoying that I am ritually dirty until evening every time I have sex; or
  • Now that I have had sex, I need to bathe, and I will not be able to go to the Tent of Meeting until evening.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 15:13–18 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this part of Leviticus, Yahweh is talking about things that make people ritually clean and ritually dirty. Yahweh is God's personal name that Yahweh told the Israelites to call Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

At the beginning of this passage, Yahweh explains that when a man with a discharge stops having the discharge, the man needs to wait seven days before the man can do his ceremonial cleansing. Use the same word or phrase for ceremonial cleansing or purification ceremony as you used in previous passages. For more information, refer to "purification ceremony" in the Master Glossary.

The man needs to wash the man's clothes and the man's body in fresh water. When Yahweh says fresh water, Yahweh means water that is flowing. The Israelites considered still, or unmoving, water unsafe, so the Israelites used running water for important purification. The Israelites often got this water from springs in the ground. Use the same word or phrase for fresh water as you used in previous passages.

When the man who had the discharge waits seven days and washes his clothes and himself, the man will be ritually clean. Use the same word or phrase for clean as you used in previous passages. For more information on clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary.

On the eighth day, the man who had the discharge needs to take two turtledoves or two pigeons to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. Turtledoves and pigeons are two different kinds of birds that Israelites sacrificed to Yahweh. The difference between the two birds is sometimes unclear. Use the same word or phrase for turtledoves or pigeons as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and look at the photos of the doves again, if needed. Pause this audio here.

The Tent of Meeting is another name for the tabernacle. Israelites made their offerings to Yahweh on the altar at the Tent of Meeting, which the Israelites sometimes called the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. Use the same words or phrases for "Tent of Meeting" and for "entrance to the Tent of Meeting" as you used in previous passages. For more information on the Tent of Meeting, refer to tabernacle in the Master Glossary.

When the man who had the discharge takes the two birds to the Tent of Meeting, the man gives the birds to a priest there. The priests were in charge of helping the Israelites make offerings to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for priest as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

The priest will use one bird to make a sin or purification offering and one bird to make a burnt offering. A purification offering is an offering that makes a person ritually clean, which means fit for service to God. A burnt offering was a sacrifice where the priest completely burned an animal on the altar. The burnt offering was a way that people showed Yahweh the people were completely devoted to Yahweh. Use the same words or phrases for purification offering and for burnt offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on purification offering and burnt offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

When a priest makes these two offerings, the priest makes atonement for the man who had the discharge. Use the same word or phrase for atonement as you used in previous passages. For more information on atonement, refer to the Master Glossary.

Next, Yahweh says that if semen comes out of a man's penis, the man needs to bathe his whole body in water, and that the man will be ritually dirty until evening. In Israel, the new day starts in the evening, so the man is ritually dirty until the next day. Yahweh also says that if the semen touches any clothing or leather item, the man or someone else needs to wash the item with water, and the item is ritually dirty until evening. Yahweh is talking about any type of clothing. Use the same general word or phrase for clothing as you used in previous passages. Leather is any material that people make from animal skins, which people clean and turn into a flexible material to use for clothes, tents, and bags.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a leather bag. Pause this audio here.

Next, Yahweh says that if a man lies with a woman and semen comes out of the man's penis, then both the man and the woman need to bathe in water. Both the man and the woman will be ritually dirty until evening. In ancient Israel, people used the phrase "lie with" to talk about when people have sex. People did that because people were sometimes uncomfortable talking about sex directly, so people talked about sex indirectly with this phrase and other phrases.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for lie with. If you have already translated this phrase in another book of the Bible, use the same phrase that you have used there.

Speaking the Word

Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 15:19–24 and put it in your hearts.
