title: Leviticus 22:17–25
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 22:17–25 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 22:17–25 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 22:17–25 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous passages, Yahweh told the Israelites the rules Yahweh had for the priests and the holy food. In this passage, Yahweh tells the Israelites the rules Yahweh has for sacrifices and offerings Yahweh will accept.

In the beginning of this passage, Yahweh tells Moses to talk to Aaron and Aaron's sons and all the people in Israel. Aaron and Aaron's sons are also Israelites, so Yahweh is talking to the Israelites and especially to Aaron and the rest of the priests. Yahweh tells Moses to say that when anyone who is an Israelite or someone who is living in Israel makes an offering, the offering needs to be physically perfect. The offering cannot have anything wrong with it. The offering could be payment for a vow, or it could be a freewill offering that someone sacrifices to Yahweh as a burnt offering. These offerings are offerings that people give when people want to or promise to, rather than offerings that Yahweh requires the people to give. These offerings are a type of peace or fellowship offering. For Yahweh to accept the offering, the offering needs to be completely perfect. The offering cannot have anything wrong with it. The offering needs to be cattle, sheep, or goats. Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to offer anything that has something wrong with it, because Yahweh will not accept it as an offering from the Israelites. When Yahweh accepts an offering from someone, Yahweh appreciates the offering and Yahweh strengthens his relationship with the person who made the sacrifice.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people think gods or spirits react to sacrifices that people make to the gods or spirits? Why would it be good that the spirits or gods accept the sacrifices? Pause this audio here.

Then, Yahweh says that when anyone offers a fellowship offering to Yahweh it needs to be completely perfect in every way. The offering needs to be perfect, whether it is bulls or sheep or goats. The offering also needs to be perfect if it is a fellowship offering to complete a vow or if it is a freewill offering. Yahweh is talking about animals with permanent physical problems, not animals that are sick for a short amount of time. Yahweh lists the reasons that an animal might not be physically perfect. If the animal is blind, or crippled, or severely cut, or if something is wrong with the animal's skin in some way, then Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to use that animal as a sacrifice. When Yahweh talks about skin problems, we are not exactly sure what Yahweh means. However, these problems are probably serious or permanent skin diseases of some kind.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What skin diseases do animals in your area have? How do people treat these animals that have these skin diseases? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to put an animal that has these physical problems on the altar for the priests to burn for Yahweh. The altar was the only place where the Israelites made sacrifices to Yahweh.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of the altar. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh will allow the Israelites to offer a bull or cow, or a sheep that has a leg that is too long or too short, if the Israelites are making a freewill offering. But Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to offer a cow or bull, or a sheep that has a leg that is too long or too short as a sacrifice when the Israelites are fulfilling a vow. Yahweh has different standards for the freewill offerings, perhaps because Yahweh thinks sacrifices for vows are more important than sacrifices people make when people are grateful.

Then, Yahweh says that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to offer an animal to Yahweh if the animal's testicles are bruised, crushed, torn, or cut. A male animal's testicles are the parts that allow a male to have babies with a female. In different cultures throughout the world, people would often remove the testicles of animals that they owned when people did not want the animals to have babies. Yahweh is probably talking about that here. Yahweh definitely does not want the Israelites to offer any animal that has something wrong with its testicles for any reason.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people stop animals that people own from having babies? Would you give that animal as a gift to someone? How much is that animal worth compared to an animal that can have babies? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to do this in Israel. Yahweh probably means that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to offer animals with something wrong with their testicles anywhere in Israel. Yahweh also might be saying that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to remove or damage an animal's testicles anywhere in Israel. Yahweh also will not allow the Israelites to offer an animal that has something wrong with it that the Israelites bought from a foreigner. Since the animal has something wrong with it, Yahweh will not accept that animal. Yahweh spends more time talking about an animal whose testicles are damaged than any other problem an animal might have because Yahweh cares more that the animal's testicles are undamaged than that the animal is undamaged in any other way. Damaging the animal's testicles stops the animal from having babies, which damages Yahweh's creation and the way Yahweh intends his creation to be.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 22:17–25 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells Moses to tell the Israelites and the priests specifically that Yahweh will not accept any animal as an offering if the animal is not physically perfect.

In the second scene: Yahweh says the Israelites may only give physically perfect animals as freewill offerings.

In the third scene: Yahweh tells the Israelites to never offer an animal that has something wrong with its testicles.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • Aaron's sons
  • The Israelites
  • And people from other countries who live in Israel

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Remember that in previous passages, Yahweh told the Israelites how to treat the holy food. Now, in this passage, Yahweh tells Moses to tell Aaron and the other priests and the other Israelites to offer animals that are physically perfect.

In the first scene, Yahweh tells Moses to talk to Aaron and Aaron's sons and all the people of Israel. Aaron is the high priest who is responsible for maintaining the relationship between Yahweh and the Israelites, and Aaron's sons are the other priests. Aaron and Aaron's sons are all Israelites. Yahweh mentions Aaron and Aaron's sons specifically because the priests are responsible for offering the sacrifices to Yahweh, so Yahweh wants the priests to pay special attention to these rules.

Yahweh starts by giving a specific situation. In this situation, someone presents an offering to Yahweh. This person could be an Israelite or someone from another country who is living in Israel. This person could be offering a peace or fellowship offering to fulfill a vow. Or the person could be making a burnt offering simply because the person wanted to. In this situation, the person needs to offer a male animal without anything wrong with it. The animal can be cattle or a sheep or a goat. You will remember that cattle is a general term that can mean a female cow, a bull, or an ox. These are the three large animals that Yahweh allows the Israelites to sacrifice. Yahweh will not accept any of these animals that have something wrong with them. Yahweh says twice that Yahweh will not allow the animal to have anything wrong with it because Yahweh really cares that the people give Yahweh animals that are valuable and perfect. Yahweh wants the people to obey Yahweh's instructions and only offer something that is good, not something that is bad.

In the second scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites more details about the physical problems an animal for sacrifice must not have. Yahweh repeats that Yahweh will not accept an animal with a defect as a freewill offering or an offering for a vow to show how important this command is. Yahweh mentions the offerings from the herds and flocks as a way to talk about the groups of animals that the Israelites can sacrifice to Yahweh. Herds refer to cattle, and flocks refer to sheep and goats. If an animal is blind, unable to walk, severely injured, or if the animal has a serious skin disease of any kind, then Yahweh will not allow anyone to offer the animal to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What kinds of defects do your animals have? How will you translate these terms for animals that have a physical problem? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that Yahweh will not allow anyone to put an animal that has one of these problems on the altar to burn as an offering to Yahweh. Yahweh says twice, in two different ways, that Yahweh will not allow anyone to give an animal with something wrong with it as an offering. Yahweh wants the Israelites to know how much Yahweh wants the animals to be valuable and undamaged. The Israelites must not give Yahweh a bad or damaged thing as a gift, which would be insulting to Yahweh.

Yahweh will allow someone to sacrifice cattle or a sheep as a freewill offering, even if the animal has a leg that is too long or a leg that is too short. But Yahweh will not allow someone to sacrifice an animal that has a leg that is too long or a leg that is too short to fulfill a vow. You will remember that people would sometimes vow to give Yahweh an offering if Yahweh did something good for them. If this happened, people had to give Yahweh a perfect animal.

Stop here and discuss this question: How do you describe an animal with a leg that is too long or too short? How will you translate this here? Pause this audio here.

In the third scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites that Yahweh will not allow anyone to offer an animal that has damaged testicles, which means that the animal has bruised, crushed, torn, or cut testicles. Yahweh lists four different ways something might damage an animal's testicles because Yahweh wants the Israelites to know how much Yahweh wants the animal's testicles to be completely undamaged. Yahweh says that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to offer an animal whose testicles are damaged in the land Yahweh will give to the Israelites. Yahweh is talking to the Israelites about the land that Yahweh has promised to give to the Israelites, but that Yahweh has not given to the Israelites yet. Yahweh probably talks about the land of Israel because Yahweh wants the Israelites to remember that Yahweh gives this land.

Stop here and discuss this question: How do you describe an animal that has damaged testicles? How will you translate this here? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also will not allow the Israelites to offer a damaged animal that the Israelites got from the hand of a foreigner. In other words, the Israelites should not buy an animal with damaged testicles from a person who is not an Israelite, and then try to give the animal to Yahweh. Yahweh wants the Israelites to follow this instruction in the future, when the Israelites are living in the land Yahweh will give to the Israelites and when foreigners are living in the land too. Yahweh will not accept damaged animals as a true sacrifice.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 22:17–25 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Aaron
  • Aaron's sons
  • The Israelites
  • And people from other countries who live in Israel

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh tells Moses to speak to Aaron and Aaron's sons and the rest of the Israelites. Yahweh wants Moses to say that when any Israelite or anyone else living in Israel gives an offering to Yahweh, the offering needs to be physically perfect. The offering could be payment for a vow or a freewill offering that the person offers to Yahweh as a burnt offering. The offering needs to be a male, and it can be cattle, sheep, or goats. Yahweh will not allow anyone to offer an animal that has something wrong with it, because Yahweh will not consider the sacrifice to be valid.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I would be insulted if someone offered a damaged animal to me, since people would not give a damaged animal as a gift to another person; or
  • When the Israelites give me only good animals, this shows other people how much the Israelites honor and respect me. This shows other people how good and powerful I am; or
  • I really want the Israelites to know what I will and will not consider valid.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh says that when anyone offers a fellowship offering, the offering needs to be physically perfect, or Yahweh will not accept the offering. This is true whether people are giving an offering to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering. The Israelites can offer a bull, a sheep, or a goat, but the animal cannot have anything wrong with it. Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to offer an animal to Yahweh if the animal is blind, or crippled, or severely damaged, or if the animal has anything wrong with its skin. Yahweh will not allow anyone to place one of these animals on an altar to burn as a sacrifice to Yahweh. Yahweh will allow someone to offer cattle or a sheep as a freewill offering, even if the animal has a leg that is too long or a leg that is too short. However, Yahweh will not allow someone to offer an animal that has a leg that is too long or a leg that is too short when that person fulfills a vow.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • Yahweh is very particular that we must offer perfect animals to Yahweh. I will learn Yahweh's laws very carefully so that I do not accidentally disobey Yahweh; or
  • I want to offer an undamaged animal to Yahweh to show how much I respect and honor Yahweh; or
  • I am worried I might have a damaged animal, and then I cannot offer the animal to Yahweh.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh will not allow anyone to sacrifice an animal with bruised, crushed, torn, or cut testicles. The Israelites cannot do this anywhere in the land that Yahweh is going to give the Israelites. The Israelites must not offer an animal with damaged testicles that the Israelites bought from a foreigner to Yahweh, either. That animal is damaged and is not physically perfect.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing a person from another country, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • Yahweh expects me to respect Yahweh even though I am not an Israelite; or
  • I am surprised that the Israelites have many rules about offering animals to Yahweh; or
  • I am surprised that the Israelites offer sacrifices differently than I do; or
  • I am impressed that the Israelites really do honor their God, Yahweh, when the Israelites give valuable animals as gifts; or
  • I am impressed that Yahweh is so careful to make sure that when people sacrifice animals to Yahweh, the animals are good animals.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh will not consider an animal with damaged testicles to be a good sacrifice.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 22:17–25 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh talks to Moses. Yahweh is the personal name that the one true God gave to the Israelites to call God. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh tells the Israelites that even foreigners who live among the Israelites in Israel but are not from Israel need to obey Yahweh's laws about offerings. A person is a foreigner when the person is in a country that is not where the person was born. Use the same words or phrases for Israel, Israelites, and foreigner as you used in previous passages. For more information on foreigner, refer to the Master Glossary.

In this passage, Yahweh talks about offerings. An offering is a gift or sacrifice that a person offers to a god in a ritual. Use the same word or phrase for offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Sometimes people made offerings to fulfill a vow. A person who is making a vow is asking God to do something for that person, and is offering to do something in return. Yahweh does not require people to make vows, but if a person makes a vow, the vow is seriously binding like an oath. Use the same word or phrase for vow as you used in previous passages. For more information on vow, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh is also talking about freewill offerings. A freewill offering is a special kind of peace or fellowship offering that Yahweh does not require people to make. Instead, people will decide to make this kind of offering when people fulfill a vow or want to thank Yahweh for something. Use the same word or phrase for freewill offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on freewill offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh talks about people who offer a freewill offering as a burnt offering. A burnt offering is an offering that a person burns completely when the person sacrifices it to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for burnt offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on burnt offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh accepts animals from herds and flocks. Herds are groups of cattle. Flocks are groups of sheep or goats. First, Yahweh accepts cattle. Use the same word for cattle as you used in Leviticus 7:23.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of cattle as needed. Pause this audio here.

Second, Yahweh accepts sheep. Use the same word for sheep as you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a sheep as needed. Pause this audio here.

Finally, Yahweh accepts goats. Use the same word for goat as you used in previous passages.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a bull as needed. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh requires that the offering be physically perfect, or blameless. When an animal is perfect, the animal does not have anything wrong with it. Use the same word or phrase for a perfect animal as you used in previous passages. For more information on perfect, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says that when people make these offerings, which are peace or fellowship offerings, that people should only use undamaged animals. A fellowship offering is a type of offering someone makes when the person wants to make their relationship with Yahweh better. Fellowship offerings include offerings to fulfill a vow, thanksgiving offerings, and freewill offerings. Use the same word or phrase for fellowship offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on "fellowship offering," refer to the Master Glossary.

The Israelites offer their offerings on the altar as a fire offering to Yahweh. An altar is a place where people make offerings or sacrifices to Yahweh. Use the same words or phrases for altar and fire offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on altar and fire offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 22:26–33
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 22:26–33 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 22:26–33 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 22:26–33 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In previous passages, Yahweh told the Israelites that Yahweh would only accept animals that were physically perfect as a sacrifice. In this passage, Yahweh gives some more rules that the Israelites need to obey when the Israelites sacrifice an animal.

Yahweh tells Moses that when a cow, sheep, or goat gives birth, the baby needs to stay with the mother for seven days. Yahweh will allow the Israelites to give a baby animal as a burnt sacrifice on the eighth day or later after the animal was born. The number seven was very important to the Israelites because the Israelites thought that the number seven represented completeness.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what numbers are special? Why are those numbers special? Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, when an animal that you eat gives birth, how long do people wait before people will eat the baby animal? Why do people wait? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also will not allow the Israelites to kill a cow, sheep, or goat on the same day that the Israelites kill any offspring that the cow, sheep, or goat has.

Yahweh also tells the Israelites that when the Israelites offer a thanksgiving sacrifice, the Israelites need to make sure that Yahweh will accept it. The Israelites need to eat the meat from the sacrifice the same day the Israelites offer the sacrifice. Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to keep any of the meat until the next day. Yahweh reminds the Israelites that he is Yahweh. This offering is a type of peace or fellowship offering.

Finally, Yahweh tells the Israelites to make sure that the Israelites do what Yahweh is telling the Israelites to do. Yahweh says that he is Yahweh. Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to profane Yahweh's holy name, or the name that represents Yahweh, which shows people that Yahweh is special. If the Israelites do not profane Yahweh's name, then the Israelites will show people that Yahweh is completely good and powerful. Yahweh tells the Israelites again that he is Yahweh and that Yahweh makes the Israelites holy. Yahweh also tells the Israelites that Yahweh brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt so that Yahweh could be the Israelites' God. Yahweh is talking about how the Israelites used to be slaves in Egypt. Yahweh wants the Israelites to understand that Yahweh is holy and that Yahweh is the one who rescued the Israelites from Egypt. Yahweh tells the Israelites a third time that he is Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, when a god or a spirit focuses or pays attention to a specific person or a specific group of people, what does that god or spirit do to those people?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 22:26–33 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells the Israelites when Yahweh will allow the Israelites to sacrifice baby animals.

In the second scene: Yahweh says that when the Israelites offer a thanksgiving offering, the Israelites must eat the meat from the offering on the same day.

In the third scene: Yahweh tells the Israelites to do what Yahweh says to do and to not profane Yahweh's reputation.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Moses
  • Yahweh
  • And the Israelites

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the previous passages, Yahweh told the Israelites some of the rules Yahweh has for when the Israelites sacrifice an animal to Yahweh. In this passage, Yahweh tells the Israelites more rules that Yahweh has for when people sacrifice an animal. Then Yahweh ends this part of Leviticus by telling the Israelites to obey the rules Yahweh has given to the Israelites.

In the first scene, Yahweh speaks to Moses. When the storyteller reminds us that Yahweh speaks to Moses, the storyteller is telling us that Yahweh will talk about a new topic. Yahweh is still giving these commands to Moses to give to the Israelites.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time someone had to give someone else a lot of rules about a lot of different things. Pay attention to the ways that the person showed that they were talking about a new part of the rules. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells Moses the rules for how soon Yahweh will allow the Israelites to sacrifice an animal after it is born. Yahweh says that when a cow, sheep, or goat gives birth to a new animal, Yahweh will require the Israelites to let the baby animal stay with its mother for seven days. After the end of the seventh day, when the animal is eight days old, Yahweh will allow the Israelites to sacrifice the baby animal to Yahweh. Yahweh calls this a fire offering because the Israelites burned the meat that the Israelites gave to Yahweh on the fire on the altar at the tabernacle.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you refer to newborn cattle, sheep, and goats? Look at a photo of each of these animals. How will you translate these terms? If, in your language, you need to choose between male and female names, you should choose male names. Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh says that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to kill a cow or a sheep or a goat on the same day that the Israelites kill that animal's baby.

In the second scene, Yahweh talks about when the Israelites sacrifice a thanksgiving sacrifice. The Israelites need to make sure that Yahweh will accept their thanksgiving offering. The Israelites need to eat the meat from the sacrifice on the same day that the Israelites offer the sacrifice, which is one of the ways to make sure Yahweh accepts the offering. Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to keep any of the meat from the sacrifice until the next morning.

In the third scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites that Yahweh wants the Israelites to obey Yahweh's commands. Yahweh also tells the Israelites why Yahweh wants the Israelites to obey Yahweh's commands. Yahweh speaks like this to show that Yahweh is ending this section of Leviticus. Next, Yahweh will talk about laws that have to do with holidays, and so Yahweh is done talking about the laws that have to do with sacrifices. Before Yahweh goes on to the next subject, Yahweh wants the Israelites to realize how much Yahweh wants the Israelites to obey the laws Yahweh has about sacrifices.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time someone really wanted people to know how much the person wanted the other people to obey a specific rule. Pay attention to how the person made sure that the other people knew the rule was important. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells the Israelites to obey Yahweh's commands. Yahweh wants the Israelites to do what Yahweh told the Israelites to do. Yahweh tells the Israelites that he is Yahweh. Yahweh tells the Israelites that he is Yahweh when Yahweh wants the Israelites to think about the things that Yahweh has done for the Israelites and how powerful Yahweh is.

Then, Yahweh tells the Israelites that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to profane Yahweh's holy name. When Yahweh talks about his name, Yahweh is using special language to talk about Yahweh's reputation, or what people think about Yahweh.

If the Israelites do not profane Yahweh's name, then the Israelites will realize and tell others how holy, or completely good and powerful, Yahweh is. Yahweh says again that he is Yahweh, and that Yahweh made the Israelites holy, because Yahweh dedicated the Israelites to himself. Yahweh tells the Israelites that Yahweh brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt so that Yahweh could be the Israelites' God. Because the Israelites are Yahweh's special people, Yahweh takes care of the Israelites and helps the Israelites be good people. Yahweh ends this scene by telling the Israelites again that he is Yahweh.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 22:26–33 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Moses
  • Yahweh
  • And the Israelites

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh talks to Moses. Yahweh tells Moses that Yahweh requires the Israelites to let a calf, sheep, or goat stay with its mother for the first seven days after it is born. Yahweh will allow the Israelites to sacrifice a calf, sheep, or goat to Yahweh on the altar on the eighth day after it is born. But Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to kill a calf, sheep, or goat on the same day that the Israelites kill one of the animal's parents.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am surprised that Yahweh cares about the mother animals and young animals too; or
  • I wonder why Yahweh asks us to do this; or
  • Yahweh is very specific about the animals that we can sacrifice to Yahweh; or
  • I am glad Yahweh tells me what Yahweh wants me to do when I sacrifice an animal.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh says to sacrifice in such a way that Yahweh will accept the sacrifice. If the Israelites follow the commands Yahweh already gave, and if the Israelites eat all the meat from the thanksgiving offering on the same day that the Israelites make the offering, then Yahweh will accept the sacrifice on the Israelites' behalf. Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to keep any of the meat from the thanksgiving offering until the morning. Yahweh says again that he is Yahweh.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I want the Israelites to enjoy the meat from their thanksgiving sacrifices; or
  • I need the Israelites to treat the meat from the thanksgiving sacrifice as special, so the Israelites cannot just keep the meat as long as the Israelites want.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh says to obey the commandments Yahweh gave the Israelites and to do what Yahweh told the Israelites to do in the commandments. Yahweh says again that he is Yahweh. Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to profane Yahweh's reputation as completely good and powerful, so that all the Israelites will acknowledge that Yahweh is completely good and powerful.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • When people know how powerful and good I am, people will know why it is important to do what I tell the people to do; or
  • I really want the Israelites to realize how much I want the Israelites to do what I tell the Israelites to do; or
  • I love the Israelites, and I want to help the Israelites do the right thing.

Ask the person playing the Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am happy that Yahweh is holy and I can tell others about Yahweh; or
  • I want other people to know how amazing Yahweh is; or
  • I can show through my actions how holy Yahweh is.
Continue the drama.

Yahweh says again that he is Yahweh, and that Yahweh makes the Israelites holy. Yahweh also reminds the Israelites that Yahweh brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt so that Yahweh could be the Israelites' God. Yahweh says again that he is Yahweh.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 22:26–33 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh talks to Moses. Yahweh is the personal name that the one true God gave to the Israelites to call God. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

In this passage, Yahweh says that Yahweh will accept an animal as a fire offering when the animal is eight days old. Use the same word or phrase for fire offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on fire offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh talks about killing a baby animal. Use the same word or phrase for killing an animal as you used in previous passages.

Yahweh requires that the Israelites eat the meat from a thanksgiving sacrifice on the day the Israelites make the offering. A thanksgiving sacrifice, or offering, is a special type of freewill offering that people offered when people wanted to thank Yahweh for doing something for those people. Use the same word or phrase for thanksgiving sacrifice as you used in previous passages. For more information on sacrifices and freewill offerings, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh tells the Israelites to obey Yahweh's commands. Yahweh's commands are all the instructions that Yahweh has given his people. Use the same word or phrase for commands as you used in previous passages. For more information on commands, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh does not want the Israelites to profane Yahweh's name. When someone profanes something, that person mistreats something holy and makes that thing not seem holy anymore. Use the same word or phrase for profane as you used in previous passages. For more information on profane, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh's name is holy, and Yahweh makes the Israelites holy. When the Bible says that Yahweh is holy, it means that Yahweh is completely good, completely pure, completely powerful, and completely majestic. When Yahweh says that a specific group of people is holy, it means that the people are dedicated to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for holy as you used in previous passages. For more information on holy, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says that Yahweh is the Israelites' God. In the Bible, God refers to God who created everything. God is the most powerful spiritual being. Use the same word or phrase for God as you used in previous passages. For more information on God, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 23:1–8
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 23:1–8 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 23:1–8 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 23:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

At this time, the Israelite people are still camped near Mount Sinai. The Israelites had recently completed building the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh is now giving Moses many instructions on how the Israelite people should live in a holy way. In this passage, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about the festivals that the Israelite people should celebrate. Yahweh tells Moses to give these instructions to the Israelite people.

Yahweh uses a second name for these special festivals. Yahweh calls these festivals "holy assemblies." An assembly is a group of people whom someone calls to meet together for a special reason. An assembly can also refer to a community reading. In this case, the Israelite people gather together to hear someone read from the part of the Bible that the Israelites had at this time: probably the books of Genesis, Exodus, and Leviticus, and eventually Numbers and Deuteronomy. These books tell the history of the Israelite people and tell the Israelites how to follow Yahweh's laws.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Why do you think it is important for people to gather and listen to the Bible together? Pause this audio here.

First, Yahweh reminds Moses about how to celebrate the Sabbath. Every seventh day should be a day of rest for the Israelite people. This is the Sabbath, the last day of the week. The Sabbath reminds the Israelite people that Yahweh created the world in six days and rested on the seventh day. Sabbath is a day to trust Yahweh and a chance to be together as a family and community to worship Yahweh. Yahweh commands the Israelite people not to do any work or business on this day. The Sabbath is the regular day of sacred assembly. This means that the Israelite people come together to worship Yahweh on that day. You heard in an earlier passage that Yahweh gave the Israelite people strict instructions to celebrate the Sabbath rest and not to ignore it. Yahweh even commanded the community to punish people who did not obey this rule.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what days are holy days or days that are important in your religion? How do people act on these holy days? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh gives instructions for the Israelite people to celebrate the Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread. The instructions for the first Passover are in the book of Exodus. The Israelite people celebrate the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month of their calendar. This date can be anytime between what we today call late March and late April.

To celebrate the Passover, the Israelite people must hold a special ceremony and not do work. It is a time when the people remember the first Passover. At the first Passover, when the people were still slaves in Egypt, each household brought a young sheep or a young goat into the house on the 10th day of the month. The people kept the animal in the house until sunset on the 14th day. Then, at sunset, the people sacrificed or killed the young sheep or young lamb. The people put the animal's blood over their doors and on their doorposts, so Yahweh would remember the people and see that the Israelites obeyed Yahweh. Yahweh protected the people who obeyed Yahweh, and Yahweh did not kill the firstborn son in the houses with blood over the doors. The Israelite people ate the roasted meat of the animal with bitter herbs and unleavened bread. Unleavened bread is bread that has no yeast in it. The bitter herbs remind the people of their slavery. The unleavened bread is a reminder to make a meal and eat it quickly, because the people would not be slaves much longer.

Stop here and look at a picture of unleavened bread together as a group. Pause this audio here.

To remember that Yahweh saved the Israelite people from slavery, the Israelites now celebrate Passover every year. The people also consider the Passover festival to be a time when Yahweh cleanses the people spiritually and gives the people new strength.

Beginning on the 15th day of the seventh month, the day after Passover, the Israelite people celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread for the next seven days. During that week, the Israelites must not eat any bread with yeast. The Israelites can only eat the unleavened bread.

Stop here and look at a diagram of a calendar together as a group. See how the Sabbath is every seventh day, how Passover is on the 14th day of that month, and how the feast of Unleavened Bread starts on the 15th and continues through the next seven days. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your culture, what kinds of bread do you normally eat? If you do not normally eat bread, what is your main food that is not meat? What types of bread do people consider to be good or filling? How would you feel if you could not eat that good and filling food for a week? Pause this audio here.

The people also must give fire offerings to Yahweh every day. These are the offerings that the Israelites give to Yahweh by burning the food on the altar. We do not know everything that was in these food offerings, but it is likely that the Israelite people had to give at least grain and drink offerings. It is very possible that the Israelites also had to sacrifice a young sheep or a young goat, and it may have even included special offerings such as a firstfruits offering. People brought a firstfruits offering at the beginning of the harvest season as a gift to thank Yahweh for giving a harvest.

On the last day, one week after Passover, the Israelite people will have another special ceremony to worship Yahweh and remember what Yahweh has done. On this day, Yahweh instructs that the people should not work again, especially any form of hard work. This is another holy assembly, a special day for the Israelite people to come together to celebrate and worship Yahweh all together as a group.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your culture, how do people talk about different kinds of work? Describe the different kinds of work people in your community do, such as working in offices, in fields, building things, and teaching people.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 23:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh gives Moses instructions about the festivals that the Israelite people should celebrate. Yahweh tells Moses to give these instructions to the Israelite people.

In the second scene: Yahweh instructs Moses that every seventh day should be a day of rest for the Israelite people. This is the Sabbath, the last day of the week.

In the third scene: Yahweh tells Moses that the Israelite people should celebrate Passover at the right time. The Israelites must hold a special ceremony and do no work. For the next seven days, the Israelite people should celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread. During that time, the Israelites must eat bread without yeast and give food offerings to Yahweh.

In the fourth scene: On the last day, one week after Passover, the Israelite people must have another special ceremony and not work.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The Israelite people were still camping in the wilderness near Mount Sinai. The Israelites had recently finished building the Tent of Meeting, following Yahweh's instructions. Yahweh is giving Moses instructions that Moses then writes down and tells to the Israelite people.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about the festivals that the Israelite people should celebrate. Yahweh tells Moses to give these instructions to the Israelite people.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how do you tell someone about what another person told you? Also, describe a situation where someone gave you instructions. Notice what language you use. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh emphasizes that Yahweh has "appointed," or chosen, these festivals for a special purpose. Therefore, Yahweh gives the Israelites special times and ways to celebrate the festivals. These special festivals happen on specific days of the year, so this makes a sort of religious calendar for the Israelite people to follow.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Talk about specific holidays or celebrations in your culture that happen on specific days, specific seasons, or specific times of year. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh uses a second name for these special festivals. Yahweh calls these "holy assemblies." An assembly is a group of people who someone calls to meet together for a special reason. Yahweh wants the Israelite people to come together as an entire nation to celebrate and worship Yahweh as a group.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what kind of events bring everyone together? What makes your people proud? What do you call these special events? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, Yahweh instructs Moses that every seventh day should be a day of rest for the Israelite people. This is the Sabbath, the last day of the week. This means that the people should not do any work or business on this day. The Sabbath is the regular day of holy assembly. This means that the Israelite people should come together to worship Yahweh on that day. Earlier in Leviticus, Yahweh gave the Israelite people strict instructions to celebrate the Sabbath rest and not to ignore it.

In the third scene, Yahweh tells Moses that the Israelite people should celebrate Passover at the right time. The Israelite people celebrate the Passover after sunset on the 14th day of the first month of their calendar. This date can be anytime between late March and late April. To celebrate the Passover, the Israelite people must hold a special ceremony and do no work. It is a time when the people look back and remember the first Passover. Passover begins at twilight, which is in the evening, right after the sun goes down. For the Israelites, a new day began after the sun set in the evening.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do you talk about the time of day after the sun sets? How will you talk about the date and time that Passover begins? Pause this audio here.

For the next seven days after Passover, the Israelite people celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread. During that time, the Israelites must not eat bread with yeast. The Israelites also must give fire offerings to Yahweh every day. These are offerings that people give to Yahweh by burning at least some of the food on the altar. You may have heard that some translations call these "food offerings," while other translations call these "fire offerings."

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How do the translations you listen to describe these offerings? How will you continue to talk about these offerings in your translation? Pause this audio here.

We do not know everything that was included in these fire offerings, but it is likely that the Israelite people had to give at least grain and drink offerings. It is very possible that the Israelites also had to sacrifice a young sheep or a young goat, and it may have even included special offerings such as a firstfruits or harvest offering.

Stop here and discuss as a group: The Passover festival begins on the 14th day of the month, then the Festival of Unleavened Bread begins on the 15th day of the month and lasts for seven days. How will you talk about the days of these festivals in your language? Pause this audio here.

In the fourth scene, on the last day, one week after Passover, the Israelite people must have another special ceremony to worship Yahweh and remember what Yahweh has done. On this day, Yahweh again instructs that the people should not work, especially any form of hard work like work in the fields or work that requires a lot of physical strength. Some translations use a term like "regular" or "usual" work. This was another holy assembly, a special day for the Israelite people to come together to celebrate and worship Yahweh together as a group.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, what are ways that people talk about different kinds of work? Discuss what word or phrase in your language works best for this type of work. Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 23:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about the festivals that the Israelite people should celebrate. Yahweh tells Moses to give these instructions to the Israelite people.

In the second scene, Yahweh instructs Moses that every seventh day should be a day of rest for the Israelite people. This is the Sabbath, the last day of the week.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so glad we get a day of rest every week! or
  • I have so much to do. How can I afford to take a day off? or
  • Even Yahweh rested after Yahweh created the earth; or
  • Yahweh wants us to be still and know that Yahweh is God; or
  • The Sabbath will be the time of the week for the family to get together and worship Yahweh; or
  • Can you explain what I can and cannot do? I am not sure what Yahweh thinks is work.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh tells Moses that the Israelite people should celebrate Passover at the right time. The Israelites must hold a special ceremony and do no work. For the next seven days, the Israelite people should celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread. During that time, the Israelites must eat bread without yeast and give food offerings to Yahweh.

In the fourth scene, on the last day, one week after Passover, the Israelite people must have another special ceremony and not work.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • This will be our time to remember when Yahweh saved us from slavery in Egypt; or
  • Oh no, the people will grumble about eating unleavened bread for a whole week! or
  • To see the Israelite people come together in one place to worship Yahweh is amazing.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 23:1–8 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about the festivals that the Israelite people should celebrate. Use the same words for Yahweh and Israelites as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and Israelites, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says that these festivals are sacred or holy assemblies and appointed festivals. An assembly is a group of people whom someone calls to meet together for a special reason. This assembly is holy because Yahweh set it apart and dedicated this gathering to Yahweh. Yahweh has "appointed," or chosen, these festivals for a special purpose.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will translate holy assemblies and appointed festivals. Remember the things you discussed in previous steps. For more information on holy, look at the Master Glossary. If you have already translated these phrases in another book of the Bible, discuss whether you can use the same phrases here. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh instructs Moses that every seventh day should be a day of rest for the Israelite people. This is the Sabbath, the last day of the week. Use the same word for Sabbath as you used in previous passages. For more information on Sabbath, refer to the Master Glossary.

Use the same word for Passover as you used in previous passages. For more information on Passover, refer to the Master Glossary.

The festivals or sacred assemblies were special times of the year when the Israelite people were to stop regular activities and focus on religious celebrations or ceremonies. In this passage, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about the Festival of Unleavened Bread. Use the same phrase for the Festival of Unleavened Bread as you used in previous passages. For more information on the Festival of Unleavened Bread, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and look at a picture of unleavened bread together as a group. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh instructs Moses that the Israelites should give a fire offering to Yahweh on each of the seven days of the Festival of Unleavened Bread. Use the same word or phrase for fire offering as you have used previously, and refer to fire offering in the Master Glossary for more information.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
