title: Leviticus 23:33–44
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 23:33–44 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 23:33–44 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 23:33–44 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

At this time, the Israelite people were still camped near Mount Sinai. The Israelites had recently completed building the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh was giving Moses many instructions on how the Israelite people should live in a holy way. In this passage, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about the festivals that the Israelite people should celebrate. Yahweh tells Moses to give these instructions to the Israelite people.

Yahweh tells Moses to instruct the Israelite people how to celebrate the Festival of Tabernacles or Shelters. Here, a tabernacle is a shelter or a home that people live in for a short time. A person could make a shelter out of many different kinds of materials. Here are some of the kinds of temporary shelters that the Israelite people would have used.

First, there are tents. In ancient times, people often lived in tents. People wove goat hair into fabric to make these tents because goat hair would keep out water. Then the people used wooden poles to hold up the fabric. People made ropes from plant or animal parts and pegs from bone, wood, or metal. People tied the tent fabric down using these ropes and pegs. This created a covered space that people could eat, move, sit, and sleep inside. At the time when Yahweh gave these instructions, most Israelite people lived in tents like this.

There is another kind of shelter, which people often call a hut. People often made these huts out of wooden beams and strong grasses like reeds. People used things like ropes and mud to hold these shelters together. In ancient times, for this festival, it is probable that Israelite people lived in whatever kind of temporary shelters the Israelites could make.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of temporary shelters. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, talk about different kinds of temporary shelters. How would you build one if you needed to? Pause this audio here.

The Israelite people lived in temporary shelters for eight days during the Festival of Tabernacles. On the first and last day of the Festival of Tabernacles, the Israelite people gather the people together to have holy assemblies or worship celebrations. No one can work on those days.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what celebrations or holidays do people celebrate by not working? Pause this audio here.

For every day of the festival, people are also supposed to give fire offerings to Yahweh. You will remember that in the original language, this is something like "fire offering" or "an offering that a person makes in the fire." This can really refer to any of the offerings where a priest burns all or part of the offering on the altar.

When Yahweh gives more specific instructions about how the people should celebrate, Yahweh mentions that this festival should happen after the people have finished the harvest.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what are the most important crop harvests? What are some things you do after you finish your harvests? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also tells Moses to tell the Israelite people to gather tree branches. While it is possible that the people used these tree branches when the people built the shelters, the people probably carried these tree branches while they walked all together and celebrated as a group. In a way, the Festival of Tabernacles may have led to the celebration we see later in Jesus' time, Palm Sunday, when people waved palm branches and put the branches on the ground in front of Jesus. For this festival, Yahweh instructs the Israelite people to gather date palm branches, willow branches, and branches from other leafy trees. Yahweh says, "branches from a tree that loves water," so some scholars think this could mean willow branches or poplar trees. It is possible that when Yahweh said "leafy trees," Yahweh meant myrtle trees.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of these different kinds of trees. How are trees in your area similar to or different from these trees? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that all generations of the Israelite people should celebrate this festival by living in temporary shelters for a week. This festival is a reminder that the Israelite people lived in shelters when Yahweh brought the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. Yahweh ends his instruction with an important statement: "I am Yahweh, your God." Yahweh says this statement often, and Yahweh is saying it again, probably for the same reason as Yahweh has before: to remind the Israelites that the Israelites must obey Yahweh because Yahweh is the Israelites' God. Then Moses tells the people about Yahweh's festivals.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what do people say or think about future generations? Why do you think it was important that the future generations would live in temporary shelters like their ancestors?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 23:33–44 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells Moses to instruct the Israelite people how to celebrate the Festival of Tabernacles or Shelters. The Israelite people are to celebrate this festival for eight days. On the first and last day of the festival, the Israelite people are to have holy assemblies or worship celebrations. No one can work on those days. On every day of the festival, the people are also supposed to give offerings to Yahweh.

In the second scene: Yahweh says that these are Yahweh's festivals. Yahweh reminds the people about the different kinds of offerings that the people are supposed to give Yahweh.

In the third scene: Yahweh gives more specific instructions about how the people should celebrate the Festival of Tabernacles. Yahweh tells Moses that the Israelites should gather tree branches and build temporary shelters for this festival. Every Israelite person is supposed to live in these temporary shelters for the seven days of the festival. Yahweh also says that all future generations of the Israelite people should do this. This celebration is a reminder that the Israelite people lived in shelters when Yahweh brought the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. Yahweh says something very important at the end of this scene. Yahweh says, "I am Yahweh, your God."

In the fourth scene: Moses tells the Israelite people about Yahweh's festivals.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the Israelite people, including those who give the offerings

Although you might not wish to represent this group with a person, Yahweh also mentions another group of people in this passage: the future descendants of the Israelite people from every generation.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how do you talk about future generations? Pause this audio here.

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The Israelite people are still camping in the wilderness near Mount Sinai. The Israelites have recently finished building the Tent of Meeting as Yahweh instructed. Now, Yahweh is giving Moses instructions that Moses then writes down and tells to the Israelite people.

In the first scene, Yahweh tells Moses to instruct the Israelite people how to observe or celebrate the Festival of Tabernacles. Remember that here, a tabernacle or a shelter is a temporary house in which people can live. A person could make a shelter out of many different kinds of materials. Translators have used many names for these temporary shelters: tabernacles, shelters, booths, huts. It is even possible that some people would live in tents during the festival, which is what the Israelites are living in as Yahweh gives these instructions. Remember that in step two, you already heard explanations about different kinds of temporary shelters that the Israelite people could make and live in. You can listen again to step two if needed.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of temporary shelters. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss if there is a word or phrase in your language that you could use for any kind of temporary shelters, and decide what you will call these temporary shelters. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells the Israelites to celebrate this festival for eight days. The first and the last day of the festival are Sabbaths, or special days of worship and rest. The two Sabbaths are one week apart. Remember that the Israelite people began their days at sunset, the time when the sun goes down.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how do you count days? What words do you use to talk about lengths of time? Pause this audio here.

On the first and last day of the festival, the Israelite people must have holy assemblies. When Yahweh tells the people to gather for an assembly, Yahweh is telling the people to all meet together for a special purpose. Yahweh wants the Israelite people to gather as an entire nation to celebrate and worship Yahweh all together as a group. These two special Sabbaths are the same as normal Sabbaths; people are not supposed to work. The people are not supposed to do hard work or physical labor. For every day of the festival, the people are also supposed to give fire offerings to Yahweh. Remember that fire offerings can really refer to any of the offerings where a priest burns all or a part of the offering on the altar.

In the second scene, Yahweh reminds the people again that these are Yahweh's appointed festivals. Something that Yahweh has appointed is something that Yahweh has chosen. It can also mean something that someone does at a special time or in a special way. In this case, it also might refer to the way that these special festivals happen on specific days of the year, which makes a sort of religious calendar for the Israelite people to follow.

Yahweh talks about four kinds of offerings in this passage: burnt offerings, grain offerings, sacrifices, and drink offerings. When Yahweh says "sacrifices" in this passage, Yahweh probably means fellowship or peace offerings.

Yahweh also mentions Yahweh's Sabbaths, which are the regular Sabbaths. The two Sabbaths that Yahweh mentions for the Festival of Tabernacles are special Sabbaths. This means that the people will celebrate the special Sabbaths as well as the other Sabbaths. Lastly, Yahweh mentions freewill offerings, which are offerings that Yahweh does not require the people to give. The Israelite people bring freewill offerings to Yahweh just because the people want to give these offerings.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, discuss something that you do or something that you give, just because you want to give it. Pause this audio here.

In the third scene, Yahweh gives more specific instructions about how the people should celebrate the Festival of Tabernacles or Shelters. Yahweh says that this festival should happen after the people have finished the harvest.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, talk about harvest time in your community. Pay attention to the words and phrases you use for things like crops, which are plants that people have harvested, and harvesting, which is the process where people gather and store these plants. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also tells Moses that the people should gather tree branches. The Israelite people should gather date palm branches, willow branches, and branches from other leafy trees.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of these different kinds of trees. Discuss what you would call these kinds of tree branches and these kinds of trees. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh instructs every Israelite person to build temporary shelters, probably for their families, and live in those shelters for the seven days of the festival. Yahweh instructs the people to celebrate together as a community.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: If someone is giving instructions that everyone in the community must follow, what language will that person use? Discuss how you want to translate the way Yahweh gives instructions here. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also says that all generations of the Israelite people should celebrate this festival. This celebration is a reminder that the Israelite people lived in shelters when Yahweh brought the people out of slavery in Egypt. Yahweh finishes his instructions with an important statement: "I am Yahweh, your God."

In the fourth scene, Moses tells the Israelite people about Yahweh's festivals.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 23:33–44 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the Israelite people, including those who give the offerings

Although you might not wish to represent this group with a person, Yahweh also mentions another group of people in this passage: the future descendants of the Israelite people from every generation.

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh tells Moses to instruct the Israelite people how to celebrate the Festival of Tabernacles. The Israelite people must celebrate this festival for eight days. On the first and last day of the festival, the Israelite people must have holy worship celebrations. No one can work on those days. On every day of the festival, people are also supposed to give offerings to Yahweh.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • Yahweh deserves our attention in every season; or
  • It is good for the people to come together to worship Yahweh. It will remind the people that we all serve Yahweh together as a community; or
  • I think the people will like a break from work, but will the people complain about living in temporary shelters?
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh says that these are Yahweh's festivals. Yahweh reminds the people about the different kinds of offerings that the people are supposed to give Yahweh. Yahweh also mentions Sabbaths and freewill offerings in this scene.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am excited that the people will have so many chances to come together and be with me; or
  • I hope the people remember these instructions; or
  • It is hard for people to leave their work and rest, but I hope the people learn how to trust me by obeying my instructions.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh gives more specific instructions about how the people should celebrate the Festival of Tabernacles. Yahweh repeats most of the information from scene one. But Yahweh also tells Moses that the people should gather tree branches and build temporary shelters for this festival. Every Israelite person is supposed to live in these temporary shelters for the seven days of the festival. Yahweh says that all generations of the Israelite people should celebrate this festival. This celebration is a reminder that the Israelite people lived in shelters when Yahweh brought the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. Yahweh finishes with an important statement: "I am Yahweh, your God."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • Right now, we sleep in temporary shelters. Someday we will not sleep here, but in comfortable houses. Will we want to come sleep in temporary shelters again at that time? or
  • This will remind us what Yahweh has saved us from; or
  • Why do we have a special celebration that includes something uncomfortable?
Continue the drama.

In the fourth scene, Moses tells the Israelite people about Yahweh's festivals.

For a possible additional exercise, you could have someone play the part of the future generations. You can also ask the future generations what they are feeling when they hear this story.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing a descendant of the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I cannot believe our ancestors lived like this all of the time; or
  • I am excited. This celebration will be a good time to be together as a family and thank Yahweh for how Yahweh has taken care of us; or
  • If we forget our past, we will not know why it is important to obey Yahweh.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 23:33–44 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about how the people of Israel should celebrate the Festival of Tabernacles. For this festival, the people had to live in temporary shelters. Use the same words for Yahweh and the Israelites as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and Israelites, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and discuss as a group what phrases you will use for Festival of Tabernacles and shelters. For more information on the Festival of Tabernacles and shelters, refer to the Master Glossary. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh mentions many kinds of offerings in this passage, as a reminder of all the different offerings which Yahweh requires from the people. Use the same phrases for burnt offering, grain offering, drink offering, fire offering, sacrifice, and freewill offering as you used in previous passages. The Israelites are to bring these offerings in addition to any offerings they bring to fulfill a vow to Yahweh. For more information on any of these offerings, and on vow, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says that these festivals are holy assemblies and appointed festivals. An assembly is a group of people that someone calls to meet together for a special reason. This assembly is holy because Yahweh set it apart and dedicated this gathering to Yahweh. Yahweh has "appointed," or chosen these festivals for a special purpose. Use the same words for holy assemblies and appointed festivals as you used in previous passages. For more information on holy, refer to the Master Glossary.

The people are supposed to celebrate these festivals as well as Yahweh's Sabbath. Use the same word for Sabbath as you used in previous passages. For more information on Sabbath, refer to the Master Glossary.

For the Festival of Tabernacles, the Israelite people took branches from leafy trees, including palm trees and willow trees, to build temporary dwellings or shelters for the people to live inside.

Stop here and look at pictures of the types of trees that the Israelite peoples would use to build these shelters. Discuss what you will call these trees and their branches in your language. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh calls these instructions a lasting statute, which means this is a rule that the people should follow every year, no matter what, for every generation. Use the same words for statute and generation as you used in previous passages. For more information on statute and generation, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 24:1–9
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 24:1–9 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 24:1–9 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 24:1–9 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

At this time, the Israelite people are still camping near Mount Sinai. The Israelites had recently completed building the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh has been giving Moses many instructions on how the Israelite people should live in a holy way. In this passage, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about how the priests should do certain rituals in the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh tells Moses to give these instructions to the Israelite people in a way that shows the Israelites that these rules are very important for the Israelites to follow.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what are some of the religious rituals that people do? What are the rules for these rituals? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh commands the Israelite people to bring a certain kind of good olive oil. To make this good olive oil, people would first collect the olives by "beating" or hitting the olive trees with a stick or shaking the branches to make the olives fall off the tree. Then the people would crush the olives, either using their feet or by using a large stone and wood mill called an olive press.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of an olive press. Pause this audio here.

Then the people put the crushed olives into an olive press that would squeeze the oil out of the olives. People called oil "beaten" oil. The first oil that came out in this process would be the most clear and of the highest quality. This is the oil that Yahweh requires the Israelite people to give to the Israelite priests for priests to use in the Tent of Meeting.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of olive oil. Pause this audio here.

This oil would go in the lamps. Ancient people made regular oil lamps out of clay. These lamps looked like little bowls that could hold oil and often had a special place to put the wick. The wick is the part of the lamp that people light on fire. People would make wicks from plants. The people would fill a lamp with olive oil, light the wick on fire, and the wick would use the oil to keep the fire burning. But the lamps that the priests used in the Tent of Meeting were very special. The Israelite people had made a lampstand from pure gold as Yahweh had instructed. The people made seven lamps and a beautiful gold stand to hold all of the lamps. This gold lampstand with its seven lamps has been an important symbol of God's light and presence with the Israelites throughout history.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of regular oil lamps and the gold lampstand with its lamps. Pause this audio here.

The priests must make sure that these lamps stay lit with fire all throughout the night until morning, without the fires going out. Yahweh says that special lamps should be in the Tent of Meeting, in the Holy Place near the "curtain of the testimony." The curtain of the testimony is the beautiful curtain that hung between the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the covenant was, and the Holy Place, where the priests would perform certain important rituals. The word "testimony" is a reminder that the main reason why this curtain is there is to make a divide between Yahweh's presence on the ark of the covenant and the place where the priests serve Yahweh and worship. The priests stand just in front of the curtain of the testimony when the priests present certain offerings before Yahweh.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of the curtain of the testimony that separates the Most Holy Place from the Holy Place. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Why do you think it was important to keep the lamps burning? What are some religious rituals that your people make sure to always do? Why do people do this? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also wants the priests to set out special offerings of bread on a gold table in the Tent of Meeting. Some translations call this bread "showbread" or "bread of the presence." People called it this because the bread was to always be in the presence of Yahweh, in the Holy Place. There were 12 loaves of bread to represent the 12 tribes of Israel. It was a special bread that was only for Yahweh and the priests. We do not know who made this bread. Yahweh says to make the bread from the finest or best-quality flour. The person should make 12 loaves of this bread of the presence as cakes, which here means in round, flat shapes.

The person must use two-tenths of an ephah of flour, which is probably about 3 kilograms of flour. That is a lot of flour for each loaf! We are not sure how big these loaves would be. Some people think that these loaves must be very big. Other people think that maybe the loaves were small but very heavy. Maybe the people made the loaves in a special way, or maybe the measurements mean something different here. We do not know exactly what the answer is. But we do know that the priests put the bread in two piles, six cakes in each pile, on the gold table in the Holy Place.

People sometimes call this special gold table in the Tent of Meeting the table of the bread of the presence. Israelite craftsmen made the table from acacia wood and covered the table all over with gold. Like the ark of the covenant, the table had rings and poles so that people could carry the table from place to place as the Israelite people moved around the wilderness.

Stop here as a group and look at a map of the Tent of Meeting. Find the location of the table of the bread of the presence. Also, look at a picture of the gold table of the bread of the presence and the bread on the table. Pause this audio here.

The priests also must put frankincense on top of the two piles of special bread. Frankincense is a mixture of sap and gum that people can collect from a certain kind of tree. The tree sap hardens into little pieces of resin, but it looks like little white rocks. Frankincense smells very good, and the Israelites would often burn the frankincense to make a good smell. The priests probably take the frankincense and put it in two gold bowls. The priest put these gold bowls on top of or beside the two piles of bread. Every Sabbath, the priests have to take this frankincense and burn it on the altar of incense. The frankincense is Yahweh's portion of the bread of the presence. This is one of the offerings that the Israelites called the food offering or fire offering.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of frankincense and the altar of incense. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what smells do people really like? If possible, try to think of something that people burn to make a nice smell. Pause this audio here.

The priests should do this every Sabbath without stopping. It is an "everlasting covenant," or an agreement that does not stop. Aaron and Aaron's male descendants can eat this special bread, but these men must eat the bread in the sanctuary, or holy place, because it is holy bread.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 24:1–9 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh gives Moses instructions about how to do important jobs that Yahweh requires Israelite priests to do in the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh tells Moses to tell these important instructions to the Israelite people.

In the second scene: Yahweh wants the Israelite people to bring olive oil to the Israelite priests. The priests will use this oil to keep the fire lit in the lamps in the special gold lampstand. Yahweh's rule is that the fire of these lamps should burn every night, always.

In the third scene: Yahweh also wants the priests to set out special bread on a gold table in the Tent of Meeting. The priests should put the bread in two piles, six loaves in each pile. The priests also put frankincense on top of the bread. The priests should offer this frankincense as an offering every Sabbath. The priests must do this ritual without stopping. Aaron and Aaron's male descendants can eat this bread, but these men must eat the bread in a holy place because it is holy bread.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Israelite people
  • Aaron
  • And Aaron's male descendants

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

The Israelite people are still camping in the wilderness near Mount Sinai. The Israelites had recently finished building the Tent of Meeting as Yahweh had instructed. Yahweh is giving Moses instructions about how the Israelite people are to live and worship Yahweh, including special instructions for how the priests should perform holy rituals.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about how to do important jobs that Yahweh requires the Israelite priests to do in the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh tells Moses to tell these important instructions to the Israelite people.

Stop here and discuss how you pass information from person to person in your language. Talk about how you want to translate something that Yahweh told to Moses, and that Yahweh wanted Moses to tell to the people. Pause this audio here.

Here, Yahweh says to Moses that Moses needs to command the Israelite people to do this. When someone commands something, they tell someone something in an important way. This means that Yahweh is about to tell Moses some very important rules, and that the Israelites need to pay attention and follow these rules carefully.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how do you tell someone that it is really important for that person to do something or to follow a certain rule or instruction? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, Yahweh commands the Israelite people to bring olive oil to the Israelite priests. This oil is supposed to be the olive oil with the best quality. Good-quality olive oil can be a deep yellow color or a deep green color, and it has a smooth texture. A person could describe this good quality by saying that the oil is pure or clear. This olive oil is clear in the sense that it does not have any impurities in it. This olive oil is so clear that you can see through it like clean water.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how do you talk about something that is the best quality? Pick something, if possible oil, and talk about what you think makes it good or not good. Notice the words you use. Pause this audio here.

The priests must make sure that these lamps stay lit with fire all throughout the night until morning, without the fires going out. The priests must do this every single night, always, no matter what. However, the lamps are only lit from evening until morning, so this does not mean without stopping. Try to find a word that explains this idea of keeping the fires going all night without going out, and of doing this repeatedly. But try to stay away from words that might make people think that the priests must keep the lamps lit during the day.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, talk about how you might keep a fire going. Notice the words you use. Also, talk about how you discuss something that must happen constantly for a time, and must happen every day, over and over. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that special lamps should be in the Tent of Meeting, in the Holy Place. These lamps should be in front of the "curtain of the testimony." This curtain is the beautiful curtain that hung between the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the covenant was, and the Holy Place, where the priests performed certain important rituals. The word "testimony" is a reminder that the main reason why this curtain was there was to make a divide between Yahweh's presence on the ark of the covenant and the place where the priests served Yahweh and worshipped.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of the curtain of the sanctuary. Pause this audio here.

Ancient people would make regular oil lamps out of clay and wicks out of plants. The people would fill the lamps with olive oil, light the wick, and the wick would use the oil to keep the fire burning. But the lamps that the priests use in the Tent of Meeting are very special. The Israelite people made the lamps from pure gold. The Israelites made seven lamps and a beautiful gold stand to hold all of the lamps.

Stop here as a group and look again at pictures of regular oil lamps and the special gold lamps and lampstand in the Tent of Meeting as needed. In your language, describe how the lamps work. You may wish to discuss what special words to use for lamps and lampstand. Pause this audio here.

In the third scene, Yahweh says the priests must set out special offerings of bread on a gold table in the Tent of Meeting. Sometimes translators call this bread "showbread" or "bread of the presence." It means it is the bread that the priests display near Yahweh's presence. People called it this because the bread was to always be in the presence of Yahweh, in the Holy Place. Sometimes it helps to have a special word or phrase for this bread, since it was a special bread that was only for Yahweh and the priests.

Stop here and discuss: What will you call this bread in your language? In your translation of this phrase, how can you show that this bread is holy and that this bread was close to Yahweh? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh instructs that the person who makes the bread should make the bread out of the finest flour, which is the best quality flour. The person must use two-tenths of an ephah of flour, which is probably about 3 kilograms. Yahweh says the person must make these loaves as cakes, which here means in round, flat shapes.

Stop here and discuss: What word can you use in your language to describe this bread as round and flat? Pause this audio here.

The person should make 12 of these loaves. The priests would put the loaves on the special gold table that people sometimes called the table of the bread of the presence. The table was a special gold table. The table was 88 centimeters long, 45 centimeters wide, and 67 centimeters tall. The priests must put the bread on the table in two piles, six loaves in each pile.

Stop here as a group and look at a map of the Tent of Meeting. Find the location of the table of the bread of the presence. Also, look at a picture of the gold table of the bread of the presence and the bread on top. Pause this audio here.

The priests must also put frankincense on top of the two piles of special bread. Frankincense is a mixture of sap and gum that people could collect from a certain kind of tree. The tree sap hardens into little pieces of resin, but it looks like little white rocks. Frankincense smells very good, and the Israelites often burned the frankincense to make a good smell. The priests should take frankincense and put it in two gold bowls. The priests put these gold bowls on top of the two piles of bread. Every Sabbath, the priests must take this frankincense and burn it on the altar of incense. The frankincense is Yahweh's portion of the bread of the presence. This is one of the offerings that the Israelites called the food offering or fire offering.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of frankincense and the altar of incense. Also, look at a map of the Tent of Meeting as a group. Find the location of the altar of incense. Pause this audio here.

The priests must do this every Sabbath without stopping. It is an "everlasting covenant," or an agreement that does not stop. Aaron and his sons, or male descendants, can eat this bread, but these men must eat the bread in a holy place because it is holy bread. This holy place is probably anywhere in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 24:1–9 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Israelite people
  • Aaron
  • And Aaron's male descendants

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives Moses instructions about how to do important jobs that Yahweh requires the Israelite priests to do in the Tent of Meeting. Yahweh tells Moses to tell these important instructions to the Israelite people.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • It is good that Yahweh gives us specific instructions for all the rituals in the Tent of Meeting; or
  • I must remember all of these things so that I can explain the instructions well to the Israelite people; or
  • I wonder if the people will be happy about these instructions or if the people will be angry again.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh says that the Israelite people must bring olive oil to the Israelite priests. The priests will use this oil to keep the fire lit in the lamps in the special gold lampstand. Yahweh's rule is that the fire from these lamps should burn every night, always.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am happy to give a special offering to Yahweh; or
  • Yahweh gets the best of our olive oil, just like Yahweh gets the best of our flocks and the best of our flour. Yahweh must be very important! or
  • Why are the priests the only ones who can go into the Tent of Meeting? Yahweh's lamp is lit all night long, but we cannot see the lamp.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh says that the priests must set out special bread on a gold table in the Tent of Meeting. The priests should put the bread in two piles, with six loaves in each pile. The priests also must put frankincense on top of the bread. The priests should offer this frankincense as a part of the offering every Sabbath. The priests must do this ritual without stopping. Aaron and Aaron's male descendants can eat this bread, but these men must eat the bread in a holy place because it is holy bread.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Aaron and his male descendants, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • It is a great honor that we can eat Yahweh's special bread offering; or
  • There are 12 special bread loaves, just like there are 12 tribes of Israel; or
  • I always look forward to this offering on the Sabbath because the frankincense fills the whole Tent of Meeting with such a nice smell.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 24:1–9 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Yahweh gives Moses instructions for the people of Israel. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh and the people of Israel as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and Israelite, refer to the Master Glossary.

In the Tent of Meeting, the Israelite priests must always have the special oil lamps burning with fire. These oil lamps were on a special gold lampstand that holds seven lamps. For more information on oil lamps, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of olive oil, everyday oil lamps, and the Tent of Meeting lampstand. If you have not done so for another book, discuss what words or phrases you will use for "oil lamp" and "special gold lampstand." Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Yahweh talks about the curtain of the testimony. This is the curtain that divides the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place inside the Tent of Meeting. The priests who served in the Tent of Meeting could not see the ark of the testimony because of this curtain.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of the curtain of the testimony. If you call this the curtain of the testimony, refer to the Master Glossary for more information about testimony. Pause this audio here.

In the Tent of Meeting, there was a gold table where the priests would put the special offering of bread. In other books of the Bible, people call this the table of the bread of the presence. Use the same word for "Tent of Meeting" as you used in previous passages. For more information on the Tent of Meeting, refer to tabernacle in the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a map of the Tent of Meeting. Find the location of the gold table of the bread of the presence. Also, look at a picture of the gold table and the bread of the presence. If you choose to call this bread the "bread of the presence," refer to the Master Glossary for more information. Pause this audio here.

People should make each loaf of bread with two-tenths of an ephah of the finest flour. This was probably about 3 kilograms of flour. If you use an ephah in your translation, use the same word or phrase for ephah as you have used previously, and remember that ephah is in the Master Glossary.

Yahweh calls these instructions a lasting statute, which means this is a rule that the people should follow every year, no matter what, for every generation. Use the same words for statute and generation as you used in previous passages. For more information on statute and generation, refer to the Master Glossary.

The priests put gold bowls of frankincense on top of the bread of the presence as a memorial portion and a fire offering. You will remember that some people think that the memorial portion was a physical way for people to remember the covenant between Yahweh and Yahweh's people. Other people think it was supposed to call Yahweh's attention to the reason the person was offering the gift. Use the same words or phrases for "memorial portion" and "fire offering" as you have used previously. For more information, refer to "memorial portion" and "fire offering" in the Master Glossary.

Every week, the priests would take the frankincense and burn the frankincense on the altar of incense. Use the same words for frankincense and altar as you used in previous passages. For more information about altar, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of frankincense and the altar of incense. Pause this audio here.

The priest must put the bread on the table every Sabbath as a lasting covenant. Use the same words for Sabbath and covenant as you used in previous passages. For more information on Sabbath and covenant, refer to the Master Glossary.

Aaron and Aaron's descendants can eat their holy portion of the bread in the sanctuary or holy place. This is not just the Holy Place in the Tent of Meeting, but includes the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting as well. Use the same word or phrase for holy and sanctuary as you used in previous passages. For more information on holy and sanctuary, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 24:10–23
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 24:10–23 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 24:10–23 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 24:10–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this passage, the storyteller of Leviticus tells a story that introduces the laws Yahweh gave about how to punish someone who hurt or killed a person or animal. In this story, a man whose mother was an Israelite and whose father was an Egyptian came into the camp where the Israelites were. This man was not a full Israelite because his father was an Egyptian.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do you determine who is part of your culture and who is not? Do you have different rules for people in your culture and for people who are not? Pause this audio here.

This man, whose mother was an Israelite, got into a fight with an Israelite. In this fight, the two people probably used their hands and their feet to hit each other.

While the two people were fighting, the man whose mother was an Israelite used Yahweh's name in a curse. When a person cursed in cultures around Israel, that person asked a god or a spirit to do something harmful to someone else. This man might have asked Yahweh to do something harmful to the person the man was fighting. Or the man might have asked another god to do something harmful to Yahweh. Either way, when the man made this curse, the man deeply insulted and dishonored Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people curse other people? Who or what do people expect to harm the person they curse? What would happen if someone spoke disrespectfully about gods or spirits? Pause this audio here.

When the man misused Yahweh's name in the curse, the people who heard the man brought the man to Moses. The mother of the man who cursed had the name "Shelomith." Shelomith's father's name was Dibri. Shelomith belonged to the tribe of Dan, which means Shelomith was one of Dan's descendants. The people put this man who cursed in a place where the man could not escape, and then the people waited for Yahweh to tell the people what to do.

Yahweh told Moses that Yahweh wanted the Israelites to take the man who blasphemed Yahweh's name outside the camp. Then everyone who heard the man blaspheme Yahweh's name needed to lay their hands on the man's head. The people probably needed to lay their hands on the man's head to show that these people were not murdering the man when these people killed the man. The people also might have laid their hands on the man's head because this man made the people impure when the people heard the man blaspheme Yahweh's name. The people wanted to show that the people were transferring their impurity onto the man before the people killed the man. After the people who heard the man blaspheme Yahweh's name put their hands on his head, all the Israelites needed to throw stones at the man until the man died.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what do people do when someone misuses the name of a powerful person, or a spirit or god? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh told Moses to talk to the Israelites. Yahweh wanted the Israelites to know that anyone who curses Yahweh has sinned. The Israelites needed to execute anyone who misused Yahweh's name. All the Israelites together needed to throw stones at a person who misused Yahweh's name until that person died. If someone misused Yahweh's name, the Israelites needed to kill that person, whether the person was an Israelite or a foreigner. Sometimes, people had different rules for someone who was a citizen and someone who was a foreigner, so Yahweh wanted the Israelites to know that Yahweh expected the people to obey this law no matter who misused Yahweh's name.

Then Yahweh talked about other reasons that the Israelites might execute someone. If someone killed an animal, that person needed to give the owner another animal as a replacement. Yahweh was talking about when a person killed an animal that belonged to someone else; Yahweh was not talking about when people kill a wild animal. Yahweh expected the Israelites to give a life when the Israelites took a life. The Israelites could give a life by replacing an animal if someone killed an animal. But the Israelites had to give a life by killing a person if that person killed another person.

Yahweh said the Israelites must punish a person by injuring that person in the same way that the person injured other people. The Israelites needed to punish someone who fractured a victim's bone by fracturing the person's bones. The Israelites needed to remove someone's eye if that person removed someone else's eye, and the Israelites needed to remove someone's tooth if that person removed someone else's tooth. Yahweh said again that a person who kills an animal needs to replace the animal, and Yahweh said again that the Israelites needed to execute someone who kills a person.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people punish someone who injures someone else? How do people punish someone who killed an animal? How do people punish someone who killed a person? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh said that Yahweh expected both Israelites and foreigners to obey the laws that Yahweh is telling the people. The people needed to obey because Yahweh is their God.

After Yahweh told Moses all this, Moses told the Israelites what Yahweh said. Then the Israelites took the man who blasphemed Yahweh's name out of the camp and threw stones at that man until he died. The Israelites did exactly what Yahweh commanded Moses to tell the Israelites to do.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 24:10–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

In the first scene: A half-Israelite man blasphemes Yahweh's name.

In the second scene: Yahweh tells the Israelites to kill the man.

In the third scene: Yahweh tells Moses to tell the Israelites what to do when someone blasphemes Yahweh's name, kills a person or an animal, or injures a person.

In the fourth scene: The Israelites kill the man who blasphemed Yahweh's name.

The characters in this passage are:

  • A man whose mother was an Israelite and whose father was an Egyptian
  • An Israelite man, who fights with the first man
  • The Israelites
  • Moses
  • Yahweh
  • And foreigners

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Remember that in previous passages, Yahweh told Moses about holidays and festivals, as well as how to make the oil and bread for the tabernacle. Also, remember that in previous passages, Yahweh was telling Moses the rules that Yahweh expects the Israelites to obey, but the storyteller has not told many stories about what people do.

In this passage, the storyteller of Leviticus tells a story. The storyteller of Leviticus may tell this story to show why Yahweh gave the laws about how to punish someone who hurt or killed an animal or human. This story shows one reason to execute someone, and reminds the Israelites that Yahweh is the one who gives the laws.

In the first scene, a man whose mother was an Israelite and whose father was an Egyptian enters the Israelites' camp and fights an Israelite. This might mean that the man comes out of the tent the man is living in and goes near other people in the camp. Or it might mean that the man lives outside the camp where the Israelites live, but then the man enters the camp.

Stop here and discuss as a group: How will you say that the man went among the Israelites in the camp? Pause this audio here.

The storyteller says that the man whose mother was an Israelite blasphemes, or speaks evil, about "the Name." While the storyteller does not say whose name this is, the Israelites would know that this is Yahweh's name. Sometimes, in order to show deep respect to Yahweh, the Israelites just say "the Name," instead of "Yahweh." To show that the Israelites really do not want to blaspheme Yahweh, the Israelites would not even say Yahweh's name as the Israelites talked about the way that people curse.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people show that they deeply respect someone? What would be disrespectful ways or times to mention someone's name? What would be the best way to translate when the storyteller of Leviticus says that the half-Israelite blasphemed the name? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, when the man blasphemes Yahweh's name, the people who hear the man take the man to Moses. The storyteller now explains that the man's mother's name was Shelomith. Shelomith is the daughter of a man whose name is Dibri. Shelomith is one of Dan's descendants. You will remember that Dan is one of the sons of Jacob, and the ancestor of one of the 12 tribes of Israel. The storyteller probably tells us who the man's ancestors are when the Israelites bring the man to Moses, because Moses probably asks the man for that information when Moses asks the man about what happened. The people who heard the man blaspheme Yahweh want Moses to ask Yahweh what Yahweh wants the people to do with this man. The Israelites probably do not know what to do with the man. The man's father is an Egyptian, so this man is not fully a part of the Israelite people group. The Israelites probably are not sure if their rules are the same for this man. Then the storyteller tells us that the Israelites put the man somewhere that the man cannot escape.

The people probably tell Moses what happened, and then Moses speaks to Yahweh. The storyteller does not tell us that part of the story, but just begins to tell us what Yahweh says. The people who first heard this story would probably assume that the people talked to Moses and that Moses then talked to Yahweh. Yahweh tells Moses that Yahweh wants the Israelites to take the man who blasphemed Yahweh's name outside the camp. The people who heard the man blaspheme Yahweh's name need to put their hand on the man's head, and then all the Israelites need to stone the man. When Yahweh says all the Israelites need to stone the man, Yahweh probably does not mean that each individual Israelite needs to throw stones at the man. The Israelites must gather together as a group, or an assembly, to throw stones until the man is dead, even if not everyone throws a stone.

In the second scene, after Yahweh tells Moses what to do in this situation, Yahweh then tells Moses what to do in other times when people curse Yahweh. Yahweh tells the Israelites that anyone who blasphemes Yahweh will lift up, or carry, their sin. When Yahweh says the person will carry their sin, Yahweh is using special language to mean that the person will be guilty and that someone must punish the person. Yahweh is talking as if that person's sin is a physical object that the person holds in their hand, and because the person is holding the sin, someone needs to punish that person.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What is the best way to translate when Yahweh says that an Israelite who curses Yahweh will carry their sin? Pause this audio here.

The Israelites need to execute anyone who blasphemes Yahweh's name. All the Israelites need to throw stones at a person who blasphemes Yahweh's name until the person dies. The Israelites need to execute both Israelites and foreigners who blaspheme Yahweh's name.

Then Yahweh tells the Israelites to execute anyone who kills a human. Yahweh also says that anyone who kills an animal needs to pay money to the person who owned the animal. Yahweh says, "life for life." When Yahweh says life for life, Yahweh is using special language to mean that a person must experience the same harmful thing that the person did to someone else. If the person caused someone to lose an animal, the person also needs to lose an animal. If the person caused someone else to die, that person must also die.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people make sure a punishment is fair? If someone does something bad, the same thing must happen to that person? How would you talk about that in your language? What is the best way to say "life for life"? Remember that Yahweh will use similar special language in the next part of the passage. Pause this audio here.

The Israelites need to punish anyone who injures someone else by injuring that person in the same way. Yahweh says, "fracture for fracture." This is special language Yahweh uses to mean that if a certain person fractures someone's bone, the Israelites need to fracture the same bone in the attacker's body. Yahweh also says "eye for eye" and "tooth for tooth." Both of these are special language that Yahweh uses to mean that if someone attacks a person and removes that person's eye or tooth, the Israelites need to remove that attacker's eye or tooth. The attacker needs to suffer from the same injury that the attacker caused to someone else. Yahweh probably means that the Israelites need to punish the attacker by giving the attacker the exact same injury the attacker gave someone else. Yahweh might mean that the Israelites need to punish an attacker in a way that is as bad as what the attacker did to another person.

Yahweh says that the person who kills an animal needs to replace the animal with a similar animal. The Israelites need to execute a person who kills a human. Yahweh probably mentions these ordinances about when a person kills an animal or a human again because Yahweh wants the Israelites to know how much Yahweh wants the Israelites to obey these rules.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time someone repeated a rule to let people know how important it was. How did that person repeat the rule? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells the Israelites that the Israelites need to follow these ordinances for both foreigners and Israelites. The Israelites need to follow these ordinances because Yahweh is their God. Yahweh wants the Israelites to clearly understand that Yahweh takes care of the Israelites and is leading the Israelites so that the Israelites will do what Yahweh tells the Israelites to do.

In the third scene, Moses tells the Israelites what Yahweh told Moses to say. The Israelites take the person who blasphemed Yahweh's name outside the camp, and the Israelites throw stones at the man until the man dies. The storyteller of Leviticus says that the Israelites do what Yahweh commanded Moses. The storyteller says that Yahweh commanded Moses because Yahweh gave the rules to Moses, but Yahweh wanted all the Israelites to do what Yahweh commanded. When the storyteller says that the Israelites did what Yahweh told Moses to tell them to do, the storyteller confirms that people who read or heard this story later should act as the Israelites acted in this story, because the Israelites acted in a right way.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a person or group of people that you want other people to act like. How do you let other people know that people should act like the person or people in the story? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 24:10–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • A man whose mother was an Israelite and whose father was an Egyptian
  • An Israelite man, who fights with the first man
  • The Israelites
  • Moses
  • Yahweh
  • And foreigners

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, a man whose mother was an Israelite and whose father was an Egyptian went into the Israelite camp where Israelites were. The man and another Israelite started fighting each other. The man whose mother was an Israelite blasphemed Yahweh's name by using Yahweh's name in a curse.

In the second scene, the people who heard the man took the man to Moses.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing a man whose mother was an Israelite and whose father was an Egyptian, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I was so angry when I fought with that other Israelite! or
  • I should have respected Yahweh even though I am not a full Israelite; or
  • I am so afraid that Yahweh will make the Israelites kill me.
Continue the drama.

This man's mother was named Shelomith, and her father was named Dibri. Dibri was one of Dan's descendants. The Israelites put the man in a place where the man could not escape until Yahweh clearly told the Israelites what Yahweh wanted the Israelites to do with the man.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • This man is only half-Israelite; what are we supposed to do with this man? Does this man follow our same laws? or
  • I am mad at this man because this man disrespected Yahweh; or
  • I am surprised that this man would say something like that! We have seen how powerful Yahweh is. I know Yahweh heard this man and will be angry with this man!
Continue the drama.

Yahweh told Moses to take the man outside the Israelite camp. Everyone who heard the man blaspheme Yahweh's name needed to put their hands on the man's head. Then all the Israelites needed to throw stones at the man until the man died.

In the second scene, Yahweh told Moses to tell the Israelites to execute anyone who blasphemes Yahweh's name. All the Israelites need to throw stones at the person who blasphemes Yahweh's name together. The Israelites need to execute any person who blasphemes Yahweh's name, whether that person is a foreigner or an Israelite.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am angry that this man would insult me; or
  • I am glad that my people want to know what the right thing to do is; or
  • My name and my reputation are very important; or
  • Even people who are not Israelites need to respect me; or
  • I want people to realize how holy I am.
Continue the drama.

Then Yahweh said that the Israelites need to execute anyone who kills a human. Yahweh also said that anyone who kills an animal needs to replace the animal with a similar animal, and give a life for a life.

Then Yahweh says that if anyone injures another person, the Israelites need to give that person the same injury that person gave. The Israelites need to fracture the same bone that a person fractures, remove the same eye that a person removes, and remove the same tooth that a person removes. In the same way any person injures someone else, the Israelites need to injure that person.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am glad that Yahweh requires the Israelites to properly punish anyone who hurts me; or
  • I wish that I could punish someone who hurt me more; or
  • I am glad that if I hurt someone, other people will not hurt me worse than I hurt someone.
Continue the drama.

Then Yahweh said that a person who kills an animal needs to repay the person who owned the animal, and that the Israelites need to kill a person who kills a human. The Israelites need to apply these ordinances equally to the Israelites and the foreigners who live with the Israelites because Yahweh is their God.

In the third scene, Moses told the Israelites what Yahweh told Moses to say. So the Israelites took the man who blasphemed Yahweh's name outside the Israelite camp and threw stones at the man until the man died. The Israelites did exactly what Yahweh commanded Moses to tell the Israelites to do.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 24:10–23 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, a man whose mother was an Israelite and whose father was an Egyptian gave a curse. When someone curses, that person asks a god or spirit to harm another person or even a god. Use the same words or phrases for Israelites and for curse as you used in previous passages. For more information on Israelites and curse, refer to the Master Glossary.

The man who was a half-Israelite blasphemed God. To blaspheme someone means to speak evil about a person, and to insult someone. A person who curses God, insults God, dishonors God, or makes God seem less powerful or important is blaspheming God. The punishment for blasphemy was death.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for "blaspheme." Use the same word or phrase for blasphemy as you used in previous books of the Bible. For more information on blasphemy, refer to the Master Glossary. Pause this audio here.

The Israelites wanted to know what Yahweh wanted the Israelites to do. Yahweh is the personal name that the one true God gave to the Israelites to call God. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh will not allow anyone to curse God. In the Bible, God refers to God who created everything. God is Yahweh, and he is the most powerful spiritual being. Use the same word or phrase for God as you used in previous passages. For more information on God, refer to the Master Glossary.

If someone curses Yahweh, that person will carry their sin, or be guilty for what they have done wrong. Any time that a person breaks one of God's laws, that person sins. Use the same word or phrase for sin as you used in previous passages. For more information on sin, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says that the entire assembly, or large group of Israelites, should throw stones at the person until he dies. Use the same word or phrase for assembly as you have used previously.

Yahweh said that even foreigners who cursed Yahweh needed to die. When someone is a foreigner, that person is living in a country that the person is not from. Use the same word or phrase for foreigner as you used in previous passages. For more information on foreigner, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh requires the Israelites to punish someone who hurts their neighbor. "Neighbor" can mean people in your community or with whom you come into contact. In the Old Testament, neighbors often referred to people groups who lived in the same land area or region. Use the same word or phrase for neighbor as you used in previous passages. For more information on neighbor, refer to the Master Glossary.

The people need to apply Yahweh's decision, or ordinances, to both Israelites and foreigners. An ordinance is a decision that a leader makes about what people should do in a specific situation. Use the same word or phrase for ordinance as you used in previous passages. For more information on ordinance, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
