title: Leviticus 25:1–7
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 25:1–7 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:1–7 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:1–7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh is giving Moses instructions to prepare the Israelite people for when the Israelites move into Canaan, the land that Yahweh has promised to the Israelites. Moses and the Israelite people are still camped near Mount Sinai at this time. Moses goes up on this mountain to talk with Yahweh. Mount Sinai is part of a very rocky mountain range in the wilderness.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of Mount Sinai. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells Moses that these instructions are for when the Israelite people come into the land. This land is Canaan, the land that Yahweh had promised to give the Israelites' ancestors: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Many of the instructions in this part of Leviticus are instructions for the people to follow later when the Israelites live in the land of Canaan. So it will be many years after the people hear these instructions before the people can follow these instructions.

Yahweh says that when the Israelite people come into the land, the Israelites need to give the land a Sabbath or rest every seven years. In the Bible, the number seven often represents things that are holy or important to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what traditions do people keep that happen at certain times or after a certain number of years? What numbers are the most important or have special meaning in your culture? Pause this audio here.

The idea of Sabbath is different in this passage than in previous passages. The word for Sabbath means seven in the original language, and the Israelites would think of the Sabbath as referring to the seventh day of the week, or Saturday. This is the holy day of the week for the Israelite people. Yahweh requires that on this holy day, the Israelites must do two things: the Israelites must worship Yahweh and the Israelites must rest from any hard work. The Israelite people would have already been familiar with the Sabbath as a day on which the Israelites worshipped and rested. So the word Sabbath has this idea of seven, but also a meaning of rest. Both of these meanings are important and would be familiar to the Israelite people listening to this instruction.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what is the most important thing that people do on holy days? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that for six years, the Israelite people may plant their fields, take care of their vineyards, and harvest their crops. The word that Yahweh uses here for "fields" can be any kind of land on which a person can grow crops. It includes fields where Israelite people can grow grains such as wheat and barley.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of grain fields and crops. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, what kind of grain or food is most common? What words would you use for these kinds of grains, or for grains in general, in your language? Pause this audio here.

But the word "fields" can also include any kind of orchard. The Israelites eventually would grow pomegranate bushes, olive trees, fig trees, and date palm trees for their fruit as well.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of pomegranates, olives, dates, and figs, and their trees. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss: In your culture, which fruit trees or plants are the most important? Pause this audio here.

During the six years, the people are also supposed to take care of their vineyards. People must cut off old, dead leaves from grapevines to help the plant grow and produce new fruit.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of a vineyard and grapes. Tell a story about a time when you saw a plant that had too many dead leaves or too many branches so that the plant could not grow food. How could someone help that plant be ready to grow food again? Pause this audio here.

After six years of planting and taking care of their fields or vineyards, the Israelites must spend the next year, the seventh year, not harvesting or taking care of the land.

Instead, the people are supposed to eat what the people can find and take what the people need from whatever is growing whenever the people need it. Even without the Israelite people actively working the land, the plants will still produce things to eat. The trees, such as the fig trees and the date palm trees, will still produce their fruit. The uncut vineyards will still produce some grapes, but not as many. And seeds that fell into the ground the year before will cause plants like barley and wheat to grow, too.

This is the rule, not just for the Israelite people, but for all the people from other people groups who live with the Israelite people, as well as the Israelite people's livestock. Livestock means every kind of animal that the people raise for meat and milk, such as cattle, sheep, and goats.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:1–7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells Moses at Mount Sinai to give these instructions to the Israelite people about how to treat the land the Israelites will one day live in.

In the second scene: Yahweh says that for six years, the Israelite people may plant their fields, take care of their vineyards, and harvest their crops.

In the third scene: Yahweh says that in the seventh year, the Israelite people must not plant their fields or take care of their vineyards or harvest their fields like the Israelites normally do. Instead, all of the people and the animals are to eat what they can find and take what they need.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Israelite people
  • Male and female servants
  • Hired workers
  • And temporary residents

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Yahweh is giving Moses instructions to prepare the Israelite people for when the Israelites move into the land that Yahweh has promised to the Israelites. Moses and the Israelite people are still camped near Mount Sinai at this point. Moses goes up on this mountain to talk with Yahweh.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of Mount Sinai. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells Moses that these instructions are for when the Israelite people come into the land. Many of the instructions in this part of Leviticus are instructions for the people to follow later. From the time the Israelites heard these instructions, it would be many years before the people could follow these instructions.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, how would you give someone instructions for something to do later? Pause this audio here.

It is also important to know that Yahweh gives these instructions for all of the Israelites to follow. Sometimes it sounds like these instructions were for one person. But these instructions were for everyone. So, translate in a way that makes it clear to your listeners that these instructions were for every person.

In the second scene, Yahweh says that for six years the Israelite people may sow seeds in their fields, take care of their vineyards, and harvest their crops. The word "sow" refers to the way that people scatter seeds on the ground so that the seeds can grow into plants. The Israelite people would plant crops such as wheat and barley, pomegranates, figs, and dates.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of grain fields and crops. How do you plant seeds in your culture? Discuss how you want to translate the way that Yahweh says the Israelites can sow their seeds. Pause this audio here.

The Israelite people can also grow and tend vineyards, where people grow grapes. The Israelite people can cut off or prune the old growth on the vines so that the new vines can grow.

Stop here as a group and look at pictures of a vineyard and grapes. How do you talk about the way that people cut off parts of a plant to help the plant grow new branches or more fruit? Discuss how you will translate the way that people prune or cut off old growth here. Pause this audio here.

The Israelite people can also harvest their crops, which is when the people gather all the crops and store the crops to eat throughout the year.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what words do you use to talk about the way people harvest and gather the food that has grown on the plants? Pause this audio here.

In the third scene, Yahweh talks about what the Israelites must do in the seventh year. The Israelite people must not plant their fields, or take care of their vineyards, or organize any harvesting. Yahweh calls this "giving the land a Sabbath." The idea of Sabbath has a few different meanings. It means "seven." It is also the name of the seventh day of the week, Saturday. Remember, Yahweh instructed the Israelite people to set aside the Sabbath as a holy day to worship Yahweh and rest from work, so the Israelites probably thought about rest when the Israelites thought about the Sabbath. When you translate this word, remember that this word refers to the number seven and is connected to the idea of rest from work. In the original language, Yahweh says the land must rest. But really, it is the people who are resting from their regular work in the fields. The Israelite people are not supposed to do this only once, but instead, the Israelites are supposed to do this every seven years.

Stop here and discuss: In your language, what do you think is the best way to translate the Sabbath rest for the land, or for the people in the land? Pause this audio here.

Instead, during this seventh year, the people can eat what the people can find and take what the people need from whatever is growing whenever they need it. Even without the Israelite people actively working the land, the plants will still grow things to eat. The trees, such as the fig trees and the date palm trees, will still produce their fruit. The uncut vineyards will still produce grapes. And seeds that fell into the ground the year before will cause plants like barley and wheat to grow, too.

This is the rule, not just for the Israelite people, but for all the people who will live with the Israelite people. This includes three groups of people besides the Israelites: the people who live in the household, such as male and female slaves, the other workers that the Israelite people hire, and any foreigner who lives among the Israelites. It is even the rule for the Israelite people's livestock. Livestock refers to every kind of animal that the people keep, such as cattle, sheep, and goats. Even wild animals will eat in this way.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:1–7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • Israelite people
  • Male and female servants
  • Hired workers
  • And temporary residents or people from other people groups

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

Yahweh tells Moses at Mount Sinai to give these instructions to the Israelite people. Yahweh says that for six years the Israelite people may plant their fields, take care of their vineyards, and harvest their crops. But during the seventh year, the Israelite people must not plant their fields or take care of their vineyards or organize any harvest. Instead, all of the people and the animals are to eat what they can find and take what they need from whatever grows.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • How can we go a whole year without growing food? or
  • Yahweh provided food for us in the wilderness. Yahweh will provide for us again; or
  • I am worried that my family will go hungry.

Ask the person playing the servants, hired workers, and the people from other people groups, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • Our gods would never tell us to take such a rest for a whole year; or
  • Who is this Yahweh, who provides even for people who do not work? or
  • Perhaps the Israelite people will not work, but we will keep growing food. Otherwise, we will all go hungry.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:1–7 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Yahweh speaks to Moses at Mount Sinai, a mountain in the wilderness. Use the same words or phrases for Yahweh and Mount Sinai as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of Mount Sinai. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh gives Moses instructions for the people of Israel. Use the same word or phrase for people of Israel as you used in previous passages. For more information on Israelites, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says the land should have a Sabbath rest. Normally, the word Sabbath means the last day of the week or the day that the Israelite people would rest for a whole day. In this passage, Yahweh commands the people to allow the land to have a Sabbath or rest for a whole year. Use the same word for Sabbath as you used in previous passages. For more information on Sabbath, refer to the Master Glossary.

During the Sabbath rest for the year, the Israelites must not plant or take care of their vineyards and fields where they grow crops. The Israelites must not harvest grapes as the Israelites normally do. Use the same words for vineyards, grapes, and fields as you used in previous passages. For more information on vineyards, refer to the Master Glossary.

This rule is for the Israelites, for the Israelites' male and female slaves and hired workers, and for foreigners. Slaves are people who work for someone else without pay, usually for a long time. Hired workers are people that someone would hire and pay, usually to do a job for a short time. Foreigners are people who live in a different country from the country in which that person was born. Use the same words for male and female slaves, hired workers, and foreigners that you have used in previous passages. For more information on slaves and foreigners, refer to the Master Glossary.

This rule is for the Israelites' livestock and for wild animals. Remember that in this situation, livestock refers to cattle, sheep, and goats—all the kinds of animals that Israelites kept to work for them, and for food and milk. Wild animals are animals that people in the household did not keep. Use the same words or phrases for livestock and wild animals as you have used previously.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 25:8–22
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 25:8–22 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:8–22 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:8–22 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh is giving Moses instructions to prepare the Israelites for when the Israelites move into the land that Yahweh has promised to the Israelites. In the last passage, Yahweh said that the Israelite people will need to give the land a Sabbath or rest every seven years. For six years, the Israelite people can plant their fields, take care of their vineyards, and harvest their crops. But in the seventh year, the Israelite people are not supposed to plant their fields or take care of their vineyards or organize a harvest. Instead, all of the people and the animals are to eat what they can find and take what they need from whatever grows on its own. This is the Sabbath year.

In this passage, Yahweh talks about a special Sabbath year. After the seventh Sabbath year, which would happen on the 49th year, the next year is also to be a Sabbath year. This year, the 50th year after seven Sabbath years, is a very special Sabbath year which Yahweh calls the Year of Jubilee. For two years, the seventh Sabbath year and the Year of Jubilee, the Israelites must not plant or harvest crops as the Israelites normally do. Yahweh tells Moses that the Israelite people must count the Sabbath years well to determine when the year of Jubilee will be.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people keep track of time and important events? Pause this audio here.

The Year of Jubilee is important for many reasons. The Year of Jubilee is a year when people return to the land that Yahweh had given to the people. Families come back together. People release other people from slavery. We know from another passage that people are supposed to forgive all debts. People are supposed to forgive others in every part of life. It gives hope to the person who feels despair because the person owes money or works as a slave. It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance to restart life as a person free from being a slave and free from owing money. It is also a time that causes people to be more equal. Even though some people naturally become richer or poorer through the years, the Year of Jubilee is meant to be something that stops people from hurting each other in an effort to get wealthy. No matter how much land a person can buy, during the Year of Jubilee, that person has to return any additional land that the person bought or rented.

The Year of Jubilee also sets a spiritual example. The Year of Jubilee teaches the Israelite people that Yahweh cares about these things. Yahweh created a way for people to no longer have debt and for people who were servants to be free. Yahweh is the God of people who have made many mistakes and the people who thought that other people ignored or forgot about them. The Year of Jubilee is meant to be a year of celebration and rest, a way to completely restart the community to the way the community should be.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In what ways do you think the Year of Jubilee was helpful to the Israelites? How would something like this be helpful, or not, in your culture? Pause this audio here.

The people will announce the Year of Jubilee on the Day of Atonement, which is the tenth day of the seventh month. The religious new year always started in the seventh month of the calendar year. The Israelite people had two new years: the calendar new year that helped the Israelites keep track of the days and times, and the religious new year, a time of year for the people to renew their relationship with God. The year of Jubilee starts on the Day of Atonement, which is the tenth day of the religious new year. You will remember that the Day of Atonement was a festival in which the high priest offered sacrifices to atone for the people and restore the people's relationship with Yahweh. To announce the start of the Year of Jubilee, people are supposed to play musical instruments all over the land. To make these instruments, people would take ram horns and take out the inner bone and bone marrow. Then someone would heat up the horn to shape it and cut off the tip of the horn to make a mouthpiece.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a ram's horn instrument. Pause this audio here.

Ancient Israelite people used these ram horns to communicate important messages to large groups of people. People would also use these instruments to make loud, joyful noises of celebration. People would even use these instruments to scare their enemies when people went to war. When the Israelite people heard the sound of the ram's horn, it was like a cry of victory, and it reminded the Israelites that Yahweh cared about them and gave them freedom. The name Jubilee comes from the people using the ram's horns to announce the beginning of the celebration.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your culture, what sounds, instruments, or songs do people use to celebrate special events? Pause this audio here.

The year of Jubilee also follows the same rules as other Sabbath years. The Israelite people must not plant their fields or take care of their vineyards or organize a harvest. In the previous passage, Yahweh called this giving the land a Sabbath. This is actually a good way to take care of the land so that the land will continue to be good for farming. But really, it is the people who are resting from their regular work in the fields. Instead, the people are to eat what people can find and take what people need from whatever grows on its own. Even without the Israelite people actively working the land, the plants will still produce things to eat. The people can take whatever the people need to eat, but the people should not store or gather the crops in the way people do in other years.

Yahweh instructs Moses that the people should change the prices for fields based on how soon or how long it is until the next Year of Jubilee. Yahweh says that when it is many years until the Year of Jubilee, the Israelites can increase the price of the land. But every year that passes, the Israelites must decrease the price as the Year of Jubilee becomes closer.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Imagine you are selling land to your brother. If it has been 10 years since the last Jubilee, how many years are left to harvest crops until the next Year of Jubilee? What if it has been 30 years since the last Jubilee? Will you sell the land to your brother for more or less? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh tells the Israelite people not to do wrong to each other. This means that the Israelite people should not cheat, trick, or gain something from another person's troubles.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your language, describe a situation where someone tricked or cheated someone else. In your culture, how do people feel about people cheating in business? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh says to fear Yahweh. The reason the Israelite people should not cheat each other is that Yahweh knows when the people cheat, even if the people try to hide it. Yahweh also punishes people who do wrong. After Yahweh says these two commands, Yahweh makes one of the most important statements in Leviticus: "I am Yahweh, your God." The people should not cheat each other out of respect and honor for Yahweh. Yahweh promises that if the people obey, then the land will grow lots of food. And Yahweh promises that Yahweh will provide for the people throughout the two Sabbath years.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:8–22 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh instructs Moses on how the Israelite people should celebrate a very special year, the year of Jubilee. The Israelite people are supposed to celebrate this special year of celebration once every 50 years. The Year of Jubilee begins on the Day of Atonement, when the people are supposed to play ram's horn instruments everywhere. Then every Israelite is supposed to go back to live with their own family on their family's own land. This is another Sabbath year, so the people are supposed to follow the same rules about not growing, harvesting, or storing food in the normal way.

In the second scene: Yahweh instructs Moses that when people buy or sell fields, the people should change the prices for fields based on how soon or how long it is until the next Year of Jubilee. Since in the Year of Jubilee all the land went back to the original owners, any land that the Israelites buy or sell is just for rent until the next Jubilee.

In the third scene: Yahweh tells Moses to warn the Israelite people to follow Yahweh's rules and instructions. If the Israelite people obey Yahweh, the Israelites will safely live in the land. Then Yahweh addresses a worry or concern that the Israelite people will probably have. What will the Israelites eat during the Sabbath years if the Israelites do not plant or harvest? Yahweh says that before every Sabbath year, Yahweh will give the Israelites so much food that the Israelites will have plenty to eat and still have more left over for the next year.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The Israelite people
  • A person selling their land
  • And a person buying land

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Yahweh is giving Moses instructions to prepare the Israelite people for when the Israelites move into the land that Yahweh has promised to the Israelites. Moses and the Israelite people are still camping near Mount Sinai at this point. Notice that even though Yahweh does not mention Moses in this passage, we know from the rest of the chapter that Yahweh is giving these instructions to Moses, and that Moses will give the same instructions to the Israelite people.

In the first scene, Yahweh instructs Moses on how the Israelite people should celebrate a very special year, the Year of Jubilee. The Israelite people are supposed to celebrate this special year once every 50 years. Yahweh says to count seven Sabbath years. The word "count" means to keep track of something, to calculate something, or to keep a record to remember something. Yahweh tells Moses that the Israelite people must count the Sabbath years to know when the Year of Jubilee will be.

In the previous passage, Yahweh told Moses that every seven years should be a year of Sabbath for the people and the land. This means that a Sabbath year will happen seven times in a period of 49 years. After the seventh Sabbath year finishes, or the 49th year finishes, Yahweh tells the people to have a very special celebration in the 50th year. This celebration is the Year of Jubilee.

Stop here and do this activity as a group: Find a way, whether drawing on paper or in the dirt, or using rocks, to make seven groups of seven. If possible, have one special item in each group to represent the Sabbath year. Then add one more item to represent the Year of Jubilee. As you make these groups of seven as a group, talk about the words for these groupings and numbers in your language. Pause this audio here.

The Year of Jubilee begins on the Day of Atonement, when the people are supposed to play musical instruments or rams' horns "throughout all the land" or everywhere in the lands that the Israelite people own. The people are supposed to play these musical instruments to show that the Year of Jubilee has begun.

Stop here as a group and look again at a picture of a ram's horn instrument as needed. Pause this audio here.

Ancient Israelite people used these horns to communicate important messages to large groups of people. People would also use these instruments to make loud, joyful noises of celebration. The word "Jubilee" refers to this celebration, especially to the loud, musical noises and sounds that told the people that it was time to celebrate. Yahweh commands the Israelites to consecrate the 50th year, or make the 50th year holy. In other words, the Israelites should make the 50th year special. Yahweh commands the Israelites to do this.

Stop here and discuss how you would give a command in your language. How do you show that someone must follow your instructions? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says to proclaim liberty throughout the land to all the people. Yahweh wants the people to cry out in a loud voice that people can be free. The idea of being free here is like an animal in a trap that has broken free from the trap.

Stop here as a group and discuss what you will use for the phrase "proclaim liberty." Pause this audio here.

Then every Israelite is supposed to go back to live with their own family on their family's own land. This does not mean that the people will just visit their families. In the land of Israel, although people could buy each other's land, it was never a final sale. It was really more like renting. In the year of Jubilee, each portion of land will go back to the original owners. In the same way, if someone sold another person as a slave, in the year of Jubilee, the master will set the slave free and send the slave back to their family to live with their family again.

The Year of Jubilee is to be another Sabbath year, so the people are supposed to follow the same rules about not growing food or harvesting or storing food in the normal way. Remember the way you translated the instructions in the previous passage to decide how to translate them again here.

In the second scene, Yahweh instructs Moses that the people should change the prices when people sell a field based on how soon or how long it is until the next Year of Jubilee. This is a rule both for the people who are trying to sell land and for the people trying to buy land. Yahweh tells the people not to do wrong to each other. This means that the Israelite people should not cheat, trick, or gain something from another person's troubles. Yahweh repeats this command in this passage a second time, so also think about how you could repeat it in your language.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your language, how would you tell someone not to cheat another person? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh gives another command after Yahweh commands the Israelites not to cheat others: fear Yahweh. The reason the Israelite people should not cheat each other is that Yahweh knows when the Israelites cheat, even if the Israelites try to hide it. Yahweh also punishes people who do wrong. After these two commands comes one of the important statements in Leviticus: "I am Yahweh, your God." The people should not cheat each other because they respect and honor Yahweh.

In the third scene, Yahweh tells Moses to warn the Israelite people to follow Yahweh's rules and instructions. These are Yahweh's "statutes" and "ordinances." If the Israelite people follow Yahweh's rules, the Israelite people will live in a safe and secure way. This means that the Israelites will live without danger or threat from enemies or lack of food. The people will live without worry.

In this passage, Yahweh says something about "the land yielding its fruit." The word "land" here can refer to soil, fields, or gardens. "Yielding its fruit" refers to a good harvest of food. Yahweh says if the Israelite people obey, the Israelites will have plenty of food, that the Israelites will have full bellies, or the Israelites will have enough food to be satisfied.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your language, how do you talk about the way that people have all the food people need? Discuss how you will translate the way that Yahweh says that the Israelites will eat their fill. Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh addresses a concern that the Israelite people will probably have. What will the Israelites eat during the Sabbath years if the Israelites do not plant or harvest? Yahweh says that before every Sabbath year, Yahweh will give the Israelites an extra harvest and so much food for the Israelites to store. Yahweh promises that the people will have enough food for the Sabbath year and still have food left over.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:8–22 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The Israelite people
  • A person selling their land
  • And a person buying land

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh instructs Moses on how the Israelite people should celebrate a very special year, the Year of Jubilee. The Israelite people are supposed to celebrate this special year once every 50 years. The Year of Jubilee begins on the Day of Atonement, when the people are supposed to play ram's horn instruments everywhere. Then every Israelite is supposed to go back to live with their own family on their family's own land. This is another Sabbath year, so the people are supposed to follow the same rules about not growing food, harvesting, or storing food in the normal way.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • That will be a very special year to look forward to; or
  • A year when debts go away, and families come together, will bring hope to many people; or
  • I cannot imagine what that celebration will be like.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh instructs Moses that the people should change the prices for fields based on how soon or how long it is until the next Year of Jubilee. Since in the Year of Jubilee all the land goes back to the original owners, any land that the Israelites buy or sell is really just land for rent until the next Jubilee.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • When I see people acting in ways that are kind and just, that makes me happy; or
  • I am angry when rich people steal from poor people; or
  • I want the people to know that I am the God who cancels debts and frees slaves and servants.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh tells Moses to warn the Israelite people to follow Yahweh's rules and instructions. If the Israelite people obey Yahweh, the Israelites will safely live in the land. Then Yahweh addresses a worry or concern that the Israelite people will probably have. What will the Israelites eat during the Sabbath years if the Israelites do not plant or harvest? Yahweh says that before every Sabbath year, Yahweh will give the Israelites so much food that the Israelites will have plenty to eat and still have more left over for the next year.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am glad Yahweh promised this because I think some people will worry about having enough food; or
  • If the Israelite people obey Yahweh, the Israelites will have lives of blessing; or
  • I want to worship Yahweh. I am amazed at how Yahweh provides for us.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:8–22 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Yahweh says to count off seven Sabbath years. Normally, the word Sabbath means the last day of the week or the day that the Israelite people would rest for a whole day. In this passage, the Sabbath year refers to the year of rest for the land and the people when the people do not plant and harvest in the seventh year. After the seventh Sabbath year, which will happen on the 49th year, the next year, or the 50th year, is also to be a Sabbath year. This is a very special Sabbath year, which Yahweh calls the Year of Jubilee. Use the same word for Sabbath as you used in previous passages. For more information on Sabbath and the Year of Jubilee, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for the Year of Jubilee. Refer to "Year of Jubilee" in the Master Glossary for more information. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh instructs the people to play musical instruments or ram's horns everywhere on the Day of Atonement of the 50th year to show that it is a Year of Jubilee. Use the same phrase for "Day of Atonement" as you used in previous passages. For more information on Day of Atonement, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word for "ram's horn instrument" as you used in previous passages. For more information on horn, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a ram's horn instrument. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says to consecrate the Year of Jubilee. To consecrate something means to set the thing apart for special service to God. The thing now belongs to God and is holy. Use the same word for consecrate as you used in previous passages. For more information on consecrate, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says that each person should return to their own clan. Clans are a group of relatives that includes a few different households or families. A tribe is several clans together.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for clan. Pause this audio here.

The Israelites must not harvest grapes from the grape vines as the Israelites normally do. People grow grape vines in a vineyard. Use the same words for grape and grapevines as you used in previous passages. For more information, refer to vineyard in the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of grape vines as needed. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that the Year of Jubilee will be holy. Any place, person, or object Yahweh has dedicated to God is holy. That means that Yahweh has set the object apart for God's special purposes. Use the same word for holy as you used in previous passages. For more information on holy, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says not to take advantage of each other, but instead to "fear your God." When someone fears God, that person has a great reverence, honor, and respect for God. That person believes that everything that God has said is true. As a result, that person obeys God because that person knows that God's commandments are good, and that God will punish the person if they disobey God. Use the same phrase for "fear your God" as you used in previous passages. For more information on "fear of God," refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says, "I am Yahweh, your God," to remind the Israelites why the Israelites should obey Yahweh's commands. Use the same words for Yahweh and God as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and God, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh warns the Israelites to obey Yahweh's statutes and ordinances. Use the same words or phrases for statutes and ordinances you used in previous passages. For more information on these two terms, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh assures the Israelites that Yahweh will give the Israelites great blessings so the Israelites will have enough food to eat during the Sabbath years. When Yahweh blesses a person, Yahweh is doing, or promising to do, something good for that person. Yahweh is promising to give the Israelites good things, specifically food, for the Sabbath years. Use the same word for blessing as you used in previous passages. For more information on blessing, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 25:23–34
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 25:23–34 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:23–34 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:23–34 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh is giving Moses instructions to prepare the Israelite people for when the Israelites move into the land that Yahweh has promised to the Israelites. In this passage, Moses and the Israelite people are still camping near Mount Sinai. Yahweh gives rules about how people could "buy" or rent land.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what are common ways that people rent or sell to each other? Try to talk about specific examples and notice what kind of words you use to talk about it. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that the Israelites must not permanently sell land. The reason that the Israelite people only rent the land is because the land does not really belong to the Israelites, but to Yahweh. Because of this, Yahweh says the Israelite people are like "foreigners" in the land. That means the Israelites are like people groups from other places who come to visit as guests. Just as Yahweh instructed the Israelite people to be kind to the foreigners who live with the Israelites, the Israelite people should also be kind to each other, when one of the Israelites becomes poor and needs to sell land for a time.

In order to understand these instructions, we must talk about why land ownership was so important for the Israelite people. When Yahweh promised the land to the Israelites' ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, these men did not own much land. These men spent much of their lives traveling from place to place, even though these men believed the promise that one day Yahweh would give their family a place to settle. When the Israelite people were slaves, the Israelites had no land of their own, and yet Yahweh promised the Israelites a place where the Israelites would belong.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: How important is it for people to have a place to belong and settle? Talk about the things in your culture that make people feel like they belong. Pause this audio here.

Eventually, Yahweh will give specific regions of land to each of the tribes of Israel. The only tribe that will not get a region of land is the Levite tribe, who instead will get towns in each territory, so that the priestly tribe will live throughout the land of Israel. Each family from each tribe will receive an area that will be for the family to live in forever. Yahweh's promise was finally becoming real after many years, so it was very important.

But the reality is, as soon as people enter the land, some will be prosperous and have plenty of everything and continue to increase wealth. Other people will have troubles and lose money. The Year of Jubilee, in many ways, is a way to make people more equal again. In many ways, the Year of Jubilee would correct much of this divide of wealth and fortune.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What do you think the Year of Jubilee teaches us about Yahweh? What do you think Yahweh thinks about these things? How do you think people who follow Yahweh should think about these things? Pause this audio here.

In the same way, it was extremely important for people to try to keep land in the family if at all possible. This is why, in this passage, Yahweh talks to the Israelites about the "redeemer." If a person becomes poor and needs to sell their land, if possible, that person's closest relative is supposed to come and buy the land. This person is the redeemer. This is extremely important because it keeps the land within the same family. Notice the language in the passage: the person sells their land because that person is so poor. The Israelite person in a normal situation would not think of selling their land, because their land was the blessing from Yahweh. But extreme circumstances might cause someone to sell their land. This is why Yahweh makes the kinsmen-redeemer rule, so that the Israelite people will take care of their extended families and do everything possible to take care of each other.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how is your land and the land of your family important? What kinds of things do you do to keep the land? What happens if you lose the land? Pause this audio here.

We know from another passage that the kinsmen-redeemer should also redeem a person who became a servant, marry a widow, or even avenge the wrongful death of a relative.

If the person does not have any relatives who can help the person redeem his land, the person can sell their land. Then the person can work until the person makes enough money to buy their own land back. The Israelite people are not supposed to keep a person like this from buying back their family's land. It is more important for each person to have their land than for one person to keep buying more land for himself.

Yahweh also gave rules about selling houses. If a person sells a house in a city, the person only has one year to redeem or buy back the land before the ownership changes to the new owner forever. A city is a group of houses that has a large stone wall around it to protect the people from attackers. However, if a person sells a house in a village, which is a smaller group of houses without a wall, then the person can redeem the land and the land will go back to the original owners in the year of Jubilee.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of what an ancient Israelite city and an ancient Israelite town might have looked like. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh gives an exception to this rule for the Levite tribe—the tribe of Israelites that descended from Jacob's son Levi. The Levite tribe was the tribe that Moses and Aaron came from. Aaron's direct descendants were the priests. The other descendants of Levi worked in the tabernacle and later, the temple. Remember, Yahweh did not give the Levite tribe a large territory of land like the other tribes. Instead, Yahweh gave the Levite tribe cities in each of the territories. The Levite tribe is always allowed to redeem their own land. Not only that, but the Levites are the only tribe that Yahweh does not permit to sell their land. The Levite people can sell their houses, but the Levites cannot sell the pasture land that came with the Levite cities. This is because these pasture lands are the only lands for the whole Levite tribe, so it is important that the Levites not lose these fields.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:23–34 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh gives rules about how people could "buy" or rent land. If a person becomes poor and needs to sell their land, if possible, that person's closest relative is supposed to come and buy the land. Yahweh calls this person the redeemer. Even if someone has to sell the land outside the family, the person can make money and buy the land back. But no matter what happens, the person will be able to claim the land that they sold in the Year of Jubilee.

In the second scene: Yahweh gives the rules about selling houses. If the house is in a city, the person can sell the house, but the sale will be final. The person will have one year to redeem the house and rebuy it. After that, the house will permanently belong to the person who bought it and their descendants. However, if the house is in a town without walls, the person who sold the house can redeem the house. Also, in the year of Jubilee, the original owner of the house will get the house back from the person who bought it.

In the third scene: Yahweh gives rules about how the Levite people redeem their property. The Levite people can always redeem their houses. In the year of Jubilee, the Levite people are supposed to get back any houses that the Levites sold. The Levite people also are not supposed to sell their land.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The Israelite people
  • A poor Israelite person selling their land
  • A kinsmen-redeemer
  • A person selling a house in a city
  • A person selling a house in a village
  • And a Levite person who wants to buy back their house

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Yahweh is giving Moses instructions to prepare the Israelite people for when the Israelites move into the land that Yahweh has promised to the Israelites. Moses and the Israelite people are still camped near Mount Sinai. Notice that even though Yahweh does not mention Moses in this passage, we know from the previous passages that Yahweh is giving these instructions to Moses, and that Moses will give the same instructions to the Israelite people.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives rules about how people can "buy" or rent land. Yahweh says that the Israelites must not sell the land permanently. The reason that the Israelite people only rent the land is that the land does not really belong to the Israelites, but to Yahweh. Translate in a way that shows that Yahweh owns the land. In some languages, it may be easier to talk about the Israelite people's ways of buying land as "renting" land, since the land must go back to the original owners eventually.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Talk about the words in your language that refer to things such as buying, lending, or renting. Pause this audio here.

One important concept in this passage is the idea of whether or not a sale is permanent or forever.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Reflect on the words you just talked about for buying and renting. In your language, how would you show the difference between a sale that will eventually go back to the original owner in the Year of Jubilee and a sale that will remain, even during the Year of Jubilee? Pause this audio here.

All of the Israelite people are to obey the rule of redemption. This redemption rule is to be a rule in all the land that Yahweh will give to the Israelite people. Here is a description of the rule of redemption: If a person becomes poor and needs to sell their land, if possible, one of that person's closest relatives is supposed to come and buy the land. Yahweh calls this person the redeemer. Try to translate this name in a way that shows that this person should be a close relative of the original owner and that it is this person's responsibility to buy the land if possible to keep it in the family.

Stop here and discuss as a group: Think about the words you just talked about for buying and renting. In your language, how would you show the difference between a sale that would eventually go away in the Year of Jubilee and a sale that would remain, even during the Year of Jubilee? Pause this audio here.

Even if the person has to sell the land outside the family, the person who sold the land can make enough money and buy the land back. The original language says something like, "if the person's hand gets enough wealth so that the person is able to redeem it." This means that the person becomes rich or that the person has enough money.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In your language, how would you talk about someone having enough money to buy something expensive? Pause this audio here.

The rule is that the person who bought the land has to allow the original landowner to buy back the land if the original landowner can. In order to determine the price of the land, the buyer and the seller are to calculate the cost of the land by how many years it will be until the next Year of Jubilee. If it is a long time until the next Year of Jubilee, the price will be more. If there is less time until the next Year of Jubilee, the price will be less. The person selling the land back must not make the price too high just because the original landowner might be eager to pay extra just to get their own land back.

Even if the original owner never has enough money to buy the land back, the original landowner will be able to reclaim the land that person sold in the Year of Jubilee.

In the second scene, Yahweh gives the rules about selling houses. If the house is in a city, the person can sell the house, but the sale will be final after one year. The person will have one year to redeem the house and rebuy it. After that, the house will permanently belong to the person who bought it and to their descendants, even in the Year of Jubilee. This is the only case where the sale will be permanent. An ancient Israelite city would have a big rock wall around the house to protect the people who lived there from any warring people groups who might be traveling through the area.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of what an ancient Israelite city might have looked like. Pause this audio here.

However, if the house is in a village, the person who sells the house can redeem the house. A town is a place where people live close together, but there is no wall to protect the people from invaders. In the Year of Jubilee, the original owner of the house can get the house back from the person who bought it.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of what an ancient Israelite town might have looked like. Pause this audio here.

In the third scene, Yahweh gives rules about how the Levite people redeem their property. The Levite people are the people from the tribe of Levi, or the descendants of Levi, the son of Jacob. Aaron, a Levite, is the ancestor of all the priests. But the people who are part of the Levite tribe who are not descended from Aaron still help in the Tent of Meeting and with religious activities.

Stop here and discuss as a group: What will you call the Levite people? If you have already translated their name in another book, you should translate the same way here. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh will not give the Levite people land like Yahweh will give the other tribes. Instead, Yahweh gives the Levites cities in all of the territories. Because of this, the Levite people can always redeem their houses. In the Year of Jubilee, the Levite people are supposed to get back any houses the Levites sold. But the Levite people are not supposed to sell the land that surrounds the Levite cities. This land is pasture land, where the Levites kept their animals. It is the Levites' only land, and it is important to keep this land in the tribe.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:23–34 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The Israelite people
  • A poor Israelite person selling their land
  • A kinsmen-redeemer
  • A person selling a house in a city
  • A person selling a house in a village
  • And a Levite person who wants to buy back their house

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh gave rules about how people could "buy" or rent land. If a person became poor and needed to sell their land, if possible, that person's closest relative was supposed to come and buy the land. Yahweh called this person the redeemer. Even if the person had to sell the land outside the family, the person could make money and buy the land back. But no matter what happened, the person would be able to claim the land that the person sold in the Year of Jubilee.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the poor person selling their land, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am so sad that I am losing my land; or
  • I have hope that my family will get the land back in the Year of Jubilee; or
  • I am so grateful to my relatives for keeping the land in the family.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh gave the rules about selling houses. If the house were in a city, the person could sell the house, but the sale would be final. The person would have one year to redeem the house and re-buy it. After that, the house would permanently belong to the person who bought it and their descendants. However, if the house was in a village, the person who sold the house could redeem the house. Also, in the Year of Jubilee, the original owner of the house would get the house back from the person who bought it.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the people selling their houses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I will work hard to redeem my house; or
  • I worry for my future; or
  • I pray that Yahweh will provide for me.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh gave rules about how the Levite people redeem their property. The Levite people could always redeem their houses. In the year of Jubilee, the Levite people were supposed to get back any houses the Levites had sold. The Levite people also were not supposed to sell their land.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Moses, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • It is good that the people of my tribe can always redeem their houses, since Yahweh did not give my tribe land like other tribes; or
  • The priestly cities will be a special symbol to the Israelite people that we are Yahweh's chosen people; or
  • The Israelite people might live in the land, but the land belongs to Yahweh.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:23–34 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh says that the Israelite people are foreigners because the land belongs to Yahweh, not to the Israelites. Yahweh calls the Israelites two words for foreigners: foreigners and strangers. A stranger is a general word for someone who is not from your people group. Together, these two words mean anyone who does not belong to the Israelite people group. Use the same words or phrases for foreigner, stranger, and Israelite as you used in previous passages. For more information on foreigner and Israelite, refer to the Master Glossary.

If an Israelite person becomes so poor that the person needs to sell their land, a close relative is supposed to come buy the land. This keeps the land with the family. Yahweh calls this relative who buys the land a "redeemer." Similarly, if the person is able to make money to buy the land back themselves, people are supposed to allow this person to redeem the land. Yahweh calls this "redemption." For more information on redeem, refer to the Master Glossary.

The land will go back to the original family in the Year of Jubilee. Use the same word for Year of Jubilee as you used in the previous passage. For more information on the Year of Jubilee, refer to the Master Glossary.

In this passage, Yahweh talks about houses that people sell in cities and villages. People built cities to be able to house a lot of people, and cities had tall and wide stone walls to protect the people who lived in the city. If another people group attacked the area, the people in the surrounding villages could come and be safe in the cities. But the villages were just groups of houses without walls.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of what an ancient Israelite city and an ancient Israelite village might have looked like. Discuss as a group what words or phrases you will use for cities and villages in your language. Pause this audio here.

If a person sold their house in the city, that person had a year to buy the house back. If the person did not, the house would belong to the buyer and the buyer's descendants. Use the same word or phrase for descendants, and refer to descendants in the Master Glossary for more information.

The Levites were the people who were from the tribe of Levi, who became the tribe from which the priests and religious workers came.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for Levites. Look up Levites in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used before. Pause this audio here.

The Levites must not sell their pastureland. Pastureland is big fields with lots of grasses and food for animals like cattle and horses to eat. This is where people keep their animals.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for pastureland. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used before.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
