title: Leviticus 25:35–46
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 25:35–46 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:35–46 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:35–46 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh is giving Moses instructions to prepare the Israelite people for when the Israelites move into the land that Yahweh has promised to the Israelites. Moses and the Israelite people are still camped near Mount Sinai. In this passage, Yahweh gives rules about how the Israelite people should take care of their poor people and guidelines for slavery.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what do people say or think about owning slaves? Pause this audio here.

In this passage, Yahweh commands the Israelite people to help Israelites who become poor. This means the other Israelites should provide and care for the poor Israelites. One reason the Israelites must help poor Israelites is that the Israelite people all know that Yahweh cares for poor people. The command to fear Yahweh is a reminder that Yahweh notices and remembers how people act, especially how people treat other people who need help. Yahweh also reminds the Israelites that Yahweh showed compassion to the Israelites and rescued the Israelites when the Israelites were poor and struggling in Egypt.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what do people think and say about poor people? Pause this audio here.

Another reason why the Israelite people must help the poor Israelite is so that the poor Israelite can keep living in the land with the other Israelites. It is very important for the Israelite people to stay in the land for many reasons. The land is the inheritance that people pass on through family generations for the tribes of Israel, a place where each family has its own place and a chance to grow together. Living in the land shows the people that Yahweh keeps Yahweh's promises. As long as the Israelite people are living in the land, this shows the Israelites are obeying Yahweh.

If a poor Israelite has to leave the land, the poor Israelite might end up forgetting about Yahweh. Instead, the poor Israelite may begin to serve idols or the false gods of other people, perhaps of their new masters. If an Israelite is in another land, the Israelite also will not be able to participate in the worship services and festivals of the Israelite people. This is why it is important for the Israelites to stay in the land that Yahweh gives to the Israelites.

Yahweh says in this passage that the Israelite people must care for poor Israelites as the people would care for a foreigner or a person from another people group. This is very interesting! In the ancient world, people usually liked people from their own people group and did not like people from groups that were different from them. Yahweh gave many instructions to the Israelite people to be kind to people who were different from the Israelites. So when Yahweh needs to tell the Israelites to treat poor Israelites kindly, Yahweh says, "treat the poor Israelites like you would treat a foreigner."

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what do people think and say about people from other people groups, tribes, or countries? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh gives the Israelites specific rules for how the Israelites should treat poor people. The Israelites should not profit from a poor Israelite's need. The Israelites also must not lend money to the poor Israelite and then expect to get more back. People call this "interest." For example, a rich person might lend a poor person some money or resources. But the rich person tells the poor person that the poor person must pay back that money, plus more. It is like the rich person asks the poor person to pay an extra fee to use the money. Yahweh does not allow the Israelites to do this to each other.

Stop here and do this activity as a group: Make a demonstration of what "interest" could look like. It might look like this: a poor person asks a rich person for a coat. The rich person gives the coat to the poor person, but the rich person tells the poor person that the poor person must give the rich person two coats when the poor person comes back. Or it might look like this: one person gives another person a rock. Decide as a group what the rock represents. It could represent cattle, or money, or a certain kind of crop. The rich person gives the poor person one rock. But the poor person must give the rich person many rocks. The longer it takes the poor person to pay the rich person, the more rocks the rich person can require from the poor person. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also gives rules about slavery. Slavery is a difficult topic, and there are some people who ask why it is in the Bible at all. Slavery was very common in ancient times, and the Bible did not ignore that it was a part of many people's lives. In fact, the theme of slavery is extremely important in the Bible. The Israelite people were slaves in Egypt until Yahweh freed the Israelites. Yahweh tells the Israelites that the Israelites should be Yahweh's servants, but not slaves to false gods or idols. We will start by talking about what slavery was like in ancient times.

The word in the original language for "slave" means "someone who is underneath another person's power." People use this word in different ways. It might mean a soldier who follows the orders of their commander. It could mean the royal advisors who served a king. It also meant slaves who had a master.

In cases of this kind of "slave," the master paid a one-time price and then got free labor from the slave. When a master bought a slave, the slave was a part of the household. The master promised to take care of and protect the slaves. Many times, the slave worshipped the same gods as their master, and the master would treat the slave as part of the family.

In this passage, a person became a slave because the person had no food or no way to provide for themselves or their families. This was a very common reason why a person might become a slave. Sometimes a person might also become a slave when that person could not repay a debt. The person sold themselves to repay the debt. The person exchanged their labor as a slave for what the person borrowed or for food. The slaves usually did not earn any money for their work.

Some masters were cruel to their slaves, and some masters were kind. In the Bible, Yahweh often commanded masters to be kind to their slaves. The Israelite masters must remember that the masters themselves were all descendants of the Israelite slaves who suffered in Egypt. Sometimes the masters were so kind that the slaves chose to stay with their masters.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Remember that Yahweh reminds the Israelites that the Israelites are Yahweh's servants. What do you think about using slavery as an example of serving Yahweh? What do you like about it? What do you not like about it? Pause this audio here.

If an Israelite has to sell himself as a slave, another Israelite person can buy the first Israelite. Again, it was better that another Israelite person buy the first Israelite than for a person from another people group to buy the first Israelite. Yahweh instructs Israelites who buy other Israelites as slaves to treat the Israelite slaves like hired workers, not like slaves. This means the Israelite person must not treat the Israelite slave the same as the other slaves, but as a hired worker. A hired worker had more honor and more freedom than a slave. Since a hired worker received a wage, the hired worker could choose to leave his employer for another employer if the worker felt his job or wages were unfair. Yahweh may mean that all Israelite people working as slaves should receive a wage, but we are not sure.

During the Year of Jubilee, the Israelites must release all their Israelite slaves. This was not just true for the first slave who sold himself, but also for the slaves' family members. Even though the Israelite people could own slaves from other people groups, the Israelites had to treat their Israelite slaves with a higher level of respect and honor.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:35–46 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh gives the Israelite people instructions on how to treat other Israelite people who become poor. The Israelites must not profit from the poor Israelites or lend to the poor Israelites while expecting more back. If the poor Israelite sells themself to another Israelite, the Israelite master must not treat the poor Israelite as a slave, but like a hired servant or worker. Twice, Yahweh reminds the Israelites that Yahweh is their God and that Yahweh brought the Israelites out of slavery. Because of this, the Israelites must treat each other well.

In the second scene: Yahweh does allow the Israelite people to own slaves who were from other people groups. However, Yahweh does not allow the Israelite people to own other Israelites in the same way that the Israelites owned slaves from other countries.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The Israelite people
  • A foreigner or stranger
  • A poor Israelite person working as a slave
  • And slaves from other people groups

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Yahweh is giving Moses instructions to prepare the Israelite people for when the Israelites move into the land that Yahweh has promised to the Israelites. Moses and the Israelite people are still camped near Mount Sinai. We know from previous passages that Yahweh is giving these instructions to Moses, and that Moses will give the same instructions to the Israelite people.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives the Israelite people instructions on how to treat other Israelite people who become poor and cannot support themselves. To say that someone cannot support themselves is to say that the person cannot provide for themselves or cannot feed themselves.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how would you say that a person does not have enough or is so poor that that person cannot eat? Pause this audio here.

The Israelite people are to strengthen and help poor Israelites, which means to provide and care for the poor Israelites. The Israelite people are to care for the poor Israelites in the same way that the Israelites would care for a foreigner or a stranger.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how do you talk about doing something in the same way as you would do something else? Try to find an example and notice the language you use. Pause this audio here.

The Israelite people must help the poor Israelites so that the poor Israelites can keep living in the land with the other Israelites. It is very important for the Israelite people to stay in the land for many reasons. The land is the inheritance passed on through family generations for the tribes of Israel, a place where each family has its own place and chance to grow together. When the people live in the land, this shows the people that Yahweh keeps Yahweh's promises.

The Israelite people are not to profit from the poor Israelite or to lend money to the poor Israelite and then expect to get more back. Sometimes a person would give a poor person something, but wanted the poor person to give much more back to repay what the poor person borrowed. Yahweh does not allow the Israelites to do this to each other.

Stop here and discuss as a group how you will translate that the Israelites should not lend money to each other and expect to get interest. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh also commands that the Israelite people must not profit from a poor person when the poor person has a need. Why? The reason is that the Israelite people should fear, or respect, Yahweh, because the people know that Yahweh judges people who treat others unfairly.

Then Yahweh repeats the instructions: The Israelite people must not profit from the poor Israelites or lend money to the poor Israelites and expect to get even more back. Yahweh also commands that the Israelite people must not profit from feeding a poor Israelite. Why? Because Yahweh is the Israelites' God, and Yahweh brought the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. Yahweh will give the Israelites the land of Canaan and promises to be their God. Yahweh will make a similar statement later, so you may want to think about how to structure your translation to emphasize these important statements.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Discuss how you want to translate the way that Yahweh reminds the Israelites of what Yahweh has done for the Israelites to show why the Israelites should obey Yahweh's commands. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says that even if a poor Israelite person has nothing and needs to sell himself, the Israelite who buys the poor Israelite must not treat the poor Israelite like an ordinary slave. In ancient times, it was a common practice for people to sell themself to another person. The master would pay one price and then would get free labor from the slave. In return, the slave was a part of the household, and the master would provide food and a place to live. This kind of labor was different from a hired worker, who a master paid for their work.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your language, how would you show the difference between a person who was a slave and a person who was a paid worker? Pause this audio here.

But Yahweh says that the Israelite people must not treat the poor Israelites like the Israelites treated other slaves. Instead, the Israelites must treat the Israelite slave as the Israelites would treat hired workers or foreigners in the land. The Israelites must give the Israelite slave dignity and choice. A hired worker could always find work in another place if the wages did not suit the worker. The poor Israelite will work for their master until the Year of Jubilee. Then the poor Israelite, along with their family, can go back to their own land and be free again.

Here, Yahweh says again that this rule is this way because the Israelite people are Yahweh's servants. This word is actually the same word as "slaves," so it is clear that Yahweh is making a comparison to show how the Israelites must be kind to slaves because the Israelite people are Yahweh's slaves. Yahweh brought the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, so it would not be right for the Israelite people to mistreat or turn their fellow Israelites into slaves in a bad way. Yahweh tells the Israelites not to rule over their Israelite slaves in a cruel or fierce way, because Yahweh was kind to their ancestors when Yahweh brought the Israelites out of Egypt. Yahweh requires the people Yahweh has shown mercy to show mercy to others. Because of this, the Israelites are to treat each other well.

Stop here and discuss as a group: In this passage, it is important to show the connection between the rules about slaves and how Yahweh freed the Israelite people from slavery. Talk about how to make these connections clear in your language. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and tell a story about a time when a leader ruled in a cruel way. How did this leader act? How would you feel if one of your people treated you in that same way? Discuss how you want to translate the way that Yahweh tells the Israelites not to rule over an Israelite slave in a cruel way, but to fear God instead. Pause this audio here.

In the second scene, Yahweh does allow the Israelite people to own slaves who are from other people groups. These might be both men and women from other lands. Or it may be people from other people groups who live in the land with the Israelite people. Because these slaves were not Israelites, the Israelites did not have to release these slaves in the year of Jubilee. If an Israelite person had slaves from other people groups and then the Israelite died, that Israelite person's children and relatives could become the new masters of those slaves. However, Yahweh did not allow the Israelite people to treat each other in the same way. The Israelites must release any Israelite slaves in the Year of Jubilee. Yahweh has told the Israelites to treat an Israelite slave like a hired worker, even if the Israelite slave sold themselves as a slave. Here, Yahweh says that the Israelites should not rule over the Israelite slaves in a cruel way.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:35–46 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • The Israelite people
  • A foreigner or stranger
  • A poor Israelite person working as a slave
  • And slaves from other people groups

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives the Israelite people instructions on how to treat other Israelite people who become poor. The Israelites must not profit from the poor Israelite. The Israelites must not lend money to a poor person and then expect to get even more money back. The Israelites must not treat their Israelite slaves like ordinary slaves, but like hired workers. Twice, Yahweh reminds the Israelites that Yahweh is their God and that Yahweh brought the Israelites out of slavery. Because of this, the Israelites are to treat each other well. Yahweh says, "Do not rule over the Israelite slaves ruthlessly, but fear your God."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • These people know how bad slavery is. I do not want the Israelites to become so greedy that the Israelites forget and choose to make each other slaves again; or
  • I saved these people from slavery. What good does that do if the Israelites just became slaves again? or
  • The people will learn that I am the God who is different from the idols. I know when people are cruel and unjust, and I will repay those people for their actions.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh says that the Israelite people can own slaves who were from other people groups. These might be people, men and women, from other lands. Or it may be people from other people groups who live in the land with the Israelite people. Because these slaves were not Israelites, the Israelites did not have to free these slaves in the Year of Jubilee. Yahweh says, "Do not rule over the Israelite slaves ruthlessly, but fear your God."

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the poor Israelite person, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I have hope that my family will be free someday in the Year of Jubilee; or
  • I worry about how we will keep our dignity when we are only slaves; or
  • I am grateful that Yahweh sees the way that people treat us, both good and bad.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:35–46 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

At the beginning of this passage, Yahweh talks about how the Israelites should treat their "brother" or "fellow Israelite." Yahweh often talked about fellow Israelites as "brothers." Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh and Israelite people as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and Israelite, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says to treat the poor Israelites as you would treat a foreigner or a stranger. A foreigner is a person who is from a different people group and who lives in another land or territory. A stranger is a general word for someone who is not from your people group. Together, these two words mean anyone who does not belong to the Israelite people group. Use the same word or phrase for foreigner as you used in previous passages. For more information on foreigner, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says not to lend money to a poor Israelite and expect to receive even more money back. Instead, the Israelites must "fear their God." When a person fears God, the person has deep respect for God and so obeys God's rules because the person knows that God can punish that person. Use the same word or phrase for fear of God as you used in previous passages. For more information on fear of God, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh is the Israelite's God. Use the same word for God as you used in previous passages. For more information on God, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt to give the Israelites the land of Canaan. Use the same word or phrase for Canaan as you used in previous passages. For more information on Canaan, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Israelites must free any Israelite slaves during the Year of Jubilee. Use the same word or phrase for the Year of Jubilee as you used in previous passages. For more information on the Year of Jubilee, refer to the Master Glossary.

When the Israelite slave becomes free, the Israelite can return to their own clan. Use the same word or phrase for clan as you used in previous passages.

In this passage, Yahweh gives the Israelite people rules about how to treat other Israelite people and how to treat slaves. Yahweh says the Israelite people should treat slaves well because the Israelites are servants of Yahweh. In the original language, people used the same word for servant and slave, and used the word to mean different things in different contexts. Yahweh also talks about both male and female slaves. You may need a separate word for female slaves. Use the same words or phrases for slaves and servants as you used in previous passages. For more information on slave and servant, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Israelites can have male and female slaves from other nations. A nation is a group of people who belong together, who live in the same country, and who have the same ruler. Use the same word or phrase for nation as you used in previous passages. For more information on nation, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 25:47–55
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 25:47–55 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:47–55 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:47–55 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh was giving Moses instructions to prepare the Israelite people for when the Israelites would move into the land that Yahweh had promised to give the Israelites. Moses and the Israelite people were still camped near Mount Sinai during this time. In this passage, Yahweh gave guidelines to the Israelite people about slavery and redemption.

Slavery is a difficult topic, and there are some people who ask why it is in the Bible at all. Slavery was very common in ancient times, and the Bible did not ignore that it was a part of many people's lives. The Israelite people were slaves in Egypt until Yahweh freed the Israelites. Yahweh told the Israelites that the Israelites should be Yahweh's servants, but not slaves to false gods or idols. Let us remind you what slavery was like in ancient times.

You will remember that the word in the original language for "slave" means "someone who is underneath another person's power." People used this word in many contexts. It might mean a soldier who follows their commander's orders. It could be the royal advisors who served a king. It also meant slaves who had a master.

In cases of this kind of "slave," the master would pay a one-time price and then would get free labor from the slave. In return, the slave was a part of the household. The master would provide food and a place to live. Many times, the slave would worship the same gods as their master, and the master sometimes treated the slave as part of the family.

In this passage, a person became a slave because the person had no food or no way to provide for themselves or their families. This was a very common reason why a person might become a slave. Sometimes a person might also become a slave when that person could not repay a debt. The person sold themselves to get enough money to repay the debt. The person exchanged their labor as a slave for what the person borrowed or for food. The slaves usually did not earn any money for their work.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people treat poor people? What do people say or think about poor people? In what ways do people in your culture take care of poor people? Pause this audio here.

If an Israelite person had to sell themself as a slave, another Israelite person could buy that first Israelite person. Again, it was better that another Israelite person bought the first Israelite than for a person from another people group to buy the first Israelite. But if this was not possible, it was possible for a person from another people group who lived in the land of Israel to buy an Israelite person. This was better than the Israelite person having to live outside the land of Israel, where the Israelite would lose connection to their people and, more importantly, to Yahweh.

Yahweh instructed Israelites who bought other Israelites as slaves to treat the Israelite slaves like hired workers, not like slaves. A hired worker had more honor and more freedom than a slave. Yahweh may have implied that all Israelite people working as slaves should receive a wage. Yahweh did clearly say that the Israelites must release any Israelite slaves in the Year of Jubilee.

Another rule was that even though an Israelite person might be a slave to a foreigner, the Israelite slave still had the rule of redemption or the rule of the kinsmen-redeemer. If an Israelite person became poor and sold themselves into slavery, if possible, the person's closest relative was supposed to come and buy that person back. Yahweh called this close relative a "redeemer." Notice the language in the passage: the person became a slave because that person was so poor. An Israelite person in a normal situation would not think of becoming a slave. A person may feel like they have no choice but to sell themself into slavery because that person was in such bad circumstances. This is why Yahweh made the redeemer rule, so that the Israelite people would take care of their relatives and do everything possible to take care of each other.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what should people do to take care of their family? Who has to take care of whom and in what ways? Pause this audio here.

We know from other passages that the relative redeemer should also redeem a person who sold their land, should marry a widow, or should even avenge the wrongful death of a relative.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:47–55 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has one scene.

In the scene: Yahweh says a rich foreigner who lives in the land of Israel can buy a poor Israelite person. But a relative can redeem the Israelite slave, or the Israelite slave can even pay for their freedom on their own. The rich foreigner and the poor Israelite are supposed to decide the price based on how many more years there are until the Year of Jubilee. The master who is a foreigner is supposed to treat the Israelite slave not like an ordinary slave, but like a hired worker. Even if no one redeems the Israelite slave, the master must free the slave and their family in the Year of Jubilee. The reason is that Yahweh brought the Israelite people out of slavery in the land of Egypt.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • A rich foreigner
  • A poor Israelite person
  • A relative of the Israelite slave
  • And children of an Israelite slave

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

Yahweh is giving Moses instructions to prepare the Israelite people for when the Israelites move into the land that Yahweh has promised to the Israelites. Moses and the Israelite people are still camped near Mount Sinai. Notice that even though the storyteller does not mention Moses in this passage, we know from the rest of the chapter that Yahweh is giving these instructions to Moses, and that Moses will give the same instructions to the Israelite people.

In the scene, Yahweh describes a situation that may happen. It is possible that one of the people from another people group may live in the land of the Israelite people and become rich. This is a contrast—the opposite of the poor Israelite in this passage and the last passage. To be rich or wealthy means that the person has more than enough for himself and his household.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do you decide if a person is rich or wealthy? As you talk about this, talk about a person who has a lot of wealth or resources. Pause this audio here.

If a poor Israelite person becomes poor and cannot provide for themselves or their household, Yahweh does allow the poor Israelite to sell themself to a person from another people group who lives in the land. While Yahweh does not say the foreigner is in Israel, we know the foreigner is someone who lives in Israel because Yahweh calls this person a foreigner, or someone who is not an Israelite but lives with the Israelites. Since the person is still in the land of Israel, the foreigner is still under the law, which allows for a close relative of the person to redeem the person.

All of the Israelite people must obey the rule of redemption. Here is a description of the rule of redemption: If a person becomes poor, that person can sell their land. If a person loses their land, that person loses their ability to make money. If a person cannot provide enough, that person can even sell themselves into slavery so that the person can get food and a place to live. The rule of redemption is that, if possible, one of the person's closest relatives is supposed to come and pay the price so that the person can be free again. The closest relative can be a brother, an uncle, a cousin, or another relative who is a "blood relative." A "blood relative" is a relative who is not connected through marriage. Yahweh calls the relative who pays the price the "kinsman," or relative redeemer.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture and language, how do you show the difference between a "blood" relative and a relative through marriage? Pause this audio here.

An Israelite slave can even buy their own freedom if the Israelite slave is able to prosper, or to get enough money or resources to do so. If a person prospers, that person succeeds or is able to get something valuable.

The rich foreigner and the Israelite slave are supposed to decide the price based on how many more years there are until the Year of Jubilee. The Israelite slave will have to pay the wage of a hired worker for however many years are left until the Year of Jubilee. The master, who is a foreigner, is supposed to treat the Israelite slave as a hired worker. This may mean that the foreigner should pay their Israelite slave, or that the foreigner should treat the Israelite slave like the master treats hired workers. Yahweh says to "make sure" that the rich foreigner does not rule over the Israelite slave in a cruel or unjust way. This means that the other Israelite people should watch how the foreigner treats Israelite slaves, to make sure that a foreign master treats Israelite slaves fairly.

Stop here and, if needed, review how you translated the way that someone rules over someone else in a cruel way in the last passage. Pause this audio here.

Even if no one redeems the Israelite slave, the foreign master must free the slave and the slave's family in the Year of Jubilee.

Yahweh says the reason why the masters must do this is that the Israelite people are Yahweh's servants or slaves. Yahweh brought the Israelite people out of slavery in the land of Egypt.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:47–55 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has one scene.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • A rich foreigner
  • A poor Israelite person
  • A relative of the Israelite slave
  • And children of an Israelite slave

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

A rich foreigner who lives in the land of Israel can buy a poor Israelite person. But a relative can redeem the Israelite slave, or the Israelite slave can even pay for their freedom on their own. The rich foreigner and the poor Israelite are supposed to decide the price based on how many more years there are until the Year of Jubilee. The foreign master is supposed to treat the Israelite slave as the master would treat a hired worker. Even if no one redeems the Israelite slave, the master must free the slave and their family in the Year of Jubilee. The reason is that Yahweh brought the Israelite people out of slavery in the land of Egypt.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite slave, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am relieved that Yahweh protects me even with a foreign master; or
  • It is good that my master will release my children along with me in the Year of Jubilee; or
  • I am grateful that my relative was able to redeem me.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 25:47–55 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

Yahweh talks about how a foreigner should treat an Israelite slave. Yahweh again says "your brother Israelite" or "fellow Israelite." "Your brother" was a way that Yahweh talked about fellow Israelites. A foreigner is a person who is from a different people group who lives in another land or territory. Use the same words or phrases for foreigner and for Israelite as you used in previous passages. For more information on foreigner and Israelite, refer to the Master Glossary.

If an Israelite person becomes so poor that the person needs to sell themselves into slavery, a close relative from the person's clan could come and buy the person back. Yahweh calls this relative a "redeemer." Similarly, if the person is able to make money to buy back their freedom, that person may redeem themselves. Yahweh calls this redemption. For more information on redeem, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words or phrases for redeem, redeemer, and clan as you used in previous passages.

The Israelite slaves will become free again during the Year of Jubilee. Use the same word for Year of Jubilee as you used in the previous passage. For more information on the Year of Jubilee, refer to the Master Glossary.

The foreign master must treat the slaves as the master would treat a hired worker. Use the same word for a hired worker as you used in the previous passage.

In this passage, Yahweh gives the Israelite people rules about how to treat slaves. Yahweh says the Israelite people should treat slaves well because the Israelites are servants of Yahweh. In the original language, people used the same word for servant and slave, and used the word to mean different things in different contexts. Use the same words or phrases for slaves and servants as you used in previous passages. For more information on slave and servant, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says, "I am Yahweh your God." Use the same words for Yahweh and God as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh and God, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 26:1–5
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 26:1–5 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 26:1–5 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 26:1–5 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the previous passage, Yahweh spoke to Moses from Mount Sinai and told Moses instructions about how Israelites should respond when an Israelite has to sell land or sell themselves into slavery because of poverty.

Until this time, Yahweh has been telling Moses what Yahweh expects from the Israelite people. Yahweh has chosen the Israelites to be Yahweh's people, and Yahweh is going with the Israelites to the land Yahweh promised to give the Israelites. But Yahweh has expectations for how the Israelites will behave and interact with Yahweh. Now, in this passage and the following ones, Yahweh explains to Moses what will happen to the Israelites if the Israelites follow Yahweh's instructions. Yahweh also explains what will happen if the Israelites do not follow Yahweh's instructions.

In this passage, Yahweh first tells Moses a summary of what Yahweh requires the Israelites to do and not do. The Israelites must not make idols or false gods to worship. The Israelites must not make images to worship, meaning that the Israelites must not create anything in the shape of a person, animal, or object to worship. The Israelites must not set up a pillar to worship, which seems like a common thing that people in neighboring cultures did to worship their gods. Finally, the Israelites must not make any kind of carved stone to bow down to in worship. In the original language, a carved stone may mean some kind of stone that is so amazing that it makes people want to look at it. However, it probably means a stone that someone has carved to look like something the person wants to worship. Yahweh describes all these different things because Yahweh wants to emphasize that the Israelites must not worship any god besides Yahweh. Yahweh also wants to emphasize that the Israelites should not make any kind of object to help the Israelites worship other gods.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What kinds of idols, objects, statues, pictures, or tools do people in your culture use to worship their gods? If people in your culture do not use any items to worship, how do people worship? Pause this audio here.

The Israelites must also observe Yahweh's Sabbaths. This means that the Israelites must observe the Sabbath day of rest every week. The Israelites must also observe the Sabbath year every seven years, where the Israelites let the land rest. The Israelites must also respect Yahweh's sanctuary, or holy place. The sanctuary refers to all of Yahweh's tabernacle or Tent of Meeting. The Israelites must treat the tabernacle and all the area around the tabernacle with respect. Yahweh finishes his summary of instructions by telling Moses to remind the people that Yahweh is Yahweh, the Israelites' God. In other words, the Israelites should not worship other gods, and the Israelites should follow Yahweh's instructions because Yahweh chose the Israelites to be Yahweh's people, so Yahweh is the Israelites' God.

After this summary, Yahweh explains to Moses what will happen to the Israelites if the Israelites obey Yahweh's instructions. If the Israelites obey what Yahweh has said, Yahweh will give the rain the Israelites need at the right time. The Israelites would need good rain to help their crops grow. The seasonal rain will come when the Israelites expect the rain to come. Yahweh will cause the ground to grow crops, and Yahweh will cause the trees to grow fruit. Yahweh means that when the Israelites work in their farms, the farms will grow many crops, and the fruit orchards will grow a lot of fruit. The Israelites' harvests will not fail. The Israelites will be busy with the grain harvest until the grape harvest starts, and the Israelites will harvest the grapes until the Israelites start planting the next grain harvest. The Israelites would harvest grain in the spring and harvest grapes in the late summer and autumn. Yahweh specifically says that the Israelites will thresh the harvest until the grape harvest starts. Threshing is when you separate stalks of grain from the kernels of grain that grow on the stalk by beating the stalk until the grain falls out. People in Israel did this by beating the stalk of grain with a sharp rock or a stick, or by stomping on the grain or having animals stomp on the grain.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of grain. Notice the stalk or stem and the kernel or edible piece. Pause this audio here.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of someone threshing grain. Pause this audio here.

When Yahweh says the Israelites will be threshing the grain harvest until the grape harvest starts, Yahweh does not mean that the Israelites will only be threshing during that time. Instead, Yahweh means that the grain harvest will be very big and healthy. The Israelites will pick the grain and prepare the grain for people to eat by threshing it, and this will take all the time before the grape harvest. Then, the Israelites will harvest grapes until it is time to start planting the next grain harvest. Again, this means that the grape harvest will be very big and healthy. The Israelites will need all the time before planting season to harvest the grapes. The Israelites made their main food, bread, from grain, and the Israelites made their main drink, wine, from grapes. The Israelites will not have to worry about their food or drink because if the Israelites follow Yahweh's instructions, the Israelites' harvests will be so successful that there will be no part of the year when nothing is growing.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your community, what time of year do people harvest crops? Which types of crops do people harvest at which times of year? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh finishes this passage by telling Moses that if the Israelites obey Yahweh's instructions, the Israelites will eat all the food the Israelites want, and the Israelites will live in safety in their land.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 26:1–5 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has two scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells Moses a summary of how Yahweh expects the Israelites to behave regarding idols and Sabbaths.

In the second scene: Yahweh tells Moses what will happen to the Israelite people if the Israelites obey Yahweh's instructions.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In this passage, Yahweh continues to give Moses instructions for the Israelite people from Mount Sinai. Yahweh has just given Moses instructions about what the Israelites should do in Sabbath years, the Years of Jubilee, and when Israelite people have to sell land or sell themselves into slavery because of poverty.

Now, the storyteller begins a new section of the book. At the time the storyteller wrote this book, it was very common for people who wrote sets of laws and instructions to include a section at the end where the storyteller explained consequences. The storyteller would explain what good things would happen to people who obey the instructions and what bad things would happen to people who do not obey the instructions. The book of Leviticus has a section like this, too. This passage starts the section of the book where Yahweh explains what will happen when the Israelite people obey Yahweh's instructions and what will happen when the Israelites do not obey Yahweh's instructions.

In the first scene of this passage, Yahweh starts by summarizing Yahweh's instructions. These are not the only instructions the Israelites must follow if the Israelites want the good things Yahweh is about to describe. Instead, Yahweh is repeating some of the main points of the instructions that Yahweh has given to the Israelites in the previous parts of the book of Leviticus. In this passage, Yahweh specifically mentions that the Israelites must not worship idols or false gods, and the Israelites must not use anything to worship other gods. Yahweh lists four things that people make or use to symbolize other gods or that people use in order to worship other gods. Bible scholars do not all agree on what these things are, but firstly, Yahweh probably says that the Israelites should not make worthless things that people use to worship other gods. Secondly, the Israelites should not make images or statues that represent other gods. Thirdly, the Israelites should not set up stones or pillars as a way to worship other gods. And fourthly, the Israelites should not carve stone into anything that the Israelites want to worship. Yahweh lists all these things to emphasize that the Israelites must not make or use anything to worship false gods.

Stop here and discuss these questions as a group: Think about which words or phrases you will use to talk about these four things that people use to symbolize or worship other gods. Remember that these four things are: worthless things that people use to worship God; an image of something that people make from metal, clay, wood, or stone; a tall stone; and a carved stone. In your language, is it best to list these four things separately or to talk about some or all of these things together? If you include these four things in a list, will people think that the Israelites could create or use anything else to worship false gods? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh gives these instructions because Yahweh is the Israelites' God. Then Yahweh says that the Israelites must follow Yahweh's Sabbaths, so the Israelites must rest on the day of rest each week and let the land rest every seven years. The Israelites must also respect Yahweh's sanctuary, which is Yahweh's holy tabernacle or Tent of Meeting, and the surrounding courtyard. Yahweh gave the exact same instruction about the Sabbaths and Yahweh's sanctuary earlier in Leviticus 19:30.

Stop here and discuss as a group: If you have translated Leviticus 19:30, you can go back and listen to your translation. How did you translate the same instruction in that passage? Pause this audio here.

In the second scene of this passage, Yahweh starts telling Moses about what will happen to the Israelites if they follow and obey Yahweh's statutes and commands. Yahweh says that the Israelites must follow or walk in Yahweh's statutes and commands. When someone walks in certain commands, it means the person listens to the commands and then does what the commands say. When the Israelites obey Yahweh's commands, Yahweh will bless the Israelites' harvests. Yahweh will send rain in the season when the Israelites expect rain, the ground will successfully grow crops, and the trees will successfully grow fruit. In fact, the harvests will be so big and healthy that the Israelites will be busy with the grain harvest until the time when the grape harvest starts. During the grain harvest, the Israelites will pick the grain and also prepare the grain for eating by threshing the grain. By the time the Israelites are done with that, the grape harvest will start. Then, the Israelites will be busy with the grape harvest until the Israelites start to plant the next grain harvest. In other words, the Israelites will have food all year because something will always be growing. Yahweh emphasizes this by telling Moses that the Israelites will eat all the food the Israelites want. Finally, Yahweh tells Moses that the Israelites will live safely in their land.

Stop here and discuss this as a group: Imagine that you are explaining to someone all the things that will happen if that person obeys a certain rule or law. You can use a community rule or a government law. How do you let that person know that all of these things will only happen if that person obeys the law, and these things will not happen if that person does not obey the law? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 26:1–5 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has two scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the Israelite people

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

For the first scene, have the person playing Yahweh tell the person playing Moses the following instructions. Then have the person playing the Israelite people act out how the Israelites follow Yahweh's instructions.

First, Yahweh tells Moses a summary of what the Israelites should do to follow Yahweh's instructions. The Israelites should not worship other gods or use any objects, statues, pillars, stones, or anything else to worship other gods. The Israelites must follow Yahweh's instructions about the Sabbaths. The Israelites must also respect Yahweh's sanctuary, which was the tabernacle or Tent of Meeting.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am confident that I can follow these instructions; or
  • I am nervous that I will not be able to follow all Yahweh's instructions; or
  • I am happy that Yahweh is my God, so I am excited to follow these instructions.
Continue the drama.

Then in the second scene, Yahweh tells Moses what will happen to the Israelites if the Israelites follow Yahweh's instructions. If the Israelites follow all Yahweh's instructions, Yahweh will give the Israelites rain at the right times, and the ground will successfully grow crops, and the trees will successfully grow fruit. Also, if the Israelites follow all Yahweh's instructions, the Israelites will be busy picking and threshing the grain harvest to prepare the harvest for eating all the way until the time when the grape harvest starts. Then the Israelites will be busy harvesting grapes until the time when the Israelites plant the next grain harvest.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelite people, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am content because Yahweh has provided so much food; or
  • I am trusting Yahweh because Yahweh said Yahweh would give us successful harvests; or
  • I am proud that my people followed Yahweh's instructions, and so Yahweh is blessing us.
Continue the drama.

Finally, Yahweh promises Moses that if the Israelites follow all Yahweh's statutes and commands, then the Israelites will eat all the food they want, and the Israelites will live safely in their land.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I love my people, so I am happy to make good things happen for my people; or
  • I am happy my people followed my instructions; or
  • I am glad to see my people enjoying what I give to my people.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 26:1–5 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh first tells Moses a summary of Yahweh's instructions for the Israelite people. For more information on Yahweh and Israelite, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words for Yahweh and Israelite as you used in previous passages.

The Israelite people must not make idols to worship. For more information on idols, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words or phrases for idols as you used in previous passages.

The Israelites also must not use any objects, statues, pillars, stones, or anything to worship other gods. People made images or statues to represent other gods. People set up stones or pillars as a way to worship other gods. People carved stone into anything that the people wanted to worship. The point of listing all of these different things is to say that the Israelites should not worship any god besides Yahweh, and the Israelites should not make any kind of object to help them worship or bow down to other gods. For more information about worship, refer to bow down in the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for worship or bow down as you used in previous passages.

Stop here and discuss what words or phrases you will use for images or statues, pillars, and sacred stones. If you have translated these words in other books of the Bible, discuss whether you can use the same words here. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh says, "I am Yahweh, your God." For more information on God, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word for God as you used in previous passages.

The Israelites must also observe Yahweh's Sabbaths. This means that the Israelites must celebrate the Sabbath day of rest every week and the Israelites must observe the Sabbath year every seven years, when the Israelites let the land rest. For more information about Sabbath, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for Sabbath as you used in previous passages.

The Israelites must also treat Yahweh's sanctuary or holy place with respect. In this passage, the sanctuary is the tabernacle or the Tent of Meeting. For more information about the tabernacle and the sanctuary, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same word or phrase for sanctuary as you used in previous passages. Yahweh also tells Moses to remind the people that Yahweh is Yahweh, the Israelites' God.

After this, Yahweh explains to Moses what will happen to the Israelites if the Israelites follow Yahweh's instructions. Here, Yahweh calls the instructions Yahweh's statutes and commands. For more information on statutes and commandments, refer to the Master Glossary. Use the same words or phrases for statutes or commands as you used in previous passages.

If the Israelites follow Yahweh's statutes and commandments, Yahweh will give the rain the Israelites need at the right time. Yahweh will cause the ground to grow crops, and Yahweh will cause the trees to grow fruit. The Israelites will be busy threshing the grain harvest until the grape harvest starts, and the Israelites will harvest the grapes until the Israelites start planting the grain harvest the next year.

Stop here as a group and look again at a picture of someone threshing grain as needed. What words or phrases will you use for threshing grain? Pause this audio here.

The grain harvest and the grape harvest will be so big and healthy that the Israelites will have food growing all year. Use the same words or phrases to talk about the harvest and grapes as you have used in previous passages.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
