title: Leviticus 27:9–15
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 27:9–15 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:9–15 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:9–15 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In the last passage, Yahweh told the Israelites what to do when the Israelites vowed to give Yahweh a person. In this passage, Yahweh tells the Israelites what to do when the Israelites vow to give an animal or a house to Yahweh.

First, Yahweh talks about an animal that Yahweh will allow the Israelites to sacrifice to Yahweh. Yahweh allows the Israelites to sacrifice cattle, goats, sheep, and doves to Yahweh. Yahweh says that when the Israelites vow to give the animal, the animal becomes holy. Yahweh will not allow any of the Israelites to give Yahweh another animal instead of the one the Israelite vowed to give. The Israelites cannot exchange another animal of the same kind as they promised or another animal of a different kind. The Israelites cannot give an animal that is better or worse than the animal the Israelites promised to give. When Yahweh talks about an animal being worse or better, Yahweh is probably talking about how healthy or big the animal is. Bigger and healthier animals are more valuable than smaller and less healthy animals.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what makes one animal more valuable than another animal? Pause this audio here.

If an Israelite gives Yahweh a different animal instead of the animal the Israelite vowed to give to Yahweh, then the different animal the Israelite gives to Yahweh becomes holy, or dedicated to Yahweh. But the animal that the Israelite first promised to give is also holy. So the Israelite will still need to give the original animal that the Israelite promised to give, even though the Israelite gave a substitute.

If an Israelite makes a vow to give an animal to Yahweh that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to sacrifice to Yahweh, then the Israelite will take the animal to a priest. The priest will look at the animal and decide how much money the animal is worth. Yahweh probably says that whatever the priest decides the value of the animal is, even if the animal is worth a lot or not worth very much, that will be the value of the animal. Yahweh will not allow the Israelite to try to get another priest or someone else to decide how valuable the animal is, even if the Israelite does not like what the priest decides. Yahweh also might mean that the priest will consider both the good qualities and the bad qualities of the animal, and that whatever the priest decides will be the animal's value. If the Israelite wants to buy the animal back from Yahweh, the Israelite needs to pay the animal's value and pay an additional 20 percent, or one-fifth, of the animal's value. Then the Israelite will own the animal again.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people dedicate animals to gods or to a specific purpose? Why do people dedicate these animals? What kinds of animals do people give? How or when can people redeem, or buy back, the animal? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh says that if someone consecrates a house, or makes a house holy by dedicating it to Yahweh, a priest will look at the house and decide how much the house is worth. When someone dedicates a house to Yahweh, the house becomes the property of the priests. Yahweh is probably talking about houses that people own inside large towns or cities. In the next passage, Yahweh will talk about houses that are part of the land that Israelites will receive when Yahweh divides up the land that Yahweh is promising to give the Israelites. The priests might sell the house for money, or a priest might start living in the house.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of an ancient Israelite house in Jerusalem. Pause this audio here.

Yahweh probably says that whatever the priest decides the value of the house is, even if the house is worth a lot or not worth very much, that will be the house's value. Yahweh will not allow the Israelite to try to get another priest or someone else to decide how valuable the house is, even if the Israelite does not like what the priest decides. Yahweh also might mean that the priest will consider both the good qualities and the bad qualities of the house, and that whatever the priest decides will be the value of the house.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, when someone gives away a house, how do people decide how valuable the house is? Pause this audio here.

If the Israelite wants to buy the house back from Yahweh, the Israelite needs to pay the value of the house and pay an additional 20 percent, or one-fifth, of the house's value. Then the Israelite will own the house again.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people dedicate houses to gods or to a specific purpose? Why do people dedicate these houses? What kinds of houses do people give? How or when can people redeem, or buy back, the house?

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:9–15 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh talks about what to do when an Israelite vows to give Yahweh an animal that Yahweh accepts as an offering.

In the second scene: Yahweh talks about what to do when an Israelite vows to give Yahweh an animal that Yahweh does not accept as an offering.

In the third scene: Yahweh tells the Israelites what to do with a house that an Israelite vows to give to Yahweh.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Moses
  • Yahweh
  • The Israelites
  • And a priest

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the previous passage, Yahweh told the Israelites what to do when an Israelite vowed to give a person to Yahweh. In this passage, Yahweh tells the Israelites what to do when an Israelite vows to give an animal or a house to Yahweh. As Yahweh continues to describe people giving an animal as a vow, Yahweh does not use the word for "vow." Moses and the Israelites know what Yahweh is talking about. However, you may need to continue to make it clear that Yahweh is talking about vows in this section. You will remember that Yahweh is talking about vows that the Israelites or people who live with the Israelites give because the people want to; Yahweh is not talking about required offerings or anything else that Yahweh requires the Israelites to do.

In the first scene, Yahweh talks about what to do when an Israelite vows to give an animal to Yahweh. First, Yahweh talks about animals that Yahweh accepts as offerings. Yahweh says that when someone vows to give Yahweh one of these animals, the animal becomes holy, or dedicated to Yahweh. Yahweh will not allow any of the Israelites to give an animal that is different from the animal that the Israelite promised to give to Yahweh. The Israelite cannot exchange the animal for a better or a worse animal. The animal that an Israelite vows to give is holy. If an Israelite tries to give a different animal, that second animal becomes holy too. That means the Israelite still needs to give Yahweh the first animal that the Israelite vowed to give to Yahweh, and the Israelite cannot take back the second animal the Israelite gave to Yahweh instead.

In the second scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites what to do when an Israelite vows to give Yahweh an animal that is unclean or ritually dirty. This is an animal that an Israelite cannot offer to Yahweh as a sacrifice in worship. Sometimes, when Yahweh talks about an animal that is ritually dirty, Yahweh means an animal that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to eat. Here, Yahweh is probably talking about all animals that Yahweh will not allow an Israelite to sacrifice to Yahweh, even if an Israelite can eat the animal.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What is the best way to explain that this is a ritually dirty animal that people cannot sacrifice to Yahweh? Pause this audio here.

The person who vowed to give Yahweh a ritually dirty animal must bring the animal to a priest. The priest will look at the animal and decide how much the animal is worth. Yahweh probably means that whatever the priest decides the animal's value is, even if the animal is worth a lot or not worth very much, that will be the animal's value. Yahweh will not allow the Israelite to try to get another priest or someone else to decide how valuable the animal is, even if the Israelite does not like what the priest decides. Yahweh also might mean that the priest will consider both the good qualities and the bad qualities of the animal, and that whatever the priest decides will be the animal's value.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What is the best way to translate that, whether good or bad, what the priest decides the animal is worth is what the animal is worth? Pause this audio here.

If the Israelite wants to buy back the ritually dirty animal that the Israelite vowed to give to Yahweh, the Israelite needs to pay the value of the animal and an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the animal's value. The Israelite will give that money to a priest. In previous parts of Leviticus, Yahweh told the Israelites to pay for any holy things the Israelites took accidentally by paying those things' value and an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent of the value. In this situation, Yahweh expects the Israelites to redeem, or pay for, animals the Israelites vowed to give to Yahweh in a similar way.

In the third scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites what to do if the Israelites vow to give a house to Yahweh. Yahweh calls this making the house holy, or dedicating the house to Yahweh. The house would probably be a house in a large town or city, not a house in a field. Whatever the priest decides the house is worth will be what the house is worth. Yahweh probably means that whatever the priest decides the value of the house is, even if the house is worth a lot or not worth very much, that will be the value of the house. Yahweh will not allow the Israelite to try to get another priest or someone else to decide how valuable the house is, even if the Israelite does not like what the priest decides. Yahweh also might mean that the priest will consider both the good qualities and the bad qualities of the house, and that whatever the priest decides will be the value of the house.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What is the best way to translate that, whether good or bad, what the priest decides the house is worth is what the house is worth? Pause this audio here.

If the person who dedicated the house to Yahweh wants to buy the house back, that person needs to pay the value of the house and an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the house's value. That person will give that money to a priest. Then the person will own the house again.

Stop here and remember together how you translated the idea of adding an additional 20 percent to the value of something in Leviticus 5:16. Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:9–15 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Moses
  • Yahweh
  • The Israelites
  • And a priest

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites that if a person vows to give Yahweh an animal that Yahweh accepts as a sacrifice, the animal will become holy, or dedicated to Yahweh. The person cannot give another animal instead of the animal that the person vowed to give to Yahweh. The Israelite cannot give an animal that is the same, different, better, or worse than the animal the Israelite vowed to give to Yahweh. If the Israelite gives Yahweh another animal instead of the animal the Israelite vowed to give to Yahweh, the animal the Israelite gives to Yahweh and the animal the Israelite vowed to give to Yahweh will both be holy, or dedicated to Yahweh.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing the Israelites, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I am frustrated because I tried not to give Yahweh the animal that I promised I would, and now I have to give two animals to Yahweh; or
  • Yahweh is very serious about us doing what we vowed to do, so I should think very carefully before I make a vow!
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites that if the Israelites vow to give a ritually dirty animal, then the Israelites need to bring the animal to a priest. The priest will look at the animal and decide how much the animal is worth. Good or bad, whatever the priest decides the animal is worth is what the animal will be worth.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing a priest, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I need to do a good job figuring out how much this animal is worth; or
  • Yahweh trusts me to figure out how much this animal is worth.
Continue the drama.

If the Israelite wants to buy the animal back from Yahweh, the Israelite needs to pay the value of the animal and pay an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the animal's value.

In the third scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites that if an Israelite consecrates a house to Yahweh, a priest will look at the house and figure out how much the house is worth. Good or bad, whatever the priest decides the house is worth is what the house will be worth. If the Israelite who dedicated the house to Yahweh wants to buy the house back from Yahweh, the Israelite needs to pay the value of the house and pay an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the value of the house. Then the Israelite will own the house again.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I love it when people dedicate things because of how grateful those people are and how much they trust me; or
  • I am very serious about when people vow to give me things; or
  • I want people to realize how important I am, so I want the people to take vows seriously.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:9–15 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh tells the Israelites what to do when the Israelites vow to give animals and houses to Yahweh. When a person makes a vow, that person promises to do something for Yahweh. Yahweh does not use the word vow because Yahweh expects the Israelites to know that Yahweh is still talking about vows like Yahweh was in the last passage. Many translations of this passage do use the word vow here. If the addition of the word vow would be useful for clarity in your translation, use it. Use the same word or phrase for vow as you used in previous passages. For more information on vow, refer to the Master Glossary.

People can give Yahweh animals that Yahweh will allow the people to offer. When a person offers something, that person gives it to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for offering as you used in previous passages. For more information on offering, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Israelites give the animals to Yahweh. Yahweh is the personal name that the one true God gave the Israelites to call God. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

The animal that the person vowed to give to Yahweh becomes holy. Any place, person, or object that is dedicated to God is holy. That means that the object or person is set apart for God's special purposes. That object or thing is no longer "common" or "ordinary." People can no longer use that holy thing for common or ordinary purposes. Use the same word or phrase for holy as you used in previous passages. For more information on holy, refer to the Master Glossary.

If a person vows to give something to Yahweh, a priest looks at that thing. Priests were responsible for offering sacrifices to Yahweh on behalf of the people. The priests also took care of the tabernacle and taught people how to worship Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for priest as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh also talks about when an Israelite sacrifices an animal that is unclean or ritually dirty. If Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to eat an animal, that animal is ritually dirty. Sometimes, if Yahweh will not accept an animal as an offering, people call that animal ritually dirty. For more information on clean and unclean, refer to the Master Glossary.

An Israelite might want to redeem, or pay for, an animal that is ritually dirty. When someone redeems a person, animal, or thing, the person pays money to the person who owns that person, animal, or thing so that the second person will give up the person, animal, or thing. Use the same word or phrase for redeem as you used in previous passages. For more information on redeem, refer to the Master Glossary.

A person can also consecrate a house. If a person consecrates something, the thing becomes holy. Use the same word or phrase for consecrate as you used in previous passages. For more information on consecrate, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 27:16–25
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 27:16–25 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:16–25 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:16–25 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

Yahweh has been telling the Israelites what to do when the Israelites vow to give things to Yahweh. Yahweh also calls this consecrating, or making something holy.

In this passage, Yahweh talks about what the Israelites need to do when the Israelites consecrate land that the Israelites inherited. This would be land that is supposed to stay with the same family forever, as people gave it to their children or closest relatives. When a person consecrated this land, the person probably continued to work the land, and the person gave the grain that the land produced to the priests.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people decide who owns what land? Pause this audio here.

Also, stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people inherit or receive land from their relatives who die? How important is the land? How important is it to keep the land in the family? Pause this audio here.

If an Israelite consecrates any of the land the Israelite inherited, a priest needs to decide how valuable the land is. Yahweh says that the priest will decide the value of the land based on the opening of its seed. Yahweh probably means that the priest needs to determine how valuable the land is based on how much seed someone needs to use to sow the whole field. Yahweh might also mean that the priest needs to determine how valuable the land is based on how much seed the land produces. To the Israelites, land was primarily valuable based on how many crops a person could grow on it.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what do people mostly use land for? Pause this audio here.

Also, stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people decide how valuable a specific section of land is? Pause this audio here.

The land will be worth 50 shekels of silver for every homer of barley seed that a person can sow on the land at a time. A shekel was a weight that the Israelites used. The Israelites mostly used the weight to measure silver. Since people used silver as money, people based how valuable something was on how many shekels of silver people would pay for that thing. A shekel weighed around 11.4 grams, so 50 shekels was about 575 grams of silver.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a shekel of silver. Pause this audio here.

A homer is a measurement of how much space something took up, and Israelites used it to measure grain. Scholars disagree on how much grain a homer measured. A homer was the amount that a donkey could carry. Some scholars think that a homer of barley weighed 220 kilograms, while others think that a homer weighed 400 kilograms. If a homer weighed 300 kilograms, then the value of the field was about 1 gram of silver for every 52 grams of barley seed that a person needed to use to sow the field. This was probably a reasonable price for a field, though it might be a low price for a field. Barley seed was the cheapest crop that a person could grow in Israel, and both people and animals ate this crop.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of barley seed. Pause this audio here.

If an Israelite consecrates the field on the Year of Jubilee, then the value of the field will be 50 shekels for every homer of barley, as Yahweh said earlier. But if the person consecrates the field after the Year of Jubilee, then the priests will decide how much less the field is worth based on the number of years until the next Year of Jubilee, and the priest will reduce the value of the field by that much. You will remember that in the Year of Jubilee, any land that an Israelite sold to someone else or consecrated to Yahweh returns back to the people or the families that sold the land, so the value goes down because the field will produce fewer crops before the land returns to its original owner. Since the price of the field was 50 shekels per homer of barley seed and there are 50 years between each Year of Jubilee, the priest probably reduced the value of the field by 1 shekel per homer of barley seed for each year after the Year of Jubilee.

If the person who consecrated the field wants to redeem the field, or buy the field back, then that person needs to pay the value of the field and an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent of the value of the field. Then the person will own the field again. If the person does not buy back the field before the Year of Jubilee, then that person will not ever be able to buy back the field after the Year of Jubilee. That person will also not be able to buy back the field if that person sells the field to someone else. Because a person probably still worked the land that they dedicated to the priests, the person might sell the land to someone else so that another person would work the land. When the Year of Jubilee happens, Yahweh will totally dedicate the field to himself, and the field will belong to the priests. No normal Israelite will ever be able to use the land again.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, what things do people completely devote to a god or spirit or person? How do people treat those things that people devoted? Pause this audio here.

Sometimes people bought land that their family did not own before. If someone consecrates a field to Yahweh that the person bought, then a priest will figure out how much the field is worth based on how many years remain until the Year of Jubilee. The person who dedicates the field will have to pay how much the field is worth on the day that the priest decides how much the field is worth. The money that the person pays will be holy money devoted to Yahweh. Then, when the Year of Jubilee happens, the person who originally owned the field and sold it to the person who dedicated it to Yahweh will own the field again, since it is their property.

Then, Yahweh gives the standard of payment, or the standard value of the shekel. Yahweh gives this important information to explain how much money people need to pay for things that people have dedicated to Yahweh. Yahweh says that whenever a priest determines the value of something, the priests will measure the value in shekels that weighed as much as the priests in the holy place decided a shekel should weigh. Yahweh also says that a shekel will weigh the same amount as 20 gerahs. A gerah was another measurement of weight. The only thing we know about a gerah is that it weighed one-twentieth, or 5 percent, of a shekel's weight, which means it probably weighed a little more than half a gram.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:16–25 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has three scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells the Israelites what to do when the Israelites dedicate land they inherited to Yahweh.

In the second scene: Yahweh tells the Israelites what to do when the Israelites dedicate land they bought to Yahweh.

In the third scene: Yahweh tells the Israelites how to measure the value of things they dedicate to Yahweh.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Moses
  • A landowner who consecrates inherited land to Yahweh and redeems that land
  • A landowner who consecrates inherited land to Yahweh but does not redeem that land
  • Yahweh
  • A priest
  • A landowner who sells land that the landowner had already consecrated to Yahweh
  • A person who buys land that the landowner had already consecrated to Yahweh
  • A person who buys land and then consecrates that land
  • And the original owner of the land that someone bought and then consecrated

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In previous passages, Yahweh has told the Israelites what to do when the Israelites vow to give a person or an animal to Yahweh, and what to do when the Israelites consecrate a house to Yahweh. In this passage, Yahweh tells the Israelites what to do when the Israelites consecrate land to Yahweh, whether the Israelites bought that land or inherited that land. Remember that the Israelites are at a place called Mount Sinai in a wilderness area without any cities or villages nearby. Yahweh has promised to give the Israelites the land of Canaan, and when Yahweh does give the Israelites the land of Canaan, Yahweh will give each family a specific part of the land that will belong to that family forever. The children in each new generation will inherit the land. Even if a person who inherits land sells that land to someone else, that person will only have control of the land until the Year of Jubilee. Inherited land is any land that a person owns because Yahweh has given that land to their family.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What is the best way to translate the idea of land that people inherit? Pause this audio here.

When a person dedicates, or consecrates, a field they inherited to Yahweh, the person probably continues to grow crops on the field, and the person just gives the crops they grow to Yahweh by giving the crops to the priests. When a person consecrates land that they inherited to Yahweh, or dedicates that land to Yahweh, a priest will look at the land and determine how valuable it is. The priest will decide the value of the land based on the opening of its seed. Yahweh probably means that the priest needs to determine how valuable the land is based on how much seed the owner needs to use to sow the whole field at one time. Yahweh might also mean that the priest needs to determine how valuable the land is based on how much seed the land produces.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What is the best way for you to translate that the value of the land is based on the opening of its seed? Pause this audio here.

The land will be worth 50 shekels of silver for every homer of barley seed. This is probably a very low cost for the land, because Yahweh wants the Israelites to be able to redeem, or buy back, the land. Because Yahweh decides that the land will go back to the families Yahweh gave the land to every Year of Jubilee, Yahweh bases the value of the land on how much a person can grow on the land before the Year of Jubilee. So if the person dedicates the land to Yahweh on the Year of Jubilee, then the field will be the full price Yahweh just said: 50 shekels of silver for every homer of barley seed that a person needs to use to sow the field at one time. But if the person dedicates the land to Yahweh after the Year of Jubilee, then the priest needs to lower the value of the land based on how many years are left until the next Year of Jubilee, and the value of the land will be reduced by what the priest decides. The priest will probably reduce the price by 1 shekel per homer of barley that a person needs to use to sow the field at one time. If the person who dedicated the land wants to redeem the land, or buy it back from Yahweh, that person needs to pay the priests the value of the land and an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the value of the land. Then the person who dedicated the land to Yahweh will own the land again.

Stop here and remind each other as a group how you will translate an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the value of something. Pause this audio here.

But if the person does not buy back the land before the next Year of Jubilee, then that person and their family will not be able to buy back the land ever again. If the person sells the land that they dedicated to Yahweh to someone else, then the person and their family will not be able to buy back the land ever again. Instead, when the Year of Jubilee happens, the field will become completely devoted to Yahweh, and no person except the priests will be able to own it again. When Yahweh completely devotes the field to himself, the situation is similar to when a field is holy. But when Yahweh completely devotes something to himself, Yahweh expects most people to never use the thing again in any way. In most situations where Yahweh completely devotes something to himself, Yahweh makes the Israelites destroy the thing Yahweh has completely devoted to himself. In this case, when Yahweh completely devotes a field to himself, the priests will own that field forever.

In the second scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites that if someone dedicates a field that they bought to Yahweh, then a priest will decide how much the field is worth. The priest will decide how many years are left before the Year of Jubilee happens, and will use that to determine the field's value. Then the person who dedicated the field to Yahweh will pay the value of the field on the same day that the priest decides how valuable the field is. The money the person pays will be holy to Yahweh. A person who buys and then dedicates a piece of land to Yahweh may not want to redeem the land as quickly as the person who inherits land and then dedicates it to Yahweh. A person who inherits land must redeem the land, or else that person risks losing the land forever. A person who buys land will lose that land anyway at the Year of Jubilee, so that person may not feel that they need to hurry to redeem the land. So Yahweh tells that person to pay to redeem the field the same day the person dedicates it.

When the Year of Jubilee does happen, the field that the person bought and then dedicated to Yahweh will become the property of the original owner or the original owner's family, because it is the land Yahweh gave the original owner's family.

In the third scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites that every time the Israelites determine the value of something that the Israelites are going to dedicate to Yahweh, the Israelites need to measure that thing in shekels that weigh as much as the priests in the sanctuary say the shekels should weigh. Yahweh also says that 20 gerahs weigh as much as a shekel. The Bible only mentions a gerah when it says that a shekel is 20 gerahs. Since a shekel is a relatively small amount, a gerah is probably the smallest measurement of weight that the Israelites used.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What is the best way to translate "gerah"? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:16–25 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has three scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Moses
  • A landowner who consecrates inherited land to Yahweh and redeems that land
  • A landowner who consecrates inherited land to Yahweh but does not redeem that land
  • Yahweh
  • A priest
  • A landowner who sells land that the landowner had already consecrated to Yahweh
  • A person who buys land that the landowner had already consecrated to Yahweh
  • A person who buys land and then consecrates that land
  • And the original owner of the land that someone bought and then consecrated

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh gives the Israelites an example situation. In this example situation, an Israelite consecrates, or makes holy, the land the Israelite inherited to Yahweh. When the Israelite consecrates the land they inherited, a priest will decide how valuable the land is. The priest will decide the value of the field based on how many barley seeds you need to use to sow it at one time. A field is worth 50 shekels of silver for every homer of barley seed a person needs to use to sow the field at one time. If an Israelite consecrates a field on the Year of Jubilee, then the field will be worth what Yahweh just said it was worth. But if the Israelite consecrates the field after the Year of Jubilee, then the priest will decide what the price will be. The priest will decide the value of the field based on the number of years that remain until the Year of Jubilee, and the priest will reduce the price by the appropriate amount. If the Israelite wants to redeem the field, then the Israelite needs to pay for the value of the field they consecrated and an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the value of the field. Then the Israelite will own the field again.

If the person does not redeem the field or the person sells it to someone else, then no one will be able to redeem the field. On the Year of Jubilee, the field will become completely devoted to Yahweh, and only the priests will ever be able to own that field.

Pause the drama.

Ask the landowner who consecrates inherited land to Yahweh but does not redeem it, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I really appreciate how Yahweh takes care of me, so I dedicated a field to Yahweh; or
  • I really wanted more money after I dedicated my land to Yahweh, so I sold the land to someone else. Now I will never get my land back; or
  • I forgot to redeem my land, and now I will never own that land again; or
  • I am so upset because my family will never own this land again; or
  • The land was very cheap to buy back, but I did not do it; or
  • Yahweh really cares that people are responsible with the things that people dedicate to Yahweh.
Continue the drama.

In the second scene, Yahweh gives another situation. In this situation, an Israelite dedicates a field that they bought to Yahweh, a field that the Israelite did not inherit. In this situation, a priest will figure out how valuable the field is. The priest will figure out the value of the field based on how many years until the Year of Jubilee happens. The person who dedicates the field to Yahweh will have to pay the value of the field on the day that the priest decides the value of the field. The money the person pays for the field will be holy to Yahweh. On the Year of Jubilee, the person who originally owned the field will own the field again. This person, who originally owned the field, owned the field before the other Israelite bought the field and then dedicated the field to Yahweh. The original owner will own the field again because it is the land Yahweh gave the original owner.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I really want families to continue to be able to use the land that I will give them; or
  • I love it when people dedicate things to me to show how much the people love and trust me; or
  • I want people to be able to dedicate their fields to me without worrying about losing their fields forever.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh talks about when people determine the value of something that people give to Yahweh. Yahweh requires people to measure the value of something that people give to Yahweh in shekels. These shekels need to weigh what the priests in the sanctuary decide a shekel should weigh. One shekel is worth twenty gerahs.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:16–25 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh talks about when people consecrate something to Yahweh. When someone consecrates something, that person dedicates that thing, or makes that thing holy, to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for consecrate as you used in previous passages. For more information on consecrate, refer to the Master Glossary.

The Israelites consecrate things to Yahweh. Yahweh is the personal name that the one true God gave to the Israelites to call God. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh says that a field will be worth 50 shekels of silver for every homer of barley that a person can plant in it at one time. A shekel is a unit of measurement that equals 11.4 grams. People used shekels as money. Use the same word or phrase for shekel as you used in previous passages. For more information on shekel, refer to the Master Glossary.

Stop here as a group and look at a picture of a shekel again. Pause this audio here.

A homer was a unit of volume, or how much space something was, that equaled what a donkey could carry. A homer might have been about 150 liters. A homer of barley might have weighed around 300 kilograms, but scholars have a lot of different ideas about how big a homer of barley is.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for homer. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

Barley is a plant that the Israelites grew. Barley produces seeds. The Israelites would sometimes eat the seeds. The Israelites would mostly grind the seeds into a powder and mix the powder with water and oil, or just water, or just oil. The mixture would become a dough, and the Israelites cooked that dough over a fire to make bread. Then the Israelites ate the bread. Barley fields produced more seeds than other plants. But when people made bread from barley, the bread was worse than when people made bread from other plants.

Stop here and look again at the photo of barley seeds. Discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for barley. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

A priest decides how much a field is worth. The priests were the people who taught the Israelites how to worship Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for priest as you used in previous passages. For more information on priest, refer to the Master Glossary.

The priest will decide the value of the field based on how many years until the Year of Jubilee. Every 50 years, Yahweh expected the Israelites to have a year-long holiday. During this holiday, any inherited land that someone had sold becomes their land again. Use the same word or phrase for Year of Jubilee as you used in previous passages. For more information on Year of Jubilee, refer to the Master Glossary.

A person who consecrates a field can redeem that field, or buy the field back from Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for redeem as you used in previous passages. For more information on redeem, refer to the Master Glossary.

The money, or shekels, a person uses to pay for a field that they dedicated to Yahweh is holy. Any place, person, or object that is dedicated to God is holy. That means that the object or person is set apart for God's special purposes. That person or object is no longer "common" or "ordinary," and people can no longer use them for common or ordinary purposes. Use the same word or phrase for holy as you used in previous passages. For more information on holy, refer to the Master Glossary.

If a person sells a field that they dedicated to Yahweh, then Yahweh will completely devote the field to himself. When Yahweh completely devotes something to himself, Yahweh does not allow any common person to use it. If Yahweh completely devotes a person, animal, or object to himself, Yahweh makes the Israelites kill the person or animal or destroy the object. If Yahweh completely devotes a field to himself, the priests use that field.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for completely devoted. If you have already translated this idea in another book of the Bible, use the same word or phrase that you have used there. Pause this audio here.

The shekels need to weigh as much as the priests in the sanctuary decide the shekels should weigh. The sanctuary was the holy place that the people went to when the people wanted to make sacrifices to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for sanctuary as you used in previous passages. For more information on sanctuary, refer to the Master Glossary.

A shekel is as much as 20 gerahs. A gerah was a unit of weight, and it probably weighed about half a gram.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for gerah. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, use the same word that you have used there.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.

title: Leviticus 27:26–34
content:
Hear and Heart

In this step, hear Leviticus 27:26–34 and put it in your hearts.

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:26–34 three times, in three different translations, if possible.

Pause this audio here.

Now, as a group, discuss the following questions:

  1. What do you like in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  2. What do you not like or not understand in this passage? Pause this audio here.
  3. What does this passage tell us about God? Pause this audio here.
  4. What does this passage tell us about people? Pause this audio here.
  5. How does this passage affect our daily lives? Pause this audio here.
  6. Who do you know who needs to hear this passage?

Setting the Stage

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:26–34 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In previous passages, Yahweh has been talking about things that people vowed to give to Yahweh. In this passage, Yahweh talks about things that already belong to Yahweh.

First, Yahweh says that the first time an animal gives birth, an Israelite cannot dedicate that baby animal to Yahweh, because that baby animal already belongs to Yahweh. Yahweh had said earlier that the first time any animal gives birth, that animal's baby belongs to Yahweh. Whether the baby animal is an ox, a goat, or a sheep, that baby animal already belongs to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people treat the firstborn animal? Pause this audio here.

If the animal is an unclean or ritually dirty animal, then Yahweh will allow the person who owns the animal to buy it back from Yahweh. When Yahweh says the animal is ritually dirty, Yahweh probably means it is an animal that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to sacrifice, not just an animal the Israelites must not eat. Again, the priests determine how much the animal is worth. If a person wants to redeem the animal, that person needs to pay that amount as well as an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of that amount. If the person does not redeem the animal, then the priests will sell the animal for the original amount.

Then Yahweh says that if a person owns something and that person completely devotes that thing to Yahweh, then the person cannot sell the thing and the person cannot buy the thing back. If a person completely devotes a human, animal, or inherited land to Yahweh, then no one can take it back. Anything that a person completely devotes to Yahweh becomes one of the most holy or most dedicated things to Yahweh. However, if any human being becomes completely devoted to destruction, no one can buy that person or save that person; the Israelites need to execute that person. Sometimes Yahweh completely devotes a person to himself, because that person has murdered someone or is a prisoner of war. For example, Yahweh later completely devotes the city of Jericho to himself after the Israelites start to conquer the land that Yahweh is giving to the Israelites. Yahweh tells the Israelites to kill every person and animal in Jericho and destroy every object.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people completely devote things to a god or some special purpose? What sorts of things do people completely devote? Pause this audio here.

Then Yahweh says that all the tithes from what the land produces are holy to Yahweh. When the Israelites produced food, Yahweh expected the Israelites to give one tenth, or 10 percent, of the food to Yahweh, which Yahweh called a tithe. This reminds the Israelites that Yahweh owns everything in the land that Yahweh gave to the Israelites. The Israelites give one-tenth of their grain or fruit to the priests and the Levites, or the Israelites give it to poor people and widows and orphans and foreigners. All the tithe from the crops that grow up from the ground and all the fruit that the trees produce are holy to Yahweh. If anyone wants to buy their tithes back from Yahweh, then that person needs to pay the value of the tithe and an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of the value of the tithe.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people give to support priests or poor people? What sorts of things do people give? Pause this audio here.

When someone tithes a herd of cattle or a flock of sheep or a flock of goats, the animals the person tithes are holy to Yahweh. Yahweh says that the Israelites must give to Yahweh every tenth animal that passes under the shepherd's staff. People who owned herds or flocks would probably count their animals with their shepherd's staff. A shepherd's staff is a long stick that the shepherds would use to help themselves walk and to fight wild animals. The shepherd would probably hold their staff over the animals as they walked and count each one as the animals passed under the staff. Yahweh tells the Israelites to set aside every tenth animal when the Israelites count the animals like this, so that the Israelites can tithe these animals to Yahweh.

Stop here as a group and look at the picture of a shepherd's staff. Pause this audio here.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: In your culture, how do people count the animals that those people own? How do people direct or herd their animals? Are there any tools that people use that are similar to a staff? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh required the person who owns the herd or the flock to give Yahweh every tenth animal that the person counted when the person counted their animals, so the person could tithe the animals. You will remember that cattle were the animals in a herd, and sheep and goats were the animals in a flock. Yahweh did not expect the person who owned the herd or flock to give Yahweh every tenth animal every time the person counted their animals. Yahweh only expected the person who owned the herd or flock to give Yahweh every tenth animal that they counted occasionally. People do not know how often the Israelites counted their animals. The Israelites may not choose which animals, whether the best or the worst animals, from the flock. Yahweh also will not allow the Israelites to give Yahweh another animal instead of the animal the Israelites were supposed to tithe. If someone gives Yahweh another animal instead of the animal the person was supposed to give Yahweh, then both of the animals will be holy, or dedicated to Yahweh. Yahweh will not allow the person to buy back either of the animals from Yahweh.

Finally, the storyteller of Leviticus says that these are all the commandments that Yahweh gave Moses on Mount Sinai for the Israelites.

Defining the Scenes

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:26–34 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will define the scenes, characters, and setting of this passage. Then the group will visualize this passage.

This passage has four scenes.

In the first scene: Yahweh tells the Israelites that the Israelites cannot consecrate, or dedicate, a firstborn animal to Yahweh.

In the second scene: Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to redeem anything that is completely devoted to Yahweh.

In the third scene: Yahweh tells the Israelites about both crop and animal tithes and how to redeem their crop tithes.

In the fourth scene: The storyteller sums up both this passage and the book of Leviticus.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • A person completely devoted to Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the Israelites

As a group, pay attention to these parts of the passage's setting:

In the previous scenes, Yahweh has told the Israelites what to do when the Israelites vow to give Yahweh something, such as a person, an animal, or a house. Yahweh also calls this "consecrating" the thing, or making it holy to Yahweh. In this passage, Yahweh talks about some of the things that already belong to Yahweh.

In the first scene, Yahweh explains that the firstborn animals already belong to Yahweh, so the Israelites cannot choose those animals to dedicate to Yahweh. When an animal that an Israelite owns gives birth to her first baby, the Israelite must give the baby to Yahweh. All the firstborn cattle, sheep, and goats belong to Yahweh. If the animal is ritually dirty, then the Israelites can buy it back. When Yahweh says the animal is ritually dirty, Yahweh probably means that Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to sacrifice the animal, not that it is one of the animals that the Israelites cannot eat. Again, the priests determine the value of the animal or how much the animal is worth. If a person wants to redeem the animal, that person needs to pay that amount as well as an additional one-fifth, or 20 percent, of that amount. If the person does not redeem the animal, then the priests will sell the animal for the original amount.

In the second scene, Yahweh will not allow a person to sell or redeem anything that the person has completely devoted to Yahweh. No one can sell or redeem any human or animal or inherited property that someone has completely devoted to Yahweh. The things that a person completely devotes to Yahweh become the things that are most holy, most special to Yahweh. Most of the time, when something gets completely devoted to Yahweh, Yahweh tells the Israelites to destroy it in some way. Yahweh does not require the Israelites to destroy inherited land; instead, the priests own any land that is completely devoted to Yahweh, and no one else may use that land. If a person becomes completely devoted to Yahweh, then Yahweh will require the Israelites to kill that person. Some translations call this "devoted to destruction."

In the third scene, Yahweh tells the Israelites how to redeem the crops that they tithe to Yahweh. When people tithe something to Yahweh, the people give one-tenth of that thing. So if a person has 100 sheep, the person will give 10 of the sheep to Yahweh. Yahweh has already told the Israelites to tithe to Yahweh earlier, in the book of Exodus. First, Yahweh tells the Israelites that everything the Israelites tithe, one-tenth of all the crops and all the fruit that the Israelites will produce in the land that Yahweh will give to them, is holy to Yahweh. When Yahweh talks about the crops and the fruit from the trees, Yahweh is using special language to talk about every plant that the Israelites grow. Crops and fruit trees were the most common plants the Israelites grew, so when Yahweh talked about these things, the Israelites would know Yahweh was talking about all the plants the Israelites grew in the land.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What is the best way to translate when Yahweh says that the Israelites will tithe from the crops and the fruit of the trees? Pause this audio here.

If anyone wants to redeem the tithe of their crops, the person needs to buy the crops back from Yahweh by paying the value of the crops and an additional 20 percent, or one-fifth, of the value of the crops.

Then, Yahweh tells the Israelites that all the tithes from their herds and flocks will be holy to Yahweh. In other words, the Israelites cannot redeem the animals that the Israelites tithe to Yahweh. Yahweh says also that the tithes are every tenth animal that passes under the shepherd's staff. When the Israelites counted their animals, the Israelites probably made the animals walk one at a time under their staff so the Israelites could count the animals.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: What is the best way to talk about the animals walking under a shepherd's staff so the shepherd can count the animals? How would you talk about the way that you count animals? Pause this audio here.

Yahweh will not allow the Israelites who tithe their animals to try to decide if the animals the Israelites are giving to Yahweh are good or bad. Yahweh also will not allow the Israelites to try to give Yahweh another animal instead of every tenth animal that walks under the shepherd's staff. If an Israelite gives Yahweh another animal instead of one of the animals that the Israelites are supposed to tithe to Yahweh, then both the animals will be holy to Yahweh. Yahweh will not allow the person to redeem, or buy back, either of the animals.

In the fourth scene, the storyteller of Leviticus sums up the book of Leviticus. The storyteller says that these are the commands, or commandments, that Yahweh gave to Moses on Mount Sinai, so that Moses could give those laws to the Israelites.

Stop here and discuss this question as a group: Tell a story about a time someone gave a lot of rules to a group. How did that person finish giving the rules? Pause this audio here.

Now, the group should storyboard, draw, or use objects to visualize the passage and the action in it.

Embodying the Text

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:26–34 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will dramatize the passage.

This passage has four scenes.

The characters in this passage are:

  • Yahweh
  • A person completely devoted to Yahweh
  • Moses
  • And the Israelites

As a group, act out the passage twice. You should act out the passage in your own language.

First, act out the passage without stopping. Pay attention to the dialogue, flow, plotline, and chronology of the passage. Make sure you do not skip acting out the difficult or important parts of the passage. Help each other remember every part of the passage.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage.

The group should act out this passage a second time. At certain points in the drama, pause the drama and ask the person playing the character, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person playing the character should answer what they would be feeling or thinking if they were that character. Then continue the drama.

Pause this audio here and act out the passage a second time.

The following is an example of the drama and possible responses.

In the first scene, Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to consecrate any firstborn animal to Yahweh because Yahweh already owns all firstborn animals, whether they are cattle, sheep, or goats. Yahweh says again that all firstborn animals are Yahweh's. If the firstborn animal is a ritually dirty animal, then Yahweh will allow the Israelite who originally owned the animal to buy the animal back. That Israelite must pay the value of the animal and an additional 20 percent, or one-fifth, of the value of the animal. If the Israelite who originally owned the animal does not buy back the animal, then the priests will sell the animal for the value the priests decided the animal is worth.

In the second scene, Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to sell or redeem any of the animals, humans, or inherited property that someone completely devoted to Yahweh. The people and animals and inherited property that someone completely devotes to Yahweh are very holy. If Yahweh completely devotes a human to Yahweh, Yahweh will not allow anyone to ransom that human, or pay to save that human. Yahweh will require the Israelites to execute that human.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing Yahweh, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • The Israelites need to understand how much I want the people to execute a bad person sometimes; or
  • The Israelites will realize how holy I am when the Israelites treat the things that are completely devoted to me the right way; or
  • I do not want the Israelites to try to take things that I own from me.
Continue the drama.

In the third scene, Yahweh says that one tenth, or 10 percent, of all the crops the Israelites produce in their land will belong to Yahweh. The crops include both the plants that the Israelites grow from the ground and harvest, and the plants that produce fruit that the Israelites pick. All these crops are holy to Yahweh. If an Israelite wants to buy back any of the tithes of the crops, the Israelite needs to pay Yahweh the value of the tithe and an additional 20 percent, or one-fifth, of the value of the crops.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing an Israelite, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I love Yahweh, and I am glad to give Yahweh one-tenth of the crops that Yahweh causes to grow; or
  • I am glad Yahweh will let me buy back the crops that I want to keep; or
  • Yahweh really wants us to respect the part of our crops that we tithe to Yahweh.
Continue the drama.

Then Yahweh says that all the tithes of the herds and the flocks that the Israelites own will be holy to Yahweh. The tithes of the animals will be every tenth animal that walks under the shepherd's staff as the people count the animals. The Israelites can not choose the best or the worst animals from the flock to tithe. Yahweh will also not allow the Israelites to give Yahweh another animal instead of any of the animals that the Israelites decided to give Yahweh as a tithe. An Israelite might try to give Yahweh another animal instead of the animal the Israelite had originally decided to give Yahweh as a tithe. If so, the animal the Israelite gives, as well as the animal that the Israelite had originally decided to give as a tithe, will be holy. That Israelite cannot buy back either animal.

Pause the drama.

Ask the person playing an Israelite, "What are you feeling or thinking?" The person might answer things like:

  • I wanted to give Yahweh a worse animal than the one I originally decided to tithe to Yahweh; or
  • I should not have tried to cheat Yahweh; or
  • I feel sad because now I have to give two animals to Yahweh instead of one.
Continue the drama.

In the fourth scene, the storyteller of Leviticus says that these are the commandments that Yahweh gave to Moses on Mount Sinai so that Moses could give the commandments to the Israelites.

Filling the Gaps

Listen to an audio version of Leviticus 27:26–34 in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this step, the group will discuss key terms and words in this passage.

In this passage, Yahweh tells the Israelites that firstborn animals belong to Yahweh. Yahweh is the personal name that the one true God gave to the Israelites to call God. Use the same word or phrase for Yahweh as you used in previous passages. For more information on Yahweh, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to consecrate the firstborn animals, or make the animals holy to Yahweh, because the animals already belong to Yahweh. When someone makes something holy, the person dedicates that thing to Yahweh so that Yahweh, instead of that person, can use that thing. Use the same word or phrase for consecrate as you used in previous passages. For more information on consecrate, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh mentions cattle and sheep. Remember that cattle refers to both male and female cows. Use the same words or phrases for cattle and sheep as you have used previously.

Firstborn unclean animals also belong to Yahweh. Unclean animals are ritually dirty, and Yahweh will not allow the Israelites to sacrifice these animals to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for unclean as you used in previous passages. For more information on unclean, refer to clean and unclean in the Master Glossary.

An Israelite can ransom a ritually dirty animal that the Israelite owned and dedicated to Yahweh. When someone ransoms an animal or a person, that person pays for that person or animal to go free. In this context, the ideas of ransom and redeem are very similar. Ransom is more focused on getting the person or animal back to their original owner or family. Redeem is more focused on paying a price to free a person or animal. Use the same word or phrase for ransom as you used in previous passages. For more information on ransom, refer to the Master Glossary.

Yahweh also says that the Israelites can redeem a ritually dirty animal that someone dedicates to Yahweh. When someone redeems a person or animal that the person had owned, the person pays money to buy back the person or animal. Use the same word or phrase for redeem as you used in previous passages. For more information on redeem, refer to the Master Glossary.

Sometimes someone will completely devote a person, animal, object, or piece of land to Yahweh. When someone completely devotes something to Yahweh, Yahweh does not allow any common person to use that thing. If someone completely devotes a person or animal or object to Yahweh, Yahweh makes the Israelites kill the person or animal or destroy the object. If Yahweh completely devotes a field to himself, the priests use that field. Yahweh will not allow anyone to redeem or ransom a person, animal, object, or piece of land that someone has completely devoted to Yahweh. Use the same word or phrase for completely devote as you used in previous passages.

People, animals, objects, and land that someone completely devotes to Yahweh are very holy to Yahweh. When something is holy, that thing is devoted to Yahweh, and Yahweh will not allow anyone to use it for common things. Use the same word or phrase for holy as you used in previous passages. For more information on holy, refer to the Master Glossary.

Animals of the Israelites' herds and flocks walk under the shepherds' staff so that people can count the animals. The animals in herds are cattle, and the animals in flocks are sheep and goats. Use the same words or phrases for herds and flocks as you have used in previous passages.

The tithes are also holy to Yahweh. When people give tithes, people give one-tenth of the things they grow or make to Yahweh.

Stop here and discuss as a group what word or phrase you will use for tithe. Look up tithe in the Master Glossary for more information. If you have already translated this word in another book of the Bible, decide if the same word is appropriate to use here. Pause this audio here.

These are the commandments that Yahweh gave Moses on Mount Sinai so that Moses could give them to the Israelites. A commandment is a law, a rule, or an instruction. Use the same word or phrase for commandment as you used in previous passages. For more information on commandment, refer to the Master Glossary.

Speaking the Word

Listen to an audio version of the passage in the easiest-to-understand translation.

Pause this audio here.

In this session, retell the passage, as a group, in your own language.

First, the whole group should practice telling the passage in your own language. Remember to include the things you decided in previous steps, like chronology, words, phrases, emotions, or anything else you discussed.

One group member should tell a few sentences of the passage and pause. Another group member should tell the next part of the passage and pause. Do this until the group has retold the whole passage. The group members can correct each other in this step.

Pause this audio here.

Next, each member of the group should tell the whole passage without interruption at least one time. A group member can use random objects, motions, or their storyboard to help them remember the passage.

Pause this audio here.

Next, the group can decide whose version of the passage you like the most. You may decide that you liked the way one group member told one scene but you liked the way a different group member told another scene.

Pause this audio here.

Finally, the group can put together a final version of the passage that everyone agrees on. Each group member should practice telling this final version of the passage.
